q.q: The Treaty of Vienna of 1815 tried to reverse the changes brought about during the Napoleonic wars.
q.explanation: The treaty's objective was to reverse those changes and restore the monarchies.

q.q: Which movement broke the religious unity of Europe and ended the supremacy of the pope?
q.explanation: The Protestant Revolution broke the religious unity of Europe and ended the supremacy of the pope.

q.q: Which countries drew the Treaty of Vienna in 1815?
q.explanation: Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria drew the treaty.

q.q: What name was given to the first years after the Napoleonic era, when rulers tried to return to the old orders?
q.explanation: The first years after the Napoleonic era were called a time of reaction.

q.q: Name the movement whose development of national language and literature helped bring about national self-consciousness.
q.explanation: The Renaissance helped bring about a national self-consciousness.

q.q: Conservative leaders after 1815 supported the spread of nationalism.
q.explanation: Conservatives opposed change, while revolutionaries spread the ideas of nationalism.

q.q: In the mid-1800s, the two major European states that were NOT united were:
q.explanation: Italy and Germany were both broken up into many smaller states in the mid-1800s.

q.q: Explain one way that trade and colonies helped build a strong state.
q.answer: brought wealth|wealth helped build a strong state
q.explanation: Trade and colonies brought in wealth that helped build a strong state.

q.q: Besides language, what shared tie helped the people of the Italian and German states feel like one nation?
q.explanation: They mostly shared the same language, culture, history and religion.

q.q: How many main obstacles to unity did Italy face in 1815?
q.explanation: The textbook names three obstacles: Austrian occupation, the Papal States and the many independent states.

q.q: The secret society of Italian unification formed to abolish foreign rule was the:
q.explanation: Mazzini was a member of the Carbonari.

q.q: Giuseppe Mazzini founded the movement called Young Italy in 1831.
q.explanation: In 1831 Mazzini founded Young Italy, which attracted tens of thousands of Italians.

q.q: Cavour was considered the architect of a united Italy because of:
options: his strong military victories against France
his strong involvement in the eventual unification processes
q.explanation: Cavour's diplomacy and reforms were central to the unification process.

q.q: In which year was the Kingdom of Italy established?
q.explanation: In 1861 the Kingdom of Italy was established with Victor Emmanuel II as king.

q.q: Which of the following was a main challenge of the Italian government after unification?
options: Tension between the North and the South
q.explanation: Tension between the industrialized North and the agrarian South was a major challenge.

q.q: Northern Italy was agrarian while southern Italy was industrialized.
q.explanation: It was the reverse: the North was industrialized and the South was agrarian.

q.q: Give the name of the secret society, a kind of state within a state, that the Italian government was powerless to control.
q.explanation: The Mafia was a secret society the central government could not control.

q.q: Explain how Italy gained Venetia in 1866.
q.answer: austria defeated in the seven weeks war|seven weeks war
q.explanation: Following Austria's defeat in the Seven Weeks War in 1866, Italy got Venetia.

q.q: Rome was proclaimed the capital of the Kingdom of Italy in:
q.explanation: In 1870 the Italians entered Rome and unification was finalized; Rome became the capital.

q.q: Arrange these events of Italian unification in the correct order.
options: The Kingdom of Italy is proclaimed in 1861
q.explanation: The order is: Young Italy in 1831, the Kingdom of Italy in 1861, Venetia in 1866 and Rome in 1870.

q.q: Which policy did Otto von Bismarck use to unify Germany?
q.explanation: Bismarck used the Blood and Iron policy of military power.

q.q: The two main rivals who competed to dominate a united Germany were:
q.explanation: Austria usually dominated the German Confederation while Prussia took the lead in unifying it.

q.q: The German Confederation created in 1815 consisted of 39 separate autonomous states.
q.explanation: The Congress of Vienna created a confederation of 39 separate autonomous states.

q.q: The Zollverein created in 1834 was:
options: an economic alliance that removed tariffs
q.explanation: The Zollverein was an economic alliance and customs union between the German states.

q.q: In which year did the Prussian king Wilhelm I choose Bismarck as prime minister?
q.explanation: In 1862 the new Prussian king, Wilhelm I, chose Bismarck as prime minister.

q.q: From which class of Prussian landed nobility did Bismarck come?
q.explanation: Bismarck came from the Junker class, the landed nobility of Prussia.

q.q: Prussia's defeat of Austria in the 1866 Austro-Prussian War resulted in the creation of:
q.explanation: The North German Confederation was formed under Prussian leadership after the Seven Weeks War.

q.q: Give the name of the carefully edited document Bismarck published to provoke France into war.
q.explanation: The Ems Telegram encouraged France to declare war on Prussia in 1870.

q.q: In the Treaty of Frankfurt, France agreed to cede Alsace and Lorraine to Germany.
q.explanation: The Treaty of Frankfurt, signed on 10 May 1871, gave these coal- and iron-rich provinces to Germany.

q.q: The German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 at:
q.explanation: The German Empire was proclaimed at the Palace of Versailles with King William as Kaiser.

q.q: Arrange the three wars of German unification in the correct order.
q.explanation: The wars ran: Danish War 1864, Seven Weeks War 1866, then Franco-Prussian War 1870-71. The Zollverein (1834) was not a war.

q.q: The American Civil War was fought between:
q.explanation: The war was fought from 1861 to 1865.

q.q: The American Civil War began as a result of disagreement over the institution of slavery.
q.explanation: The conflict began from a long-standing disagreement over slavery.

q.q: The Northern states that fought the war were known as the:
q.explanation: The Northern states were known as the Union.

q.q: The Confederacy of eleven southern states was led by:
q.explanation: Jefferson Davis, a rich plantation owner, led the Confederacy.

q.q: In which year did Abraham Lincoln win the presidential election?
q.explanation: Lincoln won the presidential election in 1860.

q.q: Give the name of the strong anti-slavery movement in the North.
q.explanation: Abolitionism was the anti-slavery movement whose followers were called abolitionists.

q.q: What did Lincoln issue in January 1863 that became a turning point of the war?
options: The Emancipation Proclamation and Homestead Law
q.explanation: In January 1863 Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation and the Homestead Law.

q.q: The Thirteenth Amendment, adopted on 6 December 1865, officially outlawed slavery.
q.explanation: The Thirteenth Amendment outlawed slavery on 6 December 1865.

q.q: Explain the main result of the American Civil War for enslaved people.
q.explanation: The war ended in the defeat of the Confederates and the abolition of slavery.

q.q: The American Civil War resulted in:
options: equality between white and Black Americans
the end of slavery in the USA
the expansion of the plantation economy
increased political domination of the Confederates
q.explanation: The war ended with the defeat of the Confederates and the abolition of slavery in the USA.

q.q: Arrange these events of the American Civil War in the correct order.
q.explanation: The order is: election 1860, Emancipation Proclamation January 1863, assassination 14 April 1865, Thirteenth Amendment 6 December 1865.

q.q: The Eastern Question was a diplomatic problem concerning:
options: the declining Ottoman Empire and the Balkans
q.explanation: It arose from Balkan nationalism, the declining Ottoman Empire and the interests of the Great Powers.

q.q: Nationalism weakened the power and unity of the Ottoman Empire in the 19th century.
q.explanation: The rise of nationalism among the Balkan peoples weakened the Ottoman Empire.

q.q: During the struggle between the Ottoman Turks and the nationalists, Britain:
options: supported the independence of the Balkan states
supported the Turks to suppress the nationalist movements
q.explanation: Britain supported the Turks to keep Russia out of the Mediterranean.

q.q: Which power supported the Balkan nationalists?
q.explanation: Russia supported the Balkan nationalists for reasons of kinship, religion and access to the seas.

q.q: By what year had Greece become an independent state?
q.explanation: By 1830 Greece became an independent state and Serbia achieved some self-rule.

q.q: Give the term for the multi-ethnic region of the decaying Ottoman Empire that was home to Serbs, Bulgarians, Rumanians and Greeks.
q.explanation: This region is the Balkans.

q.q: Give one reason Russia gave support to the Balkan nationalists besides shared Slav ancestry.
q.answer: same orthodox religion|orthodox christians|access to the black sea|access to the mediterranean
q.explanation: The Russians were Orthodox Christians like many Balkan groups, and they wanted access to the Black Sea and Mediterranean.

q.q: Which countries gained independence in 1878?
q.explanation: Romania, Montenegro and Serbia got their independence in 1878.

q.q: Between 1878 and 1913 the Ottoman Empire was reduced in size as the Great Powers shared its territories.
q.explanation: Great Britain, Austria, France and Italy shared Ottoman territories in this period.

q.q: Explain why the Eastern Question had serious consequences for Europe as a whole.
q.answer: a succession of balkan crises|balkan crises|tension rose to a dangerous level
q.explanation: Unsettled conditions produced a succession of Balkan crises, and tension rose to a dangerous level.

q.q: Arrange these events of the Eastern Question in the correct order.
options: Revolts break out across the Balkans in 1875
Romania, Montenegro and Serbia gain independence in 1878
q.explanation: The order is: Greek independence by 1830, revolts in 1875, independence in 1878, and the sharing of Ottoman territories from 1878 to 1913.

q.q: Colonialism is defined as:
options: A temporary trade agreement between equals
The direct and total dominance of one country by another
q.explanation: Colonialism is the direct and total dominance of one country by another based on the possession of state authority by a foreign power.

q.q: The concept of colonialism is inextricably tied to that of:
q.explanation: The notion of colonialism is inextricably tied to that of imperialism.

q.q: European missionaries who preached Christianity in Africa converted most Africans to Christianity.
q.explanation: They converted less than 1 percent of non-Muslim Africans outside Ethiopia in the last two decades of the nineteenth century.

q.q: A considerable number of European explorers who arrived in Africa after the 1850s were agents of European governments.
q.explanation: Explorers before the 1850s pursued scientific inquiry; many after the 1850s were government agents.

q.q: Legitimate trade in the 19th century was trade in which:
options: African raw materials were exchanged for European goods
q.explanation: Legitimate commerce exchanged African raw products and cash crops for goods from Europe.

q.q: Which factor facilitated the expansion of colonialism in the 16th century, according to the lesson?
q.explanation: Advancements in navigational technology allowed Europeans to travel to all corners of the earth.

q.q: Give the term for the commodity trade between Africans and European merchants after the slave trade was abolished.
q.explanation: This is the definition of legitimate commerce, also called legitimate trade.

q.q: Which statement about European explorers in Africa is correct?
options: All of them were government agents
Those before the 1850s pursued scientific inquiry while many after the 1850s were government agents
None of them were interested in science
q.explanation: Explorers were loosely divided into two groups based on timing and purpose.

q.q: Explain why the timing of the European missionaries in Africa is described as bad.
q.answer: they came together with colonial administrators and traders|they were linked to colonial conquest and relied on administrators for protection
q.explanation: Missionaries entered Africa along with colonial administrators and traders, depended on them for funds and protection, and thus became part of the colonial process.

q.q: Missionaries in Africa depended mainly on European traders for:
q.explanation: Missionaries depended on traders for funds and on administrators for physical security.

q.q: Arrange these developments in the order in which they occurred.
options: The Atlantic slave trade ends and legitimate trade grows
European explorers enter the interior of Africa
The Berlin Conference sets rules for partition
q.explanation: The Age of Discovery came first, followed by legitimate trade, interior exploration, and finally the Berlin Conference.

q.q: Which was one of the most visible economic motives for colonizing Africa?
options: Demand for raw materials and new markets
q.explanation: Demand for raw materials and the need for new market centres were the most visible economic motives.

q.q: Searching for new markets was one of the motives of European colonial powers in Africa.
q.explanation: The need for new market centres was a visible economic motive.

q.q: Rudyard Kipling's poem The White Man's Burden reflected the idea that:
options: the white race had become a burden on other races
the white man had a responsibility to civilize other races
colonialism was a burden brought by a white man on others
the white man should not carry the burden of colonialism
q.explanation: The poem proposes that white people should rule non-white people until they adopt western ways.

q.q: The civilizing mission as a justification for European colonization of other lands:
options: considers other peoples as agents of historical change
considers Europe as less civilized than other peoples
considers colonialism as the enslavement of other peoples
considers that colonialism is good for the colonized
q.explanation: The civilizing mission presented colonialism as beneficial to the colonized, implying they were inferior and needed European guidance.

q.q: Name one European power that competed for power and prestige in Africa besides Great Britain and France.
q.explanation: Great Britain, France and Spain are named as major world powers competing for power and prestige.

q.q: Give the term for the rationale that claimed Europeans were spreading civilization, commerce and Christianity to Africa.
q.explanation: This rationale is called the civilizing mission.

q.q: Africa was believed to have untapped resources such as groundnuts, palm oil, cotton, rubber, gold and diamonds.
q.explanation: These agricultural and mining resources are named in the lesson.

q.q: Explain why some missionaries supported European colonization of Africa.
q.answer: European control would provide a political environment that facilitated missionary activities|European rule was expected to help their missionary work
q.explanation: Missionaries believed European control would create a favourable political environment for their work.

q.q: European powers were especially interested in strategic territories mainly to:
q.explanation: They wanted favourable locations for military and naval bases and for dominance over strategic territories.

q.q: Arrange these steps of the economic motive in a logical chain, from cause to outcome.
options: Industrialization creates demand for raw materials
Europeans look to Africa for resources
Europeans bring manufactured goods to sell in Africa
New markets for European products grow
q.explanation: Industrialization came first, then the search for resources, then the export of manufactured goods to African markets.

q.q: What share of Africa was ruled by foreign powers before the 1880s?
q.explanation: Before the 1880s only 10 percent of Africa was ruled by foreign powers; 90 percent was independent.

q.q: The map of Africa of 1884 was nearly similar to that of the 1914 map.
q.explanation: The Scramble for Africa transformed the map between 1884 and 1914 through partition.

q.q: The Berlin Conference was held from:
q.explanation: The Berlin Conference was held from 1884 to 1885 in Berlin, Germany.

q.q: Who was the leader of the Berlin Conference?
q.explanation: The German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck led the conference.

q.q: Which of the following was NOT agreed upon at the Berlin Conference?
options: Free trade along major African rivers
Ground rules for future appropriation of Africa
The recognition of the Congo Free State
q.explanation: Free navigation, ground rules and recognition of the Congo Free State were all agreed, so none of the listed items was excluded.

q.q: Africa was invited to the Berlin Conference to present its interests.
q.explanation: Africa was neither invited nor involved in the conference.

q.q: Give the term for the fierce, massive and rapid European expansion in Africa from the 1880s to the first decade of the 20th century.
q.explanation: This is the definition of the Scramble for Africa.

q.q: Explain the principle of effective occupation in Article 35 of the General Act.
q.answer: treaties with local leaders plus a flag plus an administration with a police force|possession required treaties, a flag and an administration with a police force
q.explanation: A power could acquire colonial land only if it had treaties with local leaders, flew its flag there and established an administration with a police force.

q.q: The Wuchale treaty signed between Ethiopia and Italy is described as an example of:
q.explanation: The textbook names Wuchale as a good example of a fake or trickery treaty.

q.q: Name the river system besides the Niger that the conference opened to free navigation.
q.explanation: The conference provided for free navigation of the Niger and the Congo.

q.q: Arrange these events of the partition in the order they occurred.
options: Only 10 percent of Africa is foreign-ruled
The Berlin Conference sets the rules for partition
Germany proclaims Tanganyika as a protectorate
Only two parts of Africa remain independent by 1914
q.explanation: Foreign rule covered a small area first, the conference followed in 1884-1885, Tanganyika was proclaimed in 1885, and by 1914 only two parts remained independent.

q.q: Which of the following was NOT one of the methods used to administer African colonies?
q.explanation: The methods were company rule, direct rule and assimilation, indirect rule, and settler rule; all colonial systems were undemocratic.

q.q: The British colonial policy favoured direct rule rather than indirect rule.
q.explanation: The British are associated with indirect rule, whose architect was Frederick Lugard; direct rule was used by the French, Belgians, Germans and Portuguese.

q.q: The British South Africa Company was controlled by:
q.explanation: The British South Africa Company was under the control of John Cecil Rhodes.

q.q: Until what year did company rule in Africa last?
q.explanation: Company rule was exercised from the 1880s to 1924.

q.q: The French colonial policy of direct rule and assimilation was designed by:
q.explanation: The French policy of direct rule and assimilation was designed by Albert Sarrout.

q.q: Give the term for the British system that governed colonies through indigenous African rulers.
q.explanation: This system is indirect rule, whose architect was Frederick Lugard.

q.q: Under French assimilation, an African who received a French education stood a chance of becoming French.
q.explanation: This is exactly what the assimilation policy asserted.

q.q: Explain the policy of association as used by France in Africa.
q.answer: the relationship between conqueror and conquered is one of cooperation not identity and merging|cooperation between rulers and ruled
q.explanation: Association was the opposite of assimilation and emphasised cooperation between the rulers and the ruled.

q.q: In Kenya, the Kikuyu lost their ancestral territory in the white highlands and migrated in mass to:
q.explanation: The Kikuyu migrated in mass to growing urban centres like Nairobi in search of employment.

q.q: A feature shared by all colonial systems in Africa was that they:
options: were imposed without the consent of African people
q.explanation: All colonial systems were undemocratic, imposed without African consent, and used divide and rule.

q.q: Which colonial administrative policy aggravated ethnic differences by emphasising differences of dialect, dress and religion?
q.explanation: British indirect rule aggravated ethnic differences in dialect of language, dress and religion.

q.q: Which of the following was a nonviolent form of anti-colonial resistance?
options: The use of the indigenous press
q.explanation: Nonviolent forms included the indigenous press, trade unionism, organised religion, associations, literary and art forms and mass migrations.

q.q: The Africans' early resistance movements were spontaneous and lacked organization.
q.explanation: Many early risings were spontaneous; the Maji Maji movement, for example, had no previous planning and no central leadership.

q.q: Samori Ture was a Muslim leader in the:
q.explanation: Samori Ture was a Muslim leader in the Mandinka Empire who fought the French from 1882 to 1898.

q.q: How large was the army led by Samori Ture?
q.explanation: Samori Ture led a strong army of 30,000 men.

q.q: The Maji Maji uprising took place in:
q.explanation: The Maji Maji uprising in Tanganyika lasted from 1905 to 1907.

q.q: Give the name of the prophet who led the Maji Maji movement.
q.explanation: The movement was led by a prophet named Kinjikitle Ngwale.

q.q: The leader of the Egyptian resistance against Anglo-Egyptian rule was:
q.explanation: Colonel Urabi Pasha led the Egyptian revolt against the imperialist domination of Britain and France.

q.q: Explain why the early African resistance movements were not successful.
q.answer: European military superiority and poor African armament, lack of unity and absence of effective organisation|they lacked unity and effective organisation and were poorly armed
q.explanation: European powers had professional armies and superior weapons, while Africans lacked cooperation, solidarity, effective organisation and central leadership.

q.q: The Herero people rebelled against German colonial rule in 1904 and the Nama in 1905.
q.explanation: The Herero, led by Samuel Maharero, rebelled in 1904 and the Nama, led by Hendrik Witbooi, in 1905.

q.q: In which year did Egypt become a British colony after the revolt was defeated?
q.explanation: In 1882 British colonial forces entered Cairo, defeated the revolt and Egypt became a British colony.

q.q: Arrange the three stages of African response to colonial rule in order.
q.explanation: The first stage ran from about 1880 to 1914, the second from 1914 to 1945, and the third, decolonization, from the 1950s to 1980s.

q.q: What was the main economic impact of colonialism on Africa?
options: Under-development as a supplier of raw materials
q.explanation: Colonialism brought under-development; Africa remained a supplier of raw materials for Europe and manufacturing was discouraged.

q.q: What was the main reason for European countries to colonize Africa?
options: The desire to establish democratic regimes in Africa
To maintain power and promote mutual trade relationships
q.explanation: The exploitation of Africa's rich resources was the main economic reason.

q.q: Colonization brought about different types of new diseases in Africa.
q.explanation: Colonization brought different types of diseases, such as Rinderpest, which affected livestock.

q.q: Give the name of the disease introduced by settlers that affected the livestock of the Shona people and of North Ethiopia.
q.explanation: Rinderpest affected the livestock of the Shona in present day Zimbabwe and Botswana and of North Ethiopia during the Kefu Qen.

q.q: Which of the following is a positive outcome of colonial rule mentioned in the lesson?
q.explanation: Positive outcomes included the ending of tribal warfare, modern ideas and the construction of railways and roads.

q.q: Europeans drew the boundaries of African colonies with the approval of the local communities.
q.explanation: Europeans created artificial boundaries without the approval of the local community, a legacy that caused boundary conflicts.

q.q: Name one raw material or cash crop whose export volume broadened during the colonial period.
q.explanation: Exports included vegetable oils, palm oil, groundnuts, gum, ivory, gold, hides and skins, rubber, cotton and copper, and cash crops such as cocoa, coffee, tea and tobacco.

q.q: Explain the political impact of the artificial boundaries created by Europeans.
q.answer: they caused boundary conflicts among African nations after independence|they became a colonial legacy causing boundary conflicts
q.explanation: The artificial boundaries ignored existing communities and became a colonial legacy that caused boundary conflicts after independence.

q.q: Forests were cleared by the colonizers mainly to obtain timber and:
options: to create grazing land for Africans
firewood to power steam engine trains and to build rail tracks
q.explanation: Forests were cleared for timber and firewood needed to power steam engine trains and to construct rail tracks.

q.q: In one sentence, describe the overall effect of colonialism on the economic and political structure of African colonies.
q.answer: it was shaped to serve the interest of European powers|the structures served European interests
q.explanation: Colonialism shaped both the economic and political structure of African colonies to serve the interest of European powers.

q.q: Arrange these impacts in a logical chain of cause and effect.
options: Europeans partition Africa and take control
Africans lose independence and indigenous rule is destroyed
Africa is kept as a supplier of raw materials
q.explanation: Partition came first, then the loss of independence, then economic under-development, and finally the post-independence consequences of artificial borders.

q.q: Where did the two major long distance trade routes of nineteenth century Ethiopia begin?
q.explanation: Both routes started from Bonga, the capital of the Kafa Kingdom.

q.q: Which item served as a medium of exchange alongside the Maria Theresa Thaler?
q.explanation: Salt bars (amole) served as a medium of exchange side by side with the Maria Theresa Thaler.

q.q: The coin introduced from Austria to the Horn of Africa at the end of the eighteenth century was the:
q.explanation: The MTT was introduced from Austria by Arab traders at the end of the eighteenth century.

q.q: The northern Muslim merchants who dominated the long distance trade were known as the Jabarti.
q.explanation: The northern Muslim merchants were known as Jabarti, and the southwestern Oromo Muslim merchants as Afqala.

q.q: The general public held artisans in high honour, which encouraged them to improve their products.
q.explanation: Artisans were mostly disdained and marginalized, so their products showed little improvement.

q.q: Name the capital of the Kafa Kingdom from which the trade routes started.
q.explanation: Both routes started from Bonga, the capital of Kafa.

q.q: Give the name of the southwestern Oromo Muslim merchants who were active in the long distance trade.
q.explanation: The southwestern Muslim Oromo merchants were known as Afqala.

q.q: Arrange the following market centres in the correct order from Bonga toward Massawa.
q.explanation: The line runs Bonga, Saqa, Asandabo, Basso and Gondar, then onward to Massawa.

q.q: Which of the following was NOT among the principal commodities of the long distance trade?
q.explanation: The principal commodities were ivory, civet musk, salt bars and slaves.

q.q: Name one cottage industry mentioned in the lesson.
q.explanation: The common cottage industries included metalworking, pottery, tannery, carpentry, masonry, weaving, jewellery and basket making.

q.q: Explain one reason why the products of the cottage industry showed little improvement.
q.answer: artisans were marginalized and disdained|lack of public support and reward
q.explanation: Artisans were disdained and marginalized, so there was little incentive or reward for improvement.

q.q: Who was the first emperor of modern Ethiopia who attempted to unify the country?
q.explanation: Kassa Hailu of Quara, who became Tewodros II, was the first to attempt unification.

q.q: Which battle symbolized the end of the Zemene Mesafint?
q.explanation: The battle of Ayshal defeated the last ruler of the Yejju dynasty and symbolized the end of the Zemene Mesafint.

q.q: Where did Tewodros II establish an arms manufacture with European help?
q.explanation: The arms manufacture was established at Gafat near Debre Tabor.

q.q: Name the famous mortar produced at Gafat.
q.explanation: About 35 cannons were produced at Gafat, including the famous mortar Sebastopol.

q.q: Tewodros II reduced the number of priests and deacons in each church to five.
q.explanation: He confiscated church land and reduced the number of priests and deacons in each church to five.

q.q: By which agreement of 1878 did Yohannes IV recognize Menilek as Nigus of Shewa?
q.explanation: Yohannes IV recognized Menilek as Nigus of Shewa by the Liche agreement of 1878.

q.q: At which council of 1878 was Tewahdo declared the only doctrine of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahdo Church?
q.explanation: The Council of Boru Meda in 1878 declared Tewahdo the only doctrine of the church.

q.q: Name the Shewan commander who played a pivotal role in Menilek's territorial expansion.
q.explanation: Ras Gobana Dache played a pivotal role in the expansion and the creation of the modern empire.

q.q: The Arsi Oromo resistance was finally suppressed at the battle of Azule on:
q.explanation: The Arsi resistance was suppressed at Azule on 6 September 1886.

q.q: Which territory was incorporated in 1897 after its king was defeated by Ras Wolde Giorgis?
q.explanation: Kafa was incorporated in 1897 after Tato Gaki Sherocho was defeated by Ras Wolde Giorgis.

q.q: Explain the immediate cause of the Great Famine known as Kefu Qan.
q.answer: rinderpest epidemic|disease carried by cattle imported through massawa
q.explanation: The immediate cause was a rinderpest epidemic triggered by the Italian importation of infected cattle through Massawa.

q.q: In which year did Tewodros II send a letter to Queen Victoria requesting military assistance?
q.explanation: In 1862 Tewodros sent a letter to Queen Victoria through Consul Cameron.

q.q: Who commanded the British expedition sent to Ethiopia in late 1867?
q.explanation: The British expedition was commanded by Sir Robert Napier.

q.q: At which fortress did Tewodros II take his own life in 1868?
q.explanation: Tewodros released his captives on 11 April and took his own life at Maqdala on 13 April 1868.

q.q: The Egyptian invasion of 1875 was launched in three directions. Which leader was the architect of the whole scheme?
q.explanation: Werner Munzinger was the architect of Ismail's scheme for the invasion of Ethiopia.

q.q: Where did Emperor Yohannes IV and Ras Alula decisively defeat the Egyptians on 16 November 1875?
q.explanation: The Egyptians were severely defeated at the battle of Gundat on 16 November 1875.

q.q: The Hewett Treaty required Ethiopia to help evacuate Egyptian soldiers encircled by the Mahdists in return for the use of Massawa.
q.explanation: This was one of the main terms of the Hewett Treaty of 1884.

q.q: Where did Emperor Yohannes IV die fighting the Mahdists on 9 March 1889?
q.explanation: Yohannes IV marched to Metemma where he died fighting the Mahdists.

q.q: What was the key difference between the versions of Article XVII of the treaty of Wuchale?
options: The Amharic said could, the Italian made it obligatory
The Amharic gave land to Italy
q.explanation: The Amharic version said the emperor could use Italian good offices, while the Italian version made it obligatory.

q.q: In which year did Menilek II unilaterally abrogate the treaty of Wuchale?
q.explanation: After failing to get a revision, Menilek abrogated the treaty in 1893.

q.q: Which Italian premier's government collapsed after the defeat at Adwa?
q.explanation: In Italy the defeat led to the collapse of the government of Premier Francesco Crispi.

q.q: The battle of Adwa was fought on:
q.explanation: The last and decisive phase of the war was fought at Adwa on 1 March 1896.

q.q: Why is the year 1906 regarded as a watershed in post-Adwa political history?
options: Menilek suffered his first stroke and the succession question opened
q.explanation: Menilek's stroke and the death of Ras Mekonnen in 1906 opened the succession question.

q.q: Menilek established Ethiopia's first cabinet in 1907.
q.explanation: Menilek established the first cabinet to address the looming succession crisis.

q.q: Which three powers signed the Tripartite Treaty of 1906?
options: Britain, France and the United States
q.explanation: Britain, France and Italy formed the Tripartite Treaty of 1906.

q.q: What name is given to the period of shared rule by Empress Zewditu and Ras Teferi Mekonnen?
q.explanation: The period of dual governance was known as diarchy.

q.q: Lij Iyasu's reforms included all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Creating Addis Ababa's first police force
q.explanation: The 1931 constitution came later, under Haile Selassie, not Lij Iyasu.

q.q: Give the name of the traditional system, removed by Lij Iyasu, of tying a plaintiff and a defendant together.
q.explanation: Lij Iyasu removed the Quragna system of tying plaintiffs and defendants together.

q.q: At which battle was Nigus Mikael, the father of Lij Iyasu, defeated in 1916?
q.explanation: Nigus Mikael was defeated and captured at Sagale on 27 October 1916.

q.q: The 1931 constitution is best described as:
options: a document that limited the emperor's power
a document that gave the legal basis of the emperor's autocratic rule
a law that ended the diarchy
q.explanation: The first written constitution provided the legal framework for Haile Selassie's emerging autocratic rule.

q.q: By the 1931 constitution all provinces except Tigray lost their internal autonomy.
q.explanation: Only Tigray was permitted to be ruled by descendants of its local hereditary chiefs.

q.q: Where was the first officer training school established in 1934?
q.explanation: The first officer training school was established at Holeta west of the capital.

q.q: Explain why the Shewan nobles opposed Empress Taytu.
q.answer: she was seen as a danger to their dominion|they feared her growing influence
q.explanation: The Shewan nobles saw her growing influence as a significant danger to their dominion.

q.q: What event did Mussolini use as a pretext to invade Ethiopia?
q.explanation: Ethiopian and Italian forces clashed at Walawal in the Ogaden on 5 December 1934 over an ill-defined border.

q.q: On what date did Italian soldiers cross the Marab River in 1935?
q.explanation: The Italian soldiers crossed the Marab River on 3 October 1935.

q.q: Which Italian commander was replaced by Pietro Badoglio on the northern front?
q.explanation: Emilio de Bono headed the Italian troops and was subsequently succeeded by Pietro Badoglio.

q.q: The Italians used internationally banned poison gas during the invasion.
q.explanation: Three hundred planes dropped the internationally banned poison gas on Ethiopians.

q.q: Name the final battle fought on the northern front on 31 March 1936.
q.explanation: The final battle on the northern front was fought at Maychew on 31 March 1936.

q.q: The Italian colony formed by merging Ethiopia with Eritrea and Somalia was called:
q.explanation: The merged territory was called Italian East Africa, or Africa Orientale Italiana.

q.q: Who attempted to assassinate Viceroy Graziani on 19 February 1937?
options: Ras Desta Damtew and Dejjach Balcha
Abune Petros and Ras Abebe Aregay
q.explanation: Moges Asgedom and Abreha Deboch attempted to kill Italian Viceroy Graziani on 19 February 1937.

q.q: Give the local name of the Ethiopian patriotic resistance fighters during the Italian occupation.
q.explanation: The resistance fighters were locally known as Arbegnoch, or Patriots.

q.q: Approximately how many Ethiopians were killed in the Graziani Massacre of February 1937?
q.explanation: Approximately 30,000 Ethiopians were slaughtered in three days.

q.q: Name the woman patriot of Addis Alem listed among the prominent women of the resistance.
q.explanation: Shewareged Gedle of Addis Alem was a prominent woman in the patriotic resistance.

q.q: Explain how Ethiopia was finally liberated in 1941.
q.answer: combined ethiopian and british efforts|joint anglo-ethiopian operation with the patriots|gideon force and cunningham
q.explanation: The final liberation came through combined internal and external forces, with a joint Anglo-Ethiopian operation in 1941.

q.q: The immediate cause of the First World War was:
options: the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
q.explanation: The textbook states that the immediate cause was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.

q.q: The Triple Alliance of 1882 comprised Germany, Austria-Hungary and:
q.explanation: The Triple Alliance comprised Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy.

q.q: Italy left the Triple Alliance and joined the Triple Entente in:
q.explanation: Although Italy was an original member of the Triple Alliance, it left it and joined the Triple Entente in 1915.

q.q: The Triple Entente developed from the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894 and the Entente Cordiale of 1904.
q.explanation: It was completed by the Anglo-Russian Agreement of 1907.

q.q: Name the Serbian nationalist who assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand.
q.explanation: Gavrilo Princip shot the Archduke at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.

q.q: Name the battle in September 1914 that halted the German advance into France and began the trench stalemate.
q.explanation: The Battle of the Marne forced the German attack back.

q.q: The United States declared war on Germany in April 1917 mainly because of:
options: unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram
q.explanation: Germany's unrestricted submarine campaign and the Zimmermann telegram turned American opinion against Germany.

q.q: Arrange these events of the First World War in the correct order.
options: The Treaty of Versailles is signed
The United States declares war on Germany
q.explanation: The order is: assassination (28 June 1914), the German invasion of France (August 1914), the US declaration of war (6 April 1917), then the Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919).

q.q: Which four imperial dynasties collapsed as a result of the First World War?
q.explanation: The Habsburgs of Austria-Hungary, the Hohenzollerns of Germany, the Ottoman sultanate and the Romanovs of Russia all collapsed.

q.q: Explain why the Treaty of Versailles is said to have punished Germany.
q.answer: blamed germany for the war|placed sole responsibility and required reparations
q.explanation: The treaty placed sole responsibility for the war on Germany and forced it to pay reparations.

q.q: On what date was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
q.explanation: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919.

q.q: The Russian Social Democratic Labour Party was formed in:
q.explanation: The revolutionaries formed the RSDLP in 1898.

q.q: The leader of the Bolsheviks was Lenin, whose real name was:
q.explanation: Lenin's real name was Vladimir Ilich Ulyanov.

q.q: Serfdom was abolished in Russia in 1861.
q.explanation: The textbook states that serfdom was abolished in Russia in 1861.

q.q: Name the event that marked the beginning of the violent phase of the Russian Revolution of 1905.
q.explanation: The Bloody Sunday massacre of peaceful demonstrators in St. Petersburg began the violent phase.

q.q: The immediate cause of the Russian Revolution of 1905 was:
options: defeat by Japan in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-05
q.explanation: Defeat by Japan became the immediate cause of the Revolution of 1905.

q.q: Give the name for the councils of peasants, workers and soldiers formed in Petrograd in 1917.
q.explanation: These councils were called Soviets.

q.q: The Bolshevik slogan of peace, land and bread was joined by:
q.explanation: The Bolsheviks used the slogans 'All Power to the Soviets!' and 'Peace, Land and Bread!'.

q.q: The New Economic Policy of 1921 abolished all small enterprises and private trade.
q.explanation: The NEP restored smaller enterprises to their owners and allowed peasants to sell grain for profit.

q.q: In which year was the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics established?
q.explanation: The USSR was established in July 1922.

q.q: Arrange these events of the Russian Revolution in the correct order.
options: Czar Nicholas II is deposed in February
The New Economic Policy is introduced
q.explanation: The order is: February Revolution (1917), October Revolution (1917), New Economic Policy (1921), USSR (1922).

q.q: Explain how the Russian Revolution influenced colonized peoples in Africa and Asia.
q.answer: inspired anti-colonial struggle|inspired national liberation movements
q.explanation: The revolution became an inspiration for colonized peoples in their anti-colonial struggle.

q.q: The League of Nations was founded on:
q.explanation: The League was founded on 10 January 1920.

q.q: The League of Nations was headquartered in:
q.explanation: Its headquarters were in Geneva, Switzerland.

q.q: The United States joined the League of Nations at its founding.
q.explanation: The US Congress was resistant, and in the end the United States did not join the League.

q.q: Name the US president who proposed the formation of the League of Nations.
q.explanation: President Woodrow Wilson proposed the League.

q.q: The four permanent members of the League's Executive Council were:
options: Great Britain, France, Japan and Italy
the USA, Britain, France and Italy
Britain, France, the USA and Japan
q.explanation: The Council's four permanent members were Great Britain, France, Japan and Italy.

q.q: Give the term for the League's method of settling disputes through a neutral party.
q.explanation: The League aimed to settle disputes through negotiation and arbitration.

q.q: In 1926 the League negotiated a peaceful outcome to a conflict over the province of:
q.explanation: In 1926 the League settled the Iraq-Turkey dispute over Mosul.

q.q: The League failed to intervene in the Italian invasion of Ethiopia and the Spanish Civil War.
q.explanation: The League failed to intervene in these conflicts and in the Second Sino-Japanese War.

q.q: Explain why the League of Nations is described as largely weak and ineffective.
q.answer: it failed to prevent world war ii|could not stop aggression by great powers
q.explanation: It failed to prevent the Second World War and could not stop aggression by Italy, Germany and Japan.

q.q: Until which year did the League of Nations continue to operate?
q.explanation: Although it had failed, the League continued to operate until 1946.

q.q: The League's primary goals were set out in its:
q.explanation: The League's primary goals were stated in its Covenant.

q.q: The Great Depression began with:
options: the Wall Street stock market crash of October 1929
q.explanation: It began with the New York Wall Street crash of October 1929.

q.q: During the Great Depression, international trade plunged by more than:
q.explanation: International trade plunged by more than 50 percent.

q.q: Unemployment in the United States rose to 25 percent during the Great Depression.
q.explanation: Unemployment in the US rose to 25 percent, and in some countries it reached 33 percent.

q.q: In which year did the Great Depression reach its lowest point?
q.explanation: By 1933 the Great Depression had reached its lowest point.

q.q: By how much did crop prices fall during the Great Depression?
q.explanation: Crop prices fell by about 60 percent, hurting farming communities.

q.q: Give the other name for the worldwide economic crisis that began in 1929.
q.explanation: The worldwide economic crisis is known as the Great Depression.

q.q: By 1933, how many Americans were unemployed?
q.explanation: By 1933 some 15 million Americans were unemployed.

q.q: Nearly half the banks in the United States had failed by 1933.
q.explanation: The textbook states that nearly half the country's banks had failed.

q.q: One political consequence of the Great Depression was:
options: the founding of the League of Nations
the rise of aggressive leaders such as Hitler and Mussolini
the end of the First World War
the signing of the Treaty of Versailles
q.explanation: The crisis created political instability, and leaders such as Hitler and Mussolini promised a better future and pursued aggression.

q.q: Explain how falling consumer spending deepened the Depression.
q.answer: factories cut output and laid off workers|less demand meant less production and more unemployment
q.explanation: Less spending reduced industrial output and employment as failing companies laid off workers.

q.q: Which city's stock market crashed in October 1929?
q.explanation: The New York Wall Street stock market crashed in October 1929.

q.q: In what country was the Fascist party and government initially formed?
q.explanation: Fascism originated in Italy, where Mussolini formed his party in 1919.

q.q: A Fascist state was established in Italy in:
q.explanation: A Fascist state was established in Italy in 1922.

q.q: The Nazis came to power in Germany in:
q.explanation: The Nazis came into power in Germany in 1933.

q.q: Benito Mussolini formed his Fascist party in 1919.
q.explanation: Mussolini formed his Fascist party in 1919.

q.q: From which Italian word, meaning a bundle of rods, is the term Fascism derived?
q.explanation: Fascism is derived from fascio, meaning a bundle of rods.

q.q: Give the name of the government established in Germany after the First World War whose weakness helped the Nazis rise.
q.explanation: Reactionary elements took advantage of the failure of the Weimar Republic.

q.q: Hitler's autobiography, written in prison and published in 1926, was entitled:
q.explanation: Hitler wrote Mein Kampf while imprisoned, and it was published in 1926.

q.q: Italy was satisfied with its share of the German overseas territories after the Treaty of Versailles.
q.explanation: Italy was disappointed because it obtained no share in the German overseas territories.

q.q: Mussolini conquered Ethiopia in 1936, which was significant because it:
options: sounded the death knell of the League of Nations
q.explanation: Mussolini's conquest of Ethiopia in 1936 sounded the death knell of the League of Nations.

q.q: Explain two causes of the rise of Nazism in Germany.
q.answer: harsh treaty of versailles and reparations|weak weimar republic and economic crisis
q.explanation: The harsh peace settlement, reparations and the weakness of the Weimar Republic were among the main causes.

q.q: Militarism in Japan peaked during the period:
q.explanation: The period from 1931 to 1945 was considered the peak of Japanese militarism.

q.q: The Second World War broke out in 1939 with the German invasion of:
q.explanation: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, marking the beginning of the war.

q.q: The two major military blocs of the Second World War were:
options: the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente
the Allied and the Axis Powers
the Central and the Allied Powers
q.explanation: The war was fought between the Allied and the Axis Powers.

q.q: Britain and France declared war on Germany on:
q.explanation: Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939.

q.q: The United States entered the war after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941.
q.explanation: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941, and the USA then declared war on Japan.

q.q: What name did the Germans give to their lightning war in Poland?
q.explanation: The Germans called the Polish campaign Blitzkrieg, or lightning war.

q.q: The decisive Soviet victories that began the Allied counter-offensive were at:
q.explanation: The victories at Stalingrad in 1942-43 and Kursk in 1943 were decisive.

q.q: Give the name of the French marshal whose puppet government was set up at Vichy.
q.explanation: In unoccupied France the Nazis formed a puppet government headed by Marshal Petain at Vichy.

q.q: Adolf Hitler committed suicide on 30 April 1945.
q.explanation: Hitler committed suicide on 30 April 1945, and Germany soon surrendered.

q.q: On which two Japanese cities did the USA drop atomic bombs in August 1945?
q.explanation: The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August 1945.

q.q: Japan unconditionally surrendered on:
q.explanation: US forces occupied Tokyo on 2 September 1945, when Japan unconditionally surrendered.

q.q: Explain two effects of the Second World War.
q.answer: about 50 million deaths and decolonization|usa and ussr became superpowers and the united nations was founded
q.explanation: The war caused about 50 million deaths, hastened decolonization, made the USA and USSR superpowers and gave birth to the United Nations.

q.q: In which year was the United Nations established?
q.explanation: The United Nations was established in 1945.

q.q: Which country did NOT sign the Charter in San Francisco on 26 June 1945 yet became an original signatory?
q.explanation: Poland was not represented at the conference but signed the charter, bringing the total to 51.

q.q: The League of Nations existed from 1926 to 1946 and failed to prevent another global war.
q.explanation: These are the exact dates and judgement given in the textbook.

q.q: The most powerful body of the UNO is the:
q.explanation: The Security Council is the most powerful body of the UNO.

q.q: How many permanent members sit on the UN Security Council?
q.explanation: There are five permanent members: the United States, Britain, France, Russia and China.

q.q: Give the name of the power that lets a permanent member prevent any decision of the Security Council.
q.explanation: Permanent members have the power to veto any decision.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six main organs of the UN?
q.explanation: The International Monetary Fund is not one of the six main UN organs.

q.q: Which organ of the UN is the principal judicial organ, seated in The Hague?
q.explanation: The International Court of Justice is the principal judicial organ and its seat is in The Hague.

q.q: Explain why the failure of the League of Nations mattered for the founding of the UN.
q.answer: the UN replaced it|learned from its weaknesses|great powers given permanent seats
q.explanation: The League's failure to stop aggression and the absence of great powers led the founders to give the major powers permanent seats and a veto in the UN.

q.q: When was Arabic added as an official language of the UN?
q.explanation: Arabic was added in 1973; the other five languages were chosen at the founding.

q.q: Name the UN organ that helps the General Assembly promote international economic and social cooperation and development.
q.explanation: This is the role of the Economic and Social Council, or ECOSOC.

q.q: Which two countries emerged as superpowers after the Second World War?
q.explanation: The war resulted in the emergence of the USA and the USSR as superpowers.

q.q: The term Iron Curtain was coined by Winston Churchill in 1946.
q.explanation: Churchill coined the term in 1946 in his speech at Fulton, Missouri.

q.q: The architect of the containment policy was:
q.explanation: George Kennan was the architect of the Containment Doctrine.

q.q: The Soviet response to the Marshall Plan was known as the:
q.explanation: The Molotov Plan, named after the Russian foreign minister, provided aid to Eastern European states.

q.q: Give the term for the Eastern European countries under heavy political, economic and military control of Soviet Russia.
q.answer: satellite states|soviet satellite states|European People's Democracies
q.explanation: They were known as European People's Democracies or Soviet satellite states.

q.q: In which year was NATO founded?
q.explanation: NATO was founded in April 1949 by 12 nations.

q.q: How long did the Berlin Blockade last?
q.explanation: The blockade lasted from 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949.

q.q: Explain the purpose of the Marshall Plan.
q.answer: stop communism|help Europe recover|provide market for American goods
q.explanation: Its aims were to stop the spread of communism, help European economies recover and provide a market for American goods.

q.q: Which event marked the beginning of the space race?
options: The founding of the Warsaw Pact
q.explanation: The launch of Sputnik on 4 October 1957 marked the beginning of the space race.

q.q: The arms race strengthened the Soviet economy by shifting spending away from weapons.
q.explanation: The very high proportion of GDP devoted to arms aggravated the economic difficulties of the Soviet Union.

q.q: Arrange these events in the correct chronological order.
options: Churchill coins the term Iron Curtain
q.explanation: The order is: Iron Curtain speech 1946, Truman Doctrine March 1947, NATO April 1949, Warsaw Pact May 1955.

q.q: In October 1949 the Chinese communists formed the:
q.explanation: In October 1949 the People's Republic of China was formed by the Chinese communists.

q.q: Chiang Kai-shek was the founder of the Chinese Communist Party.
q.explanation: Chiang Kai-shek led the nationalists or Kuomintang; Mao Tse Tung led the Chinese Communist Party.

q.q: Korea was a colony of which country from 1910 to 1945?
q.explanation: Korea was a colony of Japan from 1910 to 1945.

q.q: Which line of latitude divided North and South Korea?
q.explanation: The dividing line was the 38th parallel of latitude.

q.q: The peace treaty that ended the Korean War in 1953 was signed at:
q.explanation: A peace treaty was signed at Panmunjom in 1953.

q.q: Give the name of the Vietnamese independence movement founded in 1941.
q.explanation: Ho Chi Minh established the Viet Minh, the Vietnamese Independent League, in 1941.

q.q: Where were the French defeated on 7 May 1954?
q.explanation: The French forces were defeated by the Viet Minh at the Battle of Dien Bien Phu on 7 May 1954.

q.q: Explain the domino theory in one sentence.
q.answer: if communists not stopped they would expand to neighbouring countries
q.explanation: The theory held that if the communists were not stopped they would expand to neighbouring countries.

q.q: The Strategic Hamlet program was introduced under which US president?
q.explanation: In spring 1961 the administration of John F. Kennedy introduced the Strategic Hamlet program.

q.q: The 'Dirty war' refers to the French-Vietnamese confrontation from 1946 to 1954.
q.explanation: The First Indochina War was unpopular in France and was known as the dirty war.

q.q: Which of the following was NOT a result of the Korean War?
options: South Korea was saved from communism
China became a major power in Asia
Korea was unified under one government
q.explanation: Korea remained divided after the war; it was not unified.

q.q: NAM was formed by states that:
options: refused formal alignment with either superpower
q.explanation: NAM states did not seek to align formally with either the United States or the Soviet Union.

q.q: The basic concept of NAM originated at a conference held in 1955 in:
q.explanation: The basic concept originated at the Asia-Africa Conference held in Bandung, Indonesia, in April 1955.

q.q: The Bandung Conference gathered 29 Heads of State from Africa and Asia.
q.explanation: It gathered 29 Heads of State from the first post-colonial generation of leaders.

q.q: The first NAM Conference took place in September 1961 in:
q.explanation: The first NAM Conference took place in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, in September 1961.

q.q: Name two of the founding leaders of the Non-Aligned Movement.
q.explanation: The founding leaders were Tito of Yugoslavia, Nasser of Egypt, Nehru of India, Nkrumah of Ghana and Sukarno of Indonesia.

q.q: Which declaration of 1979 set out the purpose of NAM?
q.explanation: The purpose of the organization was enumerated in the Havana Declaration of 1979.

q.q: Explain why NAM is not the same as neutrality.
q.answer: it was a peaceful intervention in world politics|members took positions on issues
q.explanation: The textbook states that NAM does not mean neutrality on global issues; it was always a peaceful intervention in world politics.

q.q: The Bandung Conference condemned apartheid, racial discrimination and colonialism.
q.explanation: The participants condemned apartheid, racial discrimination and colonialism.

q.q: Which continents provided almost all the members of NAM?
q.answer: Asia, Africa and Latin America|Asia Africa Latin America
q.explanation: Almost all the Asian, African and Latin American states are members.

q.q: State one purpose of NAM from the Havana Declaration of 1979.
q.answer: national independence|sovereignty|territorial integrity|security of non-aligned countries
q.explanation: The declaration aimed to ensure the national independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity and security of non-aligned countries.

q.q: The Balfour Declaration of 1917 supported:
options: The nationalization of the Suez Canal
q.explanation: In 1917 the British supported the establishment of a Jewish homeland in Palestine in the Balfour Declaration.

q.q: Who was the founder of Zionism?
q.explanation: Theodor Herzl was the founder of Zionism.

q.q: The state of Israel was proclaimed on 14 May 1948.
q.explanation: The Jews proclaimed the establishment of the state of Israel on 14 May 1948.

q.q: On what date did Egypt, Syria, Iraq and Trans-Jordan declare war on Israel?
q.explanation: On 15 May 1948 the governments of Egypt, Syria, Iraq and Trans-Jordan declared war on Israel.

q.q: Give the Arab name for the 1948 war and state what it means.
q.explanation: In the Arab world the war came to be known as the Nakbah, meaning Catastrophe.

q.q: The Suez Canal Company was nationalized in 1956 by:
q.explanation: On 26 July 1956 Gamal Abdel Nasser announced the nationalization of the Suez Canal Company.

q.q: Which war resulted in Israel controlling the Golan Heights, Jerusalem and the West Bank, the Gaza Strip and the Sinai?
q.explanation: The Six-Day War of June 1967 resulted in Israel controlling those territories.

q.q: The Yom Kippur War began on 6 October 1973 with a coordinated Egyptian and Syrian attack.
q.explanation: On 6 October 1973 Egyptian and Syrian forces launched a coordinated attack on Yom Kippur.

q.q: Explain what the oil embargo of 1973 was aimed at.
q.answer: Western nations that supported Israel|countries supporting Israel
q.explanation: An oil embargo was placed on Western nations that supported Israel, and oil prices increased drastically.

q.q: Who was Chairman of the PLO from 1969 to 2004?
q.explanation: Yasser Arafat was Chairman of the Palestinian Liberation Organization from 1969 to 2004.

q.q: Which countries forced Israel, Britain and France to stop the 1956 war?
options: Soviet Russia, the USA and the UN
q.explanation: Soviet Russia, the USA and the UN forced them to stop the war and withdraw.

q.q: In which year did Gorbachev become leader of the Soviet Communist Party?
q.explanation: Mikhail Gorbachev became the leader of the Soviet Communist Party in 1985.

q.q: The Russian word glasnost means:
q.explanation: Glasnost is a Russian word for openness or publicity.

q.q: Perestroika was aimed at allowing private ownership of some businesses.
q.explanation: Perestroika was a movement aimed at allowing private ownership of some businesses.

q.q: In which country did the 1989 revolution turn violent?
q.explanation: All overthrew their communist regimes peacefully except in Romania, where the revolution was violent.

q.q: Give the Russian word that means restructuring or reorganizing the USSR.
q.explanation: Perestroika refers to restructuring or reorganizing the USSR.

q.q: How many sovereign states emerged from the collapse of the USSR in 1991?
q.explanation: Fifteen sovereign states emerged in 1991.

q.q: Which of the following was NOT a cause of the downfall of the Soviet Union?
options: Economic troubles in the Soviet Union
A direct war with the United States

q.answer: encouraged demands for rights and freedom|regimes collapsed|nationalist movements
q.explanation: The reforms encouraged people to demand more rights and freedom, protests began, and communist regimes collapsed one after another.

q.q: The regime change of 1989 first began in which country?
q.explanation: Nationalist movements first started and brought regime change in Poland.

q.q: The Cold War ended because US military spending had fallen far below that of the USSR.
q.explanation: The USSR could no longer be on a par with US military spending, so the Cold War ended.

q.q: Arrange these events of the collapse in the correct order.
q.explanation: The order is: Gorbachev becomes leader in 1985, reforms are introduced, regime change begins in Poland in 1989, and fifteen states emerge in 1991.

q.q: The first Anglo-Ethiopian treaty was signed on:

q.explanation: The textbook states the Ogaden stayed under the British until 1954.

q.q: The Point Four Agreement of 1952 gave Ethiopia American help in:

q.q: The leading export of Ethiopia in the post-liberation period was:

q.q: Explain what Rist meant in the indigenous land tenure system.
q.answer: land owned based on a lineage system|lineage land
q.explanation: Rist refers to land owned based on a lineage system.

q.q: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
q.explanation: The order is 1942, 1944, 1950, then 1952.

q.q: Which ministry was established in 1942 to modernise education?

q.explanation: The Ministry of Education and Fine Arts was established in 1942.

q.q: The earliest noticeable revolt Haile Selassie faced after returning from exile was:
q.explanation: The Woyyane revolt took place in Tigray in 1943.

q.answer: Bilata Haile Mariam Reda|Haile Mariam Reda
q.explanation: The revolt was led by Bilata Haile Mariam Reda.

q.q: The Bale revolt received support from the Republic of Somalia.
q.explanation: Somalia, pursuing Greater Somalia, gave morale and material support to the campaign.

q.q: Name one leader of the Bale uprising.
q.explanation: Waqo Gutu was one of the leaders of the Bale uprising.

q.q: Name the new tax whose introduction triggered the Gojjam uprising of 1968.
q.answer: agricultural income tax|1967 agricultural income tax

q.q: The 1960 coup d'etat was organised by:

q.explanation: Germame Neway was the civil servant and intellectual of the coup.

q.q: The main cause for the failure of the 1960 coup was:
options: lack of support from the army
q.explanation: The coup failed chiefly because it lacked support from the army.

q.q: The famous slogan of the Ethiopian student movement was:
options: All things to the war front
q.explanation: The slogan was Meret Learashu, Land to the Tiller.

q.q: Explain what happened to Tilahun Gizaw on 28 December 1969 and why it mattered.
q.answer: he was shot by security police|his death pushed students toward revolution
q.explanation: The student union president was shot by security police, radicalising the movement.

q.q: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
q.explanation: The order is 1943, 1960, 1968, then 1969.

q.q: In which month and year did the Derg depose Haile Selassie?

q.q: The Land Reform Proclamation of March 1975 nationalised all rural land in Ethiopia.

q.q: What was the motto or slogan introduced by the Derg?

q.q: The first chairman of the PMAC was:

q.answer: Edget Behebret Zemecha|Development through Cooperation Campaign
q.explanation: The Development through Cooperation Campaign sent about 60,000 campaigners to rural areas.

q.q: Urban land and extra houses were nationalised on:
q.explanation: Urban land and extra houses were nationalised on 26 July 1975.

q.q: Which political group gave critical support to the Derg?

q.q: The Workers' Party of Ethiopia was established as a vanguard party in 1984.
q.explanation: The Derg established the WPE in 1984.

q.q: Name the state proclaimed in 1987 with a constitution under Mengistu.
q.explanation: The PDRE was proclaimed in 1987.

q.q: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
q.explanation: The order is 12 September 1974, December 1974, March 1975, then 26 July 1975.

q.q: The major reason for the Ethiopia-Somalia war was:
options: Somalia's aim to create Greater Somalia
q.explanation: Somalia pursued an irredentist policy of uniting Somali-speaking territories.

q.q: Ethiopia was supported in the 1977 war by the Soviet Union and Cuba.

q.q: Name the Eritrean organisation founded in 1973 and known as Shabia.

q.q: The federation of Eritrea with Ethiopia took place in:

q.q: Which of the following was NOT a responsibility of the Ethiopian government under the federation?

q.q: Give the name of the 1982 Derg military campaign in Eritrea that failed.

q.q: Which organisation was active in the Ogaden region during the 1975-1991 period?

q.q: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.

q.q: The first British colony in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence, in 1957, was:

q.explanation: Eighty-seven per cent of all land in South Africa was reserved for whites.

q.explanation: South Africa was freed from British rule in 1910 and the ANC was formed in 1912.

q.q: In which year was Nelson Mandela released from Robben Island?
