q.q: In permafrost, soil is permanently frozen to depths of hundreds of metres.
q.explanation: Polar tundra (ET) is defined by permafrost, soil permanently frozen to depths of hundreds of metres.

q.q: The tropical wet region extends along the equator between:
q.explanation: The tropical wet region lies between 6 degrees N and 6 degrees S under maritime tropical air masses all year.

q.q: The seasonal migration of the inter-tropical convergence zone most influences which climatic region?
q.explanation: In the tropical wet and dry region the ITCZ migration produces the wet high-sun season and dry low-sun season.

q.q: The largest tropical desert area is located near the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, usually on the western side of continents.
q.explanation: The region lies near the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, usually on the western side of continents.

q.q: Snow-covered surfaces reflect up to 90 percent of incoming insolation back to space.
q.explanation: The albedo of a snow-covered surface reflects up to 90 percent of insolation, keeping ice cap temperatures below 0 degrees C.

q.q: Name the biome that dominates the Mediterranean (Cs) climatic region.
q.explanation: The chaparral biome, made of sclerophyll plants from forests to woodland and brush, dominates the Mediterranean region.

q.q: Which tropical subtype receives most of its precipitation in the 7 to 9 hottest months? Answer with the Koppen letters.
q.explanation: The tropical monsoon climate Am has most precipitation in the 7 to 9 hottest months.

q.q: Explain why mid-latitude deserts are cooler in summer than subtropical deserts, and name a famous exception.
q.answer: higher latitude with alternating tropical and polar air keeps them cooler; exception is death valley|death valley california
q.explanation: Mid-latitude deserts receive alternating tropical and polar air masses at higher latitudes, so summers are cooler; Death Valley, California is the exception.

q.q: Describe how the albedo of snow keeps the polar ice cap cold despite high summer insolation.
q.answer: snow reflects up to 90 percent of insolation back to space|high albedo reflects sunlight
q.explanation: The snow-covered surface reflects up to 90 percent of the insolation back to space, so monthly average temperatures stay below 0 degrees C.

q.q: Which mid-latitude region is limited to the interiors of North America and Eurasia with a grassland biome?
q.explanation: The winter-dry region, with hot humid summers and dry cold continental polar winters, is limited to the interiors of North America and Eurasia.

q.q: Arrange the low-latitude regions in order from the equator poleward.
q.explanation: Poleward the order is tropical wet (to 6 degrees), tropical wet and dry (6 to 15 degrees), then dry desert and steppe (15 to 25 degrees).

q.q: Which islands experience the polar tundra climate in the Southern Hemisphere?
q.explanation: The tundra climate reaches the Southern Hemisphere islands of Macquarie, Kerguelen and South Georgia.

q.q: In the lower atmosphere, the normal temperature decrease with height is about:
q.explanation: In the troposphere the normal temperature decrease with height is 6.4 degrees C per kilometre.

q.q: The job of atmospheric circulation, according to the textbook, is to:
q.explanation: Atmospheric circulation balances energy inequities across latitudes, driven by horizontal pressure differences.

q.q: The difference in day length from December to June is bigger the closer an area is to the pole.
q.explanation: The day-length difference grows as latitude increases, from tiny change at the equator to 24-hour swings near the poles.

q.q: Friction on moving air is greatest high in the free atmosphere and least at the surface.
q.explanation: Friction is greatest at the surface and diminishes with height until it is negligible in the free atmosphere.

q.q: On June 21, how many hours of daylight does the Arctic Circle have in the northern hemisphere?
q.explanation: Day length on June 21 grows from 12 hours at the equator to 24 hours at the Arctic Circle.

q.q: What fraction of insolation can a snow-covered surface reflect back to space?
q.explanation: The albedo of a snow-covered surface reflects up to 90 percent of the insolation back to space.

q.q: Explain why solar rays are attenuated and depleted more efficiently at high latitudes.
q.answer: low sun angle means rays cross more air particles|rays strike the surface, taking a long path through the atmosphere
q.explanation: At a low sun angle the rays hit a high-latitude surface after interacting with more air particles, so they lose more energy than near-vertical equatorial rays.

q.q: A mountain is 4620 m high and the sea-level temperature is 30 degrees C. Calculate the peak temperature and show your working.
q.explanation: Temperature drop = (4620 x 6.4)/1000 = 29.57 degrees C, so the peak is 30 - 29.57 = 0.43 degrees C.

q.q: The subtropical high pressure belt, the source of the surface westerlies, is located at about:
q.explanation: The STH sits at about 30 degrees latitude and pulls surface air toward the pole and the equator.

q.q: Arrange these steps of convectional afternoon rainfall formation in a low-latitude summer.
options: Rising air expands, cools and condenses into cumulus or cumulonimbus clouds
The sun heats the ground and the air above it
Warm air rises in convection currents as it becomes lighter
Storm clouds finally produce conventional rainfall
q.explanation: First the sun heats the surface, then warm air rises, then the air expands and condenses into clouds, then rainfall follows.

q.q: Albedo is the fraction of incoming sunlight reflected by a surface.
q.explanation: Albedo measures the fraction of incoming sunlight reflected by a surface.

q.q: Ethiopia's local climate classification is based on:
options: height, temperature and growing season length
q.explanation: The local system uses height, temperature and growing season length.

q.q: In which altitude range is the Woina-Dega zone found?
q.explanation: Woina-Dega covers the temperate highlands between 1500 and 2300 metres above sea level.

q.q: The Bereha zone is mainly inhabited by pastoralists because of its harsh environment.
q.explanation: Bereha's strong winds, high temperatures, low humidity and limited cloud make it mainly a pastoralist habitat.

q.q: In the Kolla zone, rainfall along the western lowlands of Gambella can reach 64 inches.
q.explanation: In the rainy western lowlands of Gambella, Kolla rainfall can reach 64 inches although the zone average is 16.4 to 32.8 inches.

q.q: Which traditional zone includes afro-alpine plateaus such as Sena, Simien, Guna, Choke and Amara Sayint?
q.explanation: Wurch, the alpine zone above 3300 m, includes those afro-alpine sites.

q.q: Which zone lies between 2300 and 3300 metres above sea level?
q.explanation: Dega, the cold temperate highland climate, lies between 2300 and 3300 metres above sea level.

q.q: Explain why crops rarely grow in the desert and Kur agroecological zones.
q.answer: too hot and dry in desert, too cold with short growing season in kur|heat and moisture limits in desert, cold limits in kur
q.explanation: Desert zones face over 30 degrees C and under 16 inches of rain, while Kur above 3700 m is too cold with too short a growing season.

q.q: Compare the main strengths of Ethiopia's local classification and Koppen's global classification.
q.answer: local links altitude and crops for the country; koppen allows worldwide comparison with vegetation-linked codes|local is crop and altitude based, koppen global
q.explanation: The local scheme grounds farming decisions in altitude and growing season; Koppen enables global comparison through vegetation-linked temperature and precipitation codes.

q.q: Which set of crops belongs to the Kolla zone?
options: Sorghum, finger millet, groundnuts, cowpeas, sesame
q.explanation: Kolla produces sorghum, finger millet, groundnuts, cowpeas and sesame.

q.q: Arrange the traditional zones from lowest altitude to highest.
q.explanation: From lowest to highest: Bereha (under 500 m), Kolla (500 to 1500 m), Woina-Dega (1500 to 2300 m), Dega (2300 to 3300 m), Wurch (above 3300 m).

q.q: The yearly average temperature of the Wurch zone is below 10 degrees C.
q.explanation: Wurch has a yearly average temperature below 10 degrees C and annual rainfall between 35.2 and 80 inches.

q.q: Land is described as the ultimate resource because:
options: it is the most expensive commodity
without it life on Earth cannot be sustained
it cannot be bought or sold
q.explanation: Land is the ultimate resource and foundation of all human activity; without it life on Earth cannot be sustained.

q.q: Which set correctly lists land resource classes based on distribution and volume?
q.explanation: Distribution and volume classify resources as ubiquitous, unique, common and rare.

q.q: Being classified as renewable means a resource can never be depleted.
q.explanation: Renewable resources can be easily depleted through excessive use; sustainable use keeps the rate of use below the rate of regeneration.

q.q: Which resource takes a relatively long time to renew compared with crops?
q.explanation: Crops regenerate quickly, but soil may take a relatively long time to renew, and forest takes longer still.

q.q: Which spheres of the Earth are the sources of land resources? Name three.
q.explanation: Land resources are derived from the lithosphere, biosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere.

q.q: State the prime objective of land management in one sentence.
q.answer: control land degradation to balance resource exploitation and regeneration
q.explanation: The prime objective of land management is to control land degradation to balance resource exploitation and regeneration.

q.q: Which pair of non-renewable resources cannot be recycled the way metallic minerals can?
q.explanation: Coal and petroleum cannot be recycled like metallic minerals, so their use must be carefully managed.

q.q: Land serves as a sink of wastes as one of its functions.
q.explanation: The waste disposal function makes land a sink of wastes.

q.q: Explain why land is considered both a physical commodity and an abstract concept.
q.answer: rights to own or use it are part of the land|ownership and use rights belong to the land
q.explanation: The rights to own or use land are as much a part of the land as the object rooted in the soil, making it an abstract (legal) concept as well as a physical one.

q.q: Arrange these stages of resource classification by stage of development from least developed.
q.explanation: Stage of development orders resources as potential, actual and conditional.

q.q: Name the practice of letting livestock numbers match the regeneration capacity of a pasture.
q.explanation: Controlled grazing protects soils, water and vegetation from overstocking.

q.q: Which set lists the renewable resources placed under the greatest human pressure?
q.explanation: From all renewable resources, soils, water and forests are the most influenced by humans and under increased pressure.

q.q: The 'tragedy of the commons' describes what?
options: Greater pressure and degradation on common-pool resources
Urban residents moving to rural areas
q.explanation: Common-pool wealth faces greater pressure because it is repeatedly misused, mismanaged and degraded.

q.q: Nearly 33% of the world's arable land and soils have been destroyed by soil erosion.
q.explanation: The textbook states nearly 33% of the world's arable land and soils have been destroyed by soil erosion.

q.q: Salinization and acidification belong to which form of soil degradation, and crusting and compaction to which?
q.explanation: Chemical degradation includes salinization, alkalinisation and acidification; physical degradation includes crusting, compaction and depth reduction.

q.q: The textbook links which world population forecast to the water crisis feared in the middle of the 21st century?
q.explanation: The world population is likely to approach 10 billion by 2050, raising water demand for agriculture and industry.

q.q: Name the exotic water plant that pollutes lakes and rivers near urban areas.
q.explanation: Rivers and lakes closer to urban areas are polluted by plastic bags and exotic water plants like the water hyacinth.

q.q: About how much forested land is converted annually into other land uses worldwide?
q.explanation: About 13 million hectares of forested lands have been annually converted into other land uses in recent decades.

q.q: Desalination of sea water is one of the measures listed for sustaining freshwater.
q.explanation: Desalination of sea water minimizes stress on streams and lakes.

q.q: Explain why oil spills and industrial chemicals are dangerous to lakes, seas and rivers.
q.answer: excessive accumulation of nutrients and toxicity|they poison the animals inhabiting the ecosystem
q.explanation: Oil spills plus chemicals released from industries cause excessive accumulation of nutrients and toxicity over the animals inhabiting those ecosystems.

q.q: Which example of forest loss given in the textbook is from plantation agriculture and livestock ranching in the tropics?
q.explanation: Forest clearance for large-scale plantation agriculture and livestock ranching in the tropics, e.g. in the Amazon basin, caused loss of rainforest ecosystems.

q.q: Which Ethiopian program for planting trees is named in the textbook?
q.answer: the green legacy|the green legacy initiative|green legacy
q.explanation: Afforestation and reforestation programs like the Green Legacy practiced in Ethiopia are recommended measures.

q.q: Resource degradation is best defined as:
options: the overall loss of quality and quantity of land resources
changing land from farm to forest
q.explanation: Resource degradation is the overall loss (decline) of the quality and quantity of land resources such as soils, water and biological mass.

q.q: Which of these is an underlying rather than a proximate cause of degradation?
q.explanation: Underlying sources are major causes, such as rapid population growth, that promote proximate issues to happen.

q.q: Degradation is often initiated by human activity but can also be started by natural hazards such as earthquakes and flooding.
q.explanation: The textbook states degradation is often initiated by human activity and sometimes by natural hazards.

q.q: Explain how poor tenurial policy leads to resource depletion.
q.answer: tenure insecurity|farmers with insecure rights do not invest in protecting the land
q.explanation: Poor tenure policy produces tenure insecurity, the final proximate step toward resource depletion in Table 3.1.

q.q: Where does the textbook photograph degraded land in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: The textbook shows degraded land in the Atsbi-Womberta area, Tigray, Ethiopia.

q.q: Name the practice of covering soil with plant residue to save moisture and add nutrients.
q.explanation: Mulching covers soil with plant residue so it regains nutrients and reduces water loss from evaporation.

q.q: Which consequence of flooding does the textbook especially highlight for dams?
q.explanation: Flooding brings soil and biodiversity losses, health problems, and sedimentation and siltation of dams (reservoirs).

q.q: The impacts of land degradation are worse in developing countries like those in Africa.
q.explanation: The textbook states its impacts are much worse in developing countries like those in Africa.

q.q: Why does reduced rainfall almost always accompany desertification?
q.answer: climate change decreases rainfalls and increases temperatures
q.explanation: Climate change brings decreasing rainfalls and increasing temperatures, whose immediate outcome is desertification with contracted vegetation.

q.q: Arrange these conservation steps from planting to enrichment as the textbook defines afforestation, reforestation and area closure.
q.explanation: Afforestation plants on barren lands, reforestation replants deforested areas, and area closures then keep livestock away so the area recovers.

q.q: What is a check dam used for?
q.answer: to control erosion by reducing water flow velocity|conserving gullied areas|reducing water flow velocity
q.explanation: A check dam, small or temporary, is constructed across a waterway to control erosion by reducing water flow velocity, important in gullied areas.

q.q: Transboundary rivers are defined as:
options: watercourses shared by two or more countries
q.explanation: Transboundary rivers are watercourses shared by two or more countries.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the transboundary waters category?
q.explanation: Oceans, territorial seas and coastal waters are not included in the transboundary waters category.

q.q: The 263 transnational watercourses cover nearly half of the Earth's terrestrial surface.
q.explanation: The textbook states they make up around 60% of freshwater flows and cover nearly one-half of the Earth's terrestrial surface.

q.q: Name the river that flows through the most nations.
q.explanation: The Danube travels through the territory of 19 nations.

q.q: Name any three of the five basins shared between nine and eleven states.
q.explanation: The five are the Congo, Niger, Nile, Rhine and Zambezi.

q.q: How many riparian countries share the Nile basin?
q.explanation: The table lists the Nile with 11 riparian countries, a length of 6,671 km and 84 BCM flow.

q.q: The Congo river carries less water per year than the Nile.
q.explanation: The Congo carries 1,250 BCM yearly to the Atlantic, far above the Nile's 84 BCM.

q.q: Explain one economic and one ecological prospect shared rivers offer riparian states.
q.answer: hydropower and irrigation and navigation|food and habitat for aquatic life|flood and pollution control
q.explanation: Prospects include socioeconomic development (dams, power, navigation) and ecosystem services such as food, aquatic habitat, flood and pollution control.

q.q: According to the textbook, around 80% of the area of 44 countries lies within international basins. How many of these countries are in Africa?
q.explanation: Twenty of the 44 countries are in Africa, 13 in Europe, 7 in Asia and 4 in Latin America.

q.q: Which Nile basin dams and projects belong to Ethiopia according to the textbook list? Name two.
q.explanation: Ethiopian entries are Tekeze HEP, Tana Beles, Tis Abay, Fincha, Koga irrigation and the GERD.

q.q: Why might a shared watercourse become a source of dialogue rather than war, using the Nile case?
q.answer: cooperation and negotiation among riparian states|potential for cooperation like ethiopia and egypt
q.explanation: Shared watercourses implant potential for cooperation like Ethiopia and Egypt over the Nile; inter-state collaboration is the best option for diverging interests.

q.q: Why do riparian states need organizing agreements for shared basins?
options: because political and institutional complications block rational long-term management
q.explanation: Due to political and/or institutional complications, shared resources of a single basin cannot be rationally managed without an organizing agreement and governing rule.

q.q: Of the 263 shared basins, 176 (67%) had bilateral conventions.
q.explanation: The textbook states 176 of the 263 basins (67%) had bilateral conventions.

q.q: TECCONILE, begun in December 1992, was first initiated by which six riparian states?
options: Ethiopia, Egypt, Sudan, Kenya, Eritrea, Burundi
Egypt, Sudan, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania, Zaire
Egypt, Sudan, Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania
Sudan, Zaire, Rwanda, Burundi, Ethiopia, Kenya
q.explanation: TECCONILE was initiated by Egypt, Sudan, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania and Zaire; Ethiopia, Kenya, Eritrea and Burundi were observers.

q.q: On what date and in which city was the NBI first signed by Ministers of Water Resources?
q.explanation: The NBI was first signed on 22 February 1999 in Dar-es-Salaam, Tanzania.

q.q: Explain one risk of the past treaty pattern where multilateral basins were covered mostly by bilateral deals.
q.answer: intentionally excluding one or more riparian countries|exclusion of some riparian states
q.explanation: Because such covenants were bilateral in character, many agreements intentionally excluded one or more riparian countries within a catchment.

q.q: Which institution created in 1986 transfers water from the head-reaches of the Orange River to South Africa's industrial region?
q.explanation: The Lesotho Highlands Development Authority was created by the 1986 treaty between Lesotho and the RSA.

q.q: The Zambezi River Authority operates and maintains the Kariba dam.
q.explanation: ZRA objectives include operating and maintaining the Kariba dam, investigating new projects and collecting data.

q.q: State two main objectives of the Nile Basin Initiative.
q.answer: sustainable socioeconomic development|equitable utilization|recognition of the rights of all riparian states|inclusive legal framework
q.explanation: Objectives include sustainable socio-economic development, equitable utilization and benefit of basin resources, recognition of riparian rights, and an inclusive legal framework for allocating Nile waters.

q.q: Which commission created in 1909 is cited as successful in resolving all transboundary issues referred to it?
q.explanation: The US-Canada International Joint Commission, created by the 1909 Waters Treaty, resolved all issues referred to it.

q.q: Arrange the Nile cooperation sequence from earliest to latest.
q.explanation: TECCONILE opened in December 1992, structure-design ran 1997-2001, and the NBI was signed on 22 February 1999.

q.q: Name the objective of SARCCUS.
q.answer: coordinating the conservation of water and soils on shared river basins|conservation of water and soils
q.explanation: SARCCUS was established to coordinate the conservation of water and soils on the shared river basins.

q.q: The actual per capita water use of Egypt is about:
options: 830 cubic meters per person per year
q.explanation: Egypt's per capita use is about 830 cubic meters per person per year - low compared with Ethiopia and Sudan.

q.q: Egypt's per capita water use is below the 1,700 cubic meters proposed by WHO.
q.explanation: Egypt's usage of about 830 m3 is less than the 1,700 cubic meters per person per annum proposed by WHO.

q.q: Under the 1959 agreement, how much Nile water went to Egypt and how much to Sudan?
q.explanation: Egypt was granted 55.5 BCM while Sudan received 18.5 BCM per year under the 1959 treaty.

q.q: How many riparian countries share the Nile River?
q.explanation: The Nile River is shared by 11 riparian countries.

q.q: Explain the historical ties the textbook mentions between Ethiopia and Egypt.
q.answer: exchanging popes for their orthodox churches|orthodox church popes exchanged
q.explanation: Ethiopia and Egypt exchanged popes for their Orthodox Churches during their past long history.

q.q: The 1959 treaty allotted a large share of Nile water to Ethiopia.
q.explanation: All Nile water was distributed to Egypt and Sudan; Ethiopia received none, which the textbook says deliberately overlooked her right.

q.q: Which body did Egypt and Sudan create under the 1959 treaty?
q.explanation: The 1959 treaty created the Permanent Joint Technical Commission.

q.q: Why is Egypt's actual water use a paradox in the Nile dispute?
q.answer: it uses historically the most but has the lowest per capita use and falls below the who threshold
q.explanation: Historically Egypt dominated Nile irrigation and hydropower, yet its per capita use (about 830 m3) is the lowest of the three and under the WHO benchmark - so it contests any reduced flow.

q.q: Name the agreement signed later by basin states to create a permanent Nile River Basin Commission.
q.explanation: The signing of the Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) was for the creation of a permanent Nile River Basin Commission.

q.q: What is Sudan's and Egypt's stated fear about the GERD, and what does Ethiopia counter?
q.answer: gerd might affect their water supply|they say ethiopia should abide by the 1959 agreement
q.explanation: Sudan and Egypt challenge the GERD saying it might affect their water supply and argue Ethiopia should abide by 1959; Ethiopia rejects a treaty signed in her absence that gave her nothing.

q.q: In the past, the use of Nile water for hydropower and irrigation was dominated exclusively by Egypt and Sudan.
q.explanation: Past use was exclusively dominated by Egypt and Sudan, while poverty and political instability hindered upstream countries.

q.q: A natural resource conflict is best described as:
options: a war caused only by religion
a dispute over accessing, controlling and using materials found in nature
q.explanation: Resource conflicts are disputes arising over accessing, controlling and using materials found in nature.

q.q: The market value of exhaustible resources like diamonds rises when their quantities shrink.
q.explanation: The textbook states the market value of such resources rises when their quantities shrink, causing asset scarcity and conflict.

q.q: What share of civil wars of the past six decades were instigated by the control and use of natural resources?
q.explanation: Some 40-60% of the civil wars during the past six decades were instigated by the control and use of natural resources.

q.q: Which Ethiopian pastoralist groups are named as parties to a pasture land conflict?
q.explanation: Pasture land conflict in Ethiopia occurred between Somali and Afar pastoralists.

q.q: The conflict in Darfur (Sudan) is given as an example of conflict mainly due to:
q.explanation: In Darfur, much of the fighting was due to water scarcity.

q.q: Name three of the four kinds of resource conflicts recognized at the wider scope.
q.answer: secessionist|standalone projects|new national laws|cumulative small-scale clashes
q.explanation: The four kinds are secessionist conflicts; disputes within new national laws and conventions; grievances over standalone projects such as mines and dams; and cumulative impacts of multiple small-scale clashes.

q.q: Which fishing dispute does the textbook cite between the UK and Iceland?
options: The cod wars of the 1950s and 1970s
q.explanation: Fishing disputes led to 'cod wars' between the UK and Iceland in the 1950s and 1970s.

q.q: The Gulf war between Kuwait and Iraq is cited as a conflict caused by which resource?
q.explanation: Natural oil in the Middle East caused the Gulf war between Kuwait and Iraq; in Africa it caused conflict between Cameroon and Nigeria.

q.q: Name the rebel groups that used diamonds in Angola and Sierra Leone in the late 1990s.
q.explanation: The Angola National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA) and Sierra Leone's Revolutionary United Front (RUF) used diamonds as income in the late 1990s.

q.q: Arrange these conflict-handling modes from least to most third-party involvement.
q.explanation: Negotiation is voluntary and party-led, mediation adds a facilitating third party, and arbitration gives decision power to a mutually agreeable third party.

q.q: List three conditions under which conflicts arise even without absolute scarcity.
q.answer: user groups excluded from management|inequitable sharing|unclear laws|poor policy implementation|inequality in distribution
q.explanation: Conflicts arise when users are excluded from management, resources are inequitably shared, laws are unclear, information is absent, or implementation is poor.

q.q: In 1800 the world population stood at about:
q.explanation: The text states the world's population grew from one billion in 1800.

q.q: Which statement correctly describes stage two of the demographic transition model?
options: Birth and death rates are both high
Death rates fall, especially among children 0-5, while birth rates stay high
Birth rates fall due to widespread contraception
q.explanation: In stage two mortality falls first, notably among children aged 0 to 5, while births remain high, causing rapid growth.

q.q: Human population growth was modest until the mid-nineteenth century.
q.explanation: Growth was modest until the mid-1800s, when birth rates were only slightly greater than mortality rates.

q.q: The medium-variant projection for world population in 2100 is:
q.explanation: The projection is 10.7 billion in 2100, a 42 percent increase over 2019.

q.q: Which region had the highest fertility in 2019, and roughly how many births per woman?
q.explanation: Sub-Saharan Africa had 4.6 births per woman in 2019, the highest of any region.

q.q: Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to account for more than half of the world's population growth between 2019 and 2050.
q.explanation: With a predicted addition of 1.1 billion people, Sub-Saharan Africa could account for over half of global growth.

q.q: Define the demographic dividend and name one condition needed to reap it.
q.answer: falling fertility makes working age population grow faster|requires investment in education and health|invest in education and health of young people
q.explanation: Recent fertility declines make the population at working ages (25-64) expand faster, allowing faster economic growth if governments invest in education and health.

q.q: Which country has the lowest old-age potential support ratio in the world?
q.explanation: Japan's potential support ratio is 1.8, the lowest in the world.

q.q: Every less developed country is expected to gain population between 2019 and 2050.
q.explanation: At least 55 LDCs, including Bulgaria, Latvia, Lithuania and Ukraine, are expected to shrink due to low fertility and emigration.

q.q: Arrange the stages of the demographic transition model in order from first to last.
options: Birth rate rises again with low mortality
Death rates fall while births remain high
q.explanation: The order is stage 1 (high both), stage 2 (deaths fall), stage 4 (births equal deaths) and stage 5 (births rise again with low deaths); stage 3 fits between stages 2 and 4.

q.q: Which country is expected to surpass China as the world's most populated country around 2027?
q.explanation: India is expected to pass China around 2027.

q.q: The most important factor in the real expansion of population has been:
options: the overall reduction in the death rate
q.explanation: The textbook identifies the overall decline in death rates through medical and public health advances as most important.

q.q: Which weakness of the crude birth rate makes it unusable for comparing populations?
options: It is too hard to compute
It ignores age and sex structure
q.explanation: The CBR denominator includes everyone regardless of fertility contribution and ignores age-sex structure.

q.q: Breastfeeding eliminates the risk of pregnancy after delivery.
q.explanation: Breastfeeding reduces but does not eliminate the risk for up to twenty-one months after delivery.

q.q: What is the general weakness of the general fertility rate as a fertility measure?
q.answer: it does not account for differences in age groups|ignores age group differences|different age groups are not equally fertile
q.explanation: The GFR ignores that fertility is appreciably higher in the 20-29 age groups than in the 15-19 and 40-49 groups.

q.q: Region A recorded 100,000 deaths in 2021 with a mid-year population of 26,000,000. Its crude death rate is about:
What does a gross reproductive rate below 1.0 indicate about a population?
q.answer: the next generation of women will not replace themselves|population is not replacing itself|declining from fertility
q.explanation: GRR below 1.0 means the next generation of women will not replace themselves; above 1.0 they more than replace themselves.

q.q: The later a woman waits to engage in a sexual partnership, the lower the fertility rate tends to be.
q.explanation: Early marriage raises fertility because of the increased risk of pregnancy and longer periods in which pregnancy could occur.

q.q: Name the fertility measures most commonly used besides the crude birth rate.
q.answer: gfr|tfr|general fertility rate|total fertility rate|grr|gross reproductive rate
q.explanation: Fertility is commonly measured with the CBR, the general fertility rate and the total fertility rate; the GRR is also used.

q.q: In the TFR formula the sum of age-specific birth rates is multiplied by 5 because:
options: five children are expected per woman
each age-specific group represents a five-year cohort of women
q.explanation: The age groups from 15-19 to 45-49 each span five years, so each rate represents a five-year cohort.

q.q: Explain how illiteracy contributes to accelerated population growth in less developed countries.
q.answer: illiteracy makes it hard to understand consequences of rapid growth|hard to use contraceptives|rural societies lack information and oppose family planning
q.explanation: Higher illiteracy makes it difficult to comprehend the negative consequences of rapid growth and to employ methods such as contraceptives; many rural societies oppose family planning for lack of information.

q.q: The crude death rate depends on standards of living, nutrition, medical services, personal hygiene and environmental sanitation.
q.explanation: These are listed as the key factors that determine the rate of mortality.

q.q: Which country has been the world's most popular destination for migrants for the past five decades?
q.explanation: The United States has remained the world's most popular destination for the past five decades.

q.q: Migration has no direct impact on the total world population.
q.explanation: Because one country's loss is another's gain, migration does not change the global total, though it changes distribution.

q.q: Write the equation for the annual population change of a country in terms of births, deaths, immigrants and emigrants.
q.answer: (b-d)+(i-e)|births minus deaths plus immigrants minus emigrants
q.explanation: Annual change equals (B - D) + (I - E). Until the 1960s natural increase dominated in MDCs; now immigration contributes more.

q.q: Country A has 350,000 immigrants, 60,000 emigrants and a population of 110,000,000. Its net migration rate is:
List two push factors found in the source countries of international migrants.
q.answer: weak job opportunities|big populations|low salaries|low wages
q.explanation: Push factors include weak job opportunities, big populations and low salaries in the source country.

q.q: Which group of countries had both negative natural increase and net emigration during 2010-2020?
q.explanation: European nations such as Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Poland, Portugal, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova and Romania had both negative natural increase and negative net migration.

q.q: Human trafficking involves moving people by force or fraud for sexual exploitation or forced labor.
q.explanation: Trafficking is done by force or fraud for sexual exploitation or forced labor.

q.q: Name two regions that have been net recipients of international migrants for decades.
q.answer: europe|northern america|australia and new zealand|australia/new zealand
q.explanation: Europe, Northern America and Australia/New Zealand have been net recipients, with net migration tending to increase.

q.q: Explain why migration does not change the total world population but still matters to geographers.
q.answer: one country's loss is another's gain|it changes distribution, cultural diffusion and resource exploitation
q.explanation: The world total is unchanged, but movement redistributes people, spreads culture and changes how resources are exploited.

q.q: According to the lesson, what is the greatest apparent impact of immigration on receiving countries?
options: The shift in cultural and racial makeup
q.explanation: The greatest apparent impact is the change in the cultural and racial makeup of receiving countries as immigrants form a larger share of the population.

q.q: Region A recorded 400,000 births in 2021, of which 360,000 babies survived their first year. Its infant mortality rate is closest to what value per 1,000 live births?
Population policies are best defined as:
options: government declarations and measures that influence population size, growth, distribution and composition
q.explanation: Population policies are government declarations, choices and measures done openly or implicitly to affect number, growth, distribution and composition.

q.q: Historically, population policies were mainly pronatalist, restricting emigration and stimulating immigration.
q.explanation: Pronatalist restricting emigration and stimulating immigration were historically the key focus; today the concerns have reversed.

q.q: Which government action has an indirect demographic effect?
options: Increasing taxes for each additional child
Promoting female education and raising the status of women
q.explanation: Promoting female education is an indirect policy; the other three are listed as direct actions.

q.q: Name the three main instruments governments use to gather demographic data.
q.explanation: Governments gather demographic data through censuses, civil registration systems and surveys.

q.q: Explain why promoting female education lowers fertility even though it never mentions children.
q.answer: educated women marry later|higher status changes childbearing choices|indirect effect on fertility
q.explanation: Education and higher status change marriage and childbearing decisions, so fertility falls as an indirect demographic effect.

q.q: Which of the following is a direct (explicit) population policy?
options: Increasing taxes for each additional child
q.explanation: Raising taxes per additional child directly targets demographic outcomes; the others are indirect.

q.q: Urbanization and internal migration must be managed by population plans because they strain agriculture, natural resources and the environment.
q.explanation: Migration and urbanization influence spatial distribution and density and put pressure on agriculture, natural resources and the environment.

q.q: State the core objectives of population policies.
q.answer: economic development|social or individual welfare|promote economic development and social welfare
q.explanation: The core objectives aim to promote both economic development and social or individual welfare.

q.q: Put the two national-level steps of population policy work in order.
options: Develop and execute mortality, fertility and migration policies
Gather demographic data through censuses, civil registration and surveys
q.explanation: First data is gathered through censuses, registration and surveys; second, public health and population policies are developed and executed.

q.q: Give two measures a government can use to relieve pressure on crowded cities.
q.answer: decrease rural to urban migration|redistribute to smaller towns|ensure services for the urban poor|promote public transportation
q.explanation: Measures include redistribution to smaller urban and rural areas, reducing rural-to-urban migration, providing basic services to the urban poor and improving public transport.

q.q: Relocating people out of environmentally fragile areas is a recognized population distribution policy measure.
q.explanation: Relocating population out of environmentally fragile or threatened areas is one of the listed policy measures.

q.q: The Human Development Index is computed from which three dimensions?
options: Longevity, access to knowledge and standard of living
q.explanation: HDI uses life expectancy at birth, access to knowledge (literacy and years of schooling) and a decent standard of living (real per capita income), all scaled between 0 and 1.

q.q: In the 2019 UNDP ranking of 189 countries, Ethiopia's HDI of 0.485 placed it:
q.explanation: Ethiopia scored 0.485 and ranked 173 of the 189 countries ranked by UNDP in 2019.

q.q: Economic growth considers both the quantity and the quality of people's well-being.
q.explanation: Economic growth is purely quantitative; it is economic development that includes qualitative progress in welfare.

q.q: Determinist theorists explained the higher development of temperate countries by their location in distinct environments compared with tropical areas.
q.explanation: Determinists argued temperate regions are more developed than tropical areas because of their distinct cold and hot environments.

q.q: Which scholar belongs to the geographic determinism school?
q.explanation: Semple, with Ritter and Huntington, advocated determinism; Febvre and Vidal de la Blache were possibilists.

q.q: In von Thunen's model, ranching occupies the fourth ring mainly because:
options: livestock can transport themselves to market
q.explanation: Ranching takes the fourth ring because animals can be self-transporting to the market, unlike bulky or perishable goods.

q.q: Arrange von Thunen's land-use rings in order starting from the market city.
options: Intensive perishables: vegetables, fruit and dairy
q.explanation: The correct order is perishables (dairy), forest products, field crops, ranching, then wilderness beyond the fourth ring.

q.q: Name the German geographer who outlined industrial location theory in his 1909 book 'Theory of the Location of Industries'.
q.explanation: Alfred Weber, a Heidelberg economics professor, presented the least-cost location model in 1909.

q.q: In Weber's model, which of the three key factors comes first in fixing the firm's location, with the other two used only for adjustment?
q.explanation: Weber first determined the least transport-cost location and then adjusted it for labor costs and agglomeration economies, making transport the primary factor.

q.q: A firm computes a material index of 0.4. According to Weber it should locate:
options: at the mouth of a mine
q.explanation: An index below 1 means the product outweighs the used inputs, so the firm should locate nearer to the market.

q.q: Under Christaller's marketing principle, list the successive numbers of centers served starting from 1, and say what this achieves.
q.answer: 1, 3, 9, 27|serves many consumers from a few centers
q.explanation: The K = 3 rule follows 1, 3, 9, 27 ..., so several consumers are served from a small number of service centers.

q.q: Climate extremes are best defined as:
options: Weather elements taking excessive values above or below normal thresholds over an area and time
Slow climate change measured over a century
q.explanation: The textbook defines extreme climate as an excessive value of climatic elements below or above the normal thresholds in a specific area and time, and such extremes are rare but disastrous.

q.q: The daily income that marks people as extremely poor is about:
q.explanation: Extremely poor people receive only 1.90 USD per day, and about 10 percent of the global population lives within this threshold.

q.q: Human-induced warming reached about 1.0 degree C above pre-industrial levels by 2017.
q.explanation: The textbook states human-induced warming reached about 1.0 degree C above pre-industrial levels in 2017, with 1.5 degree C projected by 2040.

q.q: Rainfall in tropical and sub-tropical areas has shown increasing trends over the period of study.
q.explanation: Rainfall has decreased in tropical and sub-tropical areas, while increasing in the middle and high latitudes.

q.q: Between 2006 and 2012 the Itang District of Gambella suffered a major flood every year apart from:
q.explanation: The area suffered a major flood every year from 2006 to 2012 except 2009, when drought struck; 2007 and 2012 were the worst years.

q.q: Name the river whose annual overflow floods the households of Itang District, Gambella.
q.explanation: Households are flooded annually when the Baro River, a tributary of the Nile and the widest river in Ethiopia, overflows.

q.q: Explain why relying on social networks to cope with floods proved unsustainable in Itang.
q.answer: repeated floods erode social capital|repeated demand weakens reciprocal support
q.explanation: Each flood forces households to ask relatives again for shelter and food, so repeated floods erode the social capital on which reciprocal support depends.

q.q: Which groups does the textbook list as the most affected by climate extremes?
options: Female-headed households, slum dwellers and children
q.explanation: Households led by females, people living in slums and children are among the most affected; poor pastoralists also risk lingering poverty when feed supplies fall.

q.q: In the Burkina Faso case study, how did the 2011 disaster occur?
options: 165 small ruminants drowned in the Beli River during a sudden brutal rain
All cattle were stolen by raiders
q.explanation: In 2011, 165 small ruminants drowned in the Beli River while searching for fodder during a sudden and brutal rain.

q.q: Without rigorous action, the research cited in the textbook expects about how many extremely poor people to be living in 49 highly vulnerable countries during the 2030s?
q.explanation: Nearly 325 million extremely poor people are projected for 49 countries highly vulnerable to natural hazards, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.

q.q: Arrange the chain that turns climate extremes into a poverty trap.
options: Assets and savings are consumed or sold
Human capital and coping capacity decline
The next shock strikes an even poorer household
q.explanation: The sequence runs: shock strikes, assets are consumed or sold, human capital and coping capacity decline, chronic poverty deepens, and the cycle repeats.

q.q: How many landlocked countries are there in the world according to the lesson?
q.explanation: There are 49 landlocked countries, equal to one fifth (20 percent) of all countries in the world.

q.q: The most common characteristic of a landlocked country is that it:
options: has no seacoast and every border is land based
q.explanation: Landlocked countries lack any seacoast; rivers or lakes inside the borders do not change this, and they occur on all continents.

q.q: Landlocked states occupy the mid-regions of continents and make up about one fifth of the world's nations.
q.explanation: The textbook notes they occupy mid-continental regions and constitute about one fifth (20 percent) of all nations.

q.q: Doubling transport costs reduces a country's trade volume by about 80 percent.
q.explanation: It has been estimated that doubling transport costs reduces trade volume by around 80 percent.

q.q: Burundi's short direct passage to the sea, the so-called Central Corridor, runs over which transit country?
q.explanation: The Central Corridor crosses Tanzania to the port of Dar es Salaam, but its transit setup is too poor.

q.q: Name the two Red Sea ports Ethiopia lost the use of after the conflict with Eritrea following 1997.
q.explanation: The Ethiopia-Eritrea conflict denied Ethiopia use of the ports of Assab and Massawa after 1997.

q.q: Which pair of measures eases transit procedures in regional blocs?
options: Common warrants in SADC and COMESA allowing freight without local permits
Higher security bonds and police escorts
Compulsory conversion of local currency at ports
Closing borders during the rainy season
q.explanation: Common warrants announced in SADC and COMESA allow road freight within member countries without local permits or licenses.

q.q: Explain why the trade cost of a landlocked country is said to be determined indirectly by the development level of its transit neighbors.
q.answer: its goods must move over the neighbor's roads, railways and ports
q.explanation: Because landlocked states depend entirely on transit infrastructure, poor neighboring networks make overland trade significantly more costly.

q.q: The mean trip from Kampala to Mombasa takes about:
q.explanation: The mean trip takes about 21 days and sometimes up to 60 days, reflecting border delays of 24 to 48 hours across Africa.

q.q: Which statement about transit payments is correct?
options: All charges are paid only after delivery
Some charges are paid upfront and some during travel, often in hard currency
No licenses are required for foreign vehicles
Ports waive agency fees for landlocked states
q.explanation: Transit and custom charges include permits, licenses, tolls, bonds and escorts, paid partly upfront and partly en route, usually in hard currency.

q.q: Give three of the historical events that created landlocked countries.
q.answer: end of the first world war|end of colonization|collapse of the ussr|soviet union
q.explanation: Landlocked states were formed at the end of the First World War, following the end of colonization, and after the collapse and splitting of the former Soviet Union; in Africa, colonial border drawing enclosed some states.

q.q: How many member states does COMESA have according to the lesson?
q.explanation: COMESA has 19 member states, compared with 5 for AMU, 15 for ECOWAS and 16 for SADC.

q.q: Roughly what share of all intra-African formal exports does South Africa supply in 2016-2018?
q.explanation: South Africa exported 32.2 percent of intra-African formal exports in 2016-2018, nearly a third of the total.

q.q: Africa's trade pattern is dominated by imports of processed food products and exports of untreated nonfood products.
q.explanation: The textbook states Africa's world trade is dominated by imports of processed foods and exports of untreated nonfood products.

q.q: The value of intra-African food and agricultural trade peaked around 2013 before declining and then resuming growth in 2016.
q.explanation: The value rose steadily from about 2007, peaked in 2013, declined significantly, and resumed a general upward trend in 2016.

q.q: Which REC retained the largest share of its intra-African exports within its region in 2016-2018?
q.explanation: SADC retained 84 percent, ahead of ECOWAS (79), COMESA (66) and AMU (60), while ECCAS retained only 46 percent.

q.q: Ethiopia's top three intra-African export destinations are:
q.explanation: Ethiopia's top export destinations are Somalia, Djibouti and Kenya, while its top import sources are Morocco, South Africa and Egypt.

q.q: Name the brokers who convert black-market currency during informal trade in East Africa according to Case Study III.
q.explanation: Delalas are brokers who negotiate prices and convert agreed prices into Birr at prevailing black-market rates, often carrying small calculators.

q.q: Explain why time-sensitive agri-foods such as fruits and vegetables rely so heavily on informal trade across African borders.
q.answer: administrative delays are unworkable without cold storage|delays ruin perishable goods
q.explanation: Administrative barriers cause time delays that are unworkable for products that deteriorate without cold storage and transport, so traders turn to informal channels.

q.q: Which country saw its intra-African export share decline from 2.8 percent in 2005-2007 to 0.5 percent in 2016-2018?
q.explanation: Ethiopia's share of intra-African exports fell from 2.8 percent to 0.5 percent between the two periods, while Egypt, Uganda and Tanzania gained.

q.q: In Case Study III, the black-market rate of Birr 1 stood at 5-6 Kenyan Shillings against an official rate of 13. The economic implication is that:
options: Ethiopia's terms of trade are unfavorable and its informal export values fall below imports
Ethiopian exports become cheaper and more competitive formally
The Birr gains purchasing power against the Shilling
q.explanation: The falling purchasing power of the Birr makes Ethiopia's terms of trade unfavorable, so informal cross-border trade export values are substantially lower than import values, matching the national trade deficit.

q.q: Rank these top intra-African exporters of 2016-2018 in descending order of export share: Uganda (6.4), South Africa (32.2), Kenya (6.2), Egypt (8.7).
q.explanation: The order by export share is South Africa (32.2), Egypt (8.7), Uganda (6.4), Kenya (6.2).

q.q: A habitat is best described as:
options: The subset of physical environmental factors that permits a species to survive and reproduce
The total population of one species
q.explanation: Habitat is the subset of physical environmental factors permitting a particular species to survive and reproduce.

q.q: Humans alter landscapes spatially through five methods. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
q.explanation: The five methods are perforation, dissection, fragmentation, shrinkage and attrition; compaction is a soil effect, not a landscape alteration method.

q.q: Some species actually prefer disturbed settings to undisturbed habitat.
q.explanation: The textbook notes that while the area between remains of natural vegetation may extend, some species prefer disturbed settings.

q.q: The time it takes for a species to become extinct as a result of landscape change is called the __________.
q.explanation: This delay is termed extinction debt.

q.q: How many crop and livestock species together provide about 90 percent of all human food?
q.explanation: Only 15 crop species and 8 livestock species now provide 90 percent of all human food.

q.q: The green revolution began in the late 1960s.
q.explanation: Since the late 1960s, the green revolution has transferred high-yield varieties and pesticides to populous countries.

q.q: Pesticides poisoning water and soil for long periods and accumulating in the bodies of higher organisms as they move up the food chain is called:
q.explanation: Pesticides make their way up the food chain and end up in higher organisms - bio-magnification.

q.q: Mining an aquifer such as the Ogallala at a rate that exceeds its recharge rate is known as:
q.explanation: Over-drafting is extraction of a water resource beyond its recharge rate.

q.q: Name the emergent aquatic perennial native to South America that now infests Lake Tana.
q.explanation: The water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) deoxygenates rivers, killing fish and reducing income and food supply.

q.q: Which phase of invasion is defined by alien organisms competing through fast and efficient resource use?
q.explanation: Colonization is the third phase, in which the founding population multiplies and competes by growing quickly and efficiently.

q.q: Flooding can help spread invasive aquatic plants and can also be used to control them.
q.explanation: Flooding opens disturbed sites for invasion, yet in regulated water bodies weeds can be submerged to control them.

q.q: Which statement best describes the poverty-environment nexus?
options: Poverty and environmental harm are unrelated
A set of mutually reinforcing relationships between poverty and environmental harm
q.explanation: The nexus is the mutually reinforcing relationship, usually shown as a vicious cycle.

q.q: Poverty-environment linkages are dynamic and context-specific.
q.explanation: They reflect geographic location, scale, and economic, social and cultural characteristics of individuals, households and social groups.

q.q: A resource that can replenish itself, provided the stock stays above a certain threshold, is:
q.explanation: Renewable resources replenish themselves only while the stock or population is above a certain limit.

q.q: The analysis in which rising poverty leads to rising environmental damage, and both situations keep degrading, is called the downward __________.
q.explanation: The link is shown as a downward spiral.

q.q: Land degradation is caused only by impoverished households.
q.explanation: Land degradation is caused by both impoverished and non-poor households.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT a major component of land degradation listed in the lesson?
q.explanation: Soil degradation, biological degradation, vegetation alterations and water resources degradation are the components.

q.q: In the humid tropics of poor countries, soils are generally:
options: Poor, leached and quickly exhausted, with low yields
q.explanation: The textbook says these soils are poor, leached and quickly exhausted, resulting in low yields.

q.q: Name the four sets of options for managing land degradation.
q.answer: soil management, vegetation management, water management, integrated options|soil, vegetation, water, integrated
q.explanation: Soil management, vegetation management, water management and integrated options.

q.q: Deforestation is defined as the conversion of forest to __________ land.
q.explanation: Deforestation converts forest to non-forest land and can result in land degradation.

q.q: Which activity belongs to the third part of the forest strategy, protecting local and global environment values?
options: Strengthening rights of marginalized groups to forests
Building markets and finance for carbon sequestration
q.explanation: The third part establishes protected areas and develops markets and finance for international public goods such as biodiversity and carbon sequestration.

q.q: In one sentence, explain what poverty-environment mainstreaming tries to achieve.
q.answer: best balance between environmental preservation and poverty reduction|balance preservation with poverty reduction
q.explanation: It aims at the best balance between environmental preservation and poverty reduction for the benefit of the poor and long-term sustainability.

q.q: Environmental degradation is best defined as:
options: The deterioration of the environment through destruction of ecosystems, pollution and depletion of resources
q.explanation: It is the deterioration of the environment through destruction of ecosystems, habitat destruction, wildlife extinction, pollution and resource depletion.

q.q: Which type of degradation includes air degradation, particle pollution and depletion of the ozone layer?
q.explanation: These three belong to atmospheric degradation.

q.q: Noise and light pollution are also part of environmental degradation.
q.explanation: The textbook lists noise and light pollution among the kinds of environmental degradation.

q.q: According to the textbook, the basic cause of environmental degradation is:
q.explanation: Land disturbance is named as the basic cause.

q.q: Which human-made gases deplete the ozone layer?
q.explanation: CFCs and hydro-chloro-fluorocarbons in the atmosphere deplete the ozone layer.

q.q: Areas exposed to toxic air pollutants commonly suffer which respiratory problems?
q.explanation: Toxic air pollutants cause respiratory problems such as pneumonia and asthma.

q.q: In one sentence, explain how land clearance in the tropics leads to flooding and siltation.
q.answer: exposed soils erode rapidly and silt up rivers and dams|declining fertility plus flooding and siltation
q.explanation: Once forest biomass is cleared, exposed soils erode rapidly, fertility declines and flooding and siltation of rivers and dams often follow.

q.q: Environmental degradation has a direct link with long-term food shortage and famine.
q.explanation: The textbook states this direct link with long-term food shortage and famine.

q.q: Which triple correctly states the requirements of environmental sustainability?
options: More factories, more roads, more power plants
Maintaining ecological processes and life-support systems, preserving genetic diversity, sustainable utilization of species and ecosystems
Higher consumption, cheaper goods, faster transport
q.explanation: Environmental sustainability maintains life-support systems, preserves genetic diversity and ensures sustainable utilization of species and ecosystems.

q.q: Arrange the deforestation causal chain in the correct order.
options: Flooding and siltation of rivers and dams follow
q.explanation: Correct order: biomass cleared, exposed soils erode, fertility declines, then flooding and siltation follow.

q.q: Adapting for sustainability uses diverse crop varieties, diverse cropping systems and integrated management of two things. Name them.
q.explanation: Integrated management of crops and livestock is one of the adapting mechanisms for sustainable production.

q.q: In which period did the Developing Countries experience their highest population growth rates?
q.explanation: The highest growth rates in the DCs were experienced from 1960 to 1990.

q.q: Which region of the DCs will face the most rapid rate of population growth in the coming decades?
options: North Africa and the Middle East
q.explanation: Sub-Saharan Africa will face the most rapid rate of population growth in the coming decades.

q.q: According to the textbook, only 5 percent of the world population enjoys 23 percent of the world energy supply.
q.explanation: Resource distribution is polarized: 5 percent of people enjoy 23 percent of the energy supply, while 40 percent lack suitable hygiene services.

q.q: Malthus assumed that population grows in a geometric progression while food production increases in a(n):
q.explanation: Malthus held that population multiplies geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8...) while food increases arithmetically.

q.q: Give the title and year of the work in which Malthus developed his population theory.
q.answer: An Essay on the Principles of Population 1798|Essay on the Principles of Population|1798
q.explanation: Malthus developed the theory in 1798 in his treatise titled An Essay on the Principles of Population.

q.q: Why do many university graduates in African DCs remain unemployed even with degrees?
q.answer: lack of employable skills|skill discrepancies|skills do not match market demands
q.explanation: Graduates lack employment opportunities due to deficiencies in employable skills relative to the demands of the labour market.

q.q: Which economist argued that population growth induces technology and innovation in farming, stating that necessity is the mother of invention?
q.explanation: Boserup, in her 1965 Theory on Population and Agriculture, argued population growth triggers induced innovation.

q.q: By itself, reducing birth rates guarantees full economic development in a country.
q.explanation: The Latin America and Caribbean experience shows fertility decline alone never brings full development; institutions, policy, jobs and equity are also needed.

q.q: What does an Economic Dependency Ratio of 149 mean, as recorded for urban Ethiopia in 2018?
q.answer: 149 dependents supported by 100 employed persons|every 100 employed support 149 dependents
q.explanation: The EDR of 149 means 149 dependents could be supported by 100 employed persons, in food, clothing, health, education and other needs.

q.q: Arrange the chain of the demographic dividend in the correct order.
options: The working-age share rises relative to dependents
More investment flows into health and education
q.explanation: The order is: fertility falls, working-age share rises, more health-education investment, then per-capita income rises.

q.q: What is the minimum legal age of employment in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: The universally regulated age is 15 years, but the minimum age of employment in Ethiopia is 18 years.

q.q: Land degradation is best defined as:
options: a short-term decline of land quality in wet areas
a long-term alteration in the quality and quantity of land over a geographic area
the natural formation of deserts beside cold ocean currents
the loss of water only from freshwater ecosystems
q.explanation: Land degradation is the long-term alteration of land quality and quantity, lessening productivity and ecological integrity.

q.q: Soils becoming acidic or alkaline through changes in hydrogen and hydroxide ions is a sign of:
q.explanation: Chemical degradation changes constituent components; soils become acidic due to hydrogen ions or alkaline due to hydroxide ions.

q.q: The difference between land degradation and desertification is mainly geographic.
q.explanation: Desertification is land degradation in drylands, so the distinction is mainly geographic since land degradation can occur in wetter areas.

q.q: Which Aridity Index class corresponds to values between 0.20 and 0.50?
q.explanation: Semi-arid drylands are delimited by 0.20 < AI <= 0.50.

q.q: Which of the following is an anthropogenic cause of desertification, rather than a way natural deserts form?
q.explanation: Deserts form naturally beside cold currents and in continental interiors, but desertification arises from human forces such as dryland farming expansion.

q.q: Name two impacts of desertification on ecosystem services and species.
q.answer: reduced dryland ecosystem services and biodiversity loss|contraction of biodiversity, invasive species expansion, salinity, GHG emissions
q.explanation: Desertification minimizes dryland ecosystem services, contracts biodiversity, expands invasive species, raises salinity and GHG emissions.

q.q: Degradation reduces the rate at which ecosystems sequester carbon while releasing greenhouse gases.
q.explanation: Land degradation drives climate change by releasing GHGs and minimizing carbon sequestration rates.

q.q: Give two water-harvesting structures suggested to restrain desertification in drylands.
q.explanation: Water harvesting measures include planting pits, micro-basins and micro-ponds.

q.q: Arrange the effect chain from unsustainable dryland use into a deepening syndrome.
options: Capacity to invest in sustainable management falls
Unsustainable land use practices in drylands
q.explanation: The chain runs: unsustainable dryland practices, aggravated desertification, growing poverty, then reduced investment capacity, deepening the syndrome.

q.q: Name the Ethiopian region photographed in the textbook as showing desert-like landscapes together with the Somali Region.
q.explanation: Figure 7.5 shows desert landscapes in Ethiopia's Afar and Somali Region.

q.q: Explain why people with lower adaptation choices suffer most from land degradation.
q.answer: depend directly on raw resources and cannot adapt to climate stresses|few adaptation choices increase susceptibility
q.explanation: Livelihoods depending directly on raw resources with few adaptation choices are more susceptible to degradation-driven climate stresses.

q.q: Under-normal water flow in lakes, streams and underground sources defines:
q.explanation: Hydrological drought relates to under-normal water flows in lakes, streams and underground sources.

q.q: Agricultural drought is defined by:
options: a moisture deficit on the topsoil
q.explanation: Agricultural drought is the deficit of moisture on the topsoil, which affects crop growth.

q.q: The frequency and intensity of droughts have been increasing in West Africa and the Mediterranean region since the 1950s.
q.explanation: Global records show increasing drought trends in West Africa and the Mediterranean but decreasing trends in Central America, North America and northwest Australia.

q.q: Name three natural or human factors, besides drought, that cause famine.
q.answer: locust invasions|epidemics|wars and conflicts|floods|landslides|tsunamis|unfair share of resources|inequalities
q.explanation: Famines also result from landslides, floods, tsunamis, locust invasions, epidemics, unfair resource shares, inequalities, wars and conflicts.

q.q: Which of the following is an indirect effect of drought?
options: Damage to business, employment and income
q.explanation: Drought directly hits crops, water and biodiversity, and indirectly affects business, employment opportunities and income.

q.q: Explain how socioeconomic drought arises from the three basic drought types.
q.answer: the three types combine into environmental drought, causing imbalance between demand and supply of goods|demand exceeds supply of water food and fodder
q.explanation: Meteorological, hydrological and agricultural droughts combine to form environmental drought, which produces an imbalance between demand and supply - socioeconomic drought.

q.q: Which pair belongs to soil and water conservation practices for drought mitigation?
q.explanation: SWC practices include crop rotation, row cropping, terracing, minimum tillage, trenches, shallow wells, shelterbelts, mulching and salt-affected soil reclamation.

q.q: Herd management for drought mitigation includes the reduction of livestock heads and parasite control.
q.explanation: The textbook lists herd management as reducing livestock heads and controlling parasites.

q.q: Arrange the drought-to-crisis chain in the correct order.
options: Malnutrition, widespread famine and poverty rise
Crop failure and dry-up of wetlands
Food prices rise and food insecurity spreads
Prolonged rainfall shortfall with hydrological imbalance
q.explanation: The chain runs: rainfall shortfall and hydrological imbalance, crop failure and dry wetlands, rising prices and food insecurity, then famine and poverty.

q.q: Why is drought common in arid drylands?
q.answer: extreme climatic events, anticyclones, hot dry air advection and high moisture losses|rainless extremes in arid areas
q.explanation: Arid drylands experience extreme climatic events; anticyclones, hot dry air advection, reduced rainfall and high-temperature moisture losses drive droughts there.

q.q: Name one Ethiopian illustration of drought impacts given in the textbook figures.
q.answer: drought-affected livestock in Eastern Ethiopia|crop failure|water crisis
q.explanation: Figure 7.6 shows drought-affected livestock in Eastern Ethiopia, crop failure and water crisis in Ethiopia.

q.q: Deforestation refers to:
options: the gradual thinning of leaf colour in forests
removal of forest trees through commercial logging, clearing and burning for farmland, and cutting for construction and fuel-wood
q.explanation: Deforestation removes forest trees and their products via logging, farmland clearing and burning, and construction and fuel-wood cutting.

q.q: Climate change, as a change in rainfall levels and patterns, is listed among the underlying causes of deforestation.
q.explanation: The underlying causes include climate change and purely anthropogenic pressures such as population, culture and policy.

q.q: Which of the following is a proximate (direct) cause of deforestation?
q.explanation: Proximate causes include mining and quarrying, logging, fuel-wood, settlements, overgrazing and farmland clearing.

q.q: Explain how high population growth pushes farming onto virgin lands.
q.answer: growth creates new landless households that clear forest for farms|additional demand and landless households expand farming
q.explanation: High population growth creates additional resource demand and new landless households who clear and burn forest for farmland.

q.q: Name two forest ecosystem services mentioned in the lesson.
q.answer: stabilize local climates|control flooding|filter wastes|minimize soil erosion|carbon storage|habitat
q.explanation: Forests stabilize climate, control flooding, filter wastes, minimize erosion, store carbon and host terrestrial species.

q.q: Deforestation may lead to droughts and famines.
q.explanation: Among the consequences of forest removal are disruption of the hydrological cycle and the possible occurrence of droughts and famines.

q.q: Give two reasons why flawed government policy accelerates deforestation.
q.answer: tenure insecurity|weak law enforcement|wrong allocation of rights
q.explanation: Flawed policies cause tenure insecurities, weak law enforcement and wrong allocation of rights.

q.q: Substituting rubber panels for timber is suggested in order to:
options: help minimize the rapid loss of forests
q.explanation: Using rubber panels in place of timber is one of the listed measures against rapid forest loss.

q.q: Arrange the sequence from a proximate cause to a global consequence.
options: Carbon stock reduction and global warming
Commercial logging clears a forest stand
Soil erosion and sedimentation of rivers
Loss of biodiversity and habitat destruction
q.explanation: The chain runs: logging removes the stand, biodiversity and habitats are lost, erosion and sedimentation follow, and carbon reduction accelerates warming.

q.q: Distinguish forest degradation from deforestation in one accurate statement.
q.answer: degradation lowers size, species composition and quality while deforestation clears trees entirely|quality decline vs complete removal
q.explanation: Degradation contracts the size, species composition and quality of forests, while deforestation is total removal through logging, burning and cutting.

q.q: Which farming practice burns forest vegetation to open farmland, according to the textbook figure?
q.explanation: Figure 7.7 shows burning of forest vegetation using fire for agricultural land in shifting cultivation areas.

q.q: The digital divide refers to the gap among persons, households, companies and regions in:
options: access to information and use of the internet
q.explanation: The divide concerns access to relevant information and use of the internet for economic and political opportunities.

q.q: Which of the following is listed among the imperative indicators of the digital divide?
options: Access to televisions and mobile phones
q.explanation: Access gaps to computers, TVs, mobile phones and internet services are the key indicators.

q.q: Access and exposure to internet technology are lowest in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa compared to the MDCs.
q.explanation: The textbook states internet access is lowest among South Asian and SSA countries relative to MDCs.

q.q: Name two reasons the textbook gives for the growing digital gaps between countries.
q.answer: income and financial shortages|poor quality vs expensive connections|low education|limited access to ICT|lack of knowledge of technology|no opportunity to learn computers
q.explanation: Reasons include income shortages, poor expensive connections, low digital literacy, limited ICT access, lack of knowledge and no learning opportunities.

q.q: The divide between information haves and have-nots mainly relies on:
q.explanation: The haves and have-nots split mainly relies on income and education, with other factors playing supporting roles.

q.q: List three security hazards that the digital divide exacerbates.
q.answer: cyber terrorism|criminal networks|illegal money|hate speech|fake news
q.explanation: Digitalization hazards include cyber terrorism, criminal networks, illegal money, hate speech and fake news.

q.q: One consequence of the digital divide is that damage to old businesses takes away jobs because digital work requires more education.
q.explanation: The textbook lists damage to old business taking away jobs among the consequences.

q.q: Which advantage of digitalization most directly helps poor farmers and fishermen?
q.explanation: Digitalization provides real-time weather and market information for poor farmers and fishermen.

q.q: Explain who the 'unbanked' are and what digitalization offers them.
q.answer: people without financial services; digital financial services reach remote underserved populations|no bank access; financial services
q.explanation: The unbanked previously had no financial services; digitalization brings financial services to remote areas and underserved populations.

q.q: Arrange the government role in narrowing the divide correctly.
options: Enhance fair opportunities in the use of ICTs
Play the principal role in the breach
q.explanation: Governments should take the principal role, organize reachable e-services, implement cohesively and citizen-oriented, then enhance fair ICT opportunities.

q.q: Give one personal factor, besides income and education, that affects someone's place in the digital divide.
q.explanation: Family size, age, sex, cultural and linguistic experiences plus geographic location also play imperative roles.

q.q: A contour line is best defined as an imaginary line connecting places having the same:
q.explanation: A contour connects places of equal elevation on the ground surface above a datum or mean sea level.

q.q: On 1:50,000 toposheets, contours are generally drawn at a standard interval of:
q.explanation: Contours are drawn at about 20 m intervals on 1:50,000 sheets and 100 m intervals on 1:250,000 sheets.

q.q: Contours can merge or cross one another only at vertical cliffs, waterfalls and hanging cliffs.
q.explanation: These are the only exceptions to the rule that contours never cross or merge.

q.q: Hachures indicate the exact height of the land they represent.
q.explanation: Hachures do not indicate height and exact gradients; they give only qualitative information.

q.q: Closely spaced contour lines on a map indicate a:
q.explanation: Closely spaced contours illustrate a steep slope; widely spaced ones show a gentle slope.

q.q: What name is given to the heavier contour line drawn every fifth contour, starting from zero elevation?
q.explanation: The index contour starts from mean sea level and represents every fifth, heavier line.

q.q: Closed, more or less circular contours with tick marks pointing toward the low ground represent a:
q.explanation: Depressions have closing ticks pointing toward the low ground and values decreasing toward the center.

q.q: Explain how the V shapes of valley contours differ from those of spur contours.
q.answer: valley v points upstream toward high ground|valley bends upward, spur v points away from high ground
q.explanation: Valley contours have V shapes pointing upstream toward high ground; spur contours have U or V shapes pointing away from the high ground.

q.q: A series of increasingly small, closed contours at higher elevations with a maximum height below 1,000 m represents a:
q.explanation: Concentric closed contours below 1,000 m show a hill; the smallest circle marks the hilltop.

q.q: A tree-like drainage pattern with branches that forms in areas of homogeneous rock with horizontal strata is called:
q.explanation: Dendritic patterns are tree-like and form in areas of homogeneous rock.

q.q: Arrange the steps for tracing a watershed on a contour map in the correct order.
options: Trace the outline connecting the high points
Draw a circle at the outlet of the watershed
Put X marks at the high points and ridges
Highlight the tributaries and their flow directions
q.explanation: The order is: circle the outlet, highlight tributaries, mark high points with X, draw flow arrows, then trace the outline from the outlet connecting high points.

q.q: Two consecutive index contours read 300 m and 400 m with four intermediate contours between them. The contour interval is:
GIS is best defined as a computer-based system for:
options: capturing, storing, analyzing and displaying geographically referenced data
q.explanation: GIS captures, prepares, stores, checks, retrieves, manipulates, analyzes and displays geospatial data.

q.q: Data is the most important component of a GIS.
q.explanation: The textbook explicitly calls data the most important component of GIS.

q.q: Which of the following belongs to the input part of GIS hardware?
q.explanation: Input hardware includes computers, GPS, mobile phones, scanners and digitizers; printers and plotters are output.

q.q: Name the free, open-source GIS software that covers most of the functionality of ArcGIS.
q.explanation: QGIS is a very capable open-source GIS encompassing most ArcGIS functionality.

q.q: Which vector geometry is used to represent rivers, roads and railroads, and what can it measure?
q.explanation: One-dimensional lines or polylines represent linear features and can measure distance.

q.q: Raster data are used to represent continuous layers such as elevation and rainfall.
q.explanation: Rasters store continuous layers like elevation, slope, soil, vegetation, temperature and rainfall.

q.q: Give one example of non-spatial (attribute) data that could describe a lake.
q.explanation: Attributes independent of location include depth, water quality, pollution level, name, area and volume.

q.q: In a GIS, people are divided into GIS users and GIS specialists. Specialists are those who:
