options: collect, manage and analyze geographic data and provide technical support
q.explanation: GIS specialists make the GIS work by collecting, managing and analyzing data and supporting others.

q.q: What is the collection of point, polyline and polygon feature classes in a geodatabase that share a common coordinate system called?
q.explanation: A feature dataset shares a common coordinate system across its feature classes.

q.q: Explain how GIS supports decision making in urban planning.
q.answer: integrates diverse data into one map|visualizes scenarios like siting services
q.explanation: GIS merges project, socio-economic, census and base data, integrates information into an illustrative map, and visualizes scenarios such as siting a new service center.

q.q: A trellis drainage pattern and a new road layer, plus schools, could be analyzed together in a GIS mainly because the software provides tools for:
options: geographic query, analysis and visualization supported by a DBMS
q.explanation: Key software components are DBMS plus tools for input, manipulation, query, analysis and visualization.

q.q: ArcMap is best described as:
options: the primary application and interface of ArcGIS for making maps and performing analysis
q.explanation: ArcMap is the primary application of ArcGIS, used to add data, make maps, analyze and edit GIS data.

q.q: An ArcMap (.mxd) document stores the actual GIS data inside the file.
q.explanation: The MXD stores the map, symbology and pointers to the data; adding data only adds a reference to the original source.

q.q: How is ArcMap started with a desired pre-made map?
options: By double-clicking an ArcMap document (.mxd file) shortcut
q.explanation: Double-clicking an .mxd file on the desktop shortcut starts ArcMap with the desired map.

q.q: Which menu command closes an opened map in ArcMap?
q.explanation: Click the File menu and then Close; opening a new map also closes the current map.

q.q: Which tool allows a user to drop a point and generate the X, Y coordinate for a specific location?
q.explanation: The Add XY tool drops a point and generates the X, Y coordinate for a location.

q.q: Which ArcToolbox toolbox would you use to convert a shapefile to another data format?
q.explanation: The Conversion Toolbox contains tools that convert data between various formats.

q.q: A toolbox in ArcToolbox can contain another toolbox.
q.explanation: A toolbox cannot contain another toolbox; toolsets contain tools and other toolsets.

q.q: What is the information that explains your data, such as its field attributes, projection and how it was created, called?
q.explanation: Metadata explains a dataset's attributes, projection, creation and analysis to other users.

q.q: In which view do you arrange titles, north arrows and scale bars for a printable map, and why?
q.explanation: Layout view works with map layout elements arranged with the data frame on a page, in page space.

q.q: When data layers enter the Table of Contents, they are organized by geometry type. Which layer sits at the very bottom?
q.explanation: Points are on top of lines, lines on top of polygons, and polygons on top of raster datasets.

q.q: Arrange the steps for adding local data with the Add Data button in the correct order.
options: Click Add Data on the ArcMap toolbar
The layer is placed in the Table of Contents
Browse to and select the data you want
q.explanation: The order is: click Add Data, browse and select the data, click Add, then the layer appears in the TOC.

q.q: Name the three commands of the Add Data pull-down menu.
q.answer: add data, add basemap, add data from arcgis online
q.explanation: The menu has Add Data, Add Basemap and Add Data from ArcGIS Online.

q.q: The word history comes from the Greek word istoria, which means:
options: Inquiry or knowledge acquired by investigation
q.explanation: Istoria means inquiry or knowledge acquired by investigation.

q.q: Which date marks the beginning of the technique of writing, the line between prehistory and history?
q.explanation: The technique of writing began about 4000 B.C.

q.q: Herodotus is generally regarded as the father of history.
q.explanation: Herodotus wrote Histories and is called the father of history.

q.q: Leopold von Ranke is generally considered the father of:
q.explanation: Ranke of the German Historical School laid the foundations of modern academic history.

q.q: Which of the following is a primary source?
q.explanation: An inscription has a direct relation to the period under study.

q.q: Who wrote the account called Histories about the wars between the Greeks and the Persians?
q.explanation: Herodotus wrote Histories.

q.q: Give the term for the period before the technique of writing began about 4000 B.C.
q.explanation: This period is called prehistory.

q.q: One reason Ethiopian studies long focused on the north was that foreign writers had left information there. Which writers?
options: Ancient Greek, Roman and Arab writers
q.explanation: Ancient Greek, Roman and Arab writers left important information about the region.

q.q: No history can be entirely objective, and this is one reason histories are constantly rewritten.
q.explanation: The textbook states that no history can be entirely objective.

q.q: Arrange the main steps in writing history in the correct order.
q.explanation: The steps are: collection of evidence, source criticism, interpretation and objective writing.

q.q: Give the name of the institution established in 1963 that changed the focus of Ethiopian studies.
q.explanation: The Institute of Ethiopian Studies was established in 1963 at Haile Sellassie I University.

q.q: Which view holds that human beings came into existence through divine creation?
q.explanation: The creationist view is the religious belief in divine creation.

q.q: Charles Darwin's work Origin of Species by Natural Selection was published in:
q.explanation: It was published in 1859 and described evolution and natural selection.

q.q: Gorillas and chimpanzees belong to a separate zoological family called pongidae.
q.explanation: The two African apes are classified in the family pongidae.

q.q: Which two traits distinguished Australopithecines from apes?
q.explanation: Small canine teeth and walking on two legs separated them from apes.

q.q: Homo habilis is important because it was the first hominid to:
options: make stone tools, known as Oldowan technology
q.explanation: Homo habilis made the first stone tools, called Oldowan technology.

q.q: In which country were the fossils of Australopithecus afarensis found at Hadar in 1974?
q.explanation: Australopithecus afarensis was found at Hadar in the Afar region of Ethiopia.

q.q: Give the term for walking on two legs as the primary form of locomotion.
q.explanation: This is called bipedalism.

q.q: The Acheulean hand axe technology is identified with which hominid?
q.explanation: Acheulean tools are identified with Homo erectus.

q.q: The Neolithic Revolution means replacing hunting and gathering with food production through domestication.
q.explanation: That replacement is exactly what the Neolithic Revolution means.

q.q: Arrange these human species from earliest to latest.
q.explanation: The order is Homo habilis about 2 million years ago, Homo erectus, archaic Homo sapiens, then modern Homo sapiens.

q.q: Give the name of the cave site near Dire Dawa where a lower jaw of modern Homo sapiens was found.
q.explanation: A lower jaw of about 100,000 years was found at Porc Epic near Dire Dawa.

q.q: The earliest known states in the world emerged around how long ago?
q.explanation: The earliest known states emerged around 6,000 years ago.

q.q: The theory that kings ruled as representatives of the supreme god on earth is called:
q.explanation: Priests became kings whose authority rested on religion, giving the divine right theory.

q.q: Early states came into existence primarily as a result of the development of agriculture.
q.explanation: Agriculture provided the surplus that supported officials, soldiers and other classes.

q.q: According to the oriental despotism theory, a strong state arose in Egypt and Mesopotamia because:
q.explanation: A despotic state was needed to organize labour for irrigation and flood control.

q.q: Name the two rivers of Mesopotamia mentioned in the lesson.
q.explanation: Mesopotamia lay in the valleys of the Tigris and Euphrates.

q.q: Give the term for extra food produced beyond the farmers' own needs.
q.explanation: This regular extra food is called a surplus.

q.q: The word civilization comes from Latin words meaning:
q.explanation: Civilization comes from the Latin words for citizen and city.

q.q: In ancient empire states a person's social position was determined by birth and believed to be unchangeable.
q.explanation: Social position was believed to be god-given and thus immutable.

q.q: Which is given in the lesson as an example of a civilization with great monumental architecture?
q.explanation: Ancient Egypt and Aksum are named as civilizations with monumental architecture.

q.q: Arrange these stages in the rise of an early state in the correct order.
q.explanation: The order is: agriculture produces a surplus, officials and soldiers are supported, classes and specialization appear, then cities and monumental architecture.

q.q: Which factor explains states founded by a successful permanent leader in times of war?
q.explanation: War leadership explains how a permanent war leader became a king.

q.q: The Greek historian who called Egypt 'the gift of the Nile' was:
q.explanation: Herodotus (about 484-425 B.C.) described Egypt as the gift of the Nile.

q.q: Who united Upper and Lower Egypt about 3,100 B.C.?
q.explanation: Menes, king of Upper Egypt, united the two regions and founded Memphis.

q.q: The largest Egyptian pyramid was built for the pharaoh Khufu and stood at Giza.
q.explanation: The Great Pyramid was erected at Giza for the pharaoh Khufu.

q.q: Which Kushite king attacked Memphis in 751 B.C. and founded Egypt's 25th dynasty?
q.explanation: Piankhi attacked Memphis in 751 B.C., united Egypt and Kush and founded the 25th dynasty.

q.q: What title, meaning 'great house', was used for the king of Egypt from the New Kingdom?
q.explanation: From the New Kingdom the king of Egypt was called Pharaoh, meaning great house.

q.q: Explain why Meroe became a centre of iron production.
q.answer: close to iron ore deposits|iron ore
q.explanation: Meroe was located close to iron ore deposits, which made it ideal for producing iron.

q.q: The kingdom of Kush came to an end mainly because of:
options: the rise and invasion of Aksum
q.explanation: The rise of Aksum weakened Meroe and Ezana's invasion destroyed it.

q.q: Arrange these events in the order in which they happened.
options: Meroe replaces Napata as the Kushite capital
Menes unites Upper and Lower Egypt
q.explanation: Menes (c. 3,100 B.C.), then Piankhi (751 B.C.), then Meroe as capital (c. 590 B.C.), then Ezana (mid 4th century A.D.).

q.q: Which of these was an achievement of ancient Egypt?
q.explanation: Ancient Egyptians contributed hieroglyphic writing, architecture, medicine, mathematics, the calendar and irrigation.

q.q: Name two contributions of Kush-Meroe to civilization.
q.answer: iron smelting|own writing system|own art and architecture|trade|pyramids
q.explanation: Meroe developed new styles of art and architecture, its own language and writing, iron smelting and a prosperous trade.

q.q: Ancient Egyptian women could not inherit property or appear in court.
q.explanation: Under Egyptian law women could inherit property, enter business deals, go to court and obtain a divorce.

q.q: Mesopotamia is a Greek word meaning:
q.explanation: Mesopotamia means between rivers, pointing to the Tigris and the Euphrates.

q.q: The wedge-shaped writing system of the Sumerians was called:
q.explanation: Cuneiform was written by pressing wedge-shaped marks into soft clay tablets.

q.q: The Sumerian king was believed to be a god, just as the Egyptian pharaoh was.
q.explanation: The Sumerian king ruled as the representative of the city's god but was not a god himself.

q.q: Hammurabi ruled Babylon from 1792 to 1750 B.C. and is best known for:
q.explanation: Hammurabi was famous for developing a fair code of law.

q.q: Which Persian prophet introduced the religion that preached two opposing principles, good and evil?
q.explanation: Zoroaster, or Zarathustra, introduced Zoroastrianism in the 6th century B.C.

q.q: Explain what the 'middle way' means in Buddhism.
q.explanation: The middle way avoids the extremes of asceticism on one side and materialism on the other.

q.q: The numerals we call Arabic were first used in:
q.explanation: They were first used in India and later taken over and developed by the Arabs.

q.q: China's first dynasty was the:
q.explanation: The first dynasty in China was the Shang (c. 1700-1122 B.C.).

q.q: Give one reason scholars suggest for the destruction of the Indus Valley civilization.
q.answer: deforestation|epidemic disease|change in the course of the Indus River|climatic change
q.explanation: Suggested causes include environmental degradation, malaria, changes in the river's course and climatic change.

q.q: Which philosophy did Qin Shi Huang follow when he established China's first empire?
q.explanation: Qin Shi Huang believed in Legalism, which emphasised authority, efficient administration and strict laws.

q.q: Arrange these powers in the order in which they rose in the Near East.
q.explanation: Sumer, then Assyria (from the 9th century B.C.), then the New Babylonian Empire (626 B.C.), then Persia.

q.q: The Greek term for a city-state was:
q.explanation: The Greek term for city-states is polis.

q.q: Athenian direct democracy allowed adult citizens to take part in the Assembly but excluded:
q.explanation: Only adult male citizens were included; women and slaves were excluded.

q.q: Athens was defeated by Sparta in the Peloponnesian War (431-404 B.C.).
q.explanation: In the Peloponnesian War Athens was defeated by Sparta.

q.q: Which ancient Greek writer is called the Father of History?
q.explanation: Herodotus (484-425 B.C.) is called the Father of History.

q.q: Explain the difference between direct and representative democracy.
q.answer: direct: citizens decide themselves|representative: elected representatives decide
q.explanation: In a direct democracy citizens take part in decision making themselves, while in a representative democracy they elect others to decide for them.

q.q: The doctor Hippocrates (460-357 B.C.) is remembered because:
options: modern medicine sees him as its founder
q.explanation: Modern medicine sees its founder in Hippocrates, whose oath is still taken by doctors.

q.q: Rome became a republic in:
q.explanation: The Roman Republic was established in 509 B.C. after the Etruscans were driven out.

q.q: The Punic Wars were fought between Rome and:
q.explanation: Rome and Carthage fought three struggles called the Punic Wars for mastery of the Mediterranean.

q.q: What was the Pax Romana?
q.answer: Roman peace|about 200 years of stability begun under Augustus
q.explanation: The Pax Romana was a roughly 200-year period of stability that began with the reign of Augustus.

q.q: Arrange these Roman events in the order in which they happened.
options: Octavian becomes the first emperor as Augustus
q.explanation: Republic 509 B.C., Caesar assassinated 44 B.C., Antony and Cleopatra defeated 31 B.C., Augustus emperor 27 B.C.

q.q: Roman law became the base of many legal systems in Western Europe and Latin America.
q.explanation: Roman law became the base of many legal systems in Western Europe and Latin America.

q.q: Mesoamerica is made up of:
q.explanation: Mesoamerica is made up of Mexico and Central America.

q.q: The Maya Golden Age, also called the Classic Period, began about:
q.explanation: The Maya Golden Age, or Classic Period, began about 250 A.D.

q.q: The Maya built a single empire ruled from the city of Tikal.
q.explanation: The Maya cities never formed an empire; Tikal and Calakmul were the most powerful of many city-states.

q.q: Which two Maya city-states were the most powerful?
q.explanation: The most powerful Maya city-states were Tikal and Calakmul.

q.q: Explain what floating gardens were.
q.answer: reed baskets filled with earth anchored in the shallow lake|gardens in the lake
q.explanation: Farmers anchored reed baskets filled with earth in the shallow lake and planted crops in them.

q.q: The Aztec capital, founded in 1325 A.D., was called:
q.explanation: In 1325 A.D. the Aztecs established a capital named Tenochtitlan.

q.q: The Inca empire stretched from present-day Ecuador through:
q.explanation: The Inca empire stretched from today's Ecuador through Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina.

q.q: Name the chief Inca god, whose son the emperor was believed to be.
q.explanation: The emperor was believed to be the son of the sun god Inti, the chief god of the land.

q.q: Which medical achievement is credited to the Inca?
q.explanation: Inca priests had enough medical knowledge to perform successful brain surgery.

q.q: Give one suggestion scholars make for the decline of Maya civilization about 900 A.D.
q.explanation: Suggested causes include overpopulation, disease, drought, or peasant revolts against the priests and nobles.

q.q: The Maya developed a hieroglyphic writing system and an accurate 365-day solar calendar.
q.explanation: The Maya developed hieroglyphic writing and an accurate 365-day solar calendar.

q.q: In 63 B.C. the Romans conquered Judea, where most Jews lived and practised:
q.explanation: The Jews had long believed in the monotheistic religion of Judaism.

q.q: The first four books of the New Testament, which tell of the life of Jesus, are called:
q.explanation: Almost all information about the life of Jesus comes from the Gospel, the first four books of the New Testament.

q.q: Jesus was condemned to death by crucifixion at about 30 A.D.
q.explanation: At about 30 A.D. he was arrested, tried and condemned to death by crucifixion.

q.q: Name the five patriarchates of the early Christian Church.
q.answer: Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, Constantinople and Jerusalem
q.explanation: The five patriarchates were Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, Constantinople and Jerusalem.

q.q: The Council of Nicaea in 325 A.D. established the doctrine of:
q.explanation: The Council of Nicaea established the doctrine of the Holy Trinity.

q.q: What is a heresy?
q.answer: a doctrine rejected and condemned by the Church
q.explanation: Doctrines rejected and condemned by the Church were called heresies.

q.q: The Edict of Milan, issued in 313 A.D., guaranteed:
options: freedom of worship to all Roman Empire inhabitants
that Christianity was the only religion
q.explanation: The Edict of Milan guaranteed freedom of worship to all Roman Empire inhabitants.

q.q: Who declared Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire?
q.explanation: The Emperor Theodosius I (r. 379-395) declared Christianity the official religion and repressed other faiths.

q.q: Arrange these events in the order in which they happened.
options: The Edict of Milan is issued
Christianity splits into Catholic West and Orthodox East
The Romans destroy the Jewish temple
q.explanation: The temple was destroyed in 70 A.D., the Edict of Milan was issued in 313 A.D., Nicaea met in 325 A.D., and the split came in 1054 A.D.

q.q: Why did Roman rulers persecute the early Christians?
q.answer: they refused to sacrifice to the emperor|seen as political disloyalty
q.explanation: Christians would not sacrifice in honour of the emperor, which the Romans considered political disloyalty.

q.q: Christianity had a Western and an Eastern Church from 395 A.D., but the final split came in 1054 A.D.
q.explanation: The two churches existed from 395 A.D. and split into Catholic West and Orthodox East in 1054 A.D.

q.q: About how many languages are spoken in Ethiopia and the Horn?
q.explanation: Linguistic evidence shows about 85 languages spoken in the region.

q.q: Which super-families are spoken in Ethiopia and the Horn?
q.explanation: Of Africa's four super-families, only Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan are found in Ethiopia and the Horn.

q.q: Which Cushitic branch is the largest and most diversified?
q.explanation: East Cushitic is the most diversified and largest branch in the region.

q.q: The Omotic language family is spoken only in Ethiopia.
q.explanation: The textbook states that the Omotic family is spoken only in Ethiopia.

q.q: Name the one God worshipped in the Oromo religion, Waqefanna.
q.explanation: Waqefanna focuses on one God known as Waqa.

q.q: Give the term for the shared ancestral language from which related languages descend.
q.explanation: Linguists call this shared origin the proto-language or ancestral language.

q.q: Who converted King Ezana to Christianity according to Rufinus?
q.explanation: Rufinus records that Frumentius converted King Ezana to Christianity.

q.q: Islam was first introduced into Ethiopia by military conquest.
q.explanation: Islam entered peacefully; the Prophet ordered that Ethiopians were not to be converted by force.

q.q: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
options: Persecuted Muslims seek asylum at Aksum
q.explanation: The order is: Judaism (8th century B.C.), Christianity (4th century A.D.), the Nine Saints, then the Muslim asylum (615 A.D.).

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the Cushitic and Semitic peoples expanded over a wide area.
q.answer: they settled between the Red Sea and the Blue Nile then expanded outward|long historical processes shaped their settlement
q.explanation: They settled between the Red Sea and the Blue Nile and expanded into many directions over time.

q.q: Which language survives mainly as the literary language of the Orthodox Tewahido Church?
q.explanation: Ge'ez ceased to be spoken but survives as the church's literary language.

q.q: Which was the earliest historically known state in the Horn of Africa?
q.explanation: Punt was the earliest historically known state in the Horn of Africa.

q.q: The expedition to Punt by Queen Hatshepsut is documented at her tomb in:
q.explanation: Her expedition is documented at her tomb in Dier El Bahri.

q.q: The exact territorial limits of Punt are known to historians.
q.explanation: The textbook states that no one knows the territorial limits of the land of Punt.

q.q: Name the capital of the kingdom of Da'amat.
q.explanation: Yeha, 30 kilometres northeast of Aksum, was the capital of Da'amat.

q.q: Da'amat is dated to which period?
q.explanation: Da'amat is dated 980 B.C.-400 B.C.

q.q: Give the term for the gold and silver alloy that Sahure's expedition collected.
q.explanation: Electrum is an alloy of gold and silver.

q.q: Which goods were imported from Egypt to Punt?
q.explanation: Axes, daggers, swords, sickles, clothes, bracelets, necklaces and beads were imported to Punt.

q.q: Name one crop grown by the kingdom of Da'amat.
q.explanation: The kingdom of Da'amat grew millet.

q.q: State in one sentence why Yeha was well placed for trade.
q.answer: it had good access to the Red Sea and to Yemen|access to both the Red Sea and Yemen
q.explanation: Yeha had good access to both the Red Sea and to Yemen in the east.

q.q: Da'amat made iron tools and weapons.
q.explanation: The textbook says Da'amat made iron tools and weapons.

q.q: Arrange these pre-Aksumite events in time order.
options: Da'amat reaches its period of prosperity
q.explanation: Sahure (2743-2731 B.C.) came before Hatshepsut (1490-1468 B.C.), then Da'amat's prosperity (750-500 B.C.), then Aksum.

q.q: The nucleus of the Aksumite state was formed around:
q.explanation: The nucleus of the Aksumite state formed around 200-100 B.C.

q.q: Which port was the major port of Aksum?
q.explanation: Adulis on the western Red Sea coast was the major port of Aksum.

q.q: Aksum was one of the four great powers of the world at its height.
q.explanation: Aksum was one of four great powers alongside Rome, Persia and China.

q.q: How tall is the longest standing Aksumite stele?
q.explanation: The longest stele measures 33 metres.

q.q: Which king defeated Dhu-Nuwas with Byzantine help?
q.explanation: King Kaleb (r. 500-535 A.D.) defeated Dhu-Nuwas and appointed Abreha as governor.

q.q: Give the term for exchange carried out without the two sides meeting or speaking.
q.explanation: This is called silent trade, as practised with Sasu.

q.q: Around what year did the Arabs destroy the port of Adulis?
q.explanation: The port of Adulis was destroyed by the Arabs around 702.

q.q: Queen Yodit led a rebellion that contributed to the collapse of Aksum.
q.explanation: The rebellions of the Beja, the Agaw and Queen Bani al Hamwiyah (Yodit) helped seal Aksum's collapse.

q.q: Which saint developed the Ethiopian Orthodox Church's liturgical songs and hymns?
q.explanation: The creation of the church liturgy and hymns is attributed to Saint Yared.

q.q: Explain in one sentence how the loss of Adulis led to the decline of Aksum's political power.
q.answer: loss of trade weakened the economy which weakened the army and state|economic decline led to political and military decline
q.explanation: The loss of trade caused economic decline, which naturally led to the decline of political and military power.

q.q: Arrange these Aksumite events in time order.
q.explanation: The Ge'ez alphabet developed by the 1st century A.D., Ezana converted in the 4th century, Kaleb ruled 500-535, and Adulis fell around 702.

q.q: Who was the first ruler of the Sultanate of Shewa?
q.explanation: Khalid ibn al-Walid came to power around 896 A.D.

q.q: The ruling dynasty of the Sultanate of Shewa was called:
q.explanation: The dynasty was called Makhzumite, after the Makhzumi clan of South Arabia.

q.q: Name the capital of the Sultanate of Shewa.
q.explanation: The capital was Walele in northern Hararge.

q.q: In which year was the Makhzumite dynasty overthrown?
q.explanation: In 1285 A.D. the Walasma dynasty of Ifat overthrew the Makhzumite dynasty.

q.q: The Sultanate of Shewa was often at war with the kingdom of Damot.
q.explanation: It was often at war with Damot, which weakened its power.

q.q: Define the term sultanate in a few words.
q.answer: a state ruled by a sultan
q.explanation: A sultanate is a state ruled by a sultan.

q.q: Which sultanate's rulers led constant campaigns against Shewa?
q.explanation: The neighbouring Sultanate of Ifat to the east led constant campaigns against Shewa.

q.q: Islam entered Ethiopia and the Horn mainly by military conquest.
q.explanation: Islam entered peacefully through trade and preaching, notably via Zeila and the Dahlak Islands.

q.q: Name the port on the Gulf of Aden that was significant for the spread of Islam into the interior.
q.explanation: The port of Zeila on the Gulf of Aden was significant for the spread of Islam into the interior.

q.q: By the beginning of the 8th century A.D., Islam was firmly established in the:
q.explanation: By the beginning of the 8th century A.D., Islam was firmly established in the Dahlak Islands.

q.q: Who founded the Zagwe dynasty?
q.explanation: Mera Tekle Haymanot founded the Zagwe dynasty around the mid-12th century.

q.q: The Zagwe dynasty is dated to which period?
q.explanation: The Zagwe dynasty is dated r. 1050-1270.

q.q: Name the best known rock-hewn church of Lalibela, built in the shape of a perfect cross.
q.explanation: Bete Giyorgis, in the shape of a perfect cross, is the best of the Lalibela churches.

q.q: The Lalibela churches were registered as a UNESCO world heritage site in 1978.
q.explanation: They were registered as a UNESCO world heritage site in 1978.

q.q: Why did Lalibela want to build a second Jerusalem?
options: Because pilgrimages to Jerusalem had become difficult
q.explanation: Muslim control of the Red Sea and North Africa made pilgrimage to Jerusalem difficult.

q.q: Give the name of the district that was the center of the Zagwe dynasty.
q.explanation: The center was in the district of Bugna at Adafa near Roha.

q.q: Which last Zagwe king was killed in Gaynt?
q.explanation: Yetbarek (r. 1260-68) was killed in Gaynt.

q.q: The Zagwe dynasty ended in 1270 with the restoration of the Solomonic dynasty.
q.explanation: Yekuno-Amlak assumed power in 1270, restoring the Solomonic dynasty.

q.q: Explain in one sentence how the Kibre Negest was used politically against the Zagwe.
q.answer: its legend of Solomon and Sheba was used to claim the Zagwe were illegitimate|to justify Solomonic descent and challenge Zagwe rule
q.explanation: The legend supported claims of Solomonic descent and made the Zagwe appear illegitimate.

q.q: Which churchman supported Yekuno-Amlak against the Zagwe?
q.explanation: Abune Teklehaymanot of Debre Asbo, later Debre Libanos, supported Yekuno-Amlak.

q.q: Arrange these events in time order.
options: Mera Tekle Haymanot founds the Zagwe dynasty
Bete Giyorgis is built at Lalibela
q.explanation: Zagwe is founded first, then the churches are built, then Yetbarek is killed, then Yekuno-Amlak takes power in 1270.

q.q: The Kingdom of Damot was located to the ... of the Abay River.
q.explanation: Damot was located south of the Abay (Blue Nile) River.

q.q: Damot forced the Sultanate of Shewa to pay tribute.
q.explanation: Damot was a powerful state that forced the Sultanate of Shewa to pay tribute.

q.q: Who subdued Damot in the 14th century?
q.explanation: King Amda Tsiyon subdued Damot in the 14th century.

q.q: Which two states allied against Damot?
options: Shewa and the state under Yekuno Amlak
q.explanation: The Muslim state of Shewa and the new Christian state under Yekuno Amlak formed an alliance against Damot.

q.q: Name the river that gave the northern setting of the Kingdom of Damot.
q.explanation: Damot lay south of the Abay, the Blue Nile River.

q.q: Give the term for payment made by a weaker state to a stronger one.
q.explanation: Such payment is called tribute.

q.q: Damot conquered several Muslim and Christian territories.
q.explanation: The textbook states Damot conquered several Muslim and Christian territories.

q.q: Name the region north of the Abay where part of the people of Damot settled after Oromo attacks.
q.explanation: They settled in southern Gojjam.

q.q: What forced part of the people of Damot to migrate north?
q.explanation: Under the pressure of Oromo attacks, part of the people of Damot moved north of the Abay.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the alliance against Damot is historically interesting.
q.answer: states of different religions cooperated against a common threat|Muslim Shewa and Christian state allied despite religious difference
q.explanation: A Muslim state and a Christian state allied because of a shared political threat.

q.q: The Bete-Israel were an example of:
q.explanation: The Bete-Israel were one of the occupational castes in Ethiopia.

q.q: About which year did King Yishaq conquer the Bete-Israel in Wogera?
q.explanation: About 1413 the king conquered them in Wogera.

q.q: What did the name Felasi, proclaimed by King Yishaq, mean?
q.explanation: Felasi means exile, from which the name Felasha may be derived.

q.q: The relationship between the Christian kingdom and the Bete-Israel was always peaceful.
q.explanation: The relationship was not always peaceful; they revolted against increasing pressure.

q.q: Which king finally crushed the Bete-Israel and ended their independence?
q.explanation: They were gradually crushed by King Suseneyos and lost their independence.

q.q: Give the name of the most important Beta-Israel religious text.
q.explanation: The Te'ezaza Senbet is the most important Beta-Israel text.

q.q: Which of these was NOT an occupation of the Bete-Israel?
q.explanation: Their occupations were crafts such as blacksmithing, pottery, leather working and building.

q.q: The Bete-Israel influenced Ethiopian Orthodoxy in matters such as the Saturday Sabbath and dietary rules.
q.explanation: Their influences on Ethiopian Orthodoxy include the Saturday Sabbath, circumcision and dietary rules.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the Bete-Israel turned to handicrafts.
q.answer: they were deprived of inheritable land after refusing baptism|loss of land rights forced them to crafts
q.explanation: Deprived of land for refusing conversion, they developed handicrafts to survive.

q.q: Name one district where the Bete-Israel used to live.
q.explanation: They lived in Wogera, Quara, Tegede, Welqayt and Simen.

q.q: Arrange these events in time order.
options: They broaden their crafts to building
King Yishaq conquers them in Wogera
Blacksmiths travel with the royal court under Zera Ya'iqob
q.explanation: Yishaq (about 1413), then Zera Ya'iqob (1434-1468), then the broader crafts after 1540, then Suseneyos.

q.q: In which year did Rome fall into the hands of the Germanic tribes?
q.explanation: The textbook states that in 476 AD Rome fell into the hands of the Germanic tribes.

q.q: The Byzantine Empire reached its greatest size under:
q.explanation: The empire reached its greatest size under Justinian I (r. 527-565 AD).

q.q: The Eastern Roman Empire survived for about one thousand years after the Western Empire collapsed.
q.explanation: The East continued to survive for another one thousand years.

q.q: Who was Justinian's wife, advisor and co-ruler?
q.explanation: Empress Theodora (497-548) was Justinian's wife, advisor and co-ruler.

q.q: Charles Martel defeated Arabs from Spain in 732 AD at the:
q.explanation: Charles Martel defeated Arabs from Spain at the Battle of Tours in 732 AD.

q.q: Explain what the Justinian Code was and why it matters.
q.answer: a collection of ancient Roman laws|basis of many legal systems
q.explanation: The Byzantines organised the laws of ancient Rome into the Justinian Code, which has been the basis of the legal systems of many countries.

q.q: Which alphabet did Byzantine missionaries invent for the old Slavonic language?
q.explanation: They invented an alphabet later called Cyrillic, still used in Russia and much of the Balkans.

q.q: In 1054 AD the medieval Christian church split into:
q.explanation: The split was between the Western Catholic and the Eastern Orthodox churches.

q.q: Charlemagne was crowned emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III in 800 AD.
q.explanation: In 800 AD Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans.

q.q: Give two reasons why the Eastern Roman Empire outlasted the Western Roman Empire.
q.answer: richer|more population|more walled towns|less open to Germanic attack
q.explanation: The East was not geographically so open to German attacks, was richer and had more people and more towns with defensive walls.

q.q: Arrange these events in the correct chronological order.
options: Rome falls to the Germanic tribes
The Battle of Manzikert is fought
Constantinople is conquered by the Ottomans
q.explanation: The order is 476 AD (Rome falls), 800 AD (Charlemagne crowned), 1071 (Manzikert) and 1453 (Constantinople falls).

q.q: In feudalism, a lesser lord who pledged allegiance and military service in return for land was called a:
q.explanation: The lesser lords, or vassals, became loyal and gave service to the greater lord.

q.q: The part of the manor kept under the lord's direct control was the:
q.explanation: This land was called demesne and was cultivated by the unpaid compulsory labour of the serfs.

q.q: Serfs could leave the manor whenever they wished.
q.explanation: Serfs belonged to the lord and could not leave the manor without his permission.

q.q: What was the code of conduct adopted by knights in the Late Middle Ages called?
q.explanation: Chivalry required knights to be brave, loyal and true to their word.

q.q: Which two achievements does the textbook call the most important of the medieval period in culture?
q.explanation: The two most important achievements were the building of cathedrals and the growth of universities.

q.q: Explain how a guild protected its members and the public.
q.answer: set prices|regulated quality of goods|regulated working hours
q.explanation: Guilds made rules to protect their economic interests and the quality of their goods, regulated working hours and set prices.

q.q: The Crusades were launched mainly to recapture:
q.explanation: The Crusades were the expeditions organised by Western European Christians to recapture Palestine, the Holy Land.

q.q: In which year did Jerusalem fall to Salah al-Din?
q.explanation: In 1187 Jerusalem fell to the Muslims led by Salah al-Din.

q.q: Give two ways in which the Crusades changed Europe.
q.answer: trade increased|money economy|better maps and ships|weakened serfdom|more curiosity about the East
q.explanation: The Crusades expanded Mediterranean trade, facilitated a money economy, undermined serfdom and increased European curiosity about the East.

q.q: The Crusades succeeded in establishing lasting European control over Jerusalem.
q.explanation: The crusaders failed to accomplish their main goals and could not establish lasting control.

q.q: Arrange these medieval developments in the correct order.
q.explanation: The order is: the First Crusade recaptures Jerusalem (1099), the first universities develop (1100s), Gothic cathedrals are built (after the 12th century), and the Crusades end (1270).

q.q: In which year did the Hijira, the start of the Muslim calendar, take place?
q.explanation: In 622 AD Muhammed and his followers retreated to Medina, and the Muslim era dates from the Hijira.

q.q: The Abbasid dynasty ruled from which capital?
q.explanation: Abu al-Abbas established the Abbasid dynasty centred in Baghdad, which lasted until 1258.

q.q: Sunnis make up about 90 per cent of the world's total Muslim population.
q.explanation: The textbook states that Sunnis comprise 90 per cent of the world's total Muslim population.

q.q: What is the body of Islamic law that includes the Quran, the example of Muhammed's life and Muslim traditions called?
q.explanation: The Sharia applies all religious principles to all legal situations governing individual and community life.

q.q: The Ottoman sultan who took Constantinople in 1453 was:
q.explanation: In 1453 Sultan Mehmet II, the Conqueror, took control of the city and renamed it Istanbul.

q.q: What were the Janissaries and how were they recruited?
q.answer: ottoman infantry|recruited from christian children|tribute of Christian families in the Balkans
q.explanation: The Janissaries were the regular professional infantry, recruited from the tribute in Christian children paid by families in the Balkans and trained as Muslims at the palace school.

q.q: Which dynasty reunified China in 960 AD?
q.explanation: In 960 the Song dynasty reunified China.

q.q: Which of these was NOT an invention of the Song period?
q.explanation: Song inventions include gunpowder, the magnetic compass and movable type printing.

q.q: Explain the Mandate of Heaven.
q.answer: heaven gave the monarch the right to rule|a corrupt dynasty could lose it
q.explanation: The Mandate of Heaven was the idea that heaven gave the monarch the right to rule, which corruption could cause a dynasty to lose.

q.q: The Umayyads moved the Muslim capital from Medina to Damascus.
q.explanation: The Umayyads transferred the capital from Medina to the ancient city of Damascus in Syria.

q.q: Name two achievements of Islamic civilization in its golden age.
q.explanation: Islamic scholars advanced algebra, trigonometry, the decimal fraction, medicine, astronomy, history and geography.

q.q: The Hundred Years War (1337-1453) was fought between:
q.explanation: The Hundred Years War was fought between England and France and interrupted trade in both nations.

q.q: The Black Death killed about what share of Europe's population between 1347 and 1352?
q.explanation: The Black Death killed about a fourth of Europe's population between 1347 and 1352.

q.q: Investment means the addition or increase in capital.
q.explanation: Investment means addition or increase in capital, which gave impetus to the creation of banks.

q.q: Name the wealthiest citizens, usually merchants, who controlled a medieval town's administration.
q.explanation: Town administration was controlled by the richest citizens, the bourgeoisie, usually merchants.

q.q: Which cities probably had a population of about 100,000 in the Middle Ages?
q.explanation: Some great cities like Venice in Italy and Paris in France probably had a population of 100,000.

q.q: Explain the meaning of the German saying 'City air is free air'.
q.answer: there was no serfdom in towns|serfs who lived in a town became free
q.explanation: There was no serfdom in towns and cities, so town life meant freedom from the obligations of the manor.

q.q: Which trade was the most profitable of all in the late Middle Ages?
options: Trade in expensive or luxury goods
q.explanation: Trade in expensive or luxury goods was the most profitable of all.

q.q: What did bankers and their agents contribute to early capitalism?
q.answer: lent money at interest|financed trade|encouraged saving
q.explanation: Rich merchants lent money at interest and, through their agents all over Europe, helped to finance trade.

q.q: Legal equality of all citizens came to most of Europe during the 14th century.
q.explanation: Other characteristics of a capitalist society such as legal equality of all citizens did not come until after the French Revolution of 1789.

q.q: Arrange these economic events in the correct order.
options: Economic revival in the second half of the 15th century
q.explanation: The order is: towns grow (c.1000-1300), the Black Death (1347-1352), economic revival (after 1450), the French Revolution (1789).

q.q: In which year did Christopher Columbus make his first journey for Spain?
q.explanation: Columbus made his first journey in 1492 and reached the West Indies.

q.q: Who opened the Cape route round Africa and across the Indian Ocean to the East?
q.explanation: In 1497-98 Vasco da Gama sailed to India round the Cape and opened the Cape route.

q.q: Magellan personally completed the first voyage round the world.
q.explanation: Magellan was killed in the Philippines in April 1521; the Victoria and surviving crew completed the voyage in 1522.

q.q: Name the Portuguese prince who trained and equipped explorers and opened a school for them.
q.explanation: Prince Henry the Navigator (r. 1394-1460) devoted himself to training and equipping explorers.

q.q: Which crops were introduced to the Old World only after the European conquest of the Americas?
q.explanation: Maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava, tomatoes and others were introduced to the Old World after contact with the Americas.

q.q: Explain what the Columbian Exchange was.
q.answer: exchange of plants and animals between the Old and New Worlds|also exchanged diseases
q.explanation: It was the exchange of plants and animals, and also diseases, between the Old and the New Worlds.

q.q: Where did England establish its first permanent colony in North America in 1607?
q.explanation: England established the first permanent colony in North America at Jamestown in 1607.

q.q: Which legend about a rich Christian king increased European curiosity about distant lands?
q.explanation: The legend of Prester John of the Indies was disseminated across Europe since the crusades.

q.q: Give two technological aids that made long ocean voyages possible.
q.answer: compass|quadrant|astrolabe|better wind-driven sailing ships|knowledge of the winds
q.explanation: The compass, quadrant and astrolabe, better ships and knowledge of seasonal winds made oceanic voyages possible.

q.q: The Spanish and Portuguese led European exploration in the 15th and 16th centuries.
q.explanation: The Spanish and Portuguese led the voyages of exploration in the 15th and 16th centuries.

q.q: Arrange these voyages and settlements in the correct order.
options: Magellan's crew completes the voyage round the world
q.explanation: The order is: Columbus 1492, Vasco da Gama 1497-98, Magellan's voyage 1519-22, Jamestown 1607.

q.q: The word Renaissance means:
q.explanation: Renaissance means 'rebirth' of classical culture.

q.q: In which country did the Renaissance begin?
q.explanation: The Renaissance began in the city states of Italy in the 1400s.

q.q: Humanists placed great emphasis on the dignity, worth and uniqueness of each person.
q.explanation: Humanists placed great emphasis on the dignity, worth and uniqueness of each person.

q.q: Who developed a printing press with movable type in Germany around 1450?
q.explanation: Johann Gutenberg developed a printing press with movable type in Germany around 1450.

q.q: Who painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper?
q.explanation: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.

q.q: Explain why Italy was well placed for the birth of the Renaissance.
q.answer: strategic location on the Mediterranean|centres of trade and banking|centre of classical civilization|no single ruler
q.explanation: Italy's Mediterranean location, trading and banking cities, classical remains and politically divided city states all contributed.

q.q: Which Florentine artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
q.explanation: Michelangelo painted the giant mural of Bible scenes on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome.

q.q: The book The Prince, a guidebook on how to secure and maintain political power, was written by:
q.explanation: Niccolo Machiavelli wrote The Prince.

q.q: What does the phrase 'the end justifies the means' mean in Machiavelli's argument?
q.answer: a ruler may do whatever is necessary to hold power|success matters more than law or conscience
q.explanation: Machiavelli argued that successful rulers acted not by law or conscience but by whatever was necessary to hold power.

q.q: Renaissance architects kept the pointed arches and heavy ornamentation of the Middle Ages.
q.explanation: They abandoned the pointed arches and ornamentation of the Middle Ages and used columns and circular arches for a simpler classical style.

q.q: Name two ways in which the Renaissance changed learning or literature.
q.answer: humanists studied classical texts|writers wrote in the vernacular|new methods of criticising texts|writing on secular subjects
q.explanation: Humanists studied classical literature and philosophy, new methods of criticising texts emerged, and writers used the vernacular and secular subjects.

q.q: In which year did the Reformation begin?
q.explanation: The Reformation was a religious revolt that started in 1517 against the Roman Catholic Church.

q.q: Who was the leader of the Reformation movement?
q.explanation: The leader of the Reformation movement was a German, Martin Luther (1483-1546).

q.q: Luther denied the pope's supremacy and proclaimed that the Bible is the final authority.
q.explanation: Luther denied the pope's supremacy and proclaimed the Bible as the final authority.

q.q: What did Luther post on the church door at Wittenberg in 1517?
q.explanation: Luther posted the 95 Theses, a statement of his religious beliefs.

q.q: The doctrine of predestination was taught by:
q.explanation: John Calvin taught that only those elected beforehand by God would achieve salvation.

q.q: What was an indulgence?
q.answer: a church pardon sold for money without true repentance
q.explanation: Indulgences were church pardons accepted money for, without requiring true repentance.

q.q: In 1534, the Act of Supremacy made the monarch the head of the church in:
q.explanation: The Act of Supremacy instituted an independent Anglican Church of England with the monarch as its head.

q.q: Explain what the Counter Reformation was.
q.answer: catholic reform and resistance to protestantism|Council of Trent|Inquisition
q.explanation: The Catholic Church reacted to Protestantism with limited reforms, the Council of Trent and the Inquisition.

q.q: In which French city did John Calvin become a leading Protestant spokesperson?
q.explanation: Calvin became a leading Protestant spokesperson in Geneva, Switzerland.

q.q: Give two consequences of the Reformation for Europe.
q.answer: europe divided into catholic south and protestant north|secular rulers strengthened|wars of religion|art changed
q.explanation: Europe was divided into a Catholic south and Protestant north, religions wars followed, secular rulers grew stronger and art changed.

q.q: Arrange these Reformation events in the correct order.
options: Calvinism becomes the state religion of Scotland
q.explanation: The order is: 95 Theses (1517), excommunication (1521), Council of Trent (1545-1563), Scotland (1560).

q.q: The Scientific Revolution refers to a period stretching roughly from:
q.explanation: The term 'scientific revolution' refers to a period stretching roughly from 1500 to 1700.

q.q: Who challenged the geocentric theory in 1543 with a heliocentric theory?
q.explanation: In 1543 Nicholas Copernicus challenged the Ptolemaic geocentric theory with a sun-centred theory.

q.q: Galileo was found guilty by a court in Rome in 1633 and confined to his home.
q.explanation: In 1633 Galileo stood before the court in Rome, was found guilty and was confined to his home.

q.q: Whose law states that every object in the universe attracts every other object?
q.explanation: Isaac Newton's law of universal gravitation states that every object in the universe attracts every other object.

q.q: Which of the following was NOT one of the five core concepts of the philosophes?
q.explanation: The five concepts were reason, nature, happiness, progress and liberty.

q.q: What was the Enlightenment also known as?
q.explanation: The Enlightenment was also known as the Age of Reason.

q.q: Who invented the first microscope in 1590?
q.explanation: The first microscope was invented by a Dutch maker of eyeglasses, Zacharias Janssen, in 1590.

q.q: Explain the difference between the geocentric and heliocentric theories.
q.answer: geocentric means earth at the centre|heliocentric means sun at the centre
q.explanation: The geocentric theory put the Earth at the centre, while the heliocentric theory put the sun at the centre.

q.q: Which thinker taught the separation of powers?
q.explanation: Charles de Montesquieu taught the separation of powers, later used in several new constitutions.

q.q: Edward Jenner used cowpox to produce the world's first vaccination against smallpox.
q.explanation: Jenner used cowpox to produce the world's first vaccination, against smallpox.

q.q: Name two new scientific instruments of the period and what each measured or revealed.
q.explanation: The microscope revealed cells such as red blood cells, the barometer measured atmospheric pressure, and the thermometer measured temperature.

q.q: How many languages are spoken as a first language in Africa?
q.explanation: The number of first languages in Africa ranges between 1,000 and 2,000.

q.q: Which is the largest language family in Africa?
q.explanation: The Niger-Congo languages make up the largest language family in Africa.

q.q: About how many languages does Nigeria have?
q.explanation: Nigeria itself has around 500 languages.

q.q: The Khoisan languages are found mostly in southern Africa.
q.explanation: The Khoisan languages are located mostly in southern Africa, including Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Angola.

q.q: The Nilo-Saharan family is the largest language family in Africa.
q.explanation: The Niger-Congo family is the largest; Nilo-Saharan has around 80 languages.

q.q: Swahili is spoken as a second language by about how many people?
q.explanation: Swahili has about 16 million native speakers and 82 million second-language speakers.

q.q: Amharic, Afan Oromo and Somali belong to which African language family?
q.explanation: The Afro-Asiatic family includes Amharic, Afan Oromo and Somali in Ethiopia and the Horn.

q.q: Name the language family that includes Arabic, Amharic and Hausa.
q.explanation: Afro-Asiatic is the second biggest African language family and includes these languages.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why Africa is described as linguistically diverse.
q.answer: about one third of the world's languages are spoken in africa|between 1,000 and 2,000 languages are spoken
q.explanation: Africa has between 1,000 and 2,000 first languages, about one third of the world's total.

q.q: When the four language families are arranged from the largest to the smallest, which comes first?
q.explanation: The order from largest to smallest is Niger-Congo, Afro-Asiatic, Nilo-Saharan, Khoisan.

q.q: Name two centres of ancient or medieval African civilisation mentioned in the unit summary.
q.explanation: The unit summary names Mamluk Egypt, Kush-Meroe, Aksum, Ghana, Mali, Songhai, Kanem-Bornu, Benin and Great Zimbabwe.

q.q: The Mamluks ruled Egypt from about:
q.explanation: The Mamluks were a military aristocracy that ruled Egypt from about 1250 to 1517.

q.q: The Arabic word mamluk means:
q.explanation: Mamluk is an Arabic word meaning owned or slave.

q.q: The Mamluks were originally Turkish slaves brought to Egypt in the late 12th century.
q.explanation: They were Turkish slaves who were trained as soldiers and rose to high posts.

q.q: Before 1250 Egypt was ruled by the:
q.explanation: Egypt was under the Ayyubid Sultanate from 1170 until its collapse in 1250.

q.q: The major cause of the rise of the Mamluks was:
options: a power struggle within the Ayyubid family
q.explanation: Ayyubid princes fought for the sultanate, so the sultans depended on loyal mercenary soldiers, including the Mamluks.

q.q: Which crusade invaded Egypt under King Louis IX of France?
q.explanation: The army of the Sixth Crusade led by King Louis IX of France invaded Egypt.

q.q: The Mamluks defeated the Mongols and captured King Louis IX.
q.explanation: They defeated the crusaders, captured Louis IX, and defeated a second Mongol attempt in the 1250s.

q.q: In which year did the Mamluks control Nubia in the Sudan?
q.explanation: In 1275 they controlled Nubia and converted the people to Islam.

q.q: Which two trade activities made Mamluk Egypt wealthy?
options: The Trans-Saharan Trade and the Spice Trade
q.explanation: Gold passing through Cairo and the spice trade along the Red Sea enriched Mamluk Egypt.

q.q: In which year did the Ottoman Turks control Egypt?
q.explanation: In 1516 the Ottoman Turks controlled Egypt, ending about 260 years of actual Mamluk rule.

q.q: Explain why the rivalry between the Portuguese and the Ottoman Turks mattered for Egypt.
q.answer: control of the red sea and indian ocean trade|motivated the ottomans to control egypt
q.explanation: Rivalry over control of the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean was the main reason the Ottomans took Egypt.

q.q: The Maghreb is the name given by the Arabs to:
options: the western half of North Africa
q.explanation: The Maghreb is the western half of North Africa where Algeria, Tunisia, Morocco and Mauritania are located.

q.q: Which tribe began the Almoravid movement?
q.explanation: The Lamtuna, a nomadic Muslim and Berber tribe, began the Almoravid movement.

q.q: In which year was Marrakesh made the Almoravid capital?
q.explanation: In 1062 Marrakesh was made the capital of the Almoravids in southern Morocco.

q.q: The Almohads were settled Masmuda Berbers of the Atlas Mountains.
q.explanation: Unlike the nomadic Almoravids, the Almohads were settled Masmuda Berbers.

q.q: Who was the founder of the Almohad religious reform movement?
q.explanation: Ibn Tumart founded the Almohad religious reform movement.

q.q: The Almoravids and the Almohads were the same movement under two names.
q.explanation: They were two different movements; the Almohads replaced the Almoravids in the middle of the 12th century.

q.q: Who succeeded Ibn Tumart in 1130?
q.explanation: Abdul Mumin succeeded Ibn Tumart and led the Almohads to victory over the Almoravids.

q.q: Give the two main reasons why Almohad rule in North Africa came to an end in 1269.
q.explanation: Almohad rule in North Africa ended because of internal division and civil war.

q.q: The Almoravid movement called for:
options: a return to the primitive purity of Islam
q.explanation: The movement called for a return to the primitive purity of Islam.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the Almohads criticised the Almoravids.
q.answer: strict observance of islam|lamtuna lust for power|internal rivalries
q.explanation: The textbook gives strict observance of Islam, Lamtuna lust for power and internal rivalries as the reasons the Almohads replaced the Almoravids.

q.q: The oldest known kingdom in the western Sudan was:
q.explanation: The oldest known kingdom in the western Sudan was Ghana.

q.q: Bilad al-Sudan means:
q.explanation: Bilad al-Sudan is the Arab rendering of West Africa and means land of the blacks.

q.q: Which people founded the empire of Ghana?
q.explanation: Ghana was founded around the 4th century by the Soninke people.

q.q: Which city was the political centre of Ghana?
q.explanation: Kumbi Saleh was Ghana's political centre and Awadaghust its economic hub.

q.q: In 1076 the Almoravids controlled Kumbi Saleh, marking the end of the empire of Ghana.
q.explanation: Their control of Kumbi Saleh in 1076 marked the end of the empire of Ghana.

q.q: Who founded the empire of Mali and ruled from 1230 to 1255?
q.explanation: Sundiata crushed his enemies by 1235, founded Mali and ruled from 1230 to 1255.

q.q: Mansa Musa's famous pilgrimage to Mecca took place in:
q.explanation: In 1324 Mansa Musa made a pilgrimage to Mecca and displayed the wealth of Mali.

q.q: Who were the West African storytellers who preserved history by oral tradition?
q.explanation: Griots were storytellers who passed down history orally, often through song.

q.q: Which Songhai ruler built the largest state ever in West Africa between 1464 and 1492?
q.explanation: Between 1464 and 1492 Sunni Ali built the largest state that had ever existed in West Africa.

q.q: Kanem-Bornu was ruled by which dynasty?
q.explanation: Kanem-Bornu was ruled by the Mais sultans of the Saifuwa dynasty.

q.q: Explain why trade and agriculture formed the economic basis of the Hausa city-states.
q.answer: they were terminals of the trans-saharan caravan trade|collected and taxed trade items
q.explanation: The Hausa city-states emerged as southern terminals of the caravan trade and also farmed the surrounding areas.

q.q: The East African coastal region from Somalia to Mozambique was also known as:
q.explanation: The coastal region is known as the Zanj, also called the Swahili Coast.

q.q: Who wrote the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea?
q.explanation: It is a Greek merchant's guide from the first century A.D.

q.q: The original inhabitants of the Swahili Coast were Bantu-speaking Africans.
q.explanation: They migrated east from the interior and spread up and down the coast.

q.q: In which century did Muslim Arab traders come to settle permanently on the coast?
q.explanation: Starting with the eighth century A.D., Muslim traders, mostly Arabs, settled permanently.

q.q: Which city-state maintained an outpost at Sofala to trade with Great Zimbabwe?
q.explanation: Kilwa maintained an outpost at Sofala for trading with the gold-rich Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe.

q.q: The Swahili city-states formed one single empire before 1500.
q.explanation: They were independent sultanates and never consolidated into a single political entity.

q.q: Which Chinese admiral's fleets visited Mombasa, Malindi and Mogadishu?
q.explanation: The Chinese admiral Zheng He visited these ports on his later voyages.

q.q: The Swahili Coast reached its zenith during which period?
q.explanation: The coast reached its zenith during the Medieval Period, from around the 11th to the 15th centuries.

q.q: Which Portuguese explorer sailed from 1497 to 1498 past the Cape of Good Hope?
q.explanation: Vasco da Gama led the expedition in 1497 to 1498.

q.q: Explain what the term Swahili means and from which language it is derived.
q.answer: people of the coast|derived from arabic
q.explanation: The term Swahili is derived from Arabic and means people of the coast.

q.q: Which of the following was traded across the Indian Ocean by the Swahili city-states?
q.explanation: They traded across the Indian Ocean for items such as pottery, silks and glassware.

q.q: The name Zimbabwe comes from a Bantu word meaning:
q.explanation: Zimbabwe comes from a Bantu-based word that means stone house.

q.q: Which people apparently built Great Zimbabwe?
q.explanation: It was built by a succession of Bantu-speaking peoples, apparently the Shona.

q.q: Great Zimbabwe reached its height by about 1300 A.D.
q.explanation: The capital reached its height by the dawn of the 14th century, probably about 1300 A.D.

q.q: Which imported goods found at Great Zimbabwe show Indian Ocean trade?
options: Beads from India and porcelain from China
q.explanation: Beads from India and porcelain from China show it was part of an Indian Ocean trade network.

q.q: By about what year was Great Zimbabwe in decline?
q.explanation: By about 1500 A.D. Great Zimbabwe was in decline.

q.q: The San were pastoralists who herded cattle.
q.explanation: The San lived as hunter-gatherers; the Khoi Khoi were the pastoral people.

q.q: Which kingdom took over the place of Great Zimbabwe?
q.explanation: The place of Great Zimbabwe was taken over by the kingdom of Monopotapa.

q.q: The languages of the Khoi Khoi and the San belong to which super family?
q.explanation: Their languages are grouped under the Khoisan language super family.

q.q: Which coastal city did Great Zimbabwe trade with for gold exports?
q.explanation: Great Zimbabwe had commercial links with Sofala and Kilwa.

q.q: Give one assumed cause of the decline of Great Zimbabwe.
q.explanation: The assumed causes include overpopulation that over-exploited the environment, civil war and declining trade.

q.q: Explain how the economy of the Khoi Khoi changed over time.
q.answer: from hunting to cattle herding|they abandoned hunting and started cattle herding
q.explanation: The Khoi Khoi were originally hunters and gradually abandoned hunting to begin cattle herding.

q.q: The Trans-Saharan caravan trade began on a regular basis during which century?
q.explanation: It began to take place on a regular basis during the fourth century.

q.q: Which three commodities were essential throughout the 500 to 1590 period?
q.explanation: Salt, gold and slaves were the essential commodities throughout the 500 to 1590 period.

q.q: Which animal was the major pack animal on the North-South and West-East routes?
q.explanation: The camel formed the major pack animal that made transportation possible on those routes.

q.q: The Trans-Saharan Trade reached its peak during the 14th through 16th centuries.
q.explanation: The system reached its peak during the heydays of the Mali and Songhai Empires.

q.q: On the Southern route up to the Hausa city-states, which means of transport were used?
q.explanation: On the Southern route, donkeys, human porters or canoes were used.

q.q: Europeans had detailed knowledge of Africa before the 15th and 16th centuries.
q.explanation: Before the ages of discoveries and explorations, Europeans knew little about Africa.

q.q: Name one of the major gold fields of the Western Sudan.
q.explanation: Wangara, Bambuk, Bure and Lobi-pourra were the major gold fields of the Western Sudan.

q.q: By the eleventh century, a typical caravan included about how many camels?
q.explanation: By the eleventh century a typical caravan included one thousand camels.

q.q: Which North African market centre was the starting point of the caravan described in the textbook?
q.explanation: The caravan set out from Sijilmasa in North Africa.

q.q: Explain why it mattered which empire was in power for the Trans-Saharan trade routes.
q.answer: security for traders and trade routes depended on the empire in power
q.explanation: Routes rose and declined depending on the empire in power and the security it could maintain for traders.

q.q: Which of the following was a destination of merchants in the east on the northern routes?
q.explanation: Egypt in Africa and Mecca in the Near East were the last destinations of merchants in the east.

q.q: The Funj Sultanate was founded in 1504 with its centre at:
q.explanation: The Funj established the sultanate in 1504 with its centre at Sennar.

q.q: Which North African state was NOT ruled by the Ottoman Turks?
q.explanation: Morocco was the only North African state not ruled by the Ottoman Turks.

q.q: The Kingdom of Kongo was ruled by a king titled the Manikongo.
q.explanation: The Manikongo was the king of Kongo, ruling from Mbanza Kongo.

q.q: Name the capital city of the Kingdom of Kongo, using its modern name.
q.explanation: Mbanza Kongo is today called San Salvador.

q.q: Who founded the Mwene Mutapa state?
q.explanation: Mutota founded the state and was succeeded by his son Matope.

q.q: Give the title of the king of Buganda, which flourished northwest of Lake Victoria.
q.explanation: The king of Buganda was called the kabaka.

q.q: Ahmad al-Mansur sent an army across the Sahara in 1591 mainly to:
options: seize the gold mines of Songhay
q.explanation: The Moroccan army crossed the Sahara to seize control of the gold mines of Songhay.

q.q: The Rozwi expelled the Portuguese from the Zimbabwe plateau when Changamire defeated them in 1693.
q.explanation: In 1693 Changamire expelled the Portuguese and established the Rozwi empire.

q.q: The Empire of Oyo disintegrated in the 19th century mainly because of:
options: Fulani invasions and rebellions by subjected kingdoms
q.explanation: Oyo broke up under Fulani invasions and rebellions of its subjected kingdoms.

q.q: Explain how the Atlantic slave trade affected the rise of states such as Dahomey and Ashante.
q.answer: helped them grow|profited and became powerful|rise and consolidation
q.explanation: The trade helped these Guinea states profit and become powerful.

q.q: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
options: Shaka becomes king of the Zulu
q.explanation: The order is: Great Zimbabwe abandoned, Funj Sultanate founded, Shaka becomes king, and the Rozwi empire established.

q.q: European contact with most of Africa was begun by the:
q.explanation: European contact with the rest of Africa was begun by the Portuguese in the 15th century.

q.q: The main motive of the Portuguese for reaching West Africa by sea was to:
options: gain direct access to gold and bypass middlemen
q.explanation: They sought direct access to West African gold and to bypass Arab middlemen and the Turkish blockade.

q.q: The Portuguese occupied Ceuta in 1415.
q.explanation: The Portuguese occupied the coastal town of Ceuta in 1415.

q.q: Who was the Portuguese prince whose organisation sponsored the early voyages along Africa?
q.explanation: Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored the voyages.

q.q: Diogo Cao reached the mouth of which river in 1482?
q.explanation: Diogo Cao arrived at the mouth of the Congo River in 1482.

q.q: Give the royal title of the king of Ndongo, from which the name Angola was created.
q.explanation: The Portuguese renamed the region Angola after the royal title Ngola.

q.q: Queen Nzinga Mbande is best remembered for:
options: leading anti-colonial resistance for four decades
q.explanation: She led the early anti-colonial resistance of her people for four decades.

q.q: Portugal's attempt to control Morocco succeeded at the Battle of Alcacer Quibir in 1578.
q.explanation: The attempt ended in disaster, with the Portuguese king and many nobles killed.

q.q: Explain why the Portuguese attack of about 1665 was decisive for the Kingdom of Kongo.
q.answer: manikongo killed|independence ended|the king was captured and killed
q.explanation: The Portuguese captured and killed the Manikongo and ended Kongo's independence.

q.q: The Portuguese were finally expelled from the Zimbabwe plateau in 1693 by the:
q.explanation: In 1693 the Rozwi led by Changamire expelled the Portuguese from the plateau.

q.q: Slaves in African societies could often:
q.explanation: African slaves could marry, farm plots of land, inherit property and claim legal protection.

q.q: The Portuguese carried the first African captives directly across the Atlantic in:
q.explanation: In 1532 the first African captives were taken directly across the Atlantic.

q.q: The Trans-Saharan, Red Sea and Indian Ocean slave trades were older than the Trans-Atlantic slave trade.
q.explanation: Those three trades existed long before the Trans-Atlantic slave trade began.

q.q: Give the name of the Atlantic voyage on which as many as one sixth of the enslaved Africans died.
q.explanation: The voyage across the Atlantic was known as the Middle Passage.

q.q: The triangular trade linked:
q.explanation: The triangular trade linked the three continents of Europe, Africa and the Americas.

q.q: In the 18th century the single largest exporter of African slaves was:
q.explanation: In the course of the 18th century Britain became the single largest exporter.

q.q: The main reasons for abolishing the slave trade were purely religious.
q.explanation: The most important factors were economic, linked to the Industrial Revolution.

q.q: In which year did the British government outlaw the slave trade by its citizens?
q.explanation: Britain outlawed the slave trade in 1807.

q.q: Explain how the slave trade drained Africa's productive potential.
q.answer: removed manpower|drained labour|prevented africans producing what they needed
q.explanation: The drain of manpower and forced production for foreign traders prevented Africans from producing what they needed.

q.q: Which phase of the Trans-Atlantic slave trade is also known as the triangular trade?
q.explanation: The second, monopolistic phase is also known as the triangular trade.

q.q: The legitimate trade mainly replaced the export of:
q.explanation: West African commodities replaced the export of slaves.

q.q: Palm oil was used by Europeans mainly as:
q.explanation: Palm oil was the main source of lubricant for Europe's industrial machinery.

q.q: Groundnuts were exported from Guinea during the legitimate trade.
q.explanation: Groundnuts from Guinea were among the exports of the legitimate trade.

q.q: From which West African country did gum Arabic come?
q.explanation: Gum Arabic came from Senegal.

q.q: Gum Arabic was used in European textile industries to:
options: fix coloured dyes in printed cloth
q.explanation: Gum Arabic fixed coloured dyes in printed cloth.

q.q: Give the name European traders used for the lawful commerce that replaced the slave trade.
q.explanation: Europeans called the new lawful commerce the legitimate trade.

q.q: Only a small minority of wealthy rulers and merchants benefited from the legitimate trade.
q.explanation: The beneficiaries were a small minority of wealthy rulers and merchants.

q.q: Which imports from Europe did NOT strengthen indigenous African economies?
q.explanation: The principal imports of cloth, alcohol and firearms did nothing to strengthen African economies.

q.q: Explain how the legitimate trade contributed to the Scramble for Africa.
q.answer: european competition|control of internal trade|competition for markets
q.explanation: European competition to control West Africa's internal trade helped lead to the Scramble.

q.q: Who organised the production of legitimate trade goods?
q.explanation: Production was organised by West African rulers and merchants.

q.q: The Dutch East India Company established its settlement at the Cape of Good Hope in:
q.explanation: In 1652 the Dutch East India Company established a small permanent settlement at the Cape.

q.q: The Boers were originally:
q.explanation: Boers was the Dutch word for farmers, later called Afrikaners.

q.q: The first Khoi-Dutch war was fought in 1659.
q.explanation: The first Khoi-Dutch war was fought in 1659 over land and cattle.

q.q: What name is given to the Boers' northward migration of the 1830s and 1840s?
q.explanation: That migration is known as the Great Trek.

q.q: The main aim of the Dutch settlement of 1652 was to:
options: supply passing ships and trade meat with the Khoisan
q.explanation: The company regularised the meat trade and grew food for passing ships.

q.q: Give the term for the indigenous herding and hunting peoples whose grazing land the Boers occupied.
q.explanation: The indigenous peoples of the Cape were the Khoisan.

q.q: The Khoisan defeated the Dutch because their clans were united.
q.explanation: The Khoisan clans lacked unity and were eventually defeated.

q.q: The Khoisan were greatly reduced in number in the early 18th century mainly by:
q.explanation: Smallpox epidemics introduced by European sailors killed Khoisan in thousands.

q.q: Explain how indigenous peoples became a reservoir of cheap labour in South Africa.
q.answer: pushed onto poor land|dispossessed|less favourable land
q.explanation: Having been pushed onto poorer land, they served as cheap labour for the settler economy.

q.q: Britain took over the Cape Colony in:
q.explanation: The Cape colony was taken over by Britain in 1795.

q.q: The African Association was formed in 1788 to:
options: visit Timbuktu and investigate the Niger River
q.explanation: Its aim was to visit Timbuktu and investigate the course of the Niger River.

q.q: Which explorer completed Livingstone's work by sailing down the Zaire River in 1876?
q.explanation: Stanley sailed down the Zaire (Congo) in 1876.

q.q: David Livingstone was a former missionary who explored south-central Africa.
q.explanation: Livingstone was a former missionary who explored the Zambezi and the southern lakes.

q.q: Which drug, discovered in the early 1850s, protected Europeans from malaria?
q.explanation: Quinine protected Europeans from malaria fever.

q.q: Burton, Speke and Grant traced the source of the White Nile to:
q.explanation: They traced the source of the White Nile to Lake Victoria.

q.q: Give the abbreviation of the Anglican missionary society that helped fund a British force in Buganda.
q.explanation: The Anglican Church Missionary Society is the CMS.

q.q: By the 1880s Christian converts were a majority of non-Muslim Africans.
q.explanation: By the 1880s converts were less than one percent of non-Muslim Africans, excluding Ethiopia.

q.q: The main reason European exploration of Africa was slow before the second half of the 19th century was:
q.explanation: High mortality of Europeans from malaria fever slowed exploration.

q.q: Explain how the CMS helped prepare the way for the British Protectorate of Uganda in 1894.
q.answer: paid half the cost of a british military force|raised money|appealed to britain
q.explanation: The CMS raised money that paid for half the cost of a British military force in 1890-1891.

q.q: Europeans viewed Africa's rivers mainly as:
q.explanation: Rivers were seen as the primary trading arteries and highways into the interior.

q.q: Who founded the Solomonic dynasty around 1270?
q.explanation: Yikuno Amlak (r. 1270-85) founded the new dynasty around 1270.

q.q: The 14th century book that recorded the dynastic legend was called:
q.explanation: Kibre Negest, the Glory of Kings, enshrined the claim of descent from Solomon and Sheba.

q.q: The Solomonic dynasty claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.
q.explanation: This legendary claim, recorded in the Kibre Negest, justified the dynasty's rule.

q.q: The Christian highland kingdom had a permanent capital city between 1270 and 1636.
q.explanation: There was no permanent capital; kings ruled from moving or roving capitals until Gondar was established in 1636.

q.q: In what year was the town of Debre Birhan founded by Zer'a Ya'ekob?
q.explanation: Zer'a Ya'ekob founded Debre Birhan in 1454 and lived there for fourteen years.

q.q: Explain what the Gult system was.
q.answer: a right to levy tribute on Rist land and its produce|right to collect tribute
q.explanation: Gult was the right to levy tribute on the owners of Rist land and its produce.

q.q: Which king was the most expansionist of the medieval period?
q.explanation: Amde Tsiyon (r. 1314-44) was the most expansionist king of the medieval period.

q.q: Amba Gishen was used mainly to:
options: keep royal princes and control the succession
q.explanation: Male descendants of Yikuno Amlak were kept on Amba Gishen so that succession would be smooth.

q.q: Name the port that replaced the Red Sea coast as the main trade gateway between 1270 and 1529.
q.explanation: Zeyla became the main gateway, so the trade is sometimes called the Zeyla trade.

q.q: Explain why control of the Zeyla trade caused conflict between the Christian kingdom and the sultanates.
q.answer: both wanted to monopolise trade|economic rivalry over trade
q.explanation: The desire to monopolise long-distance trade in the region led to frequent clashes between the two sides.

q.q: Which port was the most important gateway for the spread of Islam into the interior of the Ethiopian region?
q.explanation: Zeyla on the Gulf of Aden was the most important gateway for Islam and trade.

q.q: Which was the earliest of the Muslim sultanates?
q.explanation: Shewa was the earliest of all the Muslim sultanates.

q.q: Arab and non-Arab Muslim merchants were agents of the peaceful expansion of Islam.
q.explanation: Merchants settled along the Zeyla routes and gradually converted local pastoral communities.

q.q: The economy of the Muslim sultanates depended mainly on mixed farming.
q.explanation: Their economies depended mainly on trade, although some communities practised mixed farming.

q.q: Which dynasty ruled the Sultanate of Ifat?
q.explanation: The ruling dynasty of Ifat, named after Umar Walasma, was called Walasma.

q.q: Give the title used by the rulers of Hadya and Bali.
q.explanation: The rulers of Hadya and Bali held the title Garad.

q.q: In what year was the sultan of Ifat, Sabr ad-Din, finally defeated?
q.explanation: Sabr ad-Din I was defeated in 1332 and Ifat became tributary.

q.q: Explain why the desire to monopolise the Zeyla trade led to conflict.
q.answer: both sides wanted control of trade|rivalry over trade and its routes
q.explanation: The ambition to monopolise the Zeyla trade and its commodities led to long rivalry and conflict.

q.q: The Sultanate of Adal was founded around 1380 by:
q.explanation: The Walasma militant wing retreated to the Harar lowlands and founded Adal around 1380.

q.q: Which sultanate was the most westerly among the Muslim sultanates?
q.explanation: Hadya occupied the most westerly territory, its frontiers touching the Gibe River.

q.q: The kingdom of Gojjam was inhabited mainly by the:
q.explanation: Gojjam was inhabited by the Agew ethnic group.

q.q: In about which year did Amde Tsiyon campaign against and reduce Gojjam?
q.explanation: Amde Tsiyon campaigned against Gojjam in about 1323/24.

q.q: The state of Bizamo was inhabited by Omotic language speakers such as the Shinasha.
q.explanation: Bizamo was inhabited by Omotic speakers, including the Shinasha.

q.q: The rulers of Wajj used the Muslim title Garad in the 15th century.
q.explanation: The rulers of Wajj used the Muslim title Qats.

q.q: Give the title used by the kings of Kafa and Shekka.
q.explanation: The kings of Kafa and Shekka used the royal title Tato.

q.q: Name the kingdom that was the main source of trade items for the region's long-distance trade up to the 16th century.
q.explanation: Ennarya was the main source of trade items, especially pure gold.

q.q: Pure gold from Ennarya was exported as far as:
q.explanation: Pure gold from Ennarya was exported to countries as far as Egypt, Greece and Rome.
