q.q: Which group finally defeated Ennarya and gave the kingdom a new name?
q.explanation: The Limmu Oromo, a sub-group of the Macha, defeated Ennarya and it became Limmu-Ennarya.

q.q: Explain why the Gonga states built trenches, stone fortifications and enclosures.
q.answer: to defend themselves from enemies|for defence
q.explanation: They built them in the 16th and 17th centuries to defend themselves from the enemy.

q.q: Which lake lay at the centre of the polity of Wajj?
q.explanation: The polity of Wajj was situated around Lake Ziway.

q.q: Who was the Imam of Adal known in the Christian highlands as Gragn?
q.explanation: Ahmad ibn-Ibrahim al-Ghazi was known as Gragn, the left-handed.

q.q: In which year did the battle of Shimbra Kure take place?
q.explanation: In March 1529 Ahmad crushed Libne Dingil's army at Shimbra Kure.

q.q: Emir Mahfuz was killed by the army of King Libne Dingil at Zeyla in 1517.
q.explanation: Mahfuz was killed at a battle in Zeyla in 1517.

q.q: The Portuguese soldiers arrived in Ethiopia in 1529 under Christovao da Gama.
q.explanation: The 400 Portuguese soldiers arrived in 1541 under Christovao da Gama.

q.q: In which year was Imam Ahmad killed at the battle of Woyna Dega?
q.explanation: Ahmad was shot at Woyna Dega in February 1543 and died soon after.

q.q: State the underlying cause of the conflict between the Christian kingdom and Adal.
q.answer: control of the Zeyla trade and its routes|rivalry over trade
q.explanation: The war was the last stage of the rivalry over the Zeyla trade and the lands along its routes.

q.q: Which was the only state in the south that successfully resisted Imam Ahmad's army?
q.explanation: Wolaita was the only state in the region that successfully resisted the Imam's army.

q.q: Explain why the Ottoman Turks sent troops to help Imam Ahmad.
q.answer: rivalry with Portugal|to protect their interest in the Red Sea
q.explanation: The Ottomans were locked in rivalry with Portugal for dominance of the Mediterranean and Red Sea.

q.q: Who defeated and killed King Gelawdewos in 1559?
q.explanation: The army of Adal under Emir Nur al-Wazir defeated and killed Gelawdewos in 1559.

q.q: Name the chronicle that describes Imam Ahmad's campaigns.
q.explanation: The Futuh al-Habesha is the chronicle of his campaigns and the source for his origins.

q.q: The 16th century large-scale Oromo population movement began from the:
q.explanation: Evidence shows the large-scale movement began from the Bale highlands.

q.q: Under the Gadaa system, a new grade succeeded the previous one every:
q.explanation: The Gadaa grades succeeded each other every eight years.

q.q: The Gadaa system was inscribed by UNESCO in 2016 as an intangible World Cultural Heritage of humanity.
q.explanation: UNESCO inscribed Gadaa in 2016 at its 11th intangible world heritage session.

q.q: The two Oromo confederacies on the eve of the movement were the Borana and the Walasma.
q.explanation: The two confederacies were the Borana and the Barantu; Walasma was the dynasty of Ifat and Adal.

q.q: Name the institution through which Oromo women participated in the Gadaa system.
q.explanation: Women took part through Siinqee, a parallel institution and peace-making body.

q.q: Give the term for adopting a whole Oromo or non-Oromo group in mass before the Abbaa Gadaa.
q.explanation: Moggassa was the adoption of a group in mass, giving the adopted rights as Ilma Gossa.

q.q: Which state successfully resisted the Oromo south of the Gojeb River?
q.explanation: South of the Gojeb River the kingdom of Kafa successfully repelled the Oromo.

q.q: Explain how the Oromo population movement weakened the Gadaa system.
q.answer: branches could no longer meet in one assembly|the territory was too large
q.explanation: Gadaa worked best in a limited territory, so the spread of the Oromo created separate assembly centres.

q.q: The Argoba language belongs to which language family?
q.explanation: Linguists classify the Argoba language in the Ethio-Semitic family.

q.q: By about what year did the Limmu branch of the Macha Oromo defeat Ennarya?
q.explanation: The Limmu branch of the Macha defeated Ennarya in about 1710.

q.q: Which Omotic kingdoms were ruled by kings who used the title Tato?
q.explanation: From the Omotic peoples, Kafa, Shekka and Yem had kings who used the title Tato.

q.q: The staple food of the Yem people was:
q.explanation: Enset was the staple food of the Yem people throughout the kingdom.

q.q: Name the council of seven that assisted the Tato of Kafa.
q.explanation: The Kafa king was assisted by a Council of Seven called Mikkerecho.

q.q: The Sidama Luwa institution closely resembled the Oromo Gadaa system.
q.explanation: The textbook states that the Luwa indigenous form of governance has much resemblance with the Oromo Gadaa system.

q.q: Give the title of the king in the Oromo monarchical states of the Gibe region.
q.explanation: The Gibe Oromo kings were called Mootii.

q.q: Which was the earliest of the five Gibe Oromo monarchies?
q.explanation: The earliest of the Gibe states was Limmu-Enarya, built around 1800.

q.q: The main factors that led the Gibe Oromo to change from Gadaa to monarchy were:
options: war with Egypt and the Ottoman Turks
the revival of long-distance trade and the spread of Islam
the building of the Jugol wall
q.explanation: Trade revival, Islam and the rise of Abbaa Duulaa collectively ended Gadaa rule.

q.q: Iron bars served as the main local currency of the kingdom of Gofa.
q.explanation: The textbook states that iron bars served as the main local currency of the kingdom of Gofa.

q.q: Who built the Jugol wall surrounding Harar?
q.answer: Emir Nur ibn al-Wazir|Nur ibn al-Wazir
q.explanation: Emir Nur ibn al-Wazir, the successor of Imam Ahmad, built the Jugol wall in 1552-53.

q.q: Which of these peoples or states is the earliest in the textbook account?
options: The Minjo dynasty of Kafa from about 1390
q.explanation: The Minjo dynasty began ruling Kafa from about 1390, earlier than the other options.

q.q: Explain why a state located on a long-distance trade route could become powerful.
q.answer: taxing trade brought wealth|control of trade routes|trade brought revenue for armies
q.explanation: Control of trade routes let rulers tax goods, grow rich and maintain armies, as among the Gibe states and Harar.

q.q: The political centre of the Christian highland kingdom was moved to the Lake Tana area during the reign of:
q.explanation: During the reign of King Minas (r. 1559-63) the centre shifted first to East Gojjam and then to Dembiya near Lake Tana.

q.q: The Jesuits were members of the Society of Jesus, founded in 1540 by:
q.explanation: The Society of Jesus was founded in Spain in 1540 by Saint Ignatius of Loyola.

q.q: King Gelawdewos accepted Catholicism and wrote a book in its defence.
q.explanation: Gelawdewos rejected conversion and wrote the Confessions of Gelawdewos to defend the Orthodox faith.

q.q: Which European power occupied the port of Massawa in 1557?
q.explanation: The Ottoman Turks occupied Massawa in 1557 and stayed on the coast for about 300 years.

q.q: Give the name of the policy by which Fasiledes kept Europeans out of the kingdom after 1632.
q.explanation: Fasiledes introduced the closed-door policy, which lasted until the early 19th century.

q.q: In what year did Susinyos make Catholicism the official state religion?
q.explanation: In 1622 Susinyos was officially converted and made Catholicism the state religion.

q.q: The first peasant rebellion against Susinyos and Catholicism broke out in:
q.explanation: The first peasant rebellion broke out in 1617, and from 1626 to 1632 many battles followed.

q.q: Explain why the promised Portuguese military assistance mattered to Susinyos.
q.answer: firearms to defeat enemies|strengthen his power|help against rebels
q.explanation: Susinyos leaned towards Catholicism to obtain Portuguese firearms with which to defeat his enemies and strengthen his rule.

q.q: Name one European who reached the court at Gondar during the closed-door period.
q.explanation: Poncet (1699) and James Bruce (1769-71) were the only two Europeans who reached the court during the isolation.

q.q: Ras Si'ile Kristos, the first important Catholic convert, was publicly hanged after the restoration of Orthodoxy.
q.explanation: The first victim of the reaction was Ras Si'ile Kristos, who was publicly hanged.

q.q: Which of these events happened first?
options: Susinyos makes Catholicism the state religion
q.explanation: The Ottomans occupied Massawa in 1557, before Gelawdewos rejected Rodriguez, before Mendez arrived in 1625, and before 1622.

q.q: Gondar was established as a permanent capital during the reign of:
q.explanation: During the reign of Fasiledes (r. 1632-1667) Gondar became the permanent capital around 1636.

q.q: The architectural style of Gondarine buildings contains elements from the Aksumite and Zagwe periods.
q.explanation: The textbook says the buildings' style contained many elements from the Aksumite and Zagwe periods.

q.q: Which king of the Gondarine period is nicknamed 'the Great'?
q.explanation: Iyasu I (r. 1682-1706) was nicknamed Iyasu the Great.

q.q: Which code was revised during the reign of Iyasu the Great?
q.explanation: The traditional civil code, the Fitha Negest, was revised during the reign of Iyasu I.

q.q: Give the name of the political elite organised by Etege Mintiwab from the chiefs of Qwara.
q.explanation: The political elite organised by Mintiwab were known as the Quaregnoch, after their place of origin.

q.q: Which office, equal to prime minister, did Welde Leul receive in 1732?
q.explanation: In 1732 Mintiwab appointed her brother Welde Leul as Rasbitweded, the equivalent of prime minister.

q.q: By the late 18th century the population of Gondar was about:
q.explanation: By the late 18th century Gondar had about 70,000 inhabitants of different religious and cultural groups.

q.q: Gondar was very close to the central provinces of the Christian kingdom, which strengthened royal control.
q.explanation: Gondar was far from the centre of the Christian kingdom, and the kingdom lost control over central and outlying territories.

q.q: Explain how the founding of Gondar contributed to the growth of regionalism.
q.answer: kings stayed in the city and neglected provinces|regional lords grew strong|kings stopped moving with their armies
q.explanation: Once kings remained in Gondar they neglected the provinces, and the regional lords built up their own power.

q.q: Which of the following crafts was mainly associated with the Bete-Israel at Gondar?
q.explanation: The Falashas, or Bete-Israel, were mainly engaged in masonry, pottery, basketry and metal works.

q.q: Which of these Gondarine events happened first?
options: Ras Michael Sehul arrives in Gondar
q.explanation: Gondar was founded around 1636, before the murder of Iyasu I in 1706, before Iyasu II in 1730, and before Ras Michael's arrival in 1768.

q.q: The Zemene Mesafint began with the death of which king?
q.explanation: The murder of Iyo'as in 1769 marked the beginning of the Zemene Mesafint.

q.q: During the Zemene Mesafint the kings at Gondar still commanded strong armies.
q.explanation: The kings were secluded in the castles without a military force and lived on customs, fines and charity.

q.q: Give the royal title, meaning 'the end of the kingdom', given to Tekle Giyorgis.
q.explanation: The Christian tradition nicknamed Tekle Giyorgis Fitsame Mengist because he was enthroned and dethroned six times.

q.q: Which dynasty founded in 1786 monopolised the office of Rasbitweded?
options: The Yejju or Werre Sheh dynasty
q.explanation: The Yejju Oromo established the Yejju or Werre Sheh dynasty in 1786, beginning with Ali Gwangul.

q.q: Give the name of the office described as that of king-maker.
q.explanation: The Rasbitwededs appointed and dismissed the kings, so they were the king-makers.

q.q: Which Egyptian ruler extended Egypt's rule over the Sudan in 1821, threatening Ethiopia from the west?
q.explanation: After the rise of Muhammad Ali, Egypt extended its rule over the Sudan in 1821.

q.q: At which battle in June 1853 did Kasa Hailu defeat Ras Ali II?
q.explanation: Ras Ali II was defeated at the battle of Ayshal in June 1853.

q.q: Explain how the Zemene Mesafint harmed the peasantry.
q.answer: forced to fight wars|produce plundered|farms became battlefields|became shiftas
q.explanation: Peasants were forced to fight, their produce was plundered, their farms became battlefields and many became bandits.

q.q: Which group of people suffered most directly from the political disorder of the era?
q.explanation: The immediate consequences of the political disorder mainly affected the lives of the peasantry.

q.q: Tigray and Shewa conducted their own foreign relations independently of Gondar during the era.
q.explanation: Tigray used Massawa and Shewa used Aussa and Tajura for their own foreign dealings.

q.q: Which of these events happened first?
options: Kasa Hailu is crowned Tewodros II
q.explanation: Iyo'as was murdered in 1769, before the Yejju dynasty in 1786, before the Egyptian conquest of Sudan in 1821, and before the coronation in 1855.

q.q: Who founded the Shewan dynasty at the end of the 17th century?
q.explanation: The Shewan dynasty was founded by Negasi Kirstos, who claimed descent from King Libne Dingil.

q.q: Which ruler established Ankober as the political centre of Shewa?
q.explanation: Meridazmach Amhayesus (r. 1745-1775) seized Ankober and made it his political centre.

q.q: Who was the first Shewan ruler to assume the title of Nigus (King)?
q.explanation: Sahle Selassie (r. 1813-1847) was the first Shewan ruler to assume the title of Nigus.

q.q: The kingdom of Shewa remained largely independent during the Zemene Mesafint.
q.explanation: During the Zemene Mesafint Shewa remained independent and was exempted from the chronic civil wars.

q.q: Give the common title of the governors appointed by the Shewan kings.
q.explanation: Trusted chiefs were appointed as governors and were called Abegazoch.

q.q: Name the church rebuilt by Sahle Selassie during his reign.
q.explanation: Sahle Selassie rebuilt the church of Debre Birhan Selassie.

q.q: In the 1840s the annual revenue of Sahle Selassie was estimated at between:
q.explanation: His annual revenue in the 1840s was estimated at between 80,000 and 300,000 Maria Theresa thalers.

q.q: Explain why Shewa developed a relatively stable government while the north faced constant warfare.
q.answer: it was far from the northern provinces|located far from the civil wars|stable administration
q.explanation: Shewa lay far from the northern provinces that experienced constant warfare, which allowed a fairly stable government.

q.q: Which of these Europeans visited the court of Sahle Selassie?
options: Major W.C. Harris and Rochet d'Hericourt
q.explanation: Major Harris and Rochet d'Hericourt led the British and French missions that signed treaties with Sahle Sellassie.

q.q: Wossenseged followed a policy of religious toleration and social equality to unify his diverse population.
q.explanation: Wossenseged followed a policy of religious toleration and social equality as a means of forging unity.

q.q: Which of these Shewan rulers came first?
q.explanation: Amhayesus (r. 1745-1775) ruled before Asfawossen (r. 1775-1808), Wossenseged (r. 1808-1813) and Sahle Selassie (r. 1813-1847).

q.q: Which traveler reached the court of Ras Wolde Sellassie of Tigray in 1805?
q.explanation: Henry Salt reached the court of Ras Wolde Sellassie of Tigray in 1805.

q.q: The main reason for the European visits was to prepare the ground for later colonial conquest.
q.explanation: The textbook states that the main reason was that they were preparing the ground for later European colonial conquest.

q.q: In which year was a treaty of commerce and friendship signed between Harris and Sahle Sellassie?
q.explanation: In 1841 a treaty of commerce and friendship was signed between Harris and Nigus Sahle Sellassie of Shewa.

q.q: Give the term for a person sent by a church to spread its religion and win converts.
q.explanation: A missionary is a person sent by a church to spread religion and make converts.

q.q: Which of the following was the main thing Ethiopian regional rulers sought from Europeans?
q.explanation: Regional rulers made foreign contacts mainly because they sought firearms to strengthen their power.

q.q: Which pair of British travelers later became loyal servants of Emperor Tewodros II?
q.explanation: John Bell and Walter Plowden came in the 1840s and later became loyal servants of Tewodros II.

q.q: With which Ethiopian ruler did Walter Plowden sign a treaty of friendship in 1849?
q.explanation: In 1849 a treaty of friendship was signed between Walter Plowden and Ras Ali II.

q.q: Explain why the treaties with regional rulers helped prepare the ground for colonial conquest.
q.answer: opened Ethiopia to foreign influence|Europeans dealt with regions not the centre|trade and information
q.explanation: By dealing directly with regional rulers and opening trade, the visitors increased European influence and knowledge of Ethiopia.

q.q: The Abbadie brothers represented France in Ethiopia.
q.explanation: Arnauld and Antoine de Abbadie, the Abbadie brothers, represented France.

q.q: Which of the following best describes the motives of the Europeans, according to the lesson?
options: Mixed motives behind a wider colonial interest
q.explanation: They came for adventure, religious zeal, scientific research and trade, but the main underlying reason was preparation for colonial conquest.

q.q: Which of these European contacts happened first?
options: Harris signs a treaty with Sahle Sellassie
Plowden signs a treaty with Ras Ali II
q.explanation: Henry Salt reached Tigray in 1805, before the 1841 treaty, the 1846 arrival and the 1849 treaty.

q.q: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
q.explanation: The textbook states that the Industrial Revolution began in England in the mid-18th century.

q.q: During the Industrial Revolution machines began to replace manual labour.
q.explanation: Before it people wove textiles by hand; during it machines replaced manual labour.

q.q: Who invented the flying shuttle in 1733?
q.explanation: John Kay made the flying shuttle, which doubled the work a weaver could do in a day.

q.q: The seed drill, invented about 1701, was important because it:
options: sowed seeds in well-spaced rows at specific depths
increased the number of coal mines
q.explanation: The seed drill sowed seeds in well-spaced rows at specific depths so more took root.

q.q: Name the three factors of production that Britain possessed for industrialization.
q.answer: land, labour and capital|land labour capital
q.explanation: Britain had all the factors of production the Industrial Revolution required: land, labour and capital.

q.q: James Watt's contribution in 1765 was to:
options: make the steam engine faster and more efficient while burning less fuel
q.explanation: Watt figured out how to make the steam engine work faster and more efficiently while burning less fuel.

q.q: Give the name given to the process of city building and the movement of people to cities.
q.explanation: Urbanization is the movement of people to cities and the building of cities.

q.q: Who were the Luddites?
q.explanation: The Luddites, named after Ned Ludd, attacked factories in northern England from 1811 to 1816.

q.q: The Luddites were named after Ned Ludd, who was said to have destroyed weaving machinery around 1779.
q.explanation: The textbook says the Luddites were named after Ned Ludd, a labourer said to have destroyed weaving machinery around 1779.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the Industrial Revolution at first caused human suffering.
q.answer: unhealthy working conditions and long hours|pollution, child labour and class tension|machine production brought long hours and pollution
q.explanation: Rapid industrialization brought long hours, pollution, child labour and rising class tension before conditions improved.

q.q: Arrange these textile inventions in the correct date order, earliest first.
q.explanation: The order is flying shuttle 1733, spinning jenny around 1764, spinning mule 1779, power loom 1787.

q.q: How many British colonies were there in North America in the 18th century?
q.explanation: The textbook states that Britain had 13 colonies in North America.

q.q: The Seven Years War between the English and the French lasted until 1763.
q.explanation: The war erupted in 1754 and the fighting lasted until 1763, when Britain and her colonists won.

q.q: In which city did the Continental Congress meet?
q.explanation: Representatives gathered in Philadelphia in September 1774 and again for the Second Continental Congress.

q.q: What did the Stamp Act of 1765 require from the colonies?
options: Payment of a tax for an official stamp on printed material
q.explanation: Colonists had to pay a tax to have an official stamp put on wills, deeds, newspapers and other printed material.

q.q: What phrase did the colonists use to describe being taxed without representatives in Parliament?
q.explanation: Colonial lawyers accused the government of taxation without representation.

q.q: Who was chosen to command the American army by the Second Continental Congress?
q.explanation: The Congress voted to raise an army under the command of a Virginian named George Washington.

q.q: Who drafted the Declaration of Independence?
q.explanation: The document was drafted by the political leader Thomas Jefferson, based on the ideas of John Locke.

q.q: France entered the American war in 1778 and helped the Americans at Yorktown.
q.explanation: French entry into the war in 1778 was decisive, and French forces helped trap Cornwallis at Yorktown in 1781.

q.q: Name the Enlightenment thinker whose ideas the Declaration of Independence was firmly based on.
q.explanation: The Declaration reflected the ideas of John Locke and the Enlightenment.

q.q: Give one important effect of the American Revolution that the textbook identifies.
q.answer: it liberated the American people from British rule|it created the United States of America|it influenced revolutions in France and Latin America
q.explanation: The revolution liberated the colonies, created an independent nation, and influenced France and Latin America.

q.q: Arrange these events in the correct date order, earliest first.
q.explanation: The order is Stamp Act 1765, Boston Tea Party 1773, Declaration of Independence 1776, Yorktown 1781.

q.q: The First Estate of France was made up of:
options: High-ranking members of the Catholic Church
q.explanation: The First Estate was made up of high-ranking members of the Catholic Church.

q.q: Under the Old Regime the privileged classes did not pay taxes.
q.explanation: The privileged were treated well and did not pay taxes, while the unprivileged paid taxes.

q.q: On what date did the Estates General convene in 1789?
q.explanation: On May 5, 1789 the Estates General convened and each estate was given one vote.

q.q: What was agreed at the Tennis Court Oath?
options: To stay together and create a written constitution for France
q.explanation: The Third Estate vowed to stay together and create a written constitution for France.

q.q: Give the term for a government spending more money than it takes in from tax revenues.
q.explanation: Deficit spending greatly damaged the economy of France.

q.q: The Bastille was stormed on July 14, 1789 because:
options: the king had raised the price of bread
news of the king's plan to use military force against the National Assembly reached Paris
the pope had excommunicated the Assembly
the nobles had fled the country
q.explanation: When news of the king's plan to use military force reached Paris, the people stormed the Bastille and seized weapons.

q.q: Who was guillotined on January 21, 1793?
q.explanation: Louis XVI was guillotined on January 21, 1793, followed by Marie Antoinette on October 16, 1793.

q.q: The Reign of Terror lasted from September 1793 to July 1794 and about 15,000 people died on the guillotine.
q.explanation: The Terror ran from September 5, 1793 to July 27, 1794, and approximately 15,000 people died on the guillotine.

q.q: Which body controlled the Reign of Terror, headed first by Danton and later by Robespierre?
q.answer: the Committee of Public Safety|Committee of Public Safety
q.explanation: A Committee of Public Safety headed by Danton and later Robespierre arrested those accused of treason.

q.q: Name the two major political parties that emerged during the revolution.
q.explanation: The major parties were the Girondists, moderates of the rich middle class, and the Jacobins, who represented workers.

q.q: Arrange the four phases of the French Revolution in the correct order.
q.explanation: The phases were the National Assembly 1789-1791, the Legislative Assembly 1791-1792, the Convention 1792-1795 and the Directory 1795-1799.

q.q: On what date did Napoleon Bonaparte take power, with a constitution giving him supreme power?
q.explanation: Napoleon took power on December 25, 1799, with the constitution giving him supreme power.

q.q: The Consulate period lasted from 1799 to 1804.
q.explanation: The first part of Napoleon's rule was the Consulate period, which lasted from 1799 to 1804.

q.q: In which year did Napoleon establish the Bank of France?
q.explanation: Napoleon established the Bank of France in 1800 to bring financial unity.

q.q: Napoleon's longest lasting legacy was:
q.explanation: The textbook calls the code of French law perhaps the longest lasting legacy of Napoleon's rule.

q.q: Give the name of the 1801 agreement Napoleon made with the Catholic Church.
q.explanation: The Concordat of 1801 sought to weaken the power of pro-Bourbon monarchs and granted freedom of worship.

q.q: Where was Napoleon finally defeated in June 1815?
q.explanation: His advance was halted at the Battle of Waterloo in Belgium, fought in June 1815.

q.q: Napoleon was exiled to St. Helena, an island in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.
q.explanation: He was exiled to the South Atlantic island of St. Helena and died there in 1821.

q.q: Which principles guided the settlement of the Congress of Vienna?
options: Legitimacy, compensation and balance of power
Self-interest, competition and supply and demand
q.explanation: The principles of settlement were legitimacy, compensation and balance of power.

q.q: Who represented Austria at the Congress of Vienna?
q.explanation: Klemens von Metternich represented Austria and epitomised a conservative reaction to the French Revolution.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the Continental System failed.
q.answer: the United States supported Britain|the blockade was not complete|Britain continued trading through other markets
q.explanation: America's concern for British commerce and its own development made the Continental System a failure.

q.q: Arrange these events of Napoleon's career in the correct order, earliest first.
q.explanation: The order is Concordat 1801, Emperor December 1804, Trafalgar October 1805, Waterloo June 1815.

q.explanation: Pair: same interaction, swapped bodies — apple pulls Earth equally upward.

q.q: A 40 kg object on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg). Its weight (N)?
q.explanation: W = mg = 40 × 1.6 = 64 N (mass still 40 kg).

q.q: Why do passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly?
q.answer: inertia continue moving|bodies keep velocity|no forward force
q.explanation: Their bodies maintain forward velocity (first law) while the bus decelerates beneath them — no forward force acts.

q.q: Lift accelerates down at 3 m/s². Apparent weight (N) of a 50 kg passenger? (g = 9.8)
On a frictionless incline, the down-slope acceleration depends on:
q.explanation: a = g sinθ — mass cancels from mg sinθ = ma.

q.q: Atwood with 6 kg and 4 kg (g = 10). Acceleration (m/s²)?
A horse-cart pair can't move because the horse pulls the cart and the cart pulls back equally.
q.explanation: The pairs act on different bodies; motion comes from the ground's forward reaction on the horse exceeding resistive forces on the cart.

q.q: Which is bigger: the force Earth exerts on the Moon, or the force the Moon exerts on Earth?
q.explanation: Third law: exactly equal magnitudes — the effects differ because the masses differ.

q.q: A 50 N push on a box whose maximum static friction is 80 N. The friction force is:
q.explanation: Below the cap, static friction MATCHES the applied force: 50 N.

q.q: 15 kg box, µₖ = 0.30, sliding. Kinetic friction (N)? (g = 9.8)
Which is typically larger?
q.explanation: Breakaway (static) exceeds sustained sliding (kinetic).

q.q: A block starts sliding on a tilting board at θ_c = 30°. Find µₛ (tan30° = 0.577).
q.explanation: µₛ = tanθ_c = 0.577.

q.q: When you walk forward, static friction on your foot points:
q.explanation: Your foot pushes the ground backward; friction (its reaction at the contact) pushes you FORWARD — static friction is the walking force.

q.q: Car braking with locked wheels, µₖ = 0.7, g = 10. Deceleration (m/s²)?
q.explanation: a = µₖg = 7 m/s².

q.q: Pushing a lawn mower (downward handle angle) vs pulling it (upward angle):
q.explanation: Pulling's vertical component lifts slightly → smaller N → smaller friction. Pushing presses down → more friction.

q.q: 4 kg block on 30° incline, µₖ = 0.2. Acceleration down the slope? (g = 10; sin30 = 0.5, cos30 = 0.866)
Doubling the contact area of a sliding block (same weight) doubles its kinetic friction.
q.explanation: Friction ≈ independent of apparent area; it depends on N and µ.

q.q: Name one method of reducing friction between machine parts.
q.explanation: Lubricants separate surfaces; bearings replace sliding with rolling; polishing smooths asperities.

q.q: Heat is best defined as:
options: Energy stored in a hot body
Energy transferred due to temperature difference
A fluid that flows through solids
q.explanation: Heat is a transfer process quantity, measured in joules.

q.q: Convert 40 °C to kelvin.
Convert 98.6 °F (normal body temperature) to °C.
Which has more internal energy: a red-hot nail (1000 °C, 5 g) or a bucket of warm water (40 °C, 5 kg)?
q.explanation: Internal energy depends on mass and particles too — the bucket's 1000× more matter wins despite lower temperature.

q.q: Why is the zeroth law essential for using a thermometer?
q.answer: equilibrium means same temp|thermometer reads its own T equal to body|transitivity
q.explanation: The thermometer equilibrates with the body; transitivity guarantees it then reads the same T the body has.

q.q: How many joules equal 500 cal? (1 cal = 4.186 J)
Heat can flow spontaneously from a cold object to a hot one.
q.explanation: Spontaneous heat flow is always hot → cold (second law); refrigerators force the reverse only with work input.

q.q: Temperature of a gas is directly proportional to the:
q.explanation: T ∝ mean translational KE; total energy also depends on how many particles.

q.q: State the temperature at which a substance has minimum internal energy (in kelvin).
q.explanation: Absolute zero, 0 K = −273.15 °C — motion is minimal there.

q.q: Which heat transfer requires NO material medium?
q.explanation: Radiation is EM waves — it crosses vacuum (Sun → Earth).

q.q: Metals are good heat conductors mainly because of:
q.explanation: Mobile electrons carry energy rapidly through the lattice.

q.q: Slab: k = 0.4, A = 5 m², d = 0.1 m, ΔT = 30 K. Heat flow rate (W)?
Why does warm air rise?
q.answer: expands less dense buoyant|lower density floats up|hot fluid less dense
q.explanation: Heating expands the air → density drops → buoyancy lifts it, cooler air sinks to replace it.

q.q: Best surface for RADIATING heat away:
q.explanation: Dull black = high emissivity = best emitter.

q.q: A convection oven cooks faster than a static one because:
options: Forced convection moves hot air faster
q.explanation: The fan forces hot air over food, replacing the slow natural current.

q.q: If a body's absolute temperature doubles, its radiated power increases by what factor?
q.explanation: Stefan: P ∝ T⁴ → 2⁴ = 16.

q.q: A vacuum flask's silvered walls mainly reduce conduction.
q.explanation: Silvering reduces RADIATION (reflection); the VACUUM kills conduction/convection.

q.q: Order the flask's defences against convection:
options: Vacuum gap → stopper seals top → narrow neck
q.explanation: Vacuum removes the fluid; stopper blocks air at the opening; narrow neck limits what's left.

q.q: Name the mechanism: a spoon handle warming in a cup of tea.
q.explanation: Energy conducts along the solid metal from the hot end.

q.q: Energy to heat 3 kg water by 10 K? (c = 4200)
Units of specific heat capacity:
q.explanation: Energy per kilogram per kelvin.

q.q: 0.2 kg metal needs 1800 J to warm 10 K. Find c (J/kg·K).
Which cools fastest after leaving the oven (same mass, same start T)?
q.explanation: Lowest c stores least energy per degree — iron's 450 runs out first (same loss rate).

q.q: Why does the sea moderate coastal temperatures?
q.answer: high specific heat|water heats and cools slowly|absorbs energy with small ΔT
q.explanation: Water's huge c means the ocean's temperature (and the air above it) changes slowly — mild summers, mild winters.

q.q: A 2000 W heater runs 60 s into 0.5 kg liquid, raising it 20 K. Find c (J/kg·K), assuming no losses.
In the immersion method, lagging the block reduces:
q.explanation: Insulation keeps VIt inside the block, making the energy assumption valid.

q.q: Q = mcΔT applies while ice is melting at 0 °C.
q.explanation: During melting ΔT = 0 while energy flows — use Q = mL (latent heat) instead.

q.q: How many kg of water can a 500 kJ supply heat from 15 to 85 °C? (c = 4200)
Which is larger: the heat capacity of 1 kg water or of 1 kg lead?
q.explanation: Water's c (4200) dwarfs lead's (130) — same mass, 32× the capacity.

q.q: Steel rod 10 m, +50 K, α = 12×10⁻⁶/K. Expansion in mm?
A metal plate with a circular hole is heated. The hole:
q.explanation: Every dimension scales up — the hole expands as if filled with metal.

q.q: Volume expansion coefficient γ for a solid with α = 9×10⁻⁶/K equals what in ×10⁻⁶/K?
Water's maximum density occurs at:
q.explanation: The anomaly peaks density at 4 °C.

q.q: Why are power lines strung with slack?
q.answer: contract in winter|sag for thermal contraction|avoid snapping when cold
q.explanation: Cold contracts wires; taut wires would snap — slack absorbs the length change.

q.q: A bimetallic strip bends on heating because:
options: One metal expands more than the other
q.explanation: Mismatched α forces curvature — the higher-α metal becomes the outer arc.

q.q: Aluminium (α = 24×10⁻⁶/K) rim: inner diameter 40.00 cm at 20 °C. New inner diameter at 120 °C (cm)?
Ice floats because solid water is denser than liquid water.
q.explanation: Ice is LESS dense (open crystal) — that's exactly why it floats.

q.q: Name the alloy with near-zero expansion used in precision instruments.
q.explanation: Invar (Fe-36%Ni) has α ≈ 0.6×10⁻⁶/K.

q.q: A 200 m steel rail (α = 12×10⁻⁶) is fully clamped. If it warms 30 K, what strain (fractional length) would it have had if free? Give as ×10⁻⁴.
Energy to melt 3 kg ice at 0 °C? (L_f = 334 kJ/kg) — answer in kJ.
During melting, the temperature of pure ice:
q.explanation: Energy goes into breaking the lattice (potential energy), not into kinetic energy.

q.q: Energy to boil away 0.2 kg water at 100 °C? (L_v = 2260 kJ/kg) in kJ.
Why is L_v larger than L_f for the same substance?
options: Gas separates molecules completely; liquid keeps contact
q.explanation: Vaporisation must overcome ALL attractions and create space; fusion only loosens the lattice.

q.q: Why do steam burns hurt worse than scalding water at the same 100 °C?
q.answer: condensation releases latent heat|steam dumps L_v on skin|extra 2260 kJ/kg
q.explanation: Steam first condenses, releasing 2260 kJ/kg of latent heat onto the skin before cooling as water.

q.q: A freezer must remove 4520 kJ to condense and freeze steam-derived water... simpler: how much energy does 2 kg of steam release condensing at 100 °C? (kJ)
On a heating curve, a horizontal (flat) section means:
options: Energy breaks bonds at constant T
q.explanation: Plateau = latent heat: energy input changes phase, not temperature.

q.q: Evaporation can occur at any temperature, but boiling only at the boiling point.
q.explanation: Surface molecules with enough speed escape anytime; boiling needs bulk vapour pressure = atmospheric.

q.q: How many kg of ice can 1 kW melt in 10 minutes from 0 °C? (L_f = 334 kJ/kg)
Which process releases latent heat: melting or freezing?
q.explanation: Bond-forming processes (freezing, condensation, deposition) release L.

q.q: Mix equal masses of water at 20 °C and 80 °C. Final temperature (°C)?
q.explanation: Equal masses of the same substance → midpoint: 50 °C.

q.q: 100 g at 90 °C mixed with 400 g at 10 °C (same c). Final T (°C)?
Why must the calorimeter cup's heat capacity be included?
q.answer: cup absorbs heat too|energy warms the cup|otherwise c is wrong
q.explanation: The cup changes temperature too — its share of energy is real and must appear on the gained side.

q.q: How much energy to melt 100 g ice at 0 °C then warm it to 20 °C? (L_f = 334 kJ/kg, c = 4200) in J.
Warm water (200 g, 25 °C) meets 60 g ice at 0 °C. Can all the ice melt? (Melt needs 20 kJ; water can give ~21 kJ)
q.explanation: Energy budget: 0.2×4200×25 = 21,000 J ≥ 20,040 J needed — all melts, final T near 0 °C.

q.q: In the method of mixtures, transferring the hot sample slowly causes the measured c to be:
q.explanation: The sample arrives cooler than T_s → its claimed heat output is smaller → c_m underestimates.

q.q: A 0.2 kg iron piece (c = 450) at 100 °C is dropped into 0.3 kg water (c = 4200) at 20 °C. Approximate final T (°C), ignoring the cup.
The principle of calorimetry is a statement of conservation of energy.
q.explanation: Heat lost = heat gained is energy conservation for an isolated thermal system.

q.q: Name one precaution that reduces heat loss in a mixing experiment.
q.explanation: Insulate (lag), cover (lid), minimise transfer time, use a polished/reflective cup.

q.q: Q₁ = Q₂ = 1 µC, r = 10 cm. Force (N)?
Distance triples; the force becomes:
q.explanation: Inverse square: 1/3² = 1/9.

q.q: Two charges repel. They are:
q.explanation: Like charges repel.

q.q: How many electrons make 1.6 µC of charge?
A +5 µC and a −2 µC interact. Which feels the larger force?
q.explanation: Newton's third law: interaction forces are always equal in magnitude.

q.q: Charges 2 µC and 8 µC are 60 cm apart. At what distance (cm) from the 2 µC charge is the net field zero between them?
If each charge halves and distance halves, the force:
q.explanation: Numerator ×¼ (½×½), denominator ×¼ (½²) → (¼)/(¼) = 1 — unchanged.

q.q: F = 4 N between two charges. If one charge doubles and distance doubles, new F (N)?
q.explanation: ×2 from charge, ÷4 from distance: 4×2/4 = 2 N.

q.q: The Coulomb force between two protons is attractive.
q.explanation: Both positive → repulsive.

q.q: State the value of k with units.
q.explanation: k ≈ 9×10⁹ N·m²/C².

q.q: A 2 µC charge feels 8 mN. Field strength (N/C)?
Field lines around a positive point charge point:
q.explanation: A positive test charge is repelled — arrows radiate outward.

q.q: Field 20 cm from a +4 nC charge? (k = 9e9) N/C
An electron in an electric field feels force:
q.explanation: Negative charge → F = qE flips direction.

q.q: Plates 2 mm apart, 100 V across them. E in V/m?
Why is the electric field zero inside a charged conductor in equilibrium?
q.answer: charges move until cancel|free charges rearrange to cancel|otherwise current flows
q.explanation: Any internal field would drive free electrons until their new arrangement cancels it — equilibrium demands E = 0 inside.

q.q: Two field lines crossing would imply:
options: Two field directions at one point — impossible
q.explanation: The net field at a point is unique; crossing lines would give it two directions.

q.q: Proton (q = 1.6e-19 C, m = 1.67e-27 kg) in E = 1000 N/C. Acceleration (m/s²)?
The units N/C and V/m are equivalent.
q.explanation: V/m = J/(C·m) = N·m/(C·m) = N/C — same quantity, two faces.

q.q: Where is the field strongest around a charged irregular conductor: flat face or sharp point?
q.explanation: Charge crowds at sharp points → concentrated field lines → strongest E at the tip.

q.q: Work moving 4 C through 9 V? (J)
Electric potential is:
q.explanation: V is energy per charge — a signed number, no direction.

q.q: Potential 30 cm from +6 nC? (k = 9e9) V
Equipotential lines are to field lines as:
q.explanation: No work along an equipotential → force (field) must be perpendicular to it.

q.q: A proton gains energy crossing 500 V. Its energy in eV?
q.explanation: eV = charge in units of e × volts: 500 eV.

q.q: Same proton — energy in joules? (e = 1.6e-19)
Which way does the electric field point relative to potential: increasing or decreasing?
q.explanation: E = −dV/dx: fields point downhill in potential — the direction a + charge naturally moves.

q.q: Between two plates, doubling the voltage and halving the gap changes E by factor:
No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential surface.
q.explanation: ΔV = 0 along it → W = QΔV = 0.

q.q: An electron (m = 9.1e-31) accelerated through 100 V reaches what speed? (v = √(2eV/m), ×10⁶ m/s)
Charge 300 C flows in 60 s. Current (A)?
V = 12 V across 4 Ω. Current (A)?
Which is OHMIC at constant temperature?
q.explanation: Fixed resistors obey V ∝ I; the others change with temperature/direction.

q.q: Wire: ρ = 2×10⁻⁷ Ω·m, L = 100 m, A = 1×10⁻⁶ m². R (Ω)?
A diode in reverse bias conducts:
q.explanation: Reverse: blocked (tiny leakage); forward above ~0.6–0.7 V: conducts.

q.q: Kettle: 230 V, 4 A. Power (W)?
Same kettle's resistance (Ω)?
Why does a filament lamp's resistance rise as it brightens?
q.answer: heating increases scattering|temperature raises R|non-ohmic heating
q.explanation: Current heats the filament; hotter lattice vibrates more, scattering electrons → higher R.

q.q: Battery ε = 12 V, r = 1 Ω, load 5 Ω. Terminal voltage (V)?
Conventional current flows in the same direction as electron drift.
q.explanation: Conventional current is +→−; electrons (negative) drift the opposite way.

q.q: 4 µF capacitor at 50 V. Charge (µC)?
Same capacitor — stored energy (mJ)?
Two 4 µF capacitors in SERIES give:
q.explanation: 1/C = ¼+¼ = ½ → C = 2 µF.

q.q: Same two in PARALLEL give:
q.explanation: Parallel: direct sum = 8 µF.

q.q: τ for R = 200 kΩ, C = 50 µF. Seconds?
After one time constant of charging, the capacitor voltage is about:
Why does inserting a dielectric increase capacitance?
q.answer: polarisation weakens field|more charge same voltage|permittivity rises
q.explanation: The dielectric polarises, reducing the net field per charge — so more charge fits at the same voltage.

q.q: 1000 µF charged to 5 V discharges in 0.05 s. Average power (W)?
A capacitor blocks steady direct current but passes alternating current.
q.explanation: Steady V → no charging current; changing V → continuous charge/discharge current appears to 'pass'.

q.q: State the unit of capacitance.
q.explanation: The farad = coulomb per volt.

q.q: 3 Ω + 5 Ω in series across 4 V. Current (A)?
6 Ω ∥ 3 Ω equals what (Ω)?
In a parallel circuit, each branch has the same:
q.explanation: Branches connect the same two nodes → identical pd.

q.q: An ammeter must be connected:
q.explanation: It measures flow THROUGH a point — must be in the path, with near-zero resistance.

q.q: Divider: 12 V in, R₁ = 8 kΩ top, R₂ = 4 kΩ bottom. V_out (V)?
Why are house lights wired in parallel, not series?
q.answer: independent operation|full voltage each|one fails others stay on
q.explanation: Parallel: each lamp gets full mains voltage and switching/failure is independent; series would share voltage and die together.

q.q: Kettle 2.3 kW on 230 V. Current (A)?
Adding more parallel appliances to a circuit:
q.explanation: More paths → lower R_eq → higher total current (the fuse's concern).

q.q: Order the safety chain for a live-case fault with earth:
options: Earth conducts fault current → fuse melts → case safe
Fuse melts → current flows → earth conducts
Case safe → fuse melts → earth conducts
Earth melts → fuse conducts → case safe
q.explanation: Low-resistance earth carries big fault current, which blows the fuse, removing the danger.

q.q: An RCD protects by detecting current leaking to earth (e.g. through a person).
q.explanation: It compares live vs neutral currents; any imbalance means leakage — trip within ~30 ms.

q.q: How many neutrons in ²³⁵₉₂ U?
Isotopes of an element differ in:
q.explanation: Same Z, different N — different mass numbers.

q.q: Which force overcomes proton–proton repulsion in the nucleus?
q.explanation: The strong force binds all nucleons at short range.

q.q: Mass defect 0.01 u. Binding energy in MeV? (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
Why do very heavy nuclei need proportionally more neutrons than protons?
q.answer: extra strong-force glue without repulsion|neutrons add attraction not repulsion|dilute proton repulsion
q.explanation: Protons repel over the whole nucleus while the strong force only acts between neighbours — extra neutrons add attraction without adding repulsion.

q.q: The most tightly bound nuclei (per nucleon) are near:
q.explanation: The BE/A curve peaks at iron-56 (~8.8 MeV/nucleon).

q.q: A nucleus with BE = 180 MeV has 30 nucleons. BE per nucleon (MeV)?
q.explanation: 180/30 = 6 MeV/nucleon.

q.q: The mass of a helium nucleus equals the sum of two proton and two neutron masses.
q.explanation: It's LESS — the mass defect became binding energy (E = mc²).

q.q: Which particle in the nucleus carries no charge?
q.explanation: Neutrons are neutral; protons are +e.

q.q: 200 MeV of fission energy in joules? (1 eV = 1.6e-19 J)
An alpha particle is:
q.explanation: ⁴₂He: 2 protons + 2 neutrons.

q.q: Most penetrating radiation:
q.explanation: γ needs thick lead/concrete; α stops at paper.

q.q: Sample halves from 800 to 50 Bq. How many half-lives passed?
T½ = 8 days; 24 days later, what FRACTION of the original activity remains?
q.explanation: 3 halvings: (½)³ = 1/8 = 0.125.

q.q: In β⁻ decay, the daughter nucleus has:
q.explanation: A neutron became a proton: Z increases by 1, A unchanged.

q.q: Why can't you speed up a radioactive sample by heating it?
q.explanation: Decay is a nuclear event; temperature/pressure/chemistry affect electrons, not the nucleus.

q.q: ²³⁸U (Z=92) emits an α. The daughter's Z is:
q.explanation: 92 − 2 = 90 (thorium).

q.q: Which ionises gas MOST strongly?
q.explanation: Heavy +2 charge rips electrons off — hence smoke detectors use α.

q.q: Count rate at 20 cm is 400 cpm. At 40 cm (inverse square), expected cpm?
q.explanation: Double distance → quarter: 400/4 = 100.

q.q: A radiation detector must subtract background counts before analysing a sample's half-life.
q.explanation: Ambient counts add a constant offset that would distort the exponential.

q.q: A fission of U-235 typically releases:
q.explanation: Average ~2.4 neutrons — enough to sustain a chain.

q.q: Complete: ²³⁹Pu + n → ¹⁴⁴Ba + ⁹⁴Sr + ?n. How many neutrons are released? (A: 239+1 = 240; 144+94 = 238)
q.explanation: A: 240 − 238 = 2 neutrons. Z check: 94 = 56 + 38 ✓ (Ba + Sr).

q.q: Control rods work by:
q.explanation: Boron/cadmium soak up neutrons, lowering k; insert deeper → less power.

q.q: The moderator's job is to:
q.explanation: U-235 captures SLOW neutrons far more readily; water/graphite do the slowing.

q.q: Fission Q = 200 MeV in joules? (1 MeV = 1.6e-13 J)
Why can't a commercial reactor explode like a nuclear bomb?
q.answer: fuel too dilute|3-5% U-235 vs 90%|chain can't run supercritical that fast
q.explanation: Reactor fuel is low-enriched; the runaway prompt-critical excursion of a weapon is physically impossible with it.

q.q: Fusion releases energy because:
options: Products are more tightly bound (higher BE/nucleon)
q.explanation: He-4 sits far above H isotopes on the BE/A curve — the climb releases the difference.

q.q: Q-value: reactants 5.03015 u, products 5.01126 u. Energy in MeV (×931.5)?
In the Sun, hydrogen fuses via the proton–proton chain into helium.
q.explanation: 4 ¹H → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν + 26.7 MeV — the Sun's engine.

q.q: Name the condition where exactly one neutron per fission continues the chain.
q.explanation: k = 1: steady, self-sustaining chain — a reactor at power.

q.q: A resource is renewable when:
options: regrowth can replace what is harvested at a finite rate
q.explanation: The rate, not the adjective, decides.

q.q: Maximum sustainable yield is taken from a population near:
q.explanation: Logistic growth peaks at half capacity.

q.q: An exclosure conserves land mainly by:
options: removing grazing so vegetation regrows and binds soil
q.explanation: Succession needs only a break from disturbance.

q.q: Which is ex-situ conservation?
q.explanation: Outside the habitat by definition.

q.q: High endemism makes a region a conservation priority because:
options: the same effort saves unique evolutionary history
q.explanation: Irreplaceable losses concentrate there.

q.q: Cutting 30 000 m³/yr from regrowth of 18 000 m³/yr means:
q.explanation: Deficit harvest = liquidation.

q.q: The Newfoundland cod crash (1992) illustrates:
options: stocks can be driven below recovery thresholds
q.explanation: Overharvest + Allee effects = sudden collapse.

q.q: Fortress conservation often fails because:
options: local people who depend on the resource get no benefit from protecting it
q.explanation: If conservation costs a household its livelihood, it loses.

q.q: Which is NOT a pillar of food security?
q.explanation: Four pillars: availability, access, utilisation, stability.

q.q: Kwashiorkor is distinguished from marasmus by:
q.explanation: Protein-poor: fluid and fat accumulate in liver/tissues.

q.q: Injera + shiro is nutritionally smart because:
options: cereal and pulse supply each other's limiting amino acids
q.explanation: Lysine from pulse, methionine from grain: complete protein.

q.q: Aflatoxin contamination of stored maize is best prevented by:
q.explanation: Low water activity stops the mould and its toxin.

q.q: Enset earns the name famine reserve because:
options: it stores years of underground carbohydrate harvestable on demand
q.explanation: The plant is the granary: drought invisible.

q.q: The first 1 000 days matter because:
options: growth and brain development lock in; stunting is largely irreversible after
q.explanation: Chronic deficit in the window = permanent cost.

q.q: Golden rice is engineered to:
q.explanation: Provitamin A grain aimed at deficiency blindness.

q.q: The nutrition transition means:
options: rising NCDs from fat/sugar diets alongside persistent under-nutrition
q.explanation: The double burden: same country, two malnutritions.

q.q: The Brundtland definition frames development as:
options: meeting present needs without compromising future generations
q.explanation: Options preserved across generations.

q.q: Pollination by bees is classed as a:
q.explanation: Pest/population control service: regulating.

q.q: Humanity's ecological footprint today is roughly:
q.explanation: Overshoot of ~70% since the 1970s.

q.q: Ethiopia's electric bajaj policy pays because:
q.explanation: Clean grid → electric transport cuts emissions at the socket.

q.q: The waste hierarchy ranks first:
q.explanation: Prevention beats processing.

q.q: A household's biggest food-climate lever is:
q.explanation: Wasted food wastes all its upstream footprint at zero benefit.

q.q: Church forests mainly demonstrate:
q.explanation: Faith-managed habitat islands: culture as conservation mechanism.

q.q: A genuine SDG trade-off pair is:
q.explanation: Land competition between SDG 2 and SDG 7/13 pathways.

q.q: Injera's spongy eyes come from:
q.explanation: Yeast/LAB CO₂ trapped in the batter.

q.q: Restriction enzymes are used because they:
q.explanation: Sticky ends at known sites enable paste-able fragments.

q.q: PCR requires all EXCEPT:
q.explanation: Cell-free chemistry: enzyme + primers + nucleotides.

q.q: Bacterial insulin uses cDNA because bacteria:
q.explanation: Intronless coding sequence survives the host's lack of splicing.

q.q: Tissue culture multiplies plants because cells are:
q.explanation: One cell can regenerate a whole plantlet.

q.q: CRISPR's targeting agent is:
options: a guide RNA to the target sequence
q.explanation: Cas9 is the scissors; the gRNA aims them.

q.q: Ergo's sour taste is chiefly:
q.explanation: LAB convert lactose to lactate.

q.q: Ethiopia's biotech governance (Proclamation 800/2013) covers:
options: living modified organisms under biosafety review
q.explanation: LMO handling, release and import require assessment.

q.q: The bacterial cell wall is made of:
q.explanation: NAM-NAG + peptides: the Gram and penicillin target.

q.q: Bacteria reproduce mainly by:
q.explanation: Clonal split; conjugation only shares plasmids.

q.q: Gram-negative bacteria stain:
q.explanation: Thin wall loses crystal violet; takes safranin.

q.q: Griffith's transformation experiment showed:
q.explanation: Dead smooth cells re-coated live rough ones.

q.q: Clostridium tetani grows in deep wounds because it is:
q.explanation: Oxygen-free tissue is its niche.

q.q: Antibiotic resistance plasmids spread between bacteria chiefly via:
q.explanation: The pilus bridge moves R-plasmids fast.

q.q: Sterilization uses 121 °C autoclave rather than boiling because:
q.explanation: Sporicidal heat needs pressure steam.

q.q: 20.0 cm³ NaOH neutralised by 15.0 cm³ of 0.100 M HCl: [NaOH] =
Why no indicator for weak acid + weak base?
options: no steep pH jump: the change is gradual
q.explanation: Buffering from both sides flattens the curve — use a meter.

q.q: Na₂CO₃ titrated with HCl to methyl orange end consumes:
q.explanation: Full neutralisation: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂CO₃.

q.q: Oxidation is best defined as:
q.explanation: OIL RIG: loss = oxidation.

q.q: The oxidation state of sulfur in H₂SO₄ is:
In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, the reducing agent is:
q.explanation: Zn gives the electrons — it reduces copper and is itself oxidised.

q.q: The half-equation Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ represents:
q.explanation: Electrons gained (left side): reduction.

q.q: Which reaction is disproportionation?
q.explanation: Chlorine (0) goes to −1 AND +1 in the same reaction.

q.q: How many electrons does MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ consume?
q.explanation: +7 to +2: five per manganese.

q.q: The coefficient of Fe²⁺ when balanced against dichromate is:
q.explanation: Cr₂O₇²⁻ takes 6e⁻; each Fe gives 1 ⇒ 6 iron(II).

q.q: A metal below hydrogen in the activity series will:
q.explanation: Cu, Ag, Au: no H⁺ reduction route — they need oxidising acids (HNO₃).

q.q: In an electrolytic cell, reduction occurs at the:
q.explanation: RED CAT — always, in any cell type.

q.q: Electrolysing molten lead(II) bromide gives at the cathode:
q.explanation: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb: grey metal bead.

q.q: Aqueous NaCl electrolysis at the cathode produces:
q.explanation: Water beats Na⁺: H₂ gas, OH⁻ left behind.

q.q: Concentrated CuBr₂ solution electrolysed with graphite: anode product?
q.explanation: Concentrated bromide discharges: red-brown Br₂.

q.q: Why is graphite used in chlor-alkali cells?
q.explanation: Inert: conducts without reacting into the products.

q.q: Dilute H₂SO₄ electrolysis overall equals:
q.explanation: H₂ + ½O₂ from water; acid is just the electrolyte — 2:1 gas volumes.

q.q: The 'extra' voltage oxygen evolution needs beyond its E° is:
q.explanation: Sluggish bubble-forming kinetics: why conc. Cl⁻ wins against the numbers.

q.q: Silver-plating a spoon: the spoon must be the:
q.explanation: Reduction (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag) happens at the cathode — the object plates there.

q.q: One faraday is the charge of:
A 5 A current for 2 min passes charge:
Moles of Cu from 2F through Cu²⁺ solution:
q.explanation: z = 2: n = 2F/2F = 1 mol.

q.q: Mass ratio Ag:Cu from equal charge in series cells:
To deposit 0.27 g Al (z 3, M 27) needs charge:
Doubling current and halving time changes deposit:
q.explanation: Q = It unchanged — product tracks charge only.

q.q: Current efficiency 90% means actual deposit is:
q.explanation: 10% of electrons take side paths (H₂, impurities).

q.q: H₂ and Cl₂ volumes from the same charge are:
q.explanation: Both need 2e⁻ per molecule: equal moles, equal volumes (same T,P).

q.q: Cryolite in aluminium cells serves to:
q.explanation: It drops the operating melt from 2050 to ~950 °C.

q.q: In Hall-Héroult cells the anodes are consumed because:
options: carbon reacts with oxide ions to CO₂
q.explanation: The overall equation includes C: 2Al₂O₃ + 3C → 4Al + 3CO₂.

q.q: Chlor-alkali cathode product is:
q.explanation: Water discharges: H₂ gas and hydroxide, Na⁺ crossing the membrane.

q.q: The membrane in modern cells passes:
q.explanation: Cation-exchange: sodium shuttles; products stay separated.

q.q: In copper electrorefining, the impure copper is the:
q.explanation: It dissolves; pure copper plates on the cathode sheet.

q.q: Anode slime is valuable because it contains:
q.explanation: Noble metals don't dissolve — they fall and are harvested.

q.q: Anodising makes aluminium corrode-resistant by:
q.explanation: The object as anode builds dense Al₂O₃ — the barrier is its own oxide.

q.q: Smelters historically locate near:
q.explanation: ~14 MWh/t: power dominates cost; alumina ships cheaply by comparison.

q.q: In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the:
q.explanation: Electrons are born at the anode — and it's the negative terminal here.

q.q: The salt bridge works by:
q.explanation: Wires carry e⁻; bridges carry ions, completing the circuit.

q.q: E°cell for Zn (−0.76) and Cu (+0.34) is:
Doubling the Zn/Cu cell reaction's coefficients makes E°:
q.explanation: Volts are per coulomb: intensive.

q.q: Which is the strongest reducing agent listed?
q.explanation: Most negative E° (−0.76 V) = best electron giver: Zn.

q.q: A rechargeable battery during charging acts as:
q.explanation: External current forces the reverse (non-spontaneous) reaction.

q.q: Lead-acid discharge: the electrolyte:
q.explanation: Sulfate leaves solution onto both plates: hydrometer drops.

q.q: Mg blocks protecting ship hulls are:
options: sacrificial anodes: Mg oxidises instead of Fe
q.explanation: Mg's −2.37 V makes it the cell's anode; steel becomes protected cathode.

q.q: A catalyst affects:
q.explanation: Speeds both directions equally: position unchanged.

q.q: Continuous processing is preferred for:
q.explanation: Steady state pays for capital at scale.

q.q: Low per-pass conversion can still mean a good plant because:
q.explanation: Loop economics, not single-trip.

q.q: The hottest cost in many plants is:
q.explanation: Distillation especially: energy-heavy columns.

q.q: Why preheat feed with product stream?
q.explanation: Heat integration recycles enthalpy already paid for.

q.q: Selectivity measures:
q.explanation: Wrong-product minimisation — the atom-economy of operation.

q.q: A purge stream in a recycle loop exists to:
q.explanation: Inerts have no exit otherwise and strangle conversion.

q.q: Ammonia plants locate near cheap energy because:
q.explanation: Feedstocks (air, water) are cheap; the H₂ from gas is the bill.

q.q: Liquid air distillation separates mainly by:
q.explanation: N₂ (−196) over Ar (−186) over O₂ (−183 °C).

q.q: Gangue is:
q.explanation: The matrix you reject early.

q.q: Froth flotation separates minerals by:
q.explanation: Collector-coated particles ride bubbles.

q.q: Phosphate rock is acid-treated because:
q.explanation: P availability is a solubility problem.

q.q: The Claus process converts H₂S into:
q.explanation: 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S: waste-to-feedstock.

q.q: In a solar pond, first to crystallise from seawater is:
q.explanation: Least soluble salt hits saturation first.

q.q: Ore concentration before smelting mainly saves:
q.explanation: Move the metal, not the mountain.

q.q: Argon's industrial role is best as:
q.explanation: Noble = welding blankets and bulb fill.

q.q: The catalyst in Haber is:
q.explanation: Fe with K₂O/Al₂O₃ promoters.

q.q: SO₃ is absorbed in H₂SO₄ (not water) to avoid:
q.explanation: Direct water contact fogs fine H₂SO₄.

q.q: Contact skips high pressure because:
q.explanation: No benefit left to buy — the triangle again.

q.q: Haber's H₂ commonly comes from:
q.explanation: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂ (then shift).

q.q: Ostwald's first reactor uses:
q.explanation: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO on precious-metal gauze.

q.q: Cement hardens by:
q.explanation: Why it cures underwater — dries is the wrong verb.

q.q: Soap fails in hard water because:
options: Ca²⁺ precipitates the carboxylate as scum
q.explanation: Insoluble calcium 'soap': detergents dodge this.

q.q: Increasing Haber pressure raises NH₃ yield because:
options: fewer gas moles on product side
q.explanation: 4 mol gas → 2: Le Chatelier's mole lever.

q.q: Ethiopia's largest chemical-industry output family is:
q.explanation: Construction demand + local limestone: cement leads.

q.q: Bagasse in a sugar mill is used for:
q.explanation: Biomass energy: the mill self-powers.

q.q: 'Wet blue' leather is tanned with:
q.explanation: The Cr(III) intermediate's colour names it.

q.q: Most cement CO₂ comes from:
q.explanation: Process emissions: the chemical equation itself.

q.q: Molasses → ethanol requires first:
q.explanation: Sugars → beer → spirits: biology then separation.

q.q: Ethiopia imports urea rather than making it mainly because:
options: Haber plants need cheap continuous H₂ feed + capital
q.explanation: The fertilizer topic's economics: energy and capital first.

q.q: Cyanidation needs dissolved oxygen because:
options: Au oxidation potential: O₂ is the oxidant
q.explanation: The equation puts O₂ in the reactants.

q.q: Rift volcanic ash in cement is a:
options: pozzolan: reactive silica for blended cement
q.explanation: Local pozzolans cut clinker fraction (and CO₂).

q.q: The monomer of PVC is:
q.explanation: Vinyl chloride CH₂=CHCl polymerises.

q.q: A thermoplastic is one that:
options: softens on heating and rehardens on cooling
q.explanation: Forces unstick then re-form: remouldable.

q.q: HDPE differs from LDPE mainly in:
q.explanation: Linear chains pack: denser and stronger.

q.q: Vulcanisation crosslinks rubber with:
q.explanation: S–S bridges at double-bond sites: tyres.

q.q: The repeat unit of poly(styrene) is:
q.explanation: Styrene minus the π bond.

q.q: PTFE's non-stick behaviour traces to:
options: strong C–F bonds and smooth fluorine sheath
q.explanation: Nothing sticks to a chain fully armoured in F.

q.q: A rubber band snapping back is best explained by:
q.explanation: Stretch orders the coils; the network remembers the shape.

q.q: Polystyrene's brittleness at room T comes from:
q.explanation: Bulky phenyl groups lock a glassy, no-slip arrangement.

q.q: In radical polymerization, the active site during propagation is:
q.explanation: The radical stays on the growing terminus.

q.q: Termination by disproportionation gives:
options: two dead chains, one with a vinyl end
q.explanation: H transfer: one saturated, one unsaturated end.

q.q: Condensation polymers always:
options: lose a small molecule (or are made from acid derivatives)
q.explanation: Water/HCl shed at every bond (PU the noted exception: no byproduct).

q.q: PET is made from:
q.explanation: Diol + diacid: a polyester.

q.q: Nylon-6 differs from nylon-6,6 because it comes from:
q.explanation: One monomer; no water lost.

q.q: Ziegler-Natta catalysts deliver:
q.explanation: HDPE + isotactic PP: coordination-insertion.

q.q: p = 0.990 step growth gives DP about:
q.explanation: 1/(1−p) = 100: the conversion cliff.

q.q: Interfacial nylon rope forms because:
options: HCl escapes to water and diamine+diacid chloride react at the boundary
q.explanation: Irreversible acid-chloride coupling at the interface.

q.q: Rayon (viscose) is best classed:
q.explanation: Nature's polymer, dissolved and rebuilt.

q.q: Thermoset plastics are:
q.explanation: Set during curing: never reflows.

q.q: Nylon and PET share being:
q.explanation: Both step-growth amide/ester condensations.

q.q: Fibres as a class are defined by:
q.explanation: A property class: cotton qualifies.

q.q: PLA biodegrades because:
q.explanation: Hydrolysable links: the biodegradation handle.

q.q: cis vs trans polyisoprene differ in:
q.explanation: Same atoms: kinked coil vs straight crystal.

q.q: 'Bioplastic' made from corn sugar but pure polyethene is:
q.explanation: Source vs end-of-life: two different axes.

q.q: Conducting polymers (PANi, PEDOT) require:
q.explanation: Delocalised π system, charges created by dopants.

q.q: Which is a point source of pollution?
q.explanation: One identifiable location vs diffuse.

q.q: 1 ppm in dilute water equals:
q.explanation: 1 mg per litre ≈ one part per million.

q.q: The phosphorus cycle's bottleneck is that P mainly cycles through:
options: rocks, soil and water (no gas phase)
q.explanation: Unlike C and N, phosphorus has no significant atmospheric pool.

q.q: High K_ow indicates a compound likely to:
q.explanation: Octanol = fat proxy: it prefers lipids.

q.q: Which fixes nitrogen industrially?
q.explanation: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: fertilizer's origin.

q.q: Mercury in a large predatory fish exceeding pond-water levels thousand-fold is:
q.explanation: Each trophic step concentrates the indigestible fraction.

q.q: Best practice for a trace-metal water sample:
q.explanation: Acid keeps metals dissolved; containers must not leach blank values.

q.q: Human reactive-nitrogen creation now roughly:
q.explanation: Haber fertilizer doubled the global N cycle — a textbook anthropocene shift.

q.q: Ground-level ozone forms mainly from:
q.explanation: Traffic NOx + sunlight is the smog engine.

q.q: CO's toxicity comes from:
q.explanation: Carboxyhaemoglobin starves the blood of oxygen.

q.q: Natural rain is slightly acidic (pH 5.6) because:
q.explanation: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃: baseline before any SO₂/NOx.

q.q: A water sample with high BOD means:
q.explanation: BOD = how much O₂ microbes will steal: demand, not supply.

q.q: Fish kills in eutrophied lakes occur mainly because:
options: bacterial decay of dead algae strips O₂
water is too green to see
q.explanation: The decomposers' oxygen bill arrives after the bloom crashes.

q.q: Which removes SO₂ from flue gas?
q.explanation: Basic CaCO₃/Ca(OH)₂ wash traps acidic SO₂ as sulfite.

q.q: Catalytic converters do NOT reduce:
q.explanation: The reaction PRODUCES CO₂ while destroying CO.

q.q: DDT was banned largely because it:
q.explanation: Persistence + fat-solubility + food-chain amplification.

q.q: Which gas does NOT absorb infrared?
q.explanation: N₂: homonuclear, no dipole change, invisible to IR.

q.q: Pre-industrial CO₂ was about:
q.explanation: 280 ppm; now 420+.

q.q: Ocean acidification directly reduces:
q.explanation: H⁺ converts CO₃²⁻ to HCO₃⁻: builders (corals, plankton) short of material.

q.q: The isotope evidence that extra CO₂ is fossil is its lack of:
q.explanation: Ancient carbon lost all ¹⁴C; the air's ¹⁴C ratio is falling exactly as CO₂ rises.

q.q: Melting ice accelerating warming is:
q.explanation: Dark surfaces replace reflective ones: more absorption, more melt.

q.q: The largest share of human-caused warming comes from:
q.explanation: ~2/3+ of the forcing: CO₂ — from sheer mass and lifetime.

q.q: Cutting methane helps climate quickly because it:
q.explanation: Short-lived but fierce: cuts cool within years, not centuries.

q.q: Direct air capture is energy-hungry mainly because:
q.explanation: Concentrating 420 ppm to pure CO₂ means processing mountainous volumes of air.

q.q: Green chemistry's first principle is:
q.explanation: Better never made than cleaned after.

q.q: Atom economy for addition reactions (A+B→C) is:
q.explanation: Every reactant atom lands in the product.

q.q: Which is the best green SOLVENT choice?
q.explanation: Non-toxic, non-carcinogenic, cheap — principle 5.

q.q: A process with 90% yield but 30% atom economy:
options: is efficient: still discards 70% of atoms by design
q.explanation: Yield ≠ AE: the equation itself wastes atoms; fix the route.

q.q: Using a catalyst rather than stoichiometric reagent serves principle 9 and also cuts:
q.explanation: Reagents get consumed to waste; catalysts don't (mass-basis win).

q.q: E-factor of 25 means:
q.explanation: The waste-per-product ratio — typical of old-school pharma.

q.q: Which product feature matches 'design for degradation'?
q.explanation: Engineered to hydrolyse to benign lactic acid in compost conditions.

q.q: Supercritical CO₂ extraction is 'green' because the solvent:
options: is non-toxic and leaves no residue when depressurised
q.explanation: It flashes away as gas; no organic-solvent trace in the product.

q.q: Macroeconomics is defined as the study of:
options: the structure and performance of national economies and the policies governments use
the prices in a single market
q.explanation: Macroeconomics studies the structure and performance of national economies and the policies governments use to affect economic performance.

q.q: Macroeconomics emerged as a distinct branch of economics after:
options: Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations in 1776
Keynes' The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in 1936
q.explanation: Macroeconomics emerged after the publication of Keynes' General Theory in 1936.

q.q: The word macro comes from the Greek word makro, which means large.
q.explanation: Macro is derived from the Greek makro, meaning large.

q.q: GDP includes only final goods and services to avoid double counting.
q.explanation: Only the values of final goods and services are included in the product approach to avoid double counting.

q.q: State the functional relationship between GNP, GDP and net factor income.
q.answer: GNP = GDP + NFI|GNP equals GDP plus NFI
q.explanation: GNP = GDP + NFI, where NFI is net factor income received from abroad.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT a macroeconomic question?
options: What determines how many goods and services a nation produces?
What determines how many jobs are available in an economy?
What causes a firm to grow?
How does the domestic economy interact with the rest of the world?
q.explanation: What causes a firm to grow is a microeconomic question about a single decision-making unit.

q.q: Which macroeconomic variable equals the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a year?
q.explanation: This is the definition of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

q.q: Under the expenditure approach, GDP is estimated as the sum of:
options: consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports
the value added of each sector only
q.explanation: GDP = C + I + G + NE under the expenditure approach.

q.q: Explain why a country's GNP can exceed its GDP.
q.answer: citizens earn factor income abroad so NFI is positive|net factor income from abroad is positive
q.explanation: When factor income received from abroad by citizens exceeds factor income paid to foreigners, NFI is positive and GNP exceeds GDP.

q.q: Real GDP is calculated in constant prices using a base year.
q.explanation: Real GDP is calculated in constant prices by taking a base year, unlike nominal GDP which uses actual market prices.

q.q: Economic growth is best defined as:
options: a rise in the general price level
an increase in the capacity of an economy to produce goods and services
a fall in unemployment to zero
an increase in the money supply
q.explanation: Economic growth represents an increase in the capacity of an economy to produce goods and services.

q.q: A persistent inflation rate of 15% per year is classified as:
q.explanation: Running inflation occurs when prices rise rapidly at the rate of 10 to 20% per year.

q.q: Deflation is a decrease in the general level of the prices of goods and services.
q.explanation: Deflation is the opposite of inflation: a fall in the general price level.

q.q: Printing money to raise revenue, known as seigniorage, works like an inflation tax on money holders.
q.explanation: As prices rise, the real value of the money in one's wallet falls, so seigniorage resembles an inflation tax on money holders.

q.q: In the textbook example, the CPI rose from 100 in 2000 E.C. to 140 in 2001 E.C. State the inflation rate.
q.explanation: (140 - 100) / 100 x 100 = 40%, because the basket cost rose from 200 to 280 birr.

q.q: Which type of unemployment arises from a deficiency of aggregate effective demand, such as a collapse in overseas demand for coffee?
q.explanation: Cyclical unemployment occurs due to a deficiency of aggregate effective demand resulting from business depressions.

q.q: Name the non-monetary composite index, deployed by UNDP and sometimes called the quality of life index.
q.explanation: The Human Development Index (HDI) was deployed by UNDP and is a non-monetary composite index of development.

q.q: Why does hyperinflation usually occur? Give the reason stated in the textbook.
q.answer: governments need revenue from printing money|governments print money to cover budget deficits
q.explanation: Most episodes of high inflation and hyperinflation are caused by governments' need to obtain revenue from printing money.

q.q: Arrange the phases of the business cycle in the correct order.
q.explanation: The order is: expansion, peak, contraction, trough.

q.q: In 2020 the textbook notes that Ethiopia ran a trade deficit of about:
q.explanation: In 2020 Ethiopia ran a trade deficit of about US$10.7 billion; China's surplus was about US$535 billion.

q.q: State the labour force participation rate in one sentence.
q.answer: the percentage of the adult population that is in the labour force
q.explanation: The labour force participation rate is the percentage of the adult population that is in the labour force.

q.q: According to the classical view, if an economy slips into recession it will return to full employment because:
options: falling prices eliminate the surplus of goods
the central bank expands money supply
q.explanation: With flexible prices, surplus goods are eliminated by falling prices and the economy returns to full employment GDP.

q.q: Say's Law states that supply creates its own demand.
q.explanation: Say's Law is the classical proposition that supply creates its own demand, contradicted by the Great Depression.

q.q: The two key building blocks of the Keynesian diagnosis of recession are:
options: strong aggregate demand and flexible wages
demand too low for full employment and sticky wages and prices
full crowding out and rational expectations
constant money growth and tax cuts
q.explanation: Recessions occur when aggregate demand is not automatically high enough for full employment and when wages and prices adjust only slowly (sticky).

q.q: The monetarist school is represented by:
q.explanation: The monetarist view is represented by Milton Friedman (1912-2006) and his colleagues.

q.q: Name the curve formalised by Arthur Laffer to show the relationship between tax rates and tax revenue.
q.explanation: The Laffer curve illustrates the argument that cutting tax rates can sometimes increase total tax revenue.

q.q: Which school coined the policy ineffectiveness proposition, and what does it claim?
q.answer: new classical|policy maker cannot or should not use countercyclical policy
q.explanation: The new classicals coined it: the policy maker either cannot or should not use countercyclical policy.

q.q: The neoclassical view holds that the government should worry more about recessions than about long-term growth and inflation.
q.explanation: The neoclassical key policy implication is to focus more on long-term growth and controlling inflation than on recession or cyclical unemployment.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why new Keynesians argue for government stabilization even under rational expectations.
q.answer: nominal rigidities from multi-period wage contracts invalidate the policy ineffectiveness proposition
q.explanation: Nominal rigidities arising from multi-period nominal wage contracts invalidate the policy ineffectiveness proposition, so stabilization policy still works.

q.q: Arrange these schools in the order they emerged historically.
q.explanation: The emergence order is: Classical, Neoclassical, Keynesian, Monetarist, then the new classical and new Keynesian schools.

q.q: Name one economist belonging to the new classical school.
q.explanation: Lucas, Sargent, Barro and Prescott are listed among the new classical economists.

q.q: Supply-siders such as Arthur Laffer advise governments to:
options: raise tax rates to fund spending
cut tax rates to stimulate the economy
q.explanation: Supply-siders emphasize the distorting effects of taxation and advise cutting tax rates to stimulate the economy.

q.q: Aggregate demand is defined as:
options: the output of a single industry
the total amount all sectors willingly spend on goods and services in a given period
the money supply of the economy
the total quantity of resources available
q.explanation: AD is the total expenditure of households, firms and government on goods and services produced in a given period.

q.q: AD = C + I + G + (X - M). In this equation X - M stands for:
q.explanation: X is exports, M is imports, so X - M is net export demand.

q.q: The increase in spending that occurs because the real value of money rises when the price level falls is called:
q.explanation: The real balance effect works through changes in the value of monetary wealth as the price level changes.

q.q: A firm expects a 6% return on a project. In which case will the investment be made?
q.explanation: Investment is potentially profitable when the expected return (6%) exceeds the interest rate, as at 5%.

q.q: The aggregate demand curve is downward sloping because of an inverse relationship between the price level and real GDP demanded.
q.explanation: With other factors constant, aggregate quantity demanded rises as the general price level falls.

q.q: A change in the price level shifts the aggregate demand curve.
q.explanation: A change in the price level causes a movement along the AD curve; only other spending factors shift the curve.

q.q: Name the three effects that explain why the AD curve slopes downward.
q.answer: real balance effect, interest rate effect, international trade effect
q.explanation: The inverse relationship is explained by the real balance, interest rate and international trade effects.

q.q: State one AD determinant mentioned in the lesson that lies under government control and one that is exogenous.
q.answer: fiscal or monetary policy variables under government control|foreign economic activity or technological change as exogenous
q.explanation: Policy variables include monetary and fiscal policy; exogenous variables include foreign economic activity and technological change.

q.q: Explain, in order, how a fall in the price level increases the quantity of real GDP demanded through the international trade effect.
q.answer: Ethiopian goods become cheaper relative to foreign goods|Ethiopians and foreigners buy more Ethiopian goods|quantity demanded of real GDP rises
q.explanation: A lower domestic price level makes home goods relatively cheaper, raising both home and foreign purchases of Ethiopian output.

q.q: Arrange the real balance effect in the correct causal order.
options: Quantity demanded of real GDP falls
Monetary wealth and purchasing power fall
