q.explanation: The order is: price level rises, purchasing power and monetary wealth fall, quantity demanded of real GDP falls.

q.q: If the Ethiopian Birr depreciates, foreign goods become more expensive and Ethiopian exports become cheaper for foreigners.
q.explanation: Depreciation makes imports dearer and exports cheaper, so exports rise, imports fall and net exports increase.

q.q: Aggregate supply refers to:
options: the quantity of one good supplied by one firm
the quantity supplied of all goods and services (real GDP) at various price levels
the total spending in the economy
q.explanation: AS is the quantity supplied of all goods and services at various price levels, ceteris paribus.

q.q: Real wage is calculated as:
options: nominal wage divided by the price level
price level divided by nominal wage
q.explanation: Real wage = Nominal wage / Price level.

q.q: Which of the following is a determinant that shifts the aggregate supply curve?
options: the interest rate on loans to households
q.explanation: Wage rates are a major input cost; higher wages shift SRAS leftward, while the price level only moves along the curve.

q.q: The long-run aggregate supply curve is vertical because:
options: in the long run the economy produces full-employment real GDP whatever the price level
the price level is fixed in the long run
q.explanation: In the long run wages and prices fully adjust, so output equals natural real GDP (QN) at any price level.

q.q: According to the Keynesian view, the aggregate supply curve is horizontal because:
options: the labour market is always at full employment
firms can supply any amount demanded at the existing price level when there is unemployment
q.explanation: With unemployment, firms obtain labour at the current wage and supply whatever is demanded at the existing price level.

q.q: A rise in equilibrium wage rates shifts the short-run aggregate supply curve to the left.
q.explanation: Higher wages raise cost per unit, lower profit per unit, and reduce output at each price level, shifting SRAS left.

q.q: In the short run, a fall in the price level with sticky nominal wages increases the output firms produce.
q.explanation: A lower price level raises real wages, so firms hire fewer workers and output declines.

q.q: A firm locked in a $30 nominal wage. If the price index falls from 1.50 to 1.25, what is the new real wage?
Distinguish between a change in the quantity supplied of real GDP and a change in short-run aggregate supply.
q.answer: movement along SRAS due to price level change|shift of SRAS due to other determinants
q.explanation: A change in quantity supplied is caused by a change in the price level (movement along SRAS); a change in aggregate supply shifts the whole curve.

q.q: Arrange the worker misperception story in the correct order.
options: Nominal wage and price level both fall
Workers believe the real wage fell
q.explanation: Order: nominal wage and prices fall together; workers misperceive a real wage fall; they supply less labour; firms produce less.

q.q: Profit per unit equals price per unit minus cost per unit.
q.explanation: This textbook equation links input costs to how many units managers choose to produce.

q.q: Short-run macroeconomic equilibrium occurs where:
options: the AD curve intersects the SRAS curve
the AD curve intersects the LRAS curve
the SRAS curve crosses the price axis
the economy is at full employment
q.explanation: Short-run equilibrium is where the quantity demanded of real GDP equals the short-run quantity supplied.

q.q: In long-run equilibrium, the economy produces:
q.explanation: Long-run equilibrium identifies the real GDP produced when wages and prices have fully adjusted, equal to natural real GDP.

q.q: Aggregate supply shocks cause the price level and real output to change:
q.explanation: For supply shocks, P and Y move in opposite directions; for example Y falls while P rises after a negative shock.

q.q: An increase in government spending, as an expansionary demand shock, will:
options: shift AD left and lower P and Y
shift AD right and raise both P and Y
q.explanation: An expansionary demand shock shifts AD right, increasing both the price level and real GDP.

q.q: A sudden interruption in the availability of imported inputs such as oil will:
options: shift SRAS leftward, reducing output and raising the price level
q.explanation: Higher input costs shift the AS curves leftward: output falls and prices rise.

q.q: At a price level above short-run equilibrium there is a surplus of goods, so the price level falls.
q.explanation: When quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, the price level drops, firms cut output and consumers buy more.

q.q: If the aggregate demand and aggregate supply curves remain unchanged, the economy keeps producing natural output at an equilibrium price indefinitely.
q.explanation: The textbook states the economy would continue producing the natural rate of output with an equilibrium price indefinitely.

q.q: Give one source of an unexpected exogenous positive demand shock.
q.answer: expansionary monetary policy|expansionary fiscal policy|increase in desired expenditures
q.explanation: Sources include expansionary monetary-policy action, expansionary fiscal-policy action, or increased desired expenditures.

q.q: Distinguish a demand shock from a supply shock in terms of how P and Y move.
q.answer: demand shock: P and Y same direction|supply shock: P and Y opposite directions
q.explanation: Demand shocks move price and output together; supply shocks move them in opposite directions.

q.q: A storm destroys agricultural crops across a country. Identify the type of shock and its effects on output and the price level.
q.answer: negative supply shock|output falls and price level rises
q.explanation: The storm shifts AS curves leftward: real GDP falls while the price level rises.

q.q: Arrange the shortage adjustment in the correct order.
options: Quantity supplied is less than quantity demanded
q.explanation: Order: shortage appears, the price level rises, firms increase output, and consumers decrease consumption until equilibrium.

q.q: Market failure occurs when the free market fails to:
options: allocate resources efficiently or distribute goods and services equitably
q.explanation: Market failure is defined as the failure to allocate resources efficiently or distribute goods and services equitably.

q.q: In the absence of government intervention, the textbook notes that tobacco and alcohol are:
q.explanation: The introduction states tobacco and alcohol are over-consumed while education and healthcare are under-consumed.

q.q: Allocative efficiency is achieved when marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost.
q.explanation: Allocative efficiency occurs when MSB = MSC, so no reallocation can raise society's welfare.

q.q: Marginal social cost is the sum of marginal private cost and which other component?
q.explanation: MSC = MPC + MEC, that is, marginal private cost plus marginal external cost.

q.q: Which of the following is a commonly cited market failure?
q.explanation: Commonly cited market failures include externalities, monopoly, information asymmetries and factor immobility.

q.q: Market failure can occur in government activity, for example through rent-seeking by special interest groups.
q.explanation: The lesson states market failure does not describe only inherent market imperfections; rent-seeking lobbying for tariffs is an example in government activity.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why individually rational decisions can still harm the group.
q.answer: rational self interest can make the group worse off|individual correct decisions are wrong for the group
q.explanation: Each individual makes the correct decision for himself or herself, but these may prove to be the wrong decisions for the group.

q.q: Placing a tax on tobacco is a government solution that works by:
q.explanation: A tobacco tax increases the cost of consumption, making smoking more expensive and cutting down the negative behaviour.

q.q: Dairy farmers building a co-operatively held refrigerated storage facility is an example of:
options: a private market solution by one firm
q.explanation: Consumers and producers can band together to form co-ops for services that a pure market would underprovide.

q.q: Every bad outcome from market activity counts as a market failure.
q.explanation: The lesson warns that not every bad outcome from market activity counts as a market failure.

q.q: Give two government responses to market failure other than taxation.
q.answer: legislation|subsidies|tradable permits|direct provision of merit and public goods|extension of property rights|advertising|international cooperation
q.explanation: Government responses include legislation, direct provision of merit and public goods, subsidies, tradable permits, extension of property rights, advertising and international cooperation.

q.q: The two key characteristics of public goods are:
q.explanation: Public goods are non-rivalrous in consumption and it is difficult and expensive to exclude non-payers.

q.q: Once a public good is provided, the marginal cost of allowing another person to consume it is zero.
q.explanation: Non-rivalry in consumption implies the marginal cost of allowing another person to consume the good is zero.

q.q: Which of the following is a pure public good?
q.explanation: National defence, clean air, biodiversity and wilderness are examples of pure public goods.

q.q: A good that is rival and non-excludable is a:
q.explanation: According to the review questions, a good that is rival and non-excludable is a common resource.

q.q: Technology can make a previously non-excludable good excludable, for example through encrypted broadcasts.
q.explanation: Radio or TV broadcasts can now be encrypted so that those without a special decoder are excluded.

q.q: What do we call a person who enjoys the benefits of a public good without contributing to its cost?
q.explanation: A free rider, also called a social loafer, enjoys the benefit without paying anything toward the cost.

q.q: The free rider problem was first observed in:
q.explanation: It was observed where non-members benefited from successful bargaining by union members, so they were unwilling to join and contribute.

q.q: Explain why the private market fails to supply a non-excludable public good.
q.answer: free riding|incentive not to pay|no automatic force|no one willing to purchase
q.explanation: Non-excludability means everyone has an incentive to let others pay, so no automatic force provides the good and the private market may offer no output.

q.q: Church and mosque services financed by a collection basket during the ceremony illustrate provision of public goods through:
q.explanation: Religious beliefs are listed as a mechanism, since religion can prevent free riding by convincing people that God is watching.

q.q: When a city street is congested, it is:
q.explanation: The review questions classify a congested street as a common resource: rival in use but non-excludable.

q.q: Public provision of a good necessarily means the government also produces it.
q.explanation: A municipality may provide garbage collection while hiring a private firm to produce it; provision and production are different.

q.q: An externality is best defined as:
options: an extra private cost paid by the producer
a cost or benefit of consumption or production falling on others that is not reflected in the price
the profit earned by a monopoly
q.explanation: An externality is a cost or benefit that affects an otherwise uninvolved party who did not choose to bear it.

q.q: Education and flower farming are examples of activities that generate positive externalities.
q.explanation: The lesson lists flower farming, education, street lights, parks and neatness as positive externality activities.

q.q: In the presence of a negative externality:
q.explanation: With an external cost of pollution, marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost, since MSC = MPC + MEC.

q.q: When a negative externality exists, the profit-maximizing market produces:
options: more than the social optimum, an over production of QQ*
q.explanation: Producing where MPC = P ignores the external cost, so over production of QQ* arises relative to point e*.

q.q: State the efficiency condition that the presence of an externality breaks.
q.answer: MC=P|marginal cost equals price|MSC equals P|MSC=MSB
q.explanation: The externality creates a difference between marginal cost and price, while efficiency requires MC = P.

q.q: Both negative and positive externalities create a deadweight loss to society.
q.explanation: Whether from over production or under production, welfare at e* exceeds welfare at e by the area ee*c, a deadweight loss.

q.q: The per-unit tax proposed by A.C. Pigou in 1920 should equal:
options: the difference between MSC and PMC at the socially optimal output
the total revenue of the firm
q.explanation: Pigou's per-unit tax equals the gap between social and private cost corresponding to the socially optimal output.

q.q: According to the Coase theorem (1960), private bargaining succeeds when:
options: transaction costs are zero or minimal, affected parties are few and property rights are well defined
q.explanation: Coase's assumptions are minimal transaction cost, a small number of individuals and well-defined initial property rights; the optimum then depends on bargaining power.

q.q: What is the term for making the external cost or benefit part of the decision-maker's own private cost or benefit?
q.explanation: All externality solutions recognize the need for internalizing externalities.

q.q: The optimal amount of pollution is zero pollution.
q.explanation: Optimum pollution does not mean zero pollution, because zero pollution implies zero production.

q.q: Give two characteristics of externalities from the lesson (besides being positive or negative).
q.answer: generated by consumers or producers|non-rival and non-excludable|reciprocal in nature|result from combined action of parties
q.explanation: Externalities arise from consumers or producers, are a special kind of public good or bad, and are reciprocal in nature.

q.q: Asymmetric information exists when:
options: one party to a transaction has more information than the other
a single seller controls the market
q.explanation: Asymmetric information means different agents have a different amount of information about a good.

q.q: Adverse selection is sometimes known as the hidden information problem.
q.explanation: Adverse selection is also called the hidden information, anti-selection or negative selection problem.

q.q: Health insurance being more likely purchased by people who are more likely to get sick is an example of:
q.explanation: This is the hidden information problem: the insurer cannot observe the buyer's health type.

q.q: An insured driver becoming less vigilant about locking his car illustrates:
q.explanation: The hidden action problem: the party insulated from risk behaves less carefully, since the insurer bears part of the loss.

q.q: What is the term for the situation where one side of the market cannot observe the actions of the other side?
q.explanation: Moral hazard, the hidden action problem, is the inability to observe and verify the agent's action.

q.q: A good used-car owner offers a warranty while owners of bad cars cannot afford one. Name the solution and explain why it works.
q.explanation: Signalling conveys meaningful information: only owners of good cars can profitably offer a warranty.

q.q: Banks asking borrowers for financial history, job security and reason for borrowing is an example of:
q.explanation: Screening is a strategy for combating adverse selection where the less informed lender learns about the borrower.

q.q: Symmetric information means all parties have complete information about the economic variables relevant for their decisions.
q.explanation: This is the definition of symmetric information given in the unit summary.

q.q: Explain why asymmetric information can cause a transaction to disappear.
q.answer: imbalance in power|distrust of the other side|transaction can go away
q.explanation: Information asymmetry creates an imbalance in power in transactions which can sometimes cause the transaction to go away.

q.q: Offering health insurance as a fringe benefit with rates based on the average over all employees is designed to eliminate:
q.explanation: Because all employees participate and rates are based on the employee average, adverse selection is eliminated.

q.q: State two limitations of signalling mentioned in the lesson.
q.answer: cost of time money or energy to the sender|receiver may not trust the signal|signalling equilibrium may break down
q.explanation: The limitations concern how much the sender should spend, whether the receiver can trust the signal, and when the signalling equilibrium breaks down.

q.q: Consumer protection means:
options: safeguarding the interest and rights of consumers
q.explanation: It refers to measures protecting consumers from unscrupulous and unethical malpractices by business, with speedy redressal of grievances.

q.q: Selling something of little value instead of the real product is the sale of:
q.explanation: Spurious goods mean selling something of little value instead of the real product.

q.q: Hoarding and black-marketing lead to scarcity and a rise in price.
q.explanation: This is stated among the common business malpractices leading to consumer exploitation.

q.q: Which Ethiopian law provided rights to consumers in 2013?
q.explanation: The Consumer Proclamation No. 813/2013 provides the rights to consumers.

q.q: Under Proclamation No. 813/2013, a consumer can claim compensation:
options: jointly or severally from the manufacturer, importer, wholesaler or retailer
q.explanation: Compensation may be claimed jointly or severally from persons who participated in the supply of the goods or services.

q.q: A consumer who examined quality or made price bargains can be obliged to buy the goods.
q.explanation: Consumers should not be obliged to buy because they looked into quality or options or made price bargains.

q.q: Give one reason the lesson gives for why consumers need protection.
q.answer: helpless position of consumers|lack of awareness|ignorance|laziness|vulnerability to malpractices
q.explanation: The necessity arises mainly due to the helpless position of consumers, and many do not exercise their rights due to lack of awareness, ignorance or laziness.

q.q: The principle of trusteeship states that manufacturers and producers:
options: are merely trustees of resources supplied by society
q.explanation: Resources are supplied by society, so businesses are merely trustees who should use them for society's benefit, including consumers.

q.q: One main objective of the Ethiopian Consumer Protection Act is to:
q.explanation: The Act's objectives include protecting the market from unfair practices, ensuring safe and suitable goods for the price paid, and accelerating economic development.

q.q: Consumers' satisfaction is described as the key to the success of a business.
q.explanation: The lesson states consumer satisfaction is the key to business success, so firms should serve consumer interests.

q.q: What term describes goods that do not conform to prescribed quality standards?
q.explanation: Sub-standard goods are goods which do not conform to prescribed quality standards.

q.q: The general objectives of macroeconomic policy include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: maximizing profits of a single firm
q.explanation: Micro-firm profit is not a macroeconomic objective; the list contains output, growth, employment, price stability, income distribution equality and the balance of payments.

q.q: During a recession, the economy is characterized by:
options: idle productive capacity and rising unemployment
q.explanation: In recession, income, output and employment are below potential, with idle capacity and rising unemployment.

q.q: Classical economists believed that an automatic mechanism works to restore stability in the economy.
q.explanation: Classical economists believed recession would cure itself and inflation would be automatically controlled.

q.q: Economies are always free of macroeconomic policy because prices adjust instantly.
q.explanation: The 1930s depression showed that no automatic mechanism ensures stability, so nations adopt macroeconomic policies.

q.q: Name the economist whose experience-based argument in the 1930s called for government intervention to cure depression and inflation.
q.explanation: Keynes argued for government intervention after the 1930s evidence showed no automatic stabilization.

q.q: Which type of macroeconomic policy consists of economy-wide wage and price controls, ranging from voluntary guidelines to mandatory freezes?
q.explanation: Income policy is economy-wide wage and price control, from voluntary guidelines to mandatory wage/price freezes.

q.q: Economic growth can be attained by raising:
options: the rates of saving and investment and accumulating capital
q.explanation: Growth depends on raising the rates of saving and investment and accumulating capital.

q.q: Distinguish between deficient demand and excess demand in terms of the full-employment level of output.
q.answer: deficient demand is aggregate demand below full employment output|excess demand is aggregate demand above full employment output
q.explanation: Deficient demand means aggregate demand falls short of output at full employment; excess demand exceeds the available output at full employment.

q.q: A large-scale overheated economy shows:
options: upward pressure on wages and prices
q.explanation: In an overheated economy demand is so high that there is upward pressure on wages and prices, causing inflation.

q.q: Arrange these macroeconomic policies from the one operated by the government's budget to the one operated through the currency's external value.
q.explanation: Correct order: fiscal policy (budget), monetary policy (money), income policy (wages and prices), foreign exchange policy (currency value).

q.q: The same macroeconomic instruments are used unchanged in every economy regardless of conditions.
q.explanation: Policies and instruments vary from one economy to another and according to prevailing economic conditions.

q.q: Fiscal policy refers to:
options: decisions to alter market interest rates
control of the producer price index
q.explanation: Fiscal policy is the expenditure and revenue (tax) policy of the government.

q.q: Transfer payments are commonly referred to as entitlements because they are locked in by earlier legislation.
q.explanation: Transfer payments such as social security benefits are not discretionary; earlier legislation locks them in.

q.q: To fight deficient demand, the major instruments of expansionary fiscal policy are:
options: increased expenditure and reduced tax rates
reduced expenditure and increased tax rates
increased expenditure and increased tax rates
q.explanation: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government expenditure and lowers tax rates to boost aggregate demand.

q.q: During inflation, a contractionary revenue policy would:
options: abolish taxes on lower income groups
raise tax rates, especially on rich people, to withdraw purchasing power
q.explanation: Higher taxes withdraw purchasing power from taxpayers, reducing effective demand; they should not harm production and savings.

q.q: What name is given to taxes on imported goods?
q.explanation: Taxes on imported goods are known as tariffs, part of taxes on production and imports.

q.q: Explain what happens in the AD-AS model when a very large budget deficit pushes output above potential GDP.
q.answer: overheating economy produces inflation|economy overheats with upward pressure on wages and prices
q.explanation: The intersection of AD and SRAS occurs above potential GDP; an overheating economy experiences upward pressure on wages and prices, calling for contractionary fiscal policy.

q.q: Grants in aid are expenditure for the federal government and revenue for the receiving governments.
q.explanation: Grants in aid reflect federal assistance to state and local governments, so they are spending for one side and revenue for the other.

q.q: Name the situation in which aggregate demand exceeds the available output at full employment.
q.explanation: Excess demand is the excess of aggregate demand over the available output at full employment, causing inflation.

q.q: Which item belongs under government spending (G) rather than transfer payments?
options: Purchase of weapons for the military
q.explanation: Government spending includes the purchase of weapons for the military; the others are direct payments without goods or services in return.

q.q: Put the expansionary fiscal policy chain in the correct order.
options: Government cuts taxes and raises spending
Disposable income in people's hands increases
q.explanation: First tax cuts and higher spending, then higher disposable income, then rising consumption and AD, then higher output and employment.

q.q: A reduction in the bank rate is:
q.explanation: Reducing the discount (bank) rate is a tool of expansionary monetary policy that increases money supply and lending.

q.q: The NBE cut the minimum deposit reserve from 15% to 10% in January 2012 to encourage banks to lend, particularly to the export sector.
q.explanation: In January 2012 the reserve requirement was cut from 15% to 10% and the liquid asset ratio from 25% to 20%, aiming to encourage lending to the export sector.

q.q: To control the situation of excess demand, the central bank:
q.explanation: Selling government securities absorbs liquidity and reduces banks' lending capacity, curtailing excess demand.

q.q: Give the name of the market through which the NBE actively conducts its open market operations.
q.explanation: NBE conducts OMO actively through the treasury bills market to influence liquidity and money supply.

q.q: Define the discount rate in your own words.
q.answer: the interest rate the national bank charges commercial banks to borrow|rate charged on central bank loans to banks
q.explanation: The discount rate is the interest rate the National Bank charges banks to borrow funds from it.

q.q: Normally the discount rate is set below the short-term inter-bank market rate.
q.explanation: The textbook notes the discount rate is usually set below the short-term inter-bank market rate.

q.q: Which sequence correctly describes the effect of tight monetary policy?
options: money supply rises, rates fall, AD shifts right
money supply falls, rates rise, AD shifts left
money supply rises, rates rise, AD shifts left
money supply falls, rates fall, AD shifts right
q.explanation: Tight policy shrinks money and credit, raises the interest rate, discourages borrowing, and shifts aggregate demand left.

q.q: Explain why monetary policy should be countercyclical, and give the danger of doing it poorly.
q.answer: loosen during recession unemployment and tighten when inflation threatens|danger of overreaction
q.explanation: The National Bank should loosen money in recessions and tighten when inflation threatens; doing either too strongly triggers the opposite problem.

q.q: When the central bank buys government bonds, the Birr paid increases the monetary base and the money supply.
q.explanation: Purchases of bonds raise the monetary base and then the money supply; sales do the reverse.

q.q: In which month and year did the discount window facility for commercial banks start in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: The textbook records that the Ethiopian discount window facility for commercial banks started in March 2001.

q.q: Monetary policy is formulated based on inputs from:
options: GDP and inflation figures, sector growth rates and geopolitical events
the winning numbers of treasury bill auctions only
the personal wishes of commercial bank managers
q.explanation: Inputs include macroeconomic numbers such as GDP and inflation, sector growth rates, geopolitical developments and survey results.

q.q: Order the contractionary monetary policy chain.
options: Central bank sells securities and raises the RRR
Banks lose cash reserves and lending capacity
Aggregate demand shifts left, easing inflation
q.explanation: Selling securities and raising the RRR drains reserves first, then rates rise, then lending falls, then AD eases inflation.

q.q: A minimum wage is legally a:
q.explanation: The minimum wage is a legally mandated price floor on hourly wages, below which a job may not be offered or accepted.

q.q: A price ceiling is a maximum legal price set below the equilibrium price and causes a shortage.
q.explanation: A price ceiling is a maximum legal price below equilibrium; it provides perverse incentives and causes a shortage.

q.q: When the supply of labour increases in a free market, the equilibrium wage:
q.explanation: When the supply of labour increases the equilibrium price falls; increased demand raises it.

q.q: Give the term for the economy-wide wage and price controls instituted most commonly as a response to inflation.
q.explanation: Income policies are economy-wide wages and price controls used against inflation.

q.q: State two purposes of the minimum wage.
q.answer: protect workers from unduly low pay|reduce poverty and inequality|equal remuneration for work of equal value|minimum living wage
q.explanation: Purposes include protection from unduly low pay, a just share of progress, a minimum living wage and reducing poverty and inequality.

q.q: A price floor must be higher than the equilibrium price in order to be effective.
q.explanation: Only a floor above the equilibrium price binds the market and creates a surplus.

q.q: What economic harm does a price floor above equilibrium create besides the surplus, in terms of total surplus?
q.explanation: The mandated higher price transfers consumer surplus to producer surplus and creates a deadweight loss.

q.q: Which behaviour characterizes firms and workers in a perfectly competitive labour market?
options: Government setting every wage by decree
Firms colluding to lower wages secretly
q.explanation: Wage-taking behaviour means neither workers nor firms control the market wage.

q.q: The vertical height of the market labour supply curve measures the opportunity cost of employing the last labour hour.
q.explanation: The height of the supply curve measures marginal opportunity cost, since more hours must be compensated by a higher wage.

q.q: Give the informal name for the distributional measure by which a country keeps real wages expanding in line with productivity.
q.explanation: A policy maintaining real wage expansion in line with productivity is an income policy providing sustainable demand expansion.

q.q: Under a binding price floor, consumers are likely to:
options: switch to substitutes such as from butter to margarine
q.explanation: Facing a higher price, consumers reduce purchases, switch to substitutes or drop out of the market.

q.q: Order the income policy instruments from the most permissive to the most mandatory.
q.explanation: Income policy ranges from voluntary guidelines, through wage floors and controlled prices, up to mandatory freezes.

q.q: The formula for calculating exchange rates given in the textbook is:
options: Starting amount (original currency) x Ending amount (new currency)
Starting amount (original currency) / Ending amount (new currency)
Ending amount (new currency) - Starting amount (original currency)
Starting amount (original currency) + Ending amount (new currency)
q.explanation: Exchange rate = starting amount in the original currency divided by ending amount in the new currency.

q.q: Depreciation is an increase in the exchange rate due to market forces.
q.explanation: Under a floating regime, depreciation is a market-force increase in the exchange rate; appreciation is a market-force decrease.

q.q: An undervalued fixed exchange rate acts as:
options: an import subsidy and an export tax
an import tax and an export subsidy
a price ceiling on foreign currency
q.explanation: An undervalued rate promotes domestic industries by acting as an import tax and an export subsidy.

q.q: Name the market in which people or firms use one currency to purchase another currency.
q.explanation: That is the foreign exchange market.

q.q: Explain the impact of devaluation or depreciation on the balance of payments.
q.answer: exports become cheaper and imports more expensive so the current account improves|improves the current account or overall balance of payments
q.explanation: Devaluation or depreciation improves the current account and/or overall balance of payments by making exports cheaper and imports more expensive.

q.q: An appreciation of the Ethiopian Birr relative to the US dollar would increase net exports.
q.explanation: Appreciation makes exports more expensive and imports cheaper, worsening the external balance, not increasing net exports.

q.q: Which factor causes depreciation when it grows large, as investors sell their bonds in the open market?
q.explanation: High government debt leads investors to sell bonds, decreasing the exchange rate value.

q.q: State the official exchange rate at which the Birr was first introduced in 1945.
q.answer: birr 2.48 per us dollar|2.48 birr per us dollar|2.48
q.explanation: The Birr was introduced in 1945 at an official rate of Birr 2.48 per US dollar, with a value of 0.36 grams of fine gold.

q.q: What happened when the NBE devalued the Birr by 20% in August 2010, and what does this show about inflation in Ethiopia?
q.answer: inflation rose about 33% in 2011 showing inflation responds positively to devaluation
q.explanation: The August 2010 devaluation from 13.63 to 16.35 Birr/USD was followed by inflation of about 33% in 2011, showing a positive response of inflation to devaluation.

q.q: Currently, the Ethiopian exchange rate is determined:
options: by a fixed government announcement each year
through the interbank foreign exchange market on a daily basis
by the gold content of the Birr
q.explanation: Today the exchange rate is determined through the interbank foreign exchange market on a daily basis.

q.q: The 1998 interbank foreign exchange market is a wholesale market exclusively for banks to trade foreign exchange with each other.
q.explanation: The interbank market is wholesale, bank-exclusive, with large amounts and a narrower buying-selling spread.

q.q: Put these Ethiopian exchange rate reforms in chronological order.
options: Unification of official and auction rates (1995)
q.explanation: Order: 1993 auctions, 1995 unification, 1996 weekly/wholesale auctions, 1998 interbank market.

q.q: According to the OECD definition used in the textbook, a tax is:
options: A voluntary payment for public services
A compulsory, unrequited payment to general government
A fee charged in direct proportion to benefits received
q.explanation: The OECD defines tax as compulsory, unrequited payments to general government.

q.q: The word unrequited in the definition of tax means that:
options: Benefits from government are not proportional to the tax paid
Taxpayers receive no public services at all
Taxes are paid only in cash
q.explanation: Unrequited means benefits provided are not in proportion to payments, so tax is levied without a quid pro quo.

q.q: Taxation typically accounts for 90 percent or more of total governmental receipts in times of peace.
q.explanation: The textbook states taxation typically accounts for 90 percent or more of receipts in peacetime.

q.q: Adam Smith proposed the classical canons of taxation in:
q.explanation: Adam Smith set out the canons of taxation in The Wealth of Nations, 1776.

q.q: Which canon of taxation requires that the cost of collection should be the minimum possible?
q.explanation: The canon of economy says the cost of collection should be minimum.

q.q: The canon of fiscal adequacy requires that the tax system:
options: Yields enough revenue so government is not forced into deficit financing
Taxes everyone at exactly the same rate
Collects tax only in convenient seasons
q.explanation: Fiscal adequacy means the system yields enough revenue to avoid deficit financing.

q.q: Define the incidence of a tax.
q.answer: final resting place of the tax|distribution of the tax burden among economic units
q.explanation: Incidence is the final resting place of the tax, found by who is made worse off and by how much.

q.q: Which of the following is an indirect tax?
q.explanation: VAT is a consumption tax whose impact and incidence fall on different persons, making it indirect.

q.q: A higher tax rate tends to reduce the level of the tax base because it makes the activity less attractive.
q.explanation: The textbook notes higher rates reduce the tax base by making the taxed activity less attractive.

q.q: In the UK, the basic rate of income tax is 20 percent paid on income above a threshold of:
q.explanation: The textbook gives a basic rate of 20 percent on income over the threshold of 11,500 pounds.

q.q: State any two characteristics of a good tax system.
q.answer: simple, financially adequate and elastic|broad based|administratively efficient|balanced and harmonious|reduces inequalities|ensures economic stability|instrument of economic growth|socially advantageous|optimum allocation of resources
q.explanation: Any two features from the textbook list, such as simplicity, adequacy, elasticity and administrative efficiency, are correct.

q.q: Suppose Ayele has an income of 4,000 birr and pays tax of 300 birr while Atote has an income of 20,000 birr and pays tax of 1,400 birr. This tax is:
q.explanation: Average rates are 7.5 percent for Ayele and 7 percent for Atote; the rate falls as income rises, so the tax is regressive.

q.q: Under the benefits approach, tax obligations should be based on the benefits received from the enjoyment of public services.
q.explanation: The benefits approach ties each taxpayer's contribution to the benefits received from public services.

q.q: The main weakness of the benefits approach is that:
options: Nobody ever benefits from public spending
About half of government spending cannot be attributed to specific beneficiaries
It is required by Adam Smith's canons
It ignores the expenditure side of the budget
q.explanation: It is hard, if not impossible, to determine who benefits most from spending on the army, police, diplomacy or the courts.

q.q: Define horizontal equity.
q.answer: people in the same circumstances pay the same taxes|equal ability treated equally
q.explanation: Horizontal equity means people in the same circumstances pay the same taxes.

q.q: A progressive tax is one where:
options: The average tax rate falls as income rises
Everyone pays the same percentage of income
The average tax rate rises with income
Only the rich pay any tax at all
q.explanation: Under a progressive tax the average rate rises with income, so high earners pay a higher share.

q.q: Under a proportional tax, the average tax rate is the same at all income levels.
q.explanation: A proportional tax takes the same share of income from everyone.

q.q: State the two equity principles on which the ability-to-pay approach is based.
q.answer: horizontal equity and vertical equity|horizontal and vertical equity
q.explanation: The ability-to-pay approach rests on horizontal equity and vertical equity.

q.q: Under a regressive tax, people with higher incomes pay:
options: A higher percentage of their income in taxes
The same percentage of their income in taxes
A lower percentage of their income in taxes
q.explanation: The average rate falls when income rises, so high earners pay a lower share of income.

q.q: Why is a comprehensive measure of ability to pay (covering consumption, wealth and leisure) not used in practice?
q.answer: such a measure is not practicable|it is too difficult to measure
q.explanation: The textbook states the ideal comprehensive measure is not practicable, even though it would reflect entire welfare.

q.q: Ethiopia's employment income tax applies rates from 10 to 35 percent. Which equity concept does this express?
q.explanation: Rates rise with earnings, applying vertical equity through a progressive structure.

q.q: Ethiopia introduced the concept of income taxation in 1944 with a decree requiring all peasants to pay:
options: A fixed head tax in cash
q.explanation: The 1944 decree required peasants to pay one-tenth of their agricultural products to tax officials.

q.q: Employment income tax is withheld by employers and is a final tax, so employees earning only employment income need not declare it.
q.explanation: Schedule A employment income tax is withheld by employers and is a final tax.

q.q: Under Proclamation No. 286/2002, income from rental of buildings falls under:
q.explanation: Schedule B covers income from rental of buildings.

q.q: Arrange the income tax schedules in their correct alphabetical order.
q.explanation: The order is A employment, B rental, C business, D other income, plus E exempt.

q.q: Ethiopia's standard VAT rate, applied since 1 January 2003, is:
q.explanation: The VAT Act took effect on 1 January 2003 with a standard rate of 15 percent.

q.q: For services rendered locally, the turnover tax rate is:
options: 2% on contractors, grain mills, tractors and combine harvesters and 10% on others
q.explanation: TOT is 2 percent on contractors, grain mills, tractors and combine harvesters and 10 percent on other services.

q.q: Registration for VAT is limited to persons whose annual transactions in total value exceed what amount?
q.explanation: Administrative feasibility limits VAT registration to those with annual transactions exceeding 500,000 Birr.

q.q: Which statement about Ethiopian excise tax is correct?
options: It applies to only 5 goods at 10%
It applies to 19 groups of items and 378 goods with rates from 5% to 500%
It is payable only on exports
It has a flat rate of 35%
q.explanation: Excise tax is applicable on 19 groups of items and 378 goods, with rates ranging from 5 to 500 percent.

q.q: Surtax of 10 percent applies to fertilizers, petroleum and lubricants imported into Ethiopia.
q.explanation: Surtax applies to imported goods except fertilizers, petroleum and lubricants, certain motor vehicles, aircraft, spacecraft and capital goods.

q.q: State the pension contribution shares payable by the employer and the employee to the Private Organizations Pension Fund.
q.explanation: Contributions are 11 percent from the employer and 7 percent from the employee, based on salary.

q.q: Explain how tax and accounting are linked.
q.answer: all taxation involves accounting processes|financial statements are used to make tax calculations|records determine tax liability
q.explanation: Taxation involves accounting processes: financial statements and figures are used for the tax calculations, and businesses keep records to determine liabilities.

q.q: The two biggest criticisms of tax systems around the world focus on:
options: Complexity of administration and difficulty of understanding and complying
q.explanation: The textbook names complexity of administration and the difficulty for taxpayers to understand and comply as the major criticisms.

q.q: Tax avoidance is illegal from the perspective of the law.
q.explanation: Tax avoidance is not illegal; it takes full advantage of provisions of the tax code, though it burdens administration.

q.q: Tax evasion is best described as:
options: Using deductions approved in the tax schedule
Arranging one's affairs to reduce the tax burden
Falsifying information on a tax return or not filing at all
q.explanation: Evasion means falsifying information on a return to reduce liability, or failing to file and pay legally due taxes, which is illegal.

q.q: State the two reasons the textbook gives for the existence of underground economic activities.
q.answer: illegal activities and high marginal tax rates|illegal activities; high marginal rates incentivize non-reporting
q.explanation: Underground activities exist because certain activities are illegal and want no records, and high marginal tax rates give an incentive to obtain income without reporting it.

q.q: Which of the following is listed as a problem of tax systems in developing countries including Ethiopia?
q.explanation: Developing-country problems include complexity, perception of corruption, cost of compliance, fairness perception and tax knowledge.

q.q: Tax knowledge has a positive effect on voluntary tax compliance.
q.explanation: The textbook states tax knowledge has a positive effect on voluntary tax compliance.

q.q: What term describes the degree to which taxpayers comply with the tax laws?
q.explanation: Tax compliance is the degree to which taxpayers comply with the tax laws.

q.q: In developed countries, a key tool for improving tax administration efficiency is:
options: Modernising customer services with client orientation
q.explanation: Developed countries modernise customer services, applying client-oriented or customer-oriented management techniques.

q.q: Explain how complexity of a tax system leads to lower revenue.
q.answer: complexity raises compliance costs which encourages evasion and avoidance|complex rules grow the underground economy
q.explanation: Complexity makes correct calculation costly, encouraging unreported transactions (evasion) and demand for shelters (avoidance), shrinking revenue.

q.q: Which is a need that tax administrations in Ethiopia and elsewhere must confront?
options: Reducing costs of tax assessment and collection
Increasing the complexity of fiscal legislation
q.explanation: Administrations face growing workload, legislative complexity, taxpayer attitude, and the need to improve service and reduce assessment and collection costs.

q.q: Which organisation defined poverty as the pronounced deprivation in wellbeing?
q.explanation: The World Bank (2000) defines poverty as the pronounced deprivation in wellbeing.

q.q: Which of the following correctly characterises absolute poverty?
options: It is defined only against other countries' incomes
It is the inability or barely ability to meet subsistence essentials like food, clothing and shelter
It applies only in rich countries
It is measured by the Gini coefficient
q.explanation: Absolute poverty is being unable, or only barely able, to meet subsistence essentials such as food, clothing and shelter.

q.q: A person can be poor in the relative sense even while meeting all basic needs.
q.explanation: Relative poverty is judged against other people's standing in the economy, so it can exist even when basic needs are met.

q.q: State the international absolute poverty line per day (in PPP dollars) most commonly used for extreme poverty.
q.explanation: The textbook cites people living on less than $1.25 a day in PPP dollars as one absolute poverty line.

q.q: In the three steps of measuring poverty, which comes first?
q.explanation: The first step is defining an indicator of welfare; then the poverty line, then the summary statistic.

q.q: Give the term for the minimum acceptable standard of a welfare indicator that separates the poor from the non-poor.
q.explanation: That minimum standard is called the poverty line.

q.q: A kebele has 200 residents and 40 live below the poverty line. Its headcount index is:
q.explanation: Headcount index = H/N = 40/200 = 0.2.

q.q: The Multidimensional Poverty Index uses health, education and standard of living as its three dimensions.
q.explanation: The MPI (UNDP, 2010) incorporates health, education and standard of living at the household level.

q.q: According to Sen's capability approach, poverty is best understood as:
options: low income measured by the headcount
the inability to pursue wellbeing because of a lack of economic means
q.explanation: Sen argues poverty is not low wellbeing itself but the inability to pursue wellbeing for lack of economic means; what matters is capabilities.

q.q: Arrange the three steps of poverty measurement in the correct order.
q.explanation: The order is: define the welfare indicator, set the poverty line, then generate the summary statistic.

q.q: Name one of the reasons for measuring poverty given in the lesson.
q.answer: keep poor people on the agenda|identify poor people|monitor and evaluate projects and policies|evaluate the effectiveness of institutions
q.explanation: Poverty is measured to keep the poor on the agenda, to target interventions, to monitor and evaluate projects, and to assess institutions.

q.q: The functional or factor share distribution of income compares:
options: the share of labour in total income with returns to land and capital as rent, interest and profit
q.explanation: Functional distribution asks what percentage of national income labour receives as a whole versus rent, interest and profit.

q.q: A quintile contains what fraction of the population?
q.explanation: Quintiles are fifths, so each quintile is 20% of the population; deciles are tenths.

q.q: In the textbook data, what share of total income does the bottom 40% of the population receive?
q.explanation: The first quintile receives 5% and the second 9%, so the bottom 40% receives 14% of total income.

q.q: Using the Kuznets ratio with a bottom-40% share of 14% and a top-20% share of 51%, the ratio is approximately:
q.explanation: The ratio is 14 divided by 51, approximately 0.28.

q.q: At the point halfway along the 45-degree diagonal of the Lorenz diagram:
options: 50% of income goes to 50% of the population
20% of income goes to 80% of the population
the curve is at its most bowed point
q.explanation: On the diagonal the percentage of income received always equals the percentage of recipients, so halfway means 50 to 50.

q.q: The more bowed out the Lorenz curve, the less equal the distribution of income.
q.explanation: A curve bowed further from the 45-degree line represents a more unequal distribution.

q.q: The Gini coefficient is expressed as the ratio of:
options: the area between the Lorenz curve and the 45-degree line to the total area under the 45-degree line
the top quintile share to the bottom quintile share
the poverty line to average income
q.explanation: The Gini coefficient is the area between the curve and diagonal divided by the total area under the diagonal.

q.q: Name the Italian statistician who first formulated the Gini coefficient in 1912.
q.explanation: The Gini coefficient is named after Corrado Gini.

q.q: Explain what a Lorenz curve with a Gini coefficient of 0.28 versus 0.60 tells you about two countries.
q.answer: high gini means more unequal|0.60 country is more unequal than the 0.28 country
q.explanation: The higher Gini (0.60) means the second country's income is distributed more unequally.

q.q: In the textbook data, the top 5% of the population (the richest individual) receives:
q.explanation: The richest individual receives 15% of income, exceeding the 14% received by the entire bottom 40%.

q.q: Arrange the steps of analysing the size distribution of income in order.
options: Divide the population into quintiles or deciles
Determine what proportion of national income each group receives
q.explanation: First rank incomes in ascending order, then group into quintiles or deciles, then find each group's income share.

q.q: The proportion of the world's population living in extreme poverty declined from 36% in 1990 to what level in 2015?
q.explanation: Extreme poverty declined from 36% in 1990 to 10% in 2015.

q.q: In 2010, about how many people lived on less than $2 a day?
q.explanation: Some 2.4 billion people, more than one third of the world's population, lived on less than $2 a day in 2010.

q.q: The majority of people living on less than $1.90 a day are found in:
q.explanation: The UN reported that the majority of people on less than $1.90 a day live in sub-Saharan Africa.

q.q: Sub-Saharan Africa experienced virtually no poverty rate reduction from 1950 to 2000.
q.explanation: The textbook states the region experienced virtually no rate reduction from 1950 to 2000.

q.q: SDG Goal 1 (2015-2030) aims to:
options: end poverty in all its forms
q.explanation: Goal 1 of the SDGs aims to end poverty in all its forms.

q.q: State two reasons given in the lesson for women being over-represented among the world's poor.
q.answer: lower earning capacity|female-headed households|limited control over spouses income|less access to education|less access to formal employment|less access to social security
q.explanation: Female-headed households, lower earning capacity, limited control over spouses' income and less access to education and formal employment combine against women.

q.q: Nutrition and family health programmes are more effective when they target women because:
options: most of women's marginal income goes into household nutritional intake
men refuse to eat better food
q.explanation: When household income is marginal, most of women's income goes toward household nutrition, unlike men's income.

q.q: Public poverty programmes that work exclusively with men tend to reduce gender inequality.
q.explanation: Such programmes tend to exacerbate inequalities, since training and extension services favour men and marginalise women's plots.

q.q: Give one example of unremunerated work done by women that limits their control over household resources.
q.answer: collecting firewood|cooking|parenting|unpaid family agriculture work|unpaid family business work
q.explanation: Collecting firewood, cooking and parenting are unremunerated, and much family agriculture or business work is unpaid.

q.q: Which is a stated consequence of a decline in women's economic status?
options: slower rates of economic growth in the long run
q.explanation: The low status of women is likely to translate into slower rates of economic growth, and growth that misses the worst-off fails a principal goal of development.

q.q: What should development policy do about women, according to the lesson, and why?
q.answer: integrate women into development programmes|increase female participation in education training employment extension|equal access to government resources
q.explanation: Policy must integrate women into programmes - education, training, formal employment and extension - because their welfare determines children's welfare and future growth.

q.q: Ethiopia's estimated population as of 2021 was about:
q.explanation: The textbook gives an estimated population of 118 million people as of 2021.

q.q: According to the World Bank (2020), the share of Ethiopians below the national poverty line fell from 38% to what level between 2008/09 and 2018/19?
q.explanation: The share below the national poverty line declined from 38% to 24% over 2008/09-2018/19.

q.q: Government figures show Ethiopian headcount poverty declining from 59% in 1992 to:
q.explanation: Headcount poverty declined from 59% in 1992 to 29.5% in 2011 (MoFED, 2012).

q.q: By how many percentage points did headcount poverty fall from 1992 to 2011?
q.explanation: 59 minus 29.5 equals 29.5 percentage points, meaning poverty was exactly halved.

q.q: Ethiopia's 2019 HDI of 0.485 places it at rank 173 of 189 countries, in which category?
q.explanation: An HDI of 0.485 puts the country in the low human development category (UNDP).

q.q: Which agency conducts Ethiopia's Household Income and Consumption Expenditure Surveys and the Welfare Monitoring Survey?
q.explanation: The Central Statistical Agency conducts the regular HICES and the WMS established in 1996.

q.q: Idir is Ethiopia's rotating credit association in which members contribute weekly or monthly to a common pool.
q.explanation: That describes Iqub; Idir is a traditional burial association characterised as group life insurance.

q.q: Explain why Iqub is more accessible than banks for a poor Ethiopian family.
q.answer: more flexible and accessible than banks|minimal paperwork|no discouragement of people without formal education
q.explanation: Iqub requires minimal paperwork, is flexible and accessible, and weekly or monthly contributions keep a steady flow of money on a rotational basis.

q.q: Cottage industries contribute to poverty reduction mainly because they:
options: require very little investment but employ labour-intensive techniques
q.explanation: Cottage industries need very little investment yet employ labour-intensive techniques, cutting unemployment and offering self-employment for men and women.

q.q: Name one of the oldest forms of cottage industry in Ethiopia.
q.explanation: Weaving, leather working, pottery, basket making and blacksmithing are the oldest cottage industries in Ethiopia.

q.q: Rural poverty in Ethiopia is declining faster than urban poverty.
q.explanation: Poverty is still a challenge especially in rural areas where the rate of decrease is slower than urban areas, with rain-fed agriculture exposed to climate vulnerability.

q.q: When did Ethiopia create the National Economic Council that prepared its three five-year development plans?
q.explanation: The National Economic Council was created in 1954/55 and helped prepare the three Imperial Five-Year Plans.

q.q: Which Five-Year Plan shifted focus to agricultural development in order to address rising food shortages?
q.explanation: The Third Five-Year Plan (1968-1973) shifted focus to agriculture and created the Integrated Rural Development project.

q.q: During the First Five-Year Plan, imports grew faster than exports, so the negative balance of trade was corrected.
q.explanation: Exports grew 3.5% but imports grew 6.4% a year, so the plan failed to correct the negative balance of trade that had existed since 1951.

q.q: The Derg main development strategy was agriculture-led industrialization.
q.explanation: The Derg deployed industry-led development under a centrally planned, socialist economy; agriculture-led ADLI came in 1994 under the EPRDF.

q.q: ADLI, launched in 1994, had as its main objective:
options: attaining food self-sufficiency by raising agricultural productivity and output
privatizing all state farms within one year
q.explanation: ADLI aimed at food self-sufficiency by increasing agricultural productivity so agriculture could drive industrial development.

q.q: Which EPRDF extension system distributed fertilizer, seed, credit and better farming practices to smallholder farmers?
q.answer: PADETES|Participatory Demonstration and Training Extension System
q.explanation: PADETES was the Participatory Demonstration and Training Extension System.

q.q: PASDEP (2005/06-2009/10) differed from SDPRP mainly because it aimed at:
options: private-sector development and scaling up resources to achieve the MDGs
q.explanation: PASDEP was built on SDPRP directions but aimed at private sector development and sustainable progress toward the MDGs by 2015.

q.q: GTP I and II delivered 9.2% average annual growth against an 11% target. State the size of the shortfall and one reason the textbook gives for the remaining challenges.
q.answer: 1.8 percentage points|debt, inflation, unemployment or weak structural transformation
q.explanation: Actual growth was 1.8 percentage points short of target; remaining challenges included debt distress, inflation, unemployment and sluggish structural transformation.

q.q: Put these four national development programmes in chronological order of adoption.
Explain in one sentence why the growth achieved during the GTP era still failed to improve life for many citizens.
q.answer: growth created too few jobs and was unequally shared|urban unemployment rose from 18% to 18.7% and inflation hurt the poor
q.explanation: The textbook notes job creation was inadequate, distribution unequal (Gini rose 0.30 to 0.33) and persistent inflation raised the cost of living.

q.q: In past periods of Ethiopia's economy, high inflation episodes such as the 55.2% spike of 2008 were most closely associated with:
options: macroeconomic instability driven by fuel and food price shocks and weak foreign exchange earnings
q.explanation: The 2008 inflation spike reflected high fuel and food price shocks, weaker foreign exchange earnings and rising import demand that depleted reserves.

q.q: Which best describes why the Home-grown Economic Reform was initiated?
options: To abandon growth and shrink the economy
To sustain rapid growth, reduce debt vulnerabilities and create adequate jobs
To increase reliance on debt financing
q.explanation: The HGER's central objectives are sustaining rapid growth, stable macroeconomics by reducing debt vulnerability, and adequate and sustainable job creation.

q.q: The HGER reforms are translated into action mainly through policies that enhance the supply side of the economy.
q.explanation: The textbook states the reforms are being translated into action through policies that enhance the supply side of the economy.

q.q: Which of the following is a macroeconomic reform measure under the HGER?
options: Market-based determination of interest and exchange rates
q.explanation: Financial sector reform promotes market-based interest rate and foreign exchange rate determination; the others are sectoral or structural.

q.q: Name the two international trade partnerships the textbook mentions as proof of Ethiopia's HGER commitment to global and regional integration.
q.answer: WTO and AfCFTA|World Trade Organization and African Continental Free Trade Area
q.explanation: The WTO accession negotiation and ratification of the African Continental Free Trade Area prove the HGER commitment to boosting trade and investment partnership.

q.q: Explain what crowding out means and how the HGER aims to avoid it.
q.answer: when government intervention displaces private investors|support private investors on merit and keep their participation
q.explanation: The ultimate goal of government intervention is to create strong private initiatives; intervention should not crowd out private investors but encourage their participation.

q.q: Under the HGER, the government should support development forces on the basis of their proximity to political elites.
q.explanation: Support should be based on merits and performances, not proximity to political elites or power.

q.q: Which set of commodities is targeted by the HGER import-substituting development strategy?
options: Food items, edible oil and wheat
q.explanation: Imports of food items, edible oil, wheat and similar commodities consume large sums of foreign currency and are targeted for domestic substitution.

q.q: State two reasons given in the textbook for reforming agriculture despite years of attention to the sector.
q.answer: still the lowest productive sector|improve inputs, irrigation, livestock productivity, private participation or reduce post-harvest loss
q.explanation: Agriculture has remained the lowest productive sector, so reform raises private participation, irrigation, input and finance supply, livestock productivity and reduces post-harvest loss.

q.q: Arrange the HGER reform tracks from the side closest to macroeconomic management to the side closest to people and institutions.
q.explanation: The sequence runs macroeconomic reforms, then sectoral reforms, then structural reforms.

q.q: Regarding external public debt, the HGER emphasizes:
options: minimizing commercial external loans, seeking concessional loans and rescheduling debt
q.explanation: The two main aspects are minimizing commercial external loans, searching for concessional loans and rescheduling existing debt.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why promoting remittances through the formal banking system matters for Ethiopia.
q.answer: it increases foreign currency inflow to reserves|formal remittances are cheaper and more traceable and support the reserve
q.explanation: The reform broadens incentives for the diaspora to send foreign currencies through formal banking, raising the foreign currency inflow to the economy.

q.q: Fiscal decentralization generally refers to:
options: the devolution of taxing and spending powers to sub-national government levels
q.explanation: It is the devolution of taxing and spending powers from central to sub-national (regional, provincial, municipal) authorities.

q.q: The centralization ratio is calculated as:
options: central direct government expenditure divided by total government expenditure
regional expenditure divided by federal grants
tax revenue divided by total expenditure
q.explanation: It is direct central government expenditure divided by total government expenditure, excluding federal grants and transfers.

q.q: The stated goal of Ethiopia's fiscal equalization payments is to equalize the fiscal capacity of local governments to provide services.
q.explanation: Fiscal equalization helps regional governments provide similar sets of public services with similar tax incidence.

q.q: How much money was allocated to regional states in 2017/18 under the grant formula for SDG implementation?
q.explanation: In 2017/18, Birr 7 billion was allocated to regional states to implement the SDGs and narrow regional disparities.

q.q: Which decision do most economists agree should be made by the central government?
options: Spending and taxing decisions to stabilize the economy
q.explanation: Most economists agree stabilization decisions, price stability and reducing unemployment, belong to the central government.

q.q: Define net fiscal benefits as presented in the lesson.
q.answer: the difference between utility households derive from consuming public services and the taxes they pay|utility from public services minus taxes paid
q.explanation: Net fiscal benefits equal the utility households get from public services less the taxes paid to produce them.

q.q: When each community constructs its own library instead of consolidating, the cost per user is higher than necessary.
q.explanation: Cost per person falls as the number of users increases, so each community building its own library loses scale economies.

q.q: Explain why local governments often tax capital lightly, and why economists view this as inefficient from the national point of view.
q.answer: capital is elastic locally so taxing it scares investors|inelastic nationally but elastic locally
q.explanation: Since capital may be inelastic nationally but elastic locally, local governments tax it little to promote investment, which is nationally inefficient because efficient taxes put higher rates on inelastic bases.

q.q: Put the following decentralization advantages in the textbook's order of introduction.
q.explanation: The textbook lists tailoring output to local tastes first, then fostering intergovernmental competition, then experimentation and innovation.

q.q: A pro-poor tax and spending pattern in one region eventually ends with an abandoned program because:
options: the region attracts the poor and loses rich taxpayers, shrinking the tax base
local services become free for everyone
q.explanation: Transfers to the poor attract more poor and expel rich taxpayers, leaving a small tax base and eventually abandoning the program.

q.q: State the textbook's conclusion about the best degree of decentralization.
q.answer: there is some optimal level of federalism|purely centralized or purely decentralized cannot maximize social welfare
q.explanation: A purely decentralized or purely centralized system cannot be expected to maximize social welfare; there is some optimal level of federalism.

q.q: Economics is the study of:
options: the allocation of limited resources to satisfy human wants
q.explanation: Economics is defined in the textbook as the study of the allocation of limited resources to satisfy human wants.

q.q: The commonly identified factors of production include:
q.explanation: The inputs are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship, with energy sometimes added.

q.q: Most environmental resources have become increasingly scarce as the scale of economic activity expands.
q.explanation: The textbook states that most environmental resources have become increasingly scarce as economic activity expands.

q.q: Which of the following is a non-monetized benefit from the environment?
q.explanation: Fresh air, rivers, lakes and oceans yield non-monetized benefits, while forests, exploited oil and minerals yield monetized flows.

q.q: Define ecosystem resilience in your own words.
q.answer: ability to withstand disturbances without changing parameters|extent to which a system can absorb disturbance without its parameters changing
q.explanation: Resilience measures how much disturbance an ecosystem can absorb without its parameters changing.

q.q: Underlying the pressure on planetary sources and sinks is:
options: the growth of world population and industrial production
q.explanation: The pressure on sources and sinks comes from growth of the world population and industrial production.

q.q: According to the poverty-environment nexus, the poor are both agents and victims of environmental degradation.
q.explanation: The poor both degrade resources out of necessity and suffer most from the resulting degradation.

q.q: Name the report published by the Brundtland Commission in 1987.
q.explanation: The Brundtland Commission Report was titled Our Common Future, published in 1987.

q.q: In the Ethiopian example, low income households cutting trees for firewood and cultivating marginal land leads to:
options: deforestation, erosion and a cycle of rural poverty
q.explanation: Logging, cultivation and overgrazing expose soil to flooding and erosion, feeding the cycle of poverty and environmental destruction.

q.q: State two conditions for environmental policies to succeed in countries like Ethiopia.
q.answer: address poverty and landlessness|secure land tenure|provide credit and inputs|firm government commitment
q.explanation: Policies must address poverty, landlessness and lack of institutional resources such as secure tenure, credit, inputs and information, with firm government commitment.

q.q: Arrange the early milestones of global environmental awareness in order of appearance.
q.explanation: The order is the Great Smog of 1952, Silent Spring in 1962, then Limits to Growth in 1972.

q.q: Global warming refers to:
options: increasing average air and ocean temperatures
q.explanation: Global warming is the increase in average air and ocean temperatures.

q.q: Which is the largest contributor to the greenhouse effect?
q.explanation: CO2 contributes 77% of the greenhouse effect, the largest share.

q.q: Climate and weather mean exactly the same thing.
q.explanation: Climate is the average weather pattern over many years; weather is short-term atmospheric condition of a day or week.

q.q: In developing countries, deforestation contributes about what share of harmful greenhouse gases?
q.explanation: Deforestation is said to contribute over 20% of harmful greenhouse gases in developing countries.

q.q: Which IPCC estimate gives the probable rise in mean temperatures by 2099 if fossil fuel emissions are not curbed?
q.explanation: The IPCC predicted a probable rise of between 1.5 and 4 degrees Celsius by 2099.

q.q: Why is adaptation to climate change necessary even if mitigation succeeds?
q.answer: climate lags make further change inevitable|some warming is already happening and unavoidable|changes already underway unfold for many years
q.explanation: Because lags in the climate system mean a significant amount of climate change is already happening and essentially inevitable, adaptation is needed to protect livelihoods.

q.q: According to the IPCC, sub-Saharan Africa's highly vulnerable zone faces:
q.explanation: The four zones: sub-Saharan Africa faces drying, Asia flooding, small islands multiple sensitivities, the Arctic melting glaciers.

q.q: Distinguish mitigation from adaptation in one sentence each.
q.answer: mitigation reduces causes|adaptation responds to consequences|mitigation cuts emissions and adaptation adjusts to actual or expected impacts
q.explanation: Mitigation deals with the causes of climate change; adaptation deals with the consequences.

q.q: The poorest developing countries will be hit earliest and hardest by climate change even though they contributed little to causing it.
q.explanation: Stern notes the poorest countries are hit earliest and hardest despite contributing little, so the international community has an obligation to support them.

q.q: Put the four classes of adaptation strategies in the order listed in the textbook.
q.explanation: The textbook lists mobility, storage, diversification, then communal pooling.

q.q: Name the emissions-reduction forest mechanism that engages indigenous communities alongside REDD.
q.explanation: REDD-plus adds incentives for re-establishing and maintaining forests with engagement of indigenous communities.

q.q: A green economy is best described as an economy that:
options: grows as fast as possible regardless of costs
improves wellbeing and equity while reducing environmental risks and ecological scarcities
q.explanation: The textbook defines the green economy by improved wellbeing and social equity with reduced environmental risks and scarcities.

q.q: The three defining features of a green economy are:
options: low carbon, resource efficient, socially inclusive
high tax, high debt, high growth
q.explanation: A green economy uses low carbon, is resource efficient and is socially inclusive.

q.q: Green growth means keeping natural assets able to provide the resources and environmental services wellbeing relies on.
q.explanation: This is the OECD definition of green growth.

q.q: Which of the following is a source of renewable energy according to the textbook?
q.explanation: Sources include solar, biomass and biofuel, geothermal, hydroelectricity, tidal and wind.

q.q: Which organisation defined green growth in 2011?
q.explanation: The OECD (2011) definition is cited in the textbook.

q.q: Explain the motive for adopting renewable energy apart from climate change.
q.answer: peak oil|perceived scarcity of fossil fuels|rising demand and declining fossil fuel production
q.explanation: The motive comes from the perceived scarcity of fossil fuels: peak oil implies rising demand against declining production, requiring alternatives even without climate change.

q.q: In a green economy, growth is driven by:
options: public and private investments that reduce emissions and raise resource efficiency
q.explanation: Growth is driven by investments that reduce carbon emissions and pollution, enhance efficiency and prevent biodiversity loss.

q.q: Why is the green economy described as a catalyst for poverty eradication in developing countries?
q.answer: protects natural assets the poor depend on|creates jobs and opportunities|poor countries have untapped renewable potential
q.explanation: It protects the natural resources the poor live on and, with technological support, turns untapped renewable potential into growth and jobs.

q.q: Green growth was proposed only for advanced economies.
q.explanation: The green economy is relevant to advanced economies and is a key catalyst for growth and poverty eradication in developing countries.

q.q: Arrange the OECD's cited risks from eroding natural capital into the order listed.
q.explanation: The order is water scarcity, resource bottlenecks, greater pollution, climate change and unrecoverable biodiversity loss.

q.q: Ethiopia is described as:
options: one of the most vulnerable countries to future climate change
q.explanation: The textbook cites Ethiopia as one of the most vulnerable countries to future climate change.

q.q: Ethiopia's National Adaptation Programme of Action was produced in:
q.explanation: NAPA was produced in 2007, followed by NAMA in 2011.

q.q: The CRGE strategy addresses both mitigation and adaptation.
q.explanation: CRGE addresses climate change adaptation (climate resilience) and mitigation (green economy) objectives.

q.q: What GDP per capita target does the CRGE's middle-income goal initially aim for?
q.explanation: The goal is middle-income status by 2025, initially raising GDP per capita to 1,000 US dollars.

q.q: State the three key underlying causes of Ethiopia's vulnerability to climate change identified in NAPA and NAMA.
q.answer: dependence on rain-fed agriculture|poor water resource development|high population growth rate
q.explanation: These documents cite rain-fed dependence, poor water resource development and high population growth.

q.q: The aims of the Green Legacy Initiative include:
options: preventing flooding, food insecurity and environment-related conflicts
q.explanation: The initiative aims to curb climate change and deforestation and prevent flooding, food insecurity and environment-related conflicts.

q.q: About 4.1 billion trees were planted under the Green Legacy Initiative by August 2020.
q.explanation: An estimated 4.1 billion trees were planted by August 2020 according to the Ethiopian government.

q.q: Name the ministry responsible for climate change and environmental management in Ethiopia.
q.answer: ministry of environment, forest and climate change
q.explanation: The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change is the lead, legally mandated body.

q.q: Explain how soil erosion and land degradation arise in Ethiopia according to the textbook.
q.answer: crop cultivation in marginal areas|livestock grazing pressure|increased cultivation and overgrazing expose soil
q.explanation: They result from increased crop cultivation in marginal areas and livestock grazing pressure, causing land degradation, biodiversity loss and low agricultural productivity.

q.q: Which of the following was identified as a sector most vulnerable to climate change in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: Agriculture, health, transport, natural resources, energy and industry were identified as most vulnerable.

q.q: Arrange Ethiopia's climate policy actions in chronological order.
q.explanation: The order is NAPA (2007), then the CRGE strategy (2011), then the Green Legacy Initiative (2020).

q.q: The continental drift theory was proposed in 1912 by:
q.explanation: The concept was proposed by a German meteorologist, Alfred Wegener, in 1912.

q.q: During the Carboniferous period, about 350 million years ago, Pangaea was located:
q.explanation: During the Carboniferous period Pangaea was located around the South Pole.

q.q: The northern part of Pangaea, which broke away during the Triassic period, was called:
q.explanation: The northern part of Pangaea is known as Laurasia; the southern part is Gondwanaland.

q.q: Which one of the following was part of the old Gondwanaland?
q.explanation: Gondwanaland in the south later broke into southern continents; Australia is part of old Gondwanaland, while North America, Asia and Europe belong to Laurasia.

q.q: The huge sea that existed around Pangaea was called:
q.explanation: The sea surrounding Pangaea was the Tethys sea.

q.q: Fossils of Mesosaurus are found on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean, in South America and Africa.
q.explanation: Mesosaurus fossils occur on both sides of the Atlantic, which is one of Wegener's fossil evidences.

q.q: Name the small reptile, which lived about 250 million years ago, whose fossils support continental drift.
q.explanation: Mesosaurus, a small reptile of about 250 million years ago, is found on both sides of the Atlantic.

q.q: Which statement was NOT one of the reasons Wegener's theory was rejected?
options: He was not a geologist by profession
Most influential geoscientists were based in the Northern Hemisphere while the data came from the Southern Hemisphere
