He presented direct, measured proof that continents were moving
There was no explanation for the mechanism of movement
q.explanation: The opposite was true: the lack of direct evidence for continental movement, not its presence, was the main objection.

q.q: Arrange the steps of continental breakup and drift in the correct order.
options: Through the process of drifting, the continents reached their present locations
Pangaea existed as a single landmass around the South Pole
Pangaea began to break into several parts in the Triassic period
Laurasia and Gondwanaland were further subdivided into the present continents
q.explanation: The order is: single Pangaea, breakup in the Triassic, subdivision of Laurasia and Gondwanaland, then drifting to present positions.

q.q: State the greatest problem that kept Wegener's theory from being accepted in his lifetime.
q.answer: lack of direct evidence for the movements of continents and no explanation for the mechanism
q.explanation: The greatest problem was the absence of direct evidence of movement and of a mechanism to explain it.

q.q: Wegener's most important legacy is considered to be:
options: proving mountains rise by volcanic action
introducing the idea of the lateral mobility of continents, a paradigm change from fixism to mobilism
q.explanation: Wegener's key legacy is the idea of lateral continental mobility - the shift from fixism to mobilism - which ignited the search for how continents move.

q.q: The plate tectonics theory was developed in:
q.explanation: Plate tectonics was developed in the late 1960s, based on a broad synthesis of geologic and geophysical data.

q.q: The lithosphere consists of the crust and the uppermost mantle.
q.explanation: The uppermost mantle and crust, together called the lithosphere, slide across the asthenosphere.

q.q: Which layer allows the plates to slide across the top of it?
q.explanation: The asthenosphere allows the lithosphere, made up of the crust and uppermost mantle, to slide over it.

q.q: Earth's lithosphere is broken into approximately:
options: about a dozen large plates plus smaller ones
hundreds of plates of equal size
q.explanation: The lithosphere is broken into about a dozen large pieces plus some smaller ones, called plates.

q.q: Plates move at a rate of a few centimeters per year.
q.explanation: The plates move slowly at a rate of a few centimeters per year and change size.

q.q: Continental crust is made largely of granite and is therefore:
options: the same density as oceanic crust
q.explanation: Continental crust, made largely of granite, is less dense than oceanic crust made largely of basalt.

q.q: Plate edges do not always correspond to continent boundaries. Which example proves this?
options: The South American Plate stops at the Atlantic coast
The North American Plate includes the western half of the North Atlantic seafloor
The Eurasian Plate covers only Asia
The Australian Plate lies entirely under land
q.explanation: The North American Plate extends into the North Atlantic seafloor, showing plates are larger than continents.

q.q: Name the soft layer of the upper mantle on which the tectonic plates ride.
q.explanation: The asthenosphere is the layer over which the lithospheric plates slide.

q.q: According to the text, plate tectonic process is a prime cause of:
q.explanation: Plate tectonic process serves as a prime cause of long-term climate change and shapes the environment in which life evolves.

q.q: What ultimately drives the motion of the lithospheric plates?
q.answer: convection currents in the mantle|mantle convection
q.explanation: Although debated in detail, most agree plate motion is ultimately driven by convection currents in the mantle.

q.q: A convergent plate boundary is also called:
q.explanation: Convergent boundaries are called destructive because the subducted crust is eventually destroyed.

q.q: At a convergent boundary, what happens to the denser plate?
options: It floats above the other plate
It is subducted beneath the less dense one
It melts entirely on the spot
It slides sideways past the other
q.explanation: The denser plate is forced under, or subducted beneath, the less dense one and is eventually destroyed.

q.q: The volcanoes of the Andes Mountains were formed because:
options: the Nazca Plate is being subducted under the South American Plate
the South American Plate slid past the Pacific Plate
q.explanation: The eastward-moving Nazca Plate is subducted under the westward-moving South American Plate; rising magma built the Andean volcanoes.

q.q: An arc of volcanic islands produced by the convergence of two oceanic plates is exemplified by:
options: the Mariana Islands of the western Pacific
q.explanation: When two oceanic plates converge, one subducts and volcanic islands form, as with the Mariana Islands.

q.q: The highest mountain range on earth was produced by the collision of:
options: the Nazca and South American plates
two plates sliding past each other
q.explanation: The northward-moving Indo-Australian Plate met the Eurasian Plate and the collision raised the Himalayas.

q.q: Along transform faults, crust is neither destroyed nor created.
q.explanation: As plates slide past each other along transform faults, crust is neither destroyed nor created - hence the name conservative.

q.q: Name the process in which rising magma creates new seafloor and pushes plates apart at oceanic ridges.
q.explanation: This process is known as seafloor spreading.

q.q: The East African Rift Valley is a modern example of:
q.explanation: Divergence can happen on continents, producing fracture zones called rift valleys; the East African Rift Valley is the example given.

q.q: Transform faults occur only on the continents.
q.explanation: Most transform faults are found on the seafloor along oceanic ridges, though some, like the San Andreas Fault, occur on continents.

q.q: State the mechanism most geoscientists agree drives the motion of the plates.
q.answer: convection currents in the mantle|mantle convection currents
q.explanation: Plate motion is ultimately driven by convection currents in the mantle, powered by the earth's internal energy.

q.q: Arrange the events of oceanic-continental convergence in the correct order.
options: Magma and gases rise to the surface and form volcanoes such as those of the Andes
The denser oceanic plate is subducted beneath the continental plate
Melted crust produces magma deep in the mantle
Two plates carrying crust of different densities move toward each other
q.explanation: The sequence is: plates converge, the denser plate subducts, subducted material melts into magma, then magma rises to build volcanoes.

q.q: An upfold formed when rock layers are compressed is called:
q.explanation: The layers of rock that bend up form an upfold, or anticline; those bending down form a syncline.

q.q: A crack on the earth's crust formed by the forces of tension and compression is:
q.explanation: A fault is a crack on the earth's crust formed by the forces of tension and compression.

q.q: Instruments that can detect earthquake waves are called:
q.explanation: Most earthquakes are detected only by sensitive instruments called seismographs.

q.q: Which feature is a block mountain (horst)?
q.explanation: Block mountains form where land between two parallel faults is pushed upward - the Afar Horst is the example.

q.q: The Richter scale rates earthquakes from 0 to 9, and its readings are:
q.explanation: The Richter scale measures effects on a logarithmic scale; effects increase significantly for each step up.

q.q: What name is given to the point on the earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake?
q.explanation: The point on the earth's surface immediately above the focus is the epicenter.

q.q: About what proportion of the energy released in earthquakes comes from the Circum-Pacific Belt (Ring of Fire)?
q.explanation: About 80 percent of earthquake energy comes from the Circum-Pacific Belt, also called the Ring of Fire.

q.q: Which Ethiopian volcano is cited as an example of an active volcano?
q.explanation: Erta Ale in Ethiopia is cited as an active volcano; Zuqualla is extinct and Kilimanjaro is dormant.

q.q: Lava that emerges through a fissure builds a volcano, not a plateau.
q.explanation: Lava that emerges via a vent builds a volcano; lava escaping through a fissure gently spreads and builds a lava plateau.

q.q: Name the limestone columns that hang down from a cave ceiling.
q.explanation: Deposits hanging from the ceiling of a limestone cave grow into stalactites.

q.q: Explain why surface waves rather than body waves do most of the destructive shaking far from the epicenter.
q.answer: they have larger amplitude|surface waves are the most powerful shake waves, moving slowly with larger amplitude
q.explanation: Surface waves travel more slowly but have much larger amplitude, so they are responsible for most destructive shaking far from the epicenter.

q.q: Climate refers to:
options: The atmosphere's state on one day
Atmospheric conditions in a place over many years
The temperature of the oceans only
q.explanation: Climate is the condition of the atmosphere in a place averaged over many years.

q.q: Which of the following is an important greenhouse gas?
q.explanation: CO2, CH4 and N2O are all important greenhouse gases identified from observations and ice cores.

q.q: The 1990s were the warmest decade worldwide according to the IPCC Third Assessment Report.
q.explanation: The 2001 report documented the 1990s as the warmest decade and 1998 as the warmest year since 1861.

q.q: According to the IPCC, climate change persists for:
q.explanation: The IPCC definition requires persistence for an extended period, typically decades or longer.

q.q: What term describes the average climate around the whole world?
q.explanation: The average climate around the world is called the global climate.

q.q: Explain why a single unusually hot summer is not, by itself, evidence of climate change.
q.answer: weather is short term|climate change needs decades of record|one season is weather not climate
q.explanation: Climate change is identified from persistent changes over decades, so one season is only a weather event.

q.q: When air temperatures rise, oceans absorb more heat from the atmosphere.
q.explanation: The textbook states oceans absorb more heat from a warming atmosphere and become warmer.

q.q: Which year was the warmest since instrumental records began in 1861?
q.explanation: The IPCC Third Assessment Report identified 1998 as the warmest year since records began in 1861.

q.q: State the IPCC definition of climate change in your own words.
q.answer: change in mean or variability of climate lasting decades or longer|long term change in climate state
q.explanation: A change in the state of the climate identified by changes in mean and/or variability, persisting decades or longer, from natural or human causes.

q.q: Greenhouse gases raise air temperatures near the ground because they:
q.explanation: GHGs are named because they trap heat and raise near-ground temperatures, acting like a greenhouse.

q.q: Most of the warming experienced over the past 50 years has resulted from what cause?
q.explanation: Observed evidence revealed most warming over the past 50 years resulted from human activities.

q.q: By how much did average global surface temperature warm in the past century?
q.explanation: The average global surface temperature warmed 0.8 C in the past century.

q.q: The IPCC projected that, with rising emissions, mean global temperatures by 2100 will increase from:
q.explanation: IPCC 2001 projected an increase of 1.4 C to 5.8 C by the end of the 21st century.

q.q: Global warming has begun to affect sea level, snow cover, ice sheets and rainfall.
q.explanation: The textbook states global warming has begun to affect all four of these.

q.q: Which base period is used for the global mean temperature variation index that runs from 1880 to present?
q.explanation: The index uses the base period 1951 to 1980.

q.q: Compare the warming rate of the past three decades with the past century. What does this indicate?
q.answer: recent rate is faster|warming is accelerating
q.explanation: 0.6 C in three decades is a much faster rate than 0.8 C over the entire century, indicating acceleration.

q.q: Rising air temperatures shifting regional climate patterns are already affecting:
q.explanation: Shifts in regional climate marked by rising temperatures already affect watersheds and ecosystems.

q.q: The pace of global warming slowed during the late twentieth century.
q.explanation: The average of each decade since the 1980s has been warmer than the preceding decade, showing acceleration.

q.q: Why do scientists use a base period when presenting temperature trends?
q.answer: comparable reference average|to compute departures fairly
q.explanation: A base period gives a fixed reference so departures of different years and decades can be compared fairly.

q.q: Arrange these steps of interpreting a temperature index graph in logical order.
options: Read a year's index value as a departure
Know the base period of the record
Compare several decades for the trend
q.explanation: First know the base period, then read departures, then compare decades for the trend.

q.q: What is the projected upper limit of global temperature increase by the end of the 21st century?
q.explanation: The IPCC 2001 range is 1.4 C to 5.8 C, with 5.8 C the upper limit.

q.q: Which factor is described as 'the leading cause of climate change' in the projections?
q.explanation: Greenhouse gas emissions are named as the leading cause of climate change in the IPCC projection.

q.q: Which of the following is one of the three external causes of climate change listed in the textbook?
q.explanation: The three external causes are changes in incoming solar radiation, atmospheric composition and the Earth's surface.

q.q: The Milankovitch theory was first proposed in the 1930s by the astronomer:
q.explanation: Milutin Milankovitch first proposed the orbital-variation theory in the 1930s.

q.q: Sunspots reach their maximum number and size approximately every 11 years.
q.explanation: Sunspot number and size peak approximately every 11 years.

q.q: Volcanic eruptions with the greatest impact on climate are those rich in:
q.explanation: Sulfur-rich eruptions form reflective stratospheric haze that cools the surface.

q.q: Name the three cyclic movements that combine in the Milankovitch theory.
q.explanation: Changes in the shape of the orbit (eccentricity), precession of the axis (wobbling) and changes in the tilt of the axis (obliquity).

q.q: Explain why sulfur-rich volcanic eruptions cool the Earth's surface. Why hemispheric difference?
q.answer: sulfuric acid haze reflects sunlight|cooling strongest in eruption hemisphere
q.explanation: Ejected sulfur forms reflective haze in the stratosphere for several years, reflecting incoming sunlight, and the strongest cooling occurs in the hemisphere of eruption.

q.q: Aerosols such as sulfates and nitrates mainly reflect incoming sunlight and cool surface air.
q.explanation: Sulfates and nitrates reflect sunlight, while soot absorbs it; many particles cause net surface cooling.

q.q: According to studies cited in the textbook, about half the rainfall in the Amazon River Basin is returned to the atmosphere by:
options: evaporation and transpiration from tree leaves
q.explanation: About half the basin's rainfall returns via evaporation and transpiration from leaves, so deforestation reduces evaporative cooling.

q.q: The IPCC Fifth Assessment Report said human influence on warming since the mid-twentieth century is 'extremely likely'. What probability does that phrase denote?
q.explanation: In the 2013 report, 'extremely likely' means a probability of at least 95 percent.

q.q: Arrange the IPCC in-depth assessment reports in chronological order of publication of the first three.
q.explanation: The order is 1990, then 2001, then 2007; the IPCC also assessed in 1995, 2013 and 2021.

q.q: Without greenhouse gases, by how much would the Earth's average atmospheric temperature be lower?
q.explanation: Without GHGs the Earth's average atmospheric temperature would be 33 C lower.

q.q: Climate models predict that the most rapid warming will occur over:
options: land areas, particularly northern high latitudes in winter
q.explanation: Land areas, especially northern high latitudes in winter, warm faster than the global average.

q.q: Average global sea level rose about how much during the twentieth century?
q.explanation: Average global sea level rose by about 17 cm during the twentieth century.

q.q: Since 1993, globally averaged sea level has risen roughly:
q.explanation: Since 1993 sea level has risen about twice as fast, roughly 3.4 cm per decade.

q.q: Both melting ice and the expansion of warming oceans contribute to sea level rise.
q.explanation: About half the 1900 to 2010 rise came from melting glaciers and ice sheets and half from ocean expansion.

q.q: The natural range of atmospheric CO2 over the last 800,000 years, from ice cores, was 180 to 300 ppm. What was true of the 2005 concentration?
q.answer: exceeded the natural range|above 300 ppm|higher than any in 800000 years
q.explanation: The 2005 CO2 concentration exceeded by far the natural range of 180 to 300 ppm from ice cores.

q.q: Boreal forests in the high latitudes absorb how much solar energy compared with snow-covered tundra?
options: up to three times as much
q.explanation: Dark green boreal forests absorb up to three times as much solar energy as snow-covered tundra, a warming feedback.

q.q: Since the middle of the twentieth century, precipitation has generally decreased over middle and high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere.
q.explanation: It has generally increased there, while decreasing over some subtropical land areas.

q.q: In which two summers did the extent of Arctic sea ice drop dramatically to record lows?
q.explanation: The summers of 2007 and 2012 both set record lows in Arctic sea ice extent.

q.q: Explain two ways sea level rise threatens people living near coastlines.
q.answer: storm surges on higher baseline|saltwater contamination of groundwater|damage to coral reefs and coastal ecosystems
q.explanation: Storm surges strike atop higher water levels and coastal groundwater may be contaminated with saltwater; coastal ecosystems like coral reefs also suffer.

q.q: Where are the effects of climate change on agriculture expected to reduce crop yields?
options: Tropical areas, where many developing nations are located
q.explanation: Tropical areas may see crop yields decrease, while higher latitudes may gain longer growing seasons.

q.q: What is the primary source of increased atmospheric CO2 since preindustrial times, according to the IPCC?
q.explanation: Fossil fuel use is the primary source, with land-use change a smaller but significant contribution.

q.q: Which strategy seeks to limit climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions and enhancing sinks?
q.explanation: Mitigation limits climate change by reducing emissions and enhancing sink opportunities.

q.q: The type of adaptation that takes place after the initial impacts of climate change have occurred is:
q.explanation: Reactive adaptation occurs after initial impacts have taken place.

q.q: In natural systems, anticipatory adaptation does not exist.
q.explanation: Natural systems adapt only autonomously and reactively; anticipatory adaptation belongs to human systems.

q.q: Adaptation based on a deliberate policy decision is called:
q.explanation: Planned adaptation follows deliberate policy decisions based on awareness of changed or expected conditions.

q.q: Name three adaptation strategies commonly identified in Ethiopia.
q.answer: irrigation|terracing|water harvesting|crop diversification|soil conservation|planting trees|changing crop planting date
q.explanation: Ethiopian strategies include soil conservation, terracing, water harvesting, crop diversification, changing planting date, planting trees and irrigation.

q.q: Differentiate mitigation from adaptation in one clear comparison.
q.answer: mitigation reduces causes by cutting emissions; adaptation adjusts to reduce impacts
q.explanation: Mitigation cuts emissions and enhances sinks; adaptation makes system-specific adjustments to alleviate adverse impacts.

q.q: Constructing a house on stilts is an example of public anticipatory adaptation.
q.explanation: Houses on stilts are a private adaptation example; public anticipatory examples include early-warning systems and building codes.

q.q: Which of the following acts as a greenhouse gas sink according to the lesson?
q.explanation: Sinks that accumulate and store greenhouse gases include the oceans, forests and soil.

q.q: A village builds an early-warning flood system. Classify the adaptation by motive, timing and planning, and justify your answer.
q.explanation: It is public (serves community interest), anticipatory (built before flooding worsens) and planned (a deliberate policy decision).

q.q: When did sensitivity to adaptation grow as a policy priority, marking a shift after years of mitigation focus?
options: Particularly after the IPCC Third Assessment Report
q.explanation: Sensitivity to adaptation grew over recent years, particularly after the IPCC Third Assessment Report (2001).

q.q: Explain how planting trees on degraded Ethiopian slopes can serve both mitigation and adaptation.
q.answer: trees are sinks absorbing CO2 and also conserve soil and moisture|both
q.explanation: Trees enhance a carbon sink, which is mitigation, while conserving soil and moisture for farm resilience, which is adaptation.

q.q: The First World Climate Conference, which identified climate change as an urgent world problem, was held in:
q.explanation: The First World Climate Conference of 1979 called on governments to anticipate and guard against climate hazards.

q.q: More than 340 participants from 46 countries recommended a comprehensive global framework convention at the:
options: Toronto Conference on the Changing Atmosphere
q.explanation: The Toronto Conference of 1988 recommended developing a comprehensive global framework convention.

q.q: The IPCC was established by the WMO and UNEP.
q.explanation: The WMO and UNEP established the IPCC to assess climate change magnitude, timing, impacts and response strategies.

q.q: The Kyoto Protocol came into force on:
q.explanation: The Protocol, adopted in 1997, entered into force on 16 February 2005.

q.q: State the overall Kyoto reduction goal for developed countries for the 2008 to 2012 period.
q.explanation: Developed countries were to cut emissions by at least 5 percent below 1990 levels during 2008 to 2012.

q.q: Explain two reasons global greenhouse gas emissions rose more than 25 percent from 1990 to 2012 despite the Kyoto Protocol.
q.answer: US did not ratify|developing nations like China not required to reduce|coverage too limited
q.explanation: The United States never ratified, and developing nations such as China were not required to cut emissions, so uncovered growth outweighed the cuts.

q.q: The detailed legal decisions adopted at COP 7 in Marrakesh are known as the:
q.explanation: COP 7 adopted the detailed legal texts called the Marrakesh Accords.

q.q: Under the Paris Agreement, each nation sets voluntary targets for reducing emissions and reports progress regularly.
q.explanation: Paris relies on voluntary national targets with regular reporting of progress.

q.q: Which countries have pledged to become carbon neutral, offsetting all their greenhouse gas emissions?
q.explanation: Costa Rica, Iceland and Norway pledged carbon neutrality, meaning no net emissions after offsetting.

q.q: Arrange these early climate milestones chronologically.
q.explanation: The order is 1979 conference, 1988 Toronto Conference, then the 1990 First Assessment Report.

q.q: List three benefits of cutting greenhouse gas emissions named in the lesson.
q.answer: slower greenhouse effect|reduced acid rain|less haze|less photochemical smog|health benefits|reduced global warming
q.explanation: Cutting emissions slows the greenhouse effect, reduces warming and acid rain, diminishes haze, slows smog production and improves health.

q.q: The CRGE strategy initially identified and prioritized how many initiatives?
q.explanation: The strategy initially identified and prioritized 60 initiatives to reach development goals while emitting less.

q.q: Ethiopia's CRGE plan aims to reach middle income status before:
q.explanation: The CRGE supports the national ambition of reaching middle income status before 2025.

q.q: The CRGE strategy is based on four pillars.
q.explanation: Ethiopia's green economy plan is based on four pillars.

q.q: Ethiopia needs to expand its electricity supply at a rate of:
q.explanation: Electricity supply must expand at 14 percent per annum, which natural resources such as hydro, geothermal, solar and wind can meet.

q.q: Name the CRGE measure that protects recovering vegetation from grazing and cutting to raise carbon storage.
q.explanation: Area closure promotes recovery of vegetation and increases carbon storage in forests and woodlands.

q.q: State the four pillars of the CRGE strategy.
q.answer: crop and livestock production|protecting and re-establishing forests|renewable electricity|energy-efficient technologies
q.explanation: The pillars are: improving crop and livestock production practices; protecting and re-establishing forests including carbon stocks; expanding renewable electricity for domestic and regional markets; and leapfrogging to modern energy-efficient technologies in transport, industry and buildings.

q.q: Which industrial sub-sectors does the fourth pillar name for leapfrogging?
q.explanation: The transport and industrial sub-sectors named include cement, textile, leather and fertilizer industries.

q.q: The CRGE treats agriculture only as a problem sector, with no role in growth.
q.explanation: Agriculture remains the core sector providing employment to the majority; the strategy raises its productivity while limiting emissions.

q.q: Explain two ways the forestry pillar reduces emissions and increases resilience.
q.answer: carbon sequestration through afforestation|reduced fuel wood demand|area closure increases storage
q.explanation: Reversing deforestation and degradation raises carbon sequestration and stocks through afforestation, reforestation, forest management and area closure, while lower fuel wood demand cuts emissions.

q.q: For the transport sector, the CRGE introduces which of the following?
options: Construction of an electric rail network powered by renewable energy
q.explanation: The strategy includes stricter fuel efficiency standards, an electric rail network powered by renewable energy, and improved modern transport.

q.q: Which sector of the Ethiopian economy does the first pillar identify as remaining the core provider of employment to the majority?
q.explanation: Agriculture remains the core sector providing employment to most Ethiopians.

q.q: The term sustainable development was first used in 1987 by:
options: The World Commission on Environment and Development
q.explanation: The term was first used in 1987 by the World Commission on Environment and Development, the Brundtland Commission.

q.q: The classic definition of sustainable development appears in the report:
q.explanation: The definition is given in the Brundtland Commission's report Our Common Future.

q.q: The first UN Conference on Environment and Development, held in Stockholm in 1972, led to the establishment of UNEP.
q.explanation: The 1972 Stockholm Conference introduced ecodevelopment and led to the establishment of UNEP.

q.q: The 1992 Rio de Janeiro conference is known as the Earth Summit and it produced:
q.explanation: The Rio 1992 Earth Summit developed Agenda 21.

q.q: In which country was the 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development held?
q.explanation: It was held in Johannesburg, South Africa in 2002.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three essential dimensions of sustainable development?
q.explanation: The three dimensions are economic development, social development and environmental sustainability.

q.q: Explain the nested rings view of sustainable development in one sentence.
q.answer: the economy depends on society and the environment|economy inside society inside environment
q.explanation: The nested rings view holds that the economy sits inside society and society inside the environment, so the economy depends on both.

q.q: How many targets accompany the 17 Sustainable Development Goals in the 2030 Agenda?
q.explanation: The 2030 Agenda comprises 17 goals and 169 targets.

q.q: Which Ethiopian framework integrated the SDGs for implementation from the 2015/16 fiscal year?
q.explanation: The SDGs were integrated with GTP II and implemented across the nation from the 2015/16 fiscal year.

q.q: Arrange the conferences in the correct order of their contributions.
q.explanation: The order is Stockholm 1972, Nairobi 1987, Rio 1992, Johannesburg 2002.

q.q: State one criticism of the notion of sustainable development mentioned in the textbook.
q.answer: internal logical contradiction of the term|narrowness of the term|benefits only part of humanity|diversity in understanding the goals
q.explanation: Critics note the internal logical contradiction of the term, its narrowness, unequal benefits and diversity of understanding of its goals.

q.q: Which one of the following is different from the others?
q.explanation: Coal is a non-renewable fixed or fund resource; water, vegetation and soil regenerate and are renewable.

q.q: Renewable resources are also known as flow resources because they regenerate through reproduction or recycling.
q.explanation: The textbook names renewable resources flow resources that replenish themselves.

q.q: Conflicts over renewable resources are usually driven by disputes over:
options: ownership, access, decision making and distribution of revenues
q.explanation: The four drivers are ownership, access, decision making, and distribution of revenues, benefits and burdens.

q.q: Which type of scarcity occurs when different groups in a society face unequal resource access?
q.explanation: Structural scarcity arises from unequal access among groups, caused by rules, cultural practices or poverty.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT among the three main drivers of conflict over natural resources?
q.explanation: The three drivers are scarcity, poor governance and transboundary dynamics; technological innovation is listed as a possible response, not a driver.

q.q: Since 1948 the historical record documents only 37 incidents of acute conflict over water while about 295 international water agreements were negotiated.
q.explanation: The textbook cites 37 acute incidents (30 involving Israel, the last in 1970) against about 295 agreements.

q.q: In which year was the Nile Basin Initiative formally established?
q.explanation: The NBI was formally established in 1999 as the first initiative including all basin states.

q.q: In 2010, the Nile River Basin Cooperative Framework was signed by five upstream states and strongly opposed by:
q.explanation: Egypt and Sudan strongly opposed the 2010 Cooperative Framework.

q.q: According to the lesson, when do conflicts over renewable resources become truly problematic?
q.answer: when mechanisms for managing and resolving them break down|when they give way to violence
q.explanation: Conflicts are not inherently negative; they become problematic when management mechanisms break down and give way to violence.

q.q: Arrange these livelihood approaches in order, from broad long-term strategy to last-resort support.
q.explanation: The order runs diversification, efficiency improvement, adaptation, protection, and finally emergency livelihood support.

q.q: State the obligation written in Article 7 of the ILC document on international watercourses.
q.answer: obligation not to cause significant harm|not to cause significant harm to other basin states
q.explanation: Article 7 contains the obligation not to cause significant harm to the river basin states.

q.q: Natural resource governance is best defined as:
options: the police enforcement of mining laws
the norms, institutions and processes that determine power, decisions, participation and benefits over natural resources
a system of taxes on resources
q.explanation: Governance covers exercised power, decision making, participation and benefit sharing over natural resources.

q.q: Article 10 of UNDRIP states that indigenous peoples should not be forcibly removed from their lands.
q.explanation: UNDRIP Article 10 forbids forced removal; relocation requires free, prior and informed consent and fair compensation.

q.q: Name the three pillars of public participation advanced by the Aarhus Convention.
q.answer: access to information|public participation in decision-making|access to justice
q.explanation: The three pillars are access to information, public participation in decision-making, and access to justice.

q.q: Which of the following is one of the four governance challenges at the root of resource conflicts?
options: Overlapping or poorly enforced resource rights
q.explanation: The challenges include unclear, overlapping or poor enforcement of resource rights and laws.

q.q: Which required assessment must be conducted transparently and made publicly available for all major development projects?
q.explanation: The third principle requires environmental and social impact assessments for major projects.

q.q: The CBD recognizes that communities are inextricably linked to their territories and that preservation of what is crucial to conservation?
q.explanation: The Convention on Biological Diversity holds that preserving traditional knowledge is crucial to conservation and biodiversity.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why improving natural resource governance can benefit people and biodiversity.
q.answer: securing rights and sharing power and responsibilities can benefit both people and biodiversity|better governance improves ecosystem health and wellbeing
q.explanation: Improving governance, including securing rights and sharing power, benefits both people and biodiversity through ecosystem health and wellbeing.

q.q: Which principle asks public policy to make equitable resource access a national priority?
q.explanation: The second principle makes equitable resource access a priority of public policy and an outcome of development programs.

q.q: According to the lesson, two governance solutions for natural resource conflicts can be prescribed as universally identical.
q.explanation: Conflicts are highly context dependent, so no two governance solutions are ever the same.

q.q: What does the fifth governance principle acknowledge even after the first four are implemented?
q.answer: unexpected impacts on renewable resources can emerge as a normal part of development
q.explanation: Even after clarification of rights, assessments and participation, unexpected impacts can emerge as a normal part of the development process.

q.q: The word Shimagle refers to:
q.explanation: Shimagle means elders, who played an important role in resolving conflicts.

q.q: Under the Fetha Negast, conflicts between individuals or communities were encouraged to be settled amicably at local level.
q.explanation: The Fetha Negast, the law of the kings, encouraged amicable local settlement.

q.q: The Oromo conflict resolution technique related to unintentional killing is called:
q.explanation: Gumma is the Oromo technique for unintentional killing that helps avoid grievances and revenge.

q.q: Which customary law institution does the Afar use to manage conflicts between different clans?
q.explanation: In Afar, the Mada'a manages inter-clan conflicts based on customary law and elders.

q.q: Which of the following correctly matches a pastoralist group with its overall institution?
q.explanation: The Somali, Borana and Afar are led respectively by Ogaz, Abbaa Gadaa and Kedo Abba, so Abbaa Gadaa belongs to the Borana.

q.q: Indigenous conflict resolution mechanisms in Ethiopia gain their legitimacy from the community values rather than the state.
q.explanation: The practices gain legitimacy from community values instead of the state.

q.q: Explain why indigenous resolution produces win-win outcomes while formal courts often do not.
q.answer: it takes into account the interest of every party|formal courts impose winner-takes-all agreements
q.explanation: Indigenous mechanisms weigh the interests of every party so disputants gain and lose something, whereas formal courts impose zero-sum winner-takes-all justice.

q.q: In which year was the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples adopted?
q.explanation: The Declaration was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2007.

q.q: UNDRIP Article 32 provides that indigenous peoples have the right to:
options: determine and develop priorities for the use of their lands and resources
q.explanation: Article 32 guarantees indigenous peoples' right to set development priorities and strategies for their lands and resources.

q.q: In the Somali customary system, the governing unit whose elders act as judges and jury is the:
q.explanation: The guurti is the Somali council of elders whose decisions are respected and adhered to.

q.q: Name one way elders of the guurti prevent conflict rather than only settle it.
q.answer: monitoring and punishing potential triggers|pressing clans to honor inter-clan agreements
q.explanation: Elders monitor, punish individuals planning violence, and push clans to respect inter-clan agreements.

q.q: According to the Malthusian theory, food production increases while population increases in which two ways?
q.explanation: Malthus held that food production increases linearly (1, 2, 3, 4, 5...) while population rises geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32...).

q.q: Which of the following is a preventive check suggested by Malthus?
options: Moral restraint, such as late marriage
q.explanation: The key preventive check is moral restraint: marrying late in life to have fewer or smaller families.

q.q: Positive checks, according to Malthus, include poor living conditions, disease, wars and famines that shorten the duration of human life.
q.explanation: Positive checks are every cause which contributes to shortening the natural duration of human life.

q.q: Unlike Malthus, Neo-Malthusians argue that population growth should mainly be checked by:
q.explanation: Neo-Malthusians follow Malthus on population causing poverty but see birth control as the means of checking growth.

q.q: Which of the following is a criticism of the Neo-Malthusian perspective?
options: It gives too much attention to technology
It diverts attention from the social and economic causes of poverty
q.explanation: Critics argue that Neo-Malthusianism simply blames reproduction and ignores the structure of underdevelopment.

q.q: Which Danish economist argued in The Conditions of Agricultural Growth (1965) that population growth stimulates innovation in agriculture?
q.explanation: Ester Boserup took an empirical approach, arguing that population growth stimulates agricultural development.

q.q: Julian Simon argued that the ultimate resource is:
q.explanation: Simon believed minds matter economically as much as or more than hands or mouths, so people are the ultimate resource.

q.q: Critics of Malthus note that world food production has increased more rapidly than population, making food distribution rather than supply the key issue.
q.explanation: The textbook states food production rose faster than population and that distribution of food resources is the key issue.

q.q: According to Karl Marx, poverty and hunger result primarily from what condition?
q.answer: unequal distribution of resources between classes|unequal distribution|lack of access to means of subsistence
q.explanation: Marx maintained poverty is a consequence of unequal resource distribution between classes, not of population growth.

q.q: Why are the Malthusian and Neo-Malthusian views described as ethnocentric?
options: They judge the reproductive behavior of developing countries by western European standards
q.explanation: Both views implicitly evaluate people in developing countries using criteria specific to western Europeans, while treating Europe's difficulties as purely economic issues.

q.q: Arrange these population thinkers in order of when their main ideas appeared, earliest first.
q.explanation: The order is Malthus (1798), Marx (1818-1883), Boserup (1965), then Simon (whose theory followed hers).

q.q: A population policy is best defined as a policy formulated by a government in order to:
options: plan and control population growth, spatial distribution and structure
q.explanation: A population policy plans and controls growth, distribution and structure based on the country's conditions.

q.q: The two broad categories of population policies are:
q.explanation: Population policies are broadly categorized as anti-natalist and pro-natalist.

q.q: A pro-natalist population policy seeks to increase fertility rates and population growth rates.
q.explanation: Pro-natalist policy seeks to increase fertility in particular and growth in general.

q.q: Which country used the 1939 Family Code, birth premiums, loans to young married couples and housing subsidies to raise birth rates?
q.explanation: The French government used the 1939 Family Code and such benefits to increase birth rates.

q.q: China's total fertility rate shot up to over 6.0 by the early 1960s because:
options: the 1950s campaign to promote birth control broke down
of immigration from the Global South
q.explanation: The 1950s birth control campaign broke down, and the TFR rose above 6.0 by the early 1960s.

q.q: Give the term for a population policy that seeks to lower fertility rates and population growth rates.
q.explanation: Anti-natalist policy seeks to lower fertility rates in particular and growth rates in general.

q.q: In 2016 China abandoned its decades-old one-child policy in favor of a two-child restriction, which failed to result in a sustained increase in births.
q.explanation: The textbook note states the 2016 two-child restriction did not sustainably raise births.

q.q: By the turn of the present century, roughly how many countries provided incentives for women to have children?
q.explanation: Around 88 countries provided incentives for women to have children.

q.q: Which set of European countries had pro-natalist policies in place as early as the 1930s?
options: Germany, France, Sweden, Italy and Spain
q.explanation: Germany, France, Sweden, Italy and Spain had pro-natalist policies in place by the 1930s.

q.q: Name two indirect government measures that make having a child more economically feasible.
q.answer: flexible working hours|child care assistance|tax incentives|family allowances|low cost housing loans
q.explanation: Flexible working hours, child care assistance, tax incentives, family allowances and low-cost housing loans are indirect pro-fertility measures.

q.q: Ageing societies with low fertility may recruit young workers from the Global South, but geographers note a major drawback. Which one?
options: Such immigration policies are extremely politically sensitive
Immigrants are too old to work
No country has ever used immigration
q.explanation: The textbook warns that immigration-based responses to ageing are extremely politically sensitive.

q.q: The World Population Conference of 1974, where 136 countries agreed to a World Population Plan of Action, was held in:
q.explanation: The World Population Conference was held in Bucharest in 1974.

q.q: In which year was the International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD) held in Cairo?
q.explanation: The 1994 Cairo conference aimed at linking population more effectively to core development agendas.

q.q: According to the lesson, the most popular population control method in the world is:
q.explanation: Contraception, a family planning mechanism, is the most popular population control method in the world.

q.q: Under the child tax method of population control, taxpayers receive an exemption for which children, besides which no others are exempted?
q.answer: the first two|first two children|two children
q.explanation: Taxpayers are entitled to an exemption for a specified number of children, mostly the first two, but no others.

q.q: China's one-child policy was enforced through a system of fines and was relaxed after mass bereavements such as the Sichuan Earthquake.
q.explanation: The textbook states the policy was enforced through fines and relaxed after mass bereavements such as the Sichuan Earthquake.

q.q: Which country was the first in sub-Saharan Africa to begin developing a national family-planning campaign, in the late 1960s?
q.explanation: Kenya was the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to view runaway growth as an impediment and start a national family-planning campaign in the late 1960s.

q.q: By 2050 about twenty percent of the world's population, almost two thousand million people, will live in Africa. Especially large growth is expected in:
options: Nigeria, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo
q.explanation: Large growth is expected in Nigeria, Ethiopia and the DRC, and also Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Somalia and Uganda.

q.q: Name three obstacles connected with executing policy directions for family planning and reproductive health services.
q.answer: availability of facilities|awareness|language barrier|effectiveness|accessibility|cultural acceptance|religious acceptance|wife or husband's acceptance
q.explanation: Obstacles include availability of facilities and equipment, awareness, language barrier, effectiveness and accessibility of family planning methods and services, and cultural, religious and spousal acceptance.

q.q: As recently as 1970, Africa was essentially self-sufficient in food.
q.explanation: The breakdown came after 1968, with per capita grain production falling nearly 1 percent per year while population growth approached 3 percent.

q.q: Global population increases by about 1.5 percent per year. If this rate persisted, the textbook warns the world's population would:
options: double in less than half a century
q.explanation: At about 1.5 percent a year the doubling happens in less than half a century.

q.q: The consensus document of the 1994 Cairo conference recognizes that pressure on the natural environment comes from:
options: rapid growth in poor countries and consumption in wealthy countries
only population growth in poor countries
q.explanation: Cairo recognized that consumption in wealthy countries and rapid population growth in poor countries both put pressure on the environment, locally and globally.

q.q: GDP is best defined as:
options: the total value of currently produced final goods and services within a country's borders in a year, irrespective of who owns the outputs
q.explanation: GDP counts all currently produced final goods and services within the borders, regardless of ownership.

q.q: Per capita income is calculated by:
options: dividing national income by population size
dividing the poverty line by inflation
q.explanation: Per capita income is national income divided by population.

q.q: Standard of living is directly related to both GDP and per capita income.
q.explanation: As GDP and per capita income get higher, standard of living improves, and vice versa.

q.q: According to the 2020 table of richest nations, which of these countries had the highest GDP per capita income?
q.explanation: Switzerland's 87,100.40 US dollars exceeded Norway's 67,329.70 and the USA's 63,206.50.

q.q: State Ethiopia's GDP per capita income in US dollars for 2021 as listed in the least developed countries table.
q.explanation: Table 4.3 lists Ethiopia at 812 US dollars per capita income in 2021.

q.q: A country's total income is 40.6 billion US dollars and its population is 50 million. Its per capita income is:
In developing countries the GDP is not only low but is also dominated by:
q.explanation: Developing country GDP is dominated by primary commodities, while secondary and tertiary activities dominate in developed countries.

q.q: Rapid population growth can reduce or eliminate food production gains resulting from the modernization of farming.
q.explanation: Population pressure also encourages over-irrigation and overuse of croplands, undermining the capacity to feed larger numbers.

q.q: State the three objectives that development must have in any society.
q.answer: wider distribution of basic life-sustaining goods|raise living standards, income, employment and education|expand the range of economic and social choices
q.explanation: The objectives are basic goods for all, higher living standards, and expanded choices.

q.q: Which of the following is a health and demographic indicator of development?
q.explanation: Health indicators include life expectancy, infant and child mortality rates, maternal mortality ratio and underweight children.

q.q: Some less developed countries raised the percentage of children enrolled in school, yet the number of unenrolled children also increased. Why?
options: population growth increased the absolute number of children faster than resources could meet needs
teachers migrated abroad in large numbers
q.explanation: Absolute numbers of unenrolled children grew because there were insufficient resources to meet the growing need created by population growth.

q.q: Environmental health is best described as:
options: the interconnection between people and their environment by which human health and a non-polluted environment are sustained
q.explanation: Environmental health is the interconnection that sustains human health and a non-polluted environment.

q.q: Chapter 6 of UN Agenda 21, agreed at the 1992 Earth Summit, includes which of the following target areas?
options: Reducing health risks from environmental pollution
q.explanation: The five target areas include reducing health risks from environmental pollution, primary health care, communicable disease control, vulnerable groups and urban health.

q.q: The environmental health model that addresses environmental problems from human activities and natural processes is the:
q.explanation: The Environmental Stewardship Model addresses environmental problems from human activities and natural processes.

q.q: Air pollution is the world's largest single environmental risk to health, with some 7 million people dying each year from everyday exposure to poor air quality.
q.explanation: The textbook gives the figure of about 7 million deaths a year from poor air quality.

q.q: Name one of the zoonotic diseases listed in the lesson as emerging from animals to humans.
q.explanation: Covid-19, Zika, Ebola, MERS, SARS and Marburg are listed as zoonotic diseases now emerging every four months.

q.q: Environmental degradation is estimated to cause how many times as many premature deaths as occur in conflicts annually?
q.explanation: The estimate is 174-234 times as many premature deaths as conflicts cause annually.

q.q: According to the UNEP Healthy Environment, Healthy People report, lack of access to clean water and sanitation causes what share of diarrheal disease cases in low and middle-income countries?
q.explanation: The report attributes 58 percent of diarrheal disease cases in these countries to missing clean water and sanitation.

q.q: State the five basic requirements for a healthy environment given in the lesson.
q.answer: clean air|safe and sufficient water|safe and adequate food|safe and peaceful settlements|stable global environment
q.explanation: The requirements are clean air, safe and sufficient water, safe and adequate food, safe settlements and a stable global environment.

q.q: Arrange the three intervention models moving from treating disease after it occurs to addressing the environmental root causes.
q.explanation: The progression is Clinical (treatment), then Public Health (agent control), then Environmental Stewardship (root causes).

q.q: New zoonotic diseases are currently emerging every four months, driven partly by exponential population growth and the 36 billion domestic animals on the planet.
q.explanation: The textbook cites emerging zoonoses every four months, exponential population growth, intensive livestock breeding with 36 billion domestic animals, and biodiversity loss.

q.q: Disproportionate impacts of environmental harms fall especially on which groups?
options: The poor, the young, the elderly, women and migrant workers
Male office workers in rich countries
q.explanation: The groups most affected are the poor, the young, the elderly, women and migrant workers.

q.q: In 2015, approximately what share of the world's population lived in extreme poverty on less than $1.90 per day?
q.explanation: The textbook states that in 2015 roughly 10 percent of the world's population, 736 million people, lived in extreme poverty on less than $1.90 per day.

q.q: Relative poverty is defined as households receiving:
options: 50 percent less than average household incomes
q.explanation: Relative poverty means household income is 50 percent less than average household incomes.

q.q: Even if the country is growing economically, growth has no effect on people living below the absolute poverty line.
q.explanation: The textbook states that in absolute poverty, economic growth has no effect on those living below the poverty line.

q.q: Give the term for poverty measured as 50 or 60 percent below average income in 2 out of every 3 years.
q.explanation: This defines persistent poverty, whose long-term consequences are the most damaging.

q.q: Name any three dimensions of poverty given in the textbook's dimension and indicator table.
q.answer: income|education|health care|access to social services|social security
q.explanation: The listed dimensions are income, education, health care, access to social services and social security.

q.q: Which set of causes belongs to the structural approach to poverty?
options: Discrimination, low wages and failed investment
q.explanation: The structural approach cites discrimination, the profit motive and low wages, and failure to invest in education, health care and social insurance.

q.q: The behavioural or cultural approach argues every person has free will and is ultimately responsible for their own life.
q.explanation: The textbook states this view insists each person has free will and is ultimately responsible for their own life.

q.q: Explain how conflict worsens chronic poverty through population structure.
q.answer: higher dependency ratios from old, women and disabled|deaths disablement and displacement raise dependency ratios
q.explanation: Conflict raises dependency ratios through deaths, disablement and displacement of the old, women and disabled, increasing chronic poverty.

q.q: According to World Bank research cited in the text, rebellion is mainly motivated by what?
q.explanation: The World Bank research argues rebellion is motivated by greed, not merely grievance, because civil wars occur when rebels are financially viable.

q.q: What did a global analysis of conflict-affected countries find about government finances and trade?
q.answer: falls in government revenue and expenditure|falls in exports|falls in gross investment|fall in GDP per capita and food production
q.explanation: Conflict-affected countries showed falls in GDP per capita, food production, exports, gross investment and government revenue and expenditure.

q.q: Arrange the continuum the textbook draws from famine and conflict literature, from mildest to most severe.
q.explanation: The continuum runs from vulnerability to external shocks, to entitlement collapse, to starvation and death.

q.q: Globalization is best defined as the process through which the world becomes more linked as a result of:
q.explanation: The most common definition centres on greater commerce and cultural interaction.

q.q: Globalization has been happening for hundreds of years but has accelerated dramatically in the last half century.
q.explanation: The textbook states globalization has occurred for hundreds of years and accelerated dramatically in the last half century.

q.q: In which three fields is globalization manifested in developing countries?
options: Economic and trade processes, education and health systems, and culture effects
q.explanation: The textbook lists economic and trade processes, education and health systems, and culture effects.

q.q: Name the four kinds of highly qualified professionals that globalized competition pushes to migrate to developed countries.
q.answer: scientists, doctors, engineers and IT specialists
q.explanation: The text names scientists, doctors, engineers and IT specialists as those migrating for higher wages.

q.q: Which is an advantage of globalization?
options: Reduction of the likelihood of war between developed nations
q.explanation: Reduction of war between well developed nations is probably one of the primary benefits of globalization.

q.q: Setting up companies and factories in developing nations by developed countries has no effect on the economies of the developed countries.
q.explanation: The text states it affects the developed countries badly and can increase unemployment there.

q.q: Explain why rural China suffers high poverty despite China's rapid overall growth.
q.answer: it does not tap global markets|rural areas did not integrate into the global economy
q.explanation: The textbook notes the rural areas of China which do not tap global markets also suffer greatly from high poverty.

q.q: Name two Arab countries the textbook cites where cultures have been negatively affected by globalization.
q.explanation: The text lists Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Jordan as examples of negatively affected cultures.

q.q: Give two disadvantages of globalization listed for the environment and sovereignty.
q.answer: polluting corporations take advantage of weak rules|World Trade Organization infringes on sovereignty|diseases transported between nations
q.explanation: Environmental integrity falls when polluting corporations exploit weak rules, and bodies like the WTO infringe on national and individual sovereignty.

q.q: Which statement about the future of globalization matches the textbook's conclusion?
options: It is a global economic trend that is here to stay
Only the Global South should manage it
Only the Global North should manage it
q.explanation: The text says globalization is here to stay and all countries of the Global North and Global South must work together to spread its benefits.

q.q: Arrange the chain of globalization's trade effects in the developing world in logical order.
options: Developed countries invest and create jobs
Trade barriers previously prevented world market access
World Bank and IMF encourage market reforms through large loans
Markets open as tariffs are removed
q.explanation: Barriers came first, then reforms encouraged by loans, tariff removal, foreign investment and finally growth.

q.q: The convergence hypothesis states that less developed countries should:
options: grow faster than more developed ones
q.explanation: The catching-up hypothesis expects less developed countries and regions to grow faster, so inter-country inequality should decline.

q.q: The shift of large amounts of labour from farm to industry boosts labour productivity in general.
q.explanation: This is the third argument supporting the convergence hypothesis.

q.q: A trade imbalance, or negative trade balance, occurs when:
options: the cost of imports exceeds the cost of exports
the country sells goods abroad at a loss
q.explanation: A trade imbalance occurs when the cost of a country's imports exceeds the cost of its exports.

q.q: Which indicator is the most often used metric for evaluating global economic disparity?
q.explanation: The textbook names per capita GDP as the most often used metric.

q.q: How can a trade deficit actually improve living standards and reduce inflation risk, according to the text?
q.answer: broader range of goods at lower cost|lower prices reduce the threat of inflation
q.explanation: Citizens access a broader range of goods and services at lower cost, and lower created prices reduce inflation threats.

q.q: Which evidence supports divergence in inequality?
options: Growing skill premiums and financial deepening
q.explanation: Skill premiums expand inequality in advanced nations, while financial deepening is associated with rising inequality in developing countries.

q.q: According to the text, inequality in Sub-Saharan Africa is:
options: among the greatest in the world despite low per capita income
q.explanation: Inequality in Sub-Saharan Africa was discovered to be among the greatest in the world, despite low income levels.

q.q: Asset-based and capability-based inequalities tend to be higher in urban than rural areas.
q.explanation: The textbook states these inequalities tend to be higher in rural than urban areas, though income inequality is typically more urban.

q.q: Give the four features considered in per capita GDP assessments of disparity.
q.answer: physical attributes, personal preferences, social process, public policy
q.explanation: Assessment considers physical attributes, personal preferences, social processes and public policy.

q.q: What is a trade deficit also known as?
q.explanation: It is known as a negative trade balance, and borrowing to finance imports is a current account deficit.

q.q: During 1990-2012 in advanced economies, market income inequality increased far more than net inequality after redistribution. This shows:
options: net measures rose much less than market measures, showing redistribution's role
q.explanation: The text contrasts the rise in market income inequality against the far smaller rise in the net Gini coefficient.

q.q: Corruption is most commonly defined as:
options: the abuse of entrusted power for private gain
q.explanation: The common definition is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain.

q.q: Corruption is simultaneously a political, economic, legal and moral phenomenon.
q.explanation: The textbook states corruption is simultaneously political, economic, legal and moral.

q.q: The three broad categories of corruption are:
options: bribery, theft of public assets and patronage
q.explanation: The concept includes bribery, theft of public assets and patronage.

q.q: What term describes systematic theft at a grand scale by high public officials?
q.explanation: Systematic grand-scale theft by high officials is called kleptocracy.

q.q: Explain the relationship between transaction value and the position of officials involved in corruption.
q.answer: the larger the transaction, the higher the official's position|petty involves lower staff, grand higher officials
q.explanation: Typically, the larger the value of the corrupt transaction, the higher the position in the public hierarchy of the officials involved.

q.q: On the Corruption Perceptions Index scale,:
options: 0 means most corrupt and 100 least corrupt
q.explanation: Scores are normalised on an ordinal scale of zero (most corrupt) to 100 (least corrupt).

q.q: Almost three-fourths of the world's population lives in states with CPI scores of 20-39, classed as very corrupt.
q.explanation: 82 states with scores 20-39 held 5210.2 million people, about 72.9 percent of humanity.

q.q: Name the African country the textbook singles out as the continent's least corrupt (CPI 60-79).
q.explanation: Botswana is noted as Africa's least-corrupt country in the 60-79 tier.

q.q: List the attributes the textbook gives for the most corrupt countries.
q.answer: low-income|closed economy|visible religious influence|low media freedom|low education
q.explanation: They are usually low-income, closed economies with visible religious influence, low media freedom and relatively low education.

q.q: Which is a documented effect of corruption on public finances?
options: It redirects expenditure toward maintenance of clinics
It reduces the effectiveness of public investments and infrastructure
It lowers the volume of public investment
q.explanation: Corruption reduces the effectiveness of public investments and the country's infrastructure.

q.q: Arrange the first three remedial measures in the textbook's suggested order for fighting system-level corruption.
q.explanation: The textbook lists leadership first, then credibility, then involving people, before press, oversight bodies and institutions.

q.q: Globally, approximately how many people do not have access to basic health services?
q.explanation: The textbook estimates 2 billion individuals lack access to basic health services.

q.q: Malaria causes approximately one death every 30 seconds worldwide.
q.explanation: The text equates malaria's more than one million yearly deaths with one death every 30 seconds.

q.q: How much of the $3.2 trillion spent on health care worldwide in 2002 went to low- and middle-income nations?
q.explanation: Only 12 percent was spent in low- and middle-income nations, which hold 90 percent of the illness burden.

q.q: A disease officially becomes a pandemic when:
options: it kills more than one million people
an epidemic spreads beyond a country's borders
q.explanation: When an epidemic spreads beyond a country's borders, the disease officially becomes a pandemic.

q.q: Explain the possible role of the Great Plague of Athens in the Peloponnesian War.
q.answer: it weakened the Athenians significantly and was a significant factor in their defeat
q.explanation: The suspected typhoid fever significantly weakened Athens and was a significant factor in its defeat by the Spartans.

q.q: The epidemic that passed through Libya, Ethiopia and Egypt before entering Athens is known as what?
q.explanation: The Great Plague of Athens of 430 BC passed through Libya, Ethiopia and Egypt before crossing the Athenian walls.

q.q: AIDS was first observed in Africa.
q.explanation: The textbook states AIDS was first observed in America, though first identified in 1981.

q.q: Why did Ebola hit Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone so hard? Give at least two reasons from the text.
q.answer: vulnerable public health infrastructure|aftermath of civil war|lack of basic sanitation|no minimum core capacity to detect, report and respond
q.explanation: These states had historically weak health systems, devastated by civil war, poor sanitation and lacking core outbreak response capacity.

q.q: On what date did the WHO declare COVID-19 a pandemic, and how many cases and countries had been reached?
q.explanation: The declaration came after the virus infected over 118,000 individuals in 114 nations in three months.

q.q: By December 2020, COVID-19 had:
options: infected more than 75 million people and killed more than 1.6 million
been controlled by a vaccine launched in 2020
infected fewer than one million people
q.explanation: By December 2020, more than 75 million people were infected and more than 1.6 million had died.

q.q: Arrange these events in chronological order.
options: Ebola index patient reported in Guinea
COVID-19 first reported case in Hubei, China
q.explanation: The order is Spanish Flu (1918), AIDS identified (1981), Ebola index case (December 2013), COVID-19 first case (November 17, 2019).

q.q: The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development that sparked global interest in environmental concerns took place in 1992 in:
q.explanation: Interest in global environmental concerns grew significantly after the 1992 Rio de Janeiro conference.

q.q: In the environment formula I = f(P,A,T), the letter A stands for:
options: Increasing affluence, that is consumption of goods and services
q.explanation: A is increasing affluence or consumption; P is population growth and T is environmentally unsound technology.

q.q: The ecological footprints of poorer nations and their citizens are vastly lower than those of wealthy nations.
q.explanation: Environmental analysts emphasize this disproportionate share of wealthy nations in global demands on the ecosystem.

q.q: Ozone layer depletion is highest over tropical areas.
q.explanation: Depletion occurs globally except over tropical areas, and its rate is higher in the highest latitude regions.

q.q: Which of the following is a primary pollutant?
q.explanation: Carbon monoxide is emitted directly from incomplete combustion; ozone and smog form secondarily in the atmosphere.

q.q: Name the international agreement that reduced emissions of ozone-depleting substances and protected both the ozone layer and the climate.
q.explanation: By reducing emissions of ozone-depleting substances, the Montreal Protocol protected both the ozone layer and the climate.

q.q: Distinguish point source from nonpoint source water pollution.
q.answer: point source comes from a single origin and nonpoint source from diffused sources
q.explanation: Pollution from a single source is point source pollution; from diffused sources it is nonpoint source pollution.

q.q: Over the past 50 years, the amount of zero-oxygen ocean water has:
q.explanation: Globally the amount of zero-oxygen ocean water has quadrupled, while low-oxygen zones increased 10 times.

q.q: Explain why water is easily polluted, according to the textbook.
q.answer: dissolves more substances than any other liquid|water dissolves more substances than any other liquid|dissolves more than other liquids
q.explanation: Water is able to dissolve more substances than any other liquid, which is why it is easily polluted.

q.q: Arrange the causal chain of climate change in the correct order.
options: Greenhouse gases intensify by blocking thermal radiation
Global mean temperature and sea level patterns shift
Carbon dioxide accumulates in the atmosphere
q.explanation: Order: fossil fuels are burned, carbon dioxide accumulates, greenhouse gases block thermal radiation, then surface temperature and sea level patterns shift.

q.q: The Montreal Protocol's replacement gases (HFCs, PFCs, SF6) are greenhouse gases even though they do not deplete ozone.
q.explanation: F-gases are not ozone-depleting substances but are recognized greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.

q.q: Which city was the only one with more than 10 million people in 1950?
q.explanation: In 1950 New York was the only city in the world with a population of more than 10 million.

q.q: Currently about 80 million people are added every year in less developed countries, compared with about 1.6 million in more developed countries.
q.explanation: The textbook gives exactly these figures, showing growth is fastest where it cannot be afforded.

q.q: Dividing the Earth's productive hectares among its people shows we are using:
options: About 2.2 hectares per person against 1.8 available
About 1.8 hectares per person against 2.2 available
q.explanation: 11.2 billion hectares over 6.3 billion people is about 1.8 hectares per person, while we collectively use about 2.2 - over 20 percent more than is produced annually.

q.q: State the threshold of annual renewable freshwater per capita below which a country is considered water-scarce.
q.answer: less than 1000 cubic metres per capita|1000 m3 per capita|less than 1,000 cubic metres
q.explanation: A country is water-scarce when its annual renewable freshwater is less than 1,000 cubic metres per capita.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as an impact of population growth coupled with urbanization?
q.explanation: Urban growth brings loss of natural beauty, not recovery of it.

q.q: Explain why, according to the textbook, only limited areas of the Earth are available for comfortable human settlement.
q.answer: three quarters covered by seas|half the land is desert|quarter is high mountain|only one eighth suitable
q.explanation: Seas cover three-quarters, half of terrestrial land is desert and more than a quarter is high mountain, leaving one-eighth suitable.

q.q: The world generates 2.01 billion tons of municipal solid garbage yearly. High-income nations, with 16 percent of world population, produce about:
q.explanation: High-income nations create 34 percent, or 683 million tons, of global garbage despite being 16 percent of the population.

q.q: Only about 0.3 percent of the Earth's water is the easily accessible surface water found in rivers and lakes.
q.explanation: Only 2.5 percent of water is fresh, three-quarters of that is locked in glaciers and snow, and just 0.3 percent is surface water.

q.q: According to the textbook, about half of the carbon dioxide on Earth is fixed by:
q.explanation: About half of the Earth's carbon dioxide is fixed by cyanobacteria and other ocean microbes, mainly through photosynthesis.

q.q: Name the three essential elements of a solar chimney power plant.
q.answer: glass roof collector, chimney, wind turbine|glass roof collector|chimney|turbine
q.explanation: The solar chimney consists of three essential elements: glass roof collector, chimney and wind turbine.

q.q: Arrange the sustainability challenges named in the lesson from those concerning living space to those concerning discards.
q.explanation: The lesson lists them as: population growth, urbanization, energy use and global warming, water shortages, waste management.

q.q: Environmental education is most simply described as education:
options: in, about, and for the environment
q.explanation: The textbook defines it as education in, about, and for the environment.

q.q: Environmental education engages audiences from youth to the elderly and settings from schools to museums and boardrooms.
q.explanation: Its audiences range from youth to the elderly and its settings from schools and courthouses to museums and boardrooms.

q.q: Learning from the actions of others, without any teaching, is called:
q.explanation: Tacit knowledge is obtained implicitly by living together, contacts or socializing.

q.q: State the three goals on which environmental education is built.
q.answer: awareness of interdependence|knowledge values attitudes commitment skills|new patterns of behaviour
q.explanation: Foster awareness of economic, social, political and ecological interdependence; provide knowledge, values, attitudes, commitment and skills; create new patterns of behaviour of individuals, groups and society.

q.q: Which activity type establishes a dialogue between audiences and environmental organizations for sharing experiences and priorities?
q.explanation: Communication activities establish dialogue for the mutual sharing of experiences, priorities and planning.

q.q: Environmental education ends when someone leaves school.
q.explanation: It is a lifelong strategy that also nurtures the environmental literacy of adults whose behaviours and political actions affect conservation.

q.q: Which name is given to the idea that a logical series of events shows how present activities lead to future goals in a well-designed environmental education initiative?
q.explanation: Well-designed initiatives are built around a theory of change.

q.q: Good environmental education teaches people:
q.explanation: It teaches people how to think, not what to think, and builds citizen-action skills.

q.q: Name the thinker whose 18th-century emphasis on environment-focused education marks the origins of environmental education.
q.explanation: The origins trace back to the 18th century, when Jean-Jacques Rousseau emphasized the necessity of an environment-focused education.

q.q: Arrange the strategy continuum in the order the lesson presents it, ideally each built upon the other.
q.explanation: The order is: information, communication, education, then capacity building activities.

q.q: Within a formal school setting, social studies and history are as important as geography, biology and chemistry for addressing environmental problems.
q.explanation: The textbook stresses that social studies, government studies and history are as important as the natural sciences.

q.q: An environmental movement is best described as:
options: A social movement of individuals, groups and coalitions acting to change environmental policies and practices
q.explanation: It involves an array of individuals, groups and coalitions with a common interest in environmental protection.

q.q: Free market environmentalism contends that the free market, property rights and tort law are the greatest tools for preserving the environment.
q.explanation: That is its defining claim, in contrast to reliance on legislative government action.

q.q: Which type differs from preservation in that it allows some industrial growth within sustainable bounds?
q.explanation: Conservation permits sustainable industrial growth; preservation sets resources strictly aside.

q.q: Which motto sums up the Light Green way of thinking, and what is their focus?
q.answer: green is the new black|lifestyle choice|personal responsibility
q.explanation: The motto 'Green is the new black' reflects their treatment of environmentalism as a lifestyle choice and personal responsibility.

q.q: Which group believes we can neither shop nor protest our way to sustainability and instead promotes tools, models and ideas?
q.explanation: Bright Greens rely on better designs, new technologies and widely distributed social innovations.

q.q: In what year was LEM Ethiopia founded, and by how many professionals?
q.explanation: LEM Ethiopia was founded in 1992 by 29 prominent Ethiopian professionals in environment and development.

q.q: Explain why the waste campaign of Sileshi Demise (Gash Abera Molla) is given special historical importance in Addis Ababa.
q.answer: precursor of the riparian buffer projects|great impact on the community|precursor to riparian buffer projects
q.explanation: His municipal solid waste controlling task had great impact and is seen as the precursor of Addis Ababa's current riparian buffer projects.

q.q: The Green Legacy campaign claimed over four billion seedlings planted in 2019 and raised this to five billion in 2020. This was an initiative led by:
q.explanation: Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's Green Legacy achieved over four billion seedlings in 2019 and five billion in 2020.

q.q: Ethiopian youth perspectives are largely absent from environmental and climate policy arenas.
q.explanation: The textbook highlights this as a pressing moral need - youth will inherit the environment adults create today - and a political need for global activism.

q.q: Give the name Dark Greens use for the emphasis on growth that exists within all existing ideologies.
q.explanation: Dark Greens claim environmental problems stem from the growth emphasis in all ideologies, a tendency called growth mania.

q.q: Arrange the Ethiopian green movement milestones in chronological order.
options: Green Legacy raises planting to 5 billion seedlings
First Green Legacy plants over 4 billion seedlings
Meles Zenawi leads Africa's climate negotiations
q.explanation: Order: LEM Ethiopia founded in 1992, Meles Zenawi's climate leadership, the 2019 campaign, then 2020's 5 billion seedlings.

q.q: Indigenous knowledge transmitted orally or by imitation is best described as:
options: Local, orally-transmitted knowledge rooted in everyday experience
q.explanation: It is rooted in a particular place, transmitted orally or through imitation and demonstration, and reinforced by everyday experience.
