q.explanation: Afroalpine lies above 3,300 m, with sub-Afroalpine between 3,000 and 3,300 m.

q.q: Lowland forests in Ethiopia are found on the banks of the Awash, Wabe Shebelle and Genale rivers.
q.explanation: Gallery or riverine forests grow along these banks where soil moisture is available.

q.q: Which primate, endemic to Ethiopia, lives in the Semein highlands under the name Gelada or Chilada?
q.explanation: The Gelada or Chilada baboon is endemic to the Semein highlands.

q.q: How many species of mammals and birds live in Ethiopia, in total number of species?
q.explanation: Ethiopia has about 277 mammal species and 862 bird species.

q.q: Explain why semi-desert vegetation is dominated by xerophytes.
q.answer: rainfall below 600 mm and long drought|drought-resisting plants survive dry areas
q.explanation: The lowlands receive below 600 mm annual rainfall with persistent drought, so only drought-resisting xerophytes survive.

q.q: Which animal is a game animal (herbivore grazer) of the Ethiopian lowlands?
q.explanation: Wild ass is a game herbivore grazer, along with zebra; giraffes are browsers.

q.q: Explain the relationship between altitude, vegetation and wild animals in Ethiopia.
q.answer: altitude controls climate and vegetation belts|animals concentrate where vegetation suits them
q.explanation: Altitude shapes climate and hence vegetation from Afroalpine to semi-desert, and wildlife habitats follow the vegetation belts, concentrating animals in the south and west.

q.q: Order these highland forest trees from the highest to the lowest altitudinal belt.
q.explanation: Kerkha (2,800-3,000 m) is highest, then Zigba (1,800-2,200 m), then Woira and Kosso (1,500-1,800 m).

q.q: In population studies, the term population refers to:
options: all living organisms in an area
the total number of human inhabitants of a specified area at a given time
only the working people of a country
q.explanation: Population means the total number of human inhabitants of a specified area at a given time.

q.q: The branch of geography concerned mainly with the spatial analysis of human population is:
q.explanation: Population geography focuses on population-space relationships.

q.q: Human population is studied only by geographers.
q.explanation: It is also studied by biology, sociology, medical science, history and other disciplines.

q.q: Which branch of geography studies the interaction between human population and the physical environment?
q.explanation: Population geography emphasises spatial aspects and the population-environment interaction.

q.q: Why is the study of population important for the economy?
options: Because population is the major source of labour force and creator of material wealth
q.explanation: Population supplies labour for agriculture, manufacturing, teaching, health services and more.

q.q: Change in the size, composition, structure and location of population has policy implications.
q.explanation: The textbook lists policy implications as a reason for studying population.

q.q: Name two government planning fields that use population information.
q.explanation: Planning in health, education, housing, social security, employment and environment preservation uses population data.

q.q: Population policies are formulated in order to:
options: modify demographic trends to achieve economic and social objectives
q.explanation: Population policies seek to modify demographic trends for economic and social goals.

q.q: Explain why population is described as 'very dynamic'.
q.answer: it shows quantitative and qualitative changes over time and space|size and quality change over time and place
q.explanation: Population demonstrates significant quantitative and qualitative changes over time and space.

q.q: About how many people live on the earth today?
q.explanation: The textbook states there are 7.9 billion people on the earth.

q.q: Name the population characteristic besides size that planners must also know, according to the lesson.
q.explanation: Size, composition, structure and location all change and all have policy implications.

q.q: Ethiopia's rank in world population in 2020 was:
q.explanation: With 114.9 million people, Ethiopia ranked 12th in the world in 2020.

q.q: Ethiopia is the second most populous country in Africa.
q.explanation: The textbook states Ethiopia is the second most populous country in Africa.

q.q: According to the 2007 Census, Ethiopia's population was:
q.explanation: The 2007 Census counted 73.8 million people.

q.q: Why was Ethiopia's population growth slow before 1920?
q.explanation: The slow growth before 1920 reflected the country's high mortality rate.

q.q: Between 1980 and 1990 the growth rate of Ethiopia's population was around 3.0 percent.
q.explanation: Growth was about 3.0 percent, peaking at 3.1 percent in 1984.

q.q: What was Ethiopia's population in 1900?
q.explanation: Table 4.1 gives 11.8 million people in 1900.

q.q: The population doubled between 1960 and 1990. This indicates a doubling time of about:
q.explanation: From 23.5 million in 1960 to 51.2 million in 1990 is a doubling time of about 30 years.

q.q: Put these years in order of increasing population size.
Explain how disease control affected Ethiopia's population growth after the 1950s.
q.answer: mortality fell so growth rose|malaria control lowered deaths and growth rate increased
q.explanation: Efforts to control malaria and other diseases from the 1950s reduced mortality, and the growth rate rose year by year to 2.8 percent in 1980.

q.q: What does Table 4.1 list as the doubling time of Ethiopia's population in 2020?
q.explanation: The 2020 doubling time is about 27 years at 2.6 percent growth.

q.q: A slight fall in the growth rate between censuses means the population became smaller.
q.explanation: The population still increased, from 42.6 to 53.5 to 73.8 million; only the pace slowed.

q.q: Population composition refers to aspects of population measured in terms of:
options: age, sex, marital status, language, religion and other attributes
q.explanation: Composition covers age, sex, marital status, family size, economic activities, nationality, language and religion.

q.q: A population pyramid is a graphic representation of the distribution of a population by:
q.explanation: The pyramid shows the population distribution by age and sex.

q.q: Ethiopia's population pyramid has a broad base that narrows towards the top.
q.explanation: The pyramid is triangular with a very broad base, typical of a population with high fertility.

q.q: Which broad age group is called the economically active population?
q.explanation: The 15-64 age group is the working age, economically active population.

q.q: The high percentage of young people in Ethiopia results from:
options: high birth rate and natural increase
low death rates among the old
q.explanation: The dominant young-age share is the result of a high birth rate and natural increase.

q.q: Ethiopia's small percentage of old-age people indicates a long life expectancy.
q.explanation: The small old-age share reflects high mortality, which results in low life expectancy.

q.q: What was Ethiopia's age dependency ratio in 2020?
q.explanation: There were 76.8 dependents on 100 working-age persons in 2020.

q.q: A country has 50 percent working-age population, 44 percent young and 6 percent old. Its age dependency ratio is:
q.explanation: ADR = (44 + 6) / 50 x 100 = 100 dependents per 100 workers.

q.q: Explain what a high dependency ratio means for an economy.
q.answer: workers support many dependents|greater burden to support children and elderly
q.explanation: The economically active population and the economy face a greater burden to provide services for children and the elderly.

q.q: The 2007 census sex ratio for Ethiopia was:
q.explanation: The sex ratio was 101.9 males per 100 females in 2007.

q.q: Arrange these census years from lowest to highest sex ratio.
Population density refers to:
options: the way a country is mapped
the average number of people per square kilometre
the total population of a region
the number of towns in an area
q.explanation: Population density is the average number of people per square kilometre.

q.q: About 77.5 percent of Ethiopia's population lives at altitudes above 1800 metres.
q.explanation: The textbook states 77.5 percent live above 1800 metres.

q.q: Which region, excluding urban administrations, has the highest population density?
q.explanation: SNNP has about 173 people per square kilometre, the highest of the regions.

q.q: Which river valley is the main exception where major river valleys in Ethiopia have dense settlement?
q.explanation: Irrigation agriculture in the Awash valley supports more people than other river valleys.

q.q: What is the most crucial physical factor influencing population distribution in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: Most physical factors are influenced by altitude, making it the most crucial.

q.q: In most pastoralist areas of Ethiopia, grazing land requirement is as large as 20 hectares or more per head of cattle.
q.explanation: This huge land need explains the extremely low densities of pastoralist areas.

q.q: Name two regions of Ethiopia with low population density.
q.explanation: Somali, Afar, Benishangul-Gumuz and Gambella have low densities.

q.q: Explain why the lowlands of Ethiopia are sparsely populated.
q.answer: high temperature, low rainfall, poor soils, tropical diseases such as malaria and yellow fever
q.explanation: Scarcity of rainfall, high temperature, poor vegetation and soils, and tropical diseases keep settlement sparse.

q.q: Woredas such as Wanago, Damot Gale and Aleta Wendo exceed a crude density of:
q.explanation: These woredas have crude densities exceeding 500 people per square kilometre.

q.q: The textbook generalizes that the lower the administrative unit, the greater the ... in population density.
q.explanation: Zone and woreda level densities vary far more than regional ones.

q.q: Ethiopia's crude density in 2020 was about:
q.explanation: Crude density rose from 40.7 in 1990 to 52 in 1998 and 103.9 in 2020.

q.q: The origin of settlements can be traced back to:
options: caves used for protection and defence
q.explanation: Settlements began in caves where people gathered for protection against natural forces and defence against rival tribes.

q.q: The primary bases for distinguishing rural and urban settlements are dominant economic activities and population density.
q.explanation: Occupation and density separate rural from urban settlements in Ethiopia.

q.q: A settlement is considered permanent if it remains in place for more than:
q.explanation: Settlements are permanent if their locations do not frequently change, staying more than ten years.

q.q: Which Ethiopian regime's compulsory villagization program created grouped villages in many areas?
q.explanation: The Derg's compulsory villagization formed grouped settlements, from which people later returned.

q.q: Temporary settlements in Ethiopia are inhabited mainly by:
q.explanation: Temporary settlements are mobile settlements of nomadic people who move with their herds.

q.q: Urbanization in Ethiopia was greatly influenced by European colonialism.
q.explanation: Unlike most of Africa, Ethiopia's urbanization is an unplanned, natural phenomenon of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

q.q: What minimum population size does a settlement need to be classified as an urban centre in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: The criteria require a minimum of 2000 people.

q.q: Give two criteria used in Ethiopia for granting the status of urban centre.
q.answer: minimum 2000 people|two-thirds in non-agricultural activities|chartered municipality|social services and amenities
q.explanation: The four criteria are size of at least 2000 people, two-thirds non-agricultural work, a chartered municipality, and social services.

q.q: In 1984 the share of Ethiopia's population living in urban settlements was:
q.explanation: In 1984, 322 urban settlements held 10.23 percent of the population, among the least urban in the world.

q.q: Put these settlement forms from smallest to largest in the settlement hierarchy.
q.explanation: The order is hamlet, village, town, city, metropolis.

q.q: Why did people reverse the Derg's villagization and return to their original sites?
q.answer: forced against their will and services were non-existent|coercion and no services
q.explanation: Because people were forced into villages against their will and the promised services were non-existent, they began returning even before the regime fell.

q.q: Ethiopia's life expectancy increased from 56.8 years in 2005 to about what value in 2016?
q.explanation: Life expectancy rose to 65.5 years in 2016.

q.q: The majority of ill health in Ethiopia is related to potentially preventable communicable diseases and nutritional disorders.
q.explanation: The textbook states most ill health is from preventable communicable diseases and nutritional disorders.

q.q: Which of the following are root causes of Ethiopia's poor health status?
options: Clean water everywhere and good nutrition
Lack of access to clean water and inadequate nutrition
q.explanation: Root causes include lack of clean water, malnutrition, harmful traditional practices and underfunded health services.

q.q: How many children under the age of five in Ethiopia are malnourished, stunted or wasted, according to the textbook?
q.answer: about half|half of the children under five
q.explanation: About half of children under five are malnourished, stunted or wasted.

q.q: The major killer diseases account for about what share of all deaths in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: Prenatal-maternal conditions, respiratory infection, malaria, malnutrition, diarrhea, AIDS and TB cause about 75 percent of deaths.

q.q: There is one doctor per 26,943 people in Ethiopia.
q.explanation: The workforce figures give one doctor per 26,943 people and one nurse per 2,311 people.

q.q: Name the two super families to which Ethiopian languages belong.
q.explanation: Ethiopian languages belong to the Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan super families.

q.q: Which Afro-Asiatic family has the largest number of speakers and the widest spatial coverage in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: The Cushitic family has the largest number of speakers and the widest coverage.

q.q: Arrange these religious groups of the 2007 census from most to least numerous.
q.explanation: The order is Orthodox 43.5, Islam 33.9, Protestant 18.6, then Catholic 0.7 and others 3.2.

q.q: Explain why Ethiopia has not attained food security, as reflected in widespread malnutrition.
q.answer: smallholder subsistence farming depends on rain and traditional methods|rain-fed subsistent methods and population pressure keep production low
q.explanation: Agriculture is dominated by smallholder peasant farming using traditional, subsistence, rain-fed methods, so per capita food production has deteriorated.

q.q: Show how rapid population growth causes fuel wood shortage in Ethiopia.
q.answer: wood collected faster than it can regrow|rising demand for fuel wood outpaces regrowth
q.explanation: Fuel wood is collected faster than forests regrow, and increasing needs for farmland, houses and grazing also clear forests, so supply collapses.

q.q: Economic activity is best defined as the:
options: production, distribution and exchange of goods and services
collection of taxes by the government
q.explanation: The textbook defines economic activity as the production, distribution and exchange of goods and services.

q.q: Which is the correct complete set of economic sectors?
options: Primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary
q.explanation: The five classes are primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary.

q.q: Primary economic activities focus directly on the extraction of resources from the environment.
q.explanation: Primary activities extract resources directly and produce foodstuffs and raw materials.

q.q: In which traditional zones does most Ethiopian agricultural production take place?
q.explanation: Most agricultural production takes place in the Dega and Woina Dega zones where productivity coincided with densest rural population.

q.q: Name the perennial crop that is the staple food of the peoples of southern and southwestern Ethiopia.
q.explanation: Enset is the staple food of the Woina Dega areas of southern and southwestern Ethiopia.

q.q: Shifting cultivation, the cut-and-burn system, is practiced mainly in:
options: Benishangul-Gumuz, Gambella and the Southern Regions
q.explanation: It is practiced in the western and southwestern fringes where population density is low.

q.q: Ethiopia stands first in the world in cattle population.
q.explanation: Ethiopia stands first in Africa and tenth in the world in cattle population.

q.q: Explain why the distribution of jobs among the economic activities indicates a country's level of development.
q.answer: countries with more primary jobs are less developed|advanced countries have more service and knowledge jobs|development shifts jobs to services
q.explanation: The share of jobs in each sector reflects development; advanced economies hold more secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary jobs.

q.q: Arrange the sectors from the one closest to nature to the most knowledge based.
q.explanation: The order is primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary, quinary; Primary comes first.

q.q: Which pair correctly matches a manufacturing type with an example?
q.explanation: Weaving, wood carving, pottery, metal works and basketry are cottage industries.

q.q: Mining currently contributes more than 10 percent of Ethiopia's GDP.
q.explanation: Mining contributes only 1.5 percent of GDP.

q.q: According to the textbook, agriculture contributed what percentage of GDP in 2019/20?
q.explanation: Agriculture contributed 32.7 percent of GDP in 2019/20, down from 39.6 percent in 2014/15.

q.q: After 2015/16, which sector became the dominant sector of the Ethiopian economy?
q.explanation: The service sector emerged as dominant after 2015/16 due to natural and economic factors.

q.q: Agriculture supplies more than 90 percent of Ethiopia's export commodities.
q.explanation: Agriculture supplies more than 90 percent of export commodities and is the main source of export earnings.

q.q: Name Ethiopia's most important export commodity, which accounted for about 28.6 percent of export value in 2019/20.
q.explanation: Coffee is the most important export commodity at about 28.6 percent of export value.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a problem of Ethiopian agriculture?
q.explanation: The problems listed are land degradation, rainfall variability, fragmentation, backward technology and poor infrastructure.

q.q: According to Table 5.2, what share of farming households accesses less than 0.5 hectares?
q.explanation: 38 percent of households access less than 0.5 hectares when the two smallest classes are combined.

q.q: Subsistence farming produces mainly for family needs, leaving little surplus for the market.
q.explanation: Nearly all crops or livestock raised are used to maintain the farmer and family.

q.q: Explain why households farming less than one hectare often face food shortages.
q.answer: the plot is too small to produce enough food|fragmented plots cannot fulfill household needs
q.explanation: Households with less than one hectare are often unable to fulfill household needs including necessary food consumption.

q.q: Arrange the steps of traditional smallholder farming in the order the textbook describes.
options: Land preparation with an oxen drawn plough
q.explanation: The order is land preparation, planting by broadcasting, manual weeding, then harvesting with the sickle.

q.q: Cash crop production contributes to the Ethiopian economy mainly by:
options: raising capital through taxation and exports while creating rural employment
q.explanation: Cash crops supply raw materials, raise capital via agricultural taxation and exports, and bring wage employment to the rural economy.

q.q: Bad road conditions in rural areas raise transport costs and reduce farmers' income.
q.explanation: The bad condition of rural roads raises transport costs, which in turn reduces farmers' income.

q.q: Trade is best defined as:
options: the buying and selling of goods and services
q.explanation: Trade involves buying and selling of goods and services with compensation paid by a buyer to a seller.

q.q: Internal (domestic) trade differs from foreign trade because it takes place:
q.explanation: Internal trade is the exchange of goods and services within the country and is the base for foreign trade.

q.q: More than 95 percent of Ethiopia's trade passes through Djibouti.
q.explanation: The new railway links Addis Ababa with Djibouti and its Port of Doraleh, through which more than 95 percent of trade passes.

q.q: In 2019/20, the second largest export item by value share was:
q.explanation: Flower and oilseeds held the second and third positions with 14.1 percent and 11.5 percent.

q.q: Name the only navigable river in Ethiopia.
q.explanation: The Baro is the only navigable river, with small-scale transport also on lakes Tana, Abbaya and Ziway.

q.q: The use of Ethiopian rivers for inland navigation is extremely limited mainly because of:
options: the rugged topography and the seasonal nature of rainfall
q.explanation: Ruggedness of topography and seasonal rainfall make river use extremely limited.

q.q: Ethiopia imports mainly agricultural raw materials.
q.explanation: Ethiopia imports mainly finished products such as machinery, transport equipment, electrical goods and fuel.

q.q: Explain what a trade balance is and describe Ethiopia's trade balance.
q.answer: yearly difference between export and import values|imports exceed exports so deficit|negative trade balance
q.explanation: Trade balance is the yearly difference between exports and imports; in Ethiopia imports exceed exports, giving a deficit.

q.q: Arrange these transport milestones from earliest to latest.
options: Addis Ababa - Djibouti meter gauge railway built (1897-1917)
q.explanation: The order is the old railway, Ethiopian Airlines, the AA-LRT, then the new railway.

q.q: The total length of the two AA-LRT lines with their 39 stations is about:
q.explanation: The north-south and east-west lines total about 31.6 kilometres with 39 stations, carrying about 60,000 people daily.

q.q: Road transport is more widespread and more flexible than railway transport in Ethiopia.
q.explanation: Road transport is more widespread and more flexible, and roads give access to rural and urban areas.

q.q: Under Ethiopia's current definition, a fatal accident is one in which:
options: one or more individuals die within 30 days of the accident
q.explanation: A fatal accident causes one or more deaths within the same 30 days of occurrence.

q.q: According to the WHO 2020 report, about how many people die on the world's roads each year?
q.explanation: An estimated 1.3 million people die and about 50 million are injured each year, mostly in low- and middle-income countries.

q.q: Road traffic deaths in Ethiopia more than doubled between 2007 and 2018.
q.explanation: Deaths rose from 2,161 in 2007 to 4,597 in 2018.

q.q: How many people does Ethiopia lose per day in road traffic crashes, according to the tablebased statistics?
q.explanation: Ethiopia loses 13 people per day, and one person is killed every two hours.

q.q: About how many people were killed per 10,000 vehicles in Ethiopia in 2018?
q.explanation: With 4,597 deaths and 1,071,345 vehicles, nearly 43 people were killed per 10,000 vehicles.

q.q: Road traffic injuries in Ethiopia mostly affect:
q.explanation: Road traffic injuries mostly affect passengers and pedestrians.

q.q: Oromia, Amhara, SNNPR and Addis Ababa together accounted for almost 85 percent of road traffic fatalities.
q.explanation: Four regional states accounted for almost 85 percent of fatalities, concentrated in central Ethiopia.

q.q: Explain why impaired driving is considered the most dangerous of the listed causes.
q.answer: it causes more than half of all car crashes|prevention of normal driving skill
q.explanation: Impairment by illness, alcohol, drugs or sleepiness prevents normal driving and causes more than half of all crashes.

q.q: Arrange the pedestrian safety steps from planning to night-time visibility.
options: Prepare a safe walking route in advance
Stay on well-lit paths at night
q.explanation: The order starts with preparing the safe route, then crossing safely, then night-time steps.

q.q: Which of the following is a vehicle-related cause of accidents?
q.explanation: Mechanical failure includes flat tires, brake failure, axle failure and steering mechanism failure.

q.q: A property damage only accident is one in which no person is injured.
q.explanation: In property damage only accidents only the vehicles involved are damaged.

q.q: A cultural landscape is best described as:
options: the combined works of nature and man
q.explanation: Cultural landscapes represent the combined works of nature and man, tied to historic events, activities or persons.

q.q: The Konso cultural landscape is characterised by:
options: dry stone terrace agriculture and walled towns
q.explanation: It is characterised by dry stone terrace agriculture and walled town settlement at the edge of the Rift Valley.

q.q: UNESCO officially recognised the Konso Cultural Landscape in 2011.
q.explanation: UNESCO officially recognised it in 2011.

q.q: What name is given to tourism because it produces income without factories?
q.explanation: Tourism is known as a smokeless industry.

q.q: Which of the following is a natural tourist attraction?
q.explanation: The Simien Mountains National Park is natural; Lalibela, Tiya and Gonder Castle are human-made.

q.q: Which set contains only human-made tourist attractions?
options: Lake Tana, Sof Omar Cave, Rift Valley
q.explanation: Harar, Axum, Gonder Castle and Tiya are human-made sites.

q.q: The Konso dry stone terraces can reach up to 5 meters high at some places.
q.explanation: The terraces contoured on the hills reach, at some places, up to 5 meters high.

q.q: Explain why dry stone terracing suits the Konso environment.
q.answer: the land is mountainous barren and rocky and terraces retain soil from erosion|terraces stop erosion and create farm saddles
q.explanation: Terracing is an indigenous adaptation that retains soil from erosion and creates terrace saddles for agriculture.

q.q: Which statement best explains the importance of tourism to Ethiopia's economy?
options: It creates jobs and income as a smokeless industry
q.explanation: Tourism is a source of both job opportunities and income, known as a smokeless industry.

q.q: The Blue Nile Falls is also known as the Tis Isat Falls.
q.explanation: The Blue Nile Falls is called Tis Isat Falls and is a natural attraction.

q.q: Define a cultural landscape in one sentence.
q.answer: a geographic area with cultural and natural resources linked to a historic event activity or person|an area showing combined works of nature and man
q.explanation: It is a geographic area associated with a historic event, activity or person, or exhibiting cultural or aesthetic values.

q.q: The three modes of human-environment interaction are:
q.explanation: The textbook groups the relationship into dependence, modification and adaptation.

q.q: The two main types of links between human activities and the environment are:
options: Use of natural resources and production of wastes
q.explanation: All links fall into using resources and producing wastes.

q.q: Every living thing on the planet depends on the environment it lives in.
q.explanation: Beings cannot survive without interaction with their environment for air, water, food or shelter.

q.q: According to the textbook, fossil fuel burning is the main cause of climate change.
q.explanation: The textbook states fossil fuels are the main energy source of industrialization and their burning is the main cause of climate change.

q.q: What is the term for catching fish faster than they can reproduce?
q.explanation: Overfishing is defined as catching fish faster than they reproduce.

q.q: Globally, which sector uses the most water?
q.explanation: Agriculture, principally irrigation, is the largest water-using sector worldwide.

q.q: Define pollution in one sentence as given in the lesson.
q.answer: introduction of harmful substances into the environment|harmful substances introduced into the environment
q.explanation: Pollution is the introduction into the environment of substances liable to harm humans and other living organisms.

q.q: Between 1980 and 2005, global population and natural resource extraction both increased by about:
q.explanation: The textbook states both population and resource extraction increased by almost 50 percent in those 25 years.

q.q: Give one ecological service that forests and microorganisms provide people.
q.answer: providing oxygen|cleaning the air|purifying water|controlling erosion|breaking down wastes
q.explanation: Forests and microbes provide oxygen, clean air, purify water, break down wastes and control erosion.

q.q: Arrange these water use categories as the textbook lists them.
q.explanation: The textbook lists domestic first (drinking, washing, cooking), then agricultural (irrigation), then industrial.

q.q: Which dam, under construction in Ethiopia, is named in the lesson as part of planned hydropower?
q.explanation: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam is the prominent planned hydropower project mentioned.

q.q: Optimum population exists when:
options: resources available equal the population's needs
q.explanation: Optimum population means resource availability matches population needs.

q.q: With existing resources and a given state of technology, the optimum population yields:
q.explanation: The optimum is the size that gives the highest income per capita under the given resources and technology.

q.q: The indications of optimum population are precise criteria that measure it exactly.
q.explanation: They are signs such as full employment and high living standards, but the textbook says they are not precise criteria.

q.q: Name one indication of optimum population.
q.answer: high average living standards|full employment|rational development of resources|balanced demographic structure
q.explanation: Any of high living standards, full employment, rational resource development or balanced demographic structure.

q.q: Explain why the optimum range is narrower in isolated, specialized economies.
q.answer: little flexibility|shocks can be disastrous to the population-resource balance
q.explanation: In specialized or isolated communities, population growth, crises, war or drought can break the delicate balance, so their optimum band is narrower.

q.q: Which factor is NOT listed as making optima vary?
q.explanation: State size, geography, social structure, technical progress and communications make optima vary.

q.q: At optimum population each person has access to adequate food, water, energy, medical care and cultural outlets.
q.explanation: This describes the highest quality of life that optimum population yields.

q.q: Order these elements of the textbook definition correctly.
options: The size is the best and most desirable
q.explanation: First resources and needs balance, giving the most desirable size, which then yields the highest income per capita.

q.q: If a locality's population and resources were at an optimum, what would happen to water, forest, soil and farmland?
q.answer: used rationally and renewed|sustainable use without degradation
q.explanation: At the optimum, these resources are used at rates they can sustain, with no shortages and no lasting degradation.

q.q: The average income of each person in a country is called what?
q.explanation: Income per capita is highest when population is at its optimum.

q.q: Optimum population supports sustainable development mainly because:
options: resources are used rationally and preserved for the future
it removes the need for technology
q.explanation: At the optimum, rational resource use keeps resources available, allowing development to continue.

q.q: Overpopulation occurs when there is:
options: an excess of population over utilized or potential resources
a balance of population and resources
too few workers for the resources
q.explanation: Overpopulation is an excess of population over utilized or potential resources.

q.q: Relative overpopulation is more common than absolute overpopulation.
q.explanation: The textbook states relative overpopulation is more common than the absolute form.

q.q: Which is NOT a cause of rural overpopulation listed in the lesson?
q.explanation: The listed causes are uneven land distribution, mechanization, the shift to livestock farming and rapid rural population growth.

q.q: Distinguish absolute from relative overpopulation in one sentence each.
q.answer: absolute: limit of production reached; relative: production could increase|limit reached vs output below potential
q.explanation: Absolute means the limit of production is attained with low living standards; relative means production is inadequate though more is feasible.

q.q: Industrial overpopulation hits hardest among:
q.explanation: Industrial overpopulation affects the unskilled and semi-skilled workers.

q.q: Name one diet-deficiency disease mentioned as an effect of overpopulation.
q.explanation: Rickets is cited among poor diet and diet-deficiency diseases.

q.q: Overpopulation can result from a decline in resources, not only from growth of population.
q.explanation: It may result from an increase in population, a decline in resources, a decline in demand for labor, or a combination.

q.q: Mention two environmental and two socio-economic effects of overpopulation.
q.answer: deforestation and pollution; migration and conflict|any listed environmental and social effects
q.explanation: Environmental effects include deforestation, pollution, erosion, desertification; social effects include migration, starvation, low life expectancy, high crime and conflict.

q.q: Which Asian country's demographic evolution has been frequently interrupted by famines, floods, droughts and epidemics?
q.explanation: The textbook cites China's demographic evolution interrupted by natural and epidemic shocks.

q.q: Order the rural overpopulation causes as effectiveness of long-term solutions suggests.
q.explanation: Beyond emigration, solutions are slow, but in the long run social and cultural revolutions are more effective.

q.q: Which of the following is listed among the effects of overpopulation on infrastructure and prices?
options: Over-utilization of mass transit, highways and public health systems
q.explanation: Overpopulation over-uses infrastructure such as mass transit, highways and public health systems and raises land prices.

q.q: Underpopulation may be said to exist where:
options: the population is too small to utilize its resources fully
q.explanation: Underpopulation means the population is too small to use resources fully, or more people could be supported harmlessly.

q.q: Absolute under population is quite rare.
q.explanation: The textbook says absolute underpopulation is quite rare except in isolated populations.

q.q: Relative under-population occurs where:
options: there is insufficient development of the resources available
birth rates are the world's highest
q.explanation: Relative under-population stems from insufficient development of available resources.

q.q: In which broadly defined regions is relative under-population most common?
q.explanation: The textbook says nowhere is it more common than in the southern continents.

q.q: Explain one positive and one negative impact of underpopulation on resource use.
q.answer: less depletion good; less production bad|lower demand reduces depletion but fewer workers cut output
q.explanation: Lower demand reduces depletion and environmental impact, but fewer workers also lower resource production.

q.q: Most under-populated areas today are typically:
options: small in area and poor in resources
large in area and rich in resources
q.explanation: Under-populated lands are usually large with rich resource endowments.

q.q: Under population can result in a shortage of workforce and fewer people to pay taxes.
q.explanation: The textbook lists workforce shortage and a smaller tax base among its disadvantages.

q.q: Order the underpopulation chain correctly.
q.explanation: Population decline first, causing fewer workers and aging, which then deepen the fall in production.

q.q: Why can exports of surplus food, energy and minerals signal underpopulation?
q.answer: surplus means more resources than people can use|unused resources are exported
q.explanation: Exporting surplus shows the local population does not use what the area can produce, an indicator of underpopulation.

q.q: With fewer people, what happens to the demand for services?
q.explanation: Fewer people mean decreased demand for services.

q.q: Which feature belongs to under-populated countries according to the lesson?
q.explanation: Under-populated lands enjoy high incomes, good living conditions and immigration, and can export surpluses.

q.q: By 2016, Ethiopia's population was estimated at over 101 million and was growing at about:
q.explanation: The textbook gives a growth rate of 2.6 percent for Ethiopia.

q.q: At the early 1950s, high forests covered about 16 percent of Ethiopia's land area.
q.explanation: High forests covered 16 percent of land in the early 1950s.

q.q: The estimated current annual loss of high forests in Ethiopia is:
q.explanation: Annual high forest loss is estimated at 150,000-200,000 hectares.

q.q: What percentage of Ethiopia's domestic energy consumption comes from biomass?
q.explanation: Biomass offers over 99 percent of total domestic energy consumption.

q.q: Explain why burning dung and crop residues instead of wood deepens land degradation.
q.answer: nutrients are not recycled into the soil|soil loses nutrients and organic matter
q.explanation: Dung and residues otherwise return nutrients and organic matter to the soil; burning them drains soil fertility and cuts crop productivity.

q.q: How much of Ethiopia's land is moderately to very severely degraded?
q.explanation: Over 85 percent of the land is moderately to very severely degraded, and about 75 percent is affected by desertification.

q.q: Name the three areas the textbook cites as land degradation hotspots.
q.explanation: Hotspots cover about 23 percent of the land, mainly in Tigray, Wollo and Gondar.

q.q: Indoor air pollution from biomass fuel contributes to about 50,320 annual deaths of children under five.
q.explanation: It causes 50,320 under-five deaths yearly, about 4.9 percent of the national burden of disease.

q.q: Order the forest-cover figures from earliest to latest.
q.explanation: The correct order is 16 percent, then 3.6 percent, then 2.7 percent.

q.q: State the textbook definition of deforestation.
q.answer: removal of forest cover without adequate replacement|indiscriminate destruction of natural vegetation
q.explanation: Deforestation is removal of forest cover without adequate replacement.

q.q: A 1 percent increase in soil organic matter reduces erodibility by about:
q.explanation: Each 1 percent rise in organic matter cuts erodibility by roughly 15 percent.

q.q: The most serious problem of Ethiopia's soil resource is:
q.explanation: Among others, erosion by running water is the most serious problem of the soil resource in Ethiopia.

q.q: Soil erosion is a natural process, but human activities frequently aggravate it.
q.explanation: The textbook states erosion is natural and that human activities frequently aggravate it.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT a natural factor that accelerates soil erosion in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: Deforestation is a human-made factor; slope, rainfall, soil type, torrent rivers and vegetation cover are natural.

q.q: About how many tons of topsoil are washed away from the Ethiopian highlands every year?
q.explanation: About 1.9 billion tons of topsoil are washed from the highlands annually.

q.q: Which river alone carries away 3000-4000 million cubic metric tons of soil annually?
q.explanation: The river Abbay carries away 3000-4000 million cubic metric tons of soil every year.

q.q: Planting different crops in alternating strips in order to retain water and soil is known as strip cultivation.
q.explanation: Strip cultivation means planting different crops in alternating strips; intercropping means two or more crops on the same field.

q.q: Building level surfaces at right angles to the slope in order to retain water and reduce erosion is called what?
q.explanation: This is the definition of terracing.

q.q: Why are goats particularly damaging to the land?
options: They destroy all kinds and parts of vegetation, including the roots
They compact the soil with their hooves
They drink large quantities of water
q.explanation: Goats destroy all kinds and parts of an area's vegetation, including the roots, leaving land bare.

q.q: Explain why lost topsoil is described as essentially irreplaceable.
q.answer: topsoil production rates are so slow|it forms very slowly
q.explanation: Because topsoil production rates are so slow, lost topsoil cannot effectively be replaced.

q.q: Distinguish between over cropping and over cultivation.
q.answer: over cropping is planting too densely, over cultivation is tilling every year|density vs yearly tilling
q.explanation: Over cropping is planting an area too densely; over cultivation is tilling land every year.

q.q: Soil is a non-renewable resource that cannot be restored once eroded.
q.explanation: Soil is renewable and can be replenished indefinitely by applying appropriate conservation measures.

q.q: Which of the following is listed as a major cause of deforestation in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: Demand for fuelwood heads the list of causes of deforestation.

q.q: Forest fires in Ethiopia may be both natural and artificial.
q.explanation: The textbook lists forest fires as natural and artificial.

q.q: Slash and burn as a way of gaining farmland is commonly practiced in:
q.explanation: This approach to gaining farmland is commonly practiced in southwestern Ethiopia.

q.q: What share of the country did Ethiopia's forest stock cover in the past, and about what share remains?
q.answer: 40 percent to less than 3 percent|40% down to under 3%
q.explanation: The forest stock that covered 40 percent of the country has come to less than 3 percent.

q.q: Explain how overgrazing leads to deforestation in pasture areas.
q.answer: forest land is converted to pasture land|grazing expands at the expense of forest
q.explanation: People increasingly convert forest land to pasture land, expanding grazing at the expense of forest.

q.q: Developing forest-related curricula for schools and forestry institutions belongs to which approach?
q.explanation: Education and curricula are capacity-building measures.

q.q: The three mitigation approaches suggested in the textbook are enough on their own to defeat deforestation.
q.explanation: The textbook states that despite their great potential, these approaches alone are not enough.

q.q: Name the practice of planting trees on bare and unproductive lands.
q.explanation: Afforestation means planting trees, including on bare and unproductive lands.

q.q: What are built-up areas, and why do they matter for forest conservation?
q.answer: areas occupied by factories, residence, recreational sites|they consume forestland
q.explanation: Built-up areas cover factories, residences and recreational sites, and some land converted to them is forestland.

q.q: The textbook says conserving and preserving Ethiopia's forest resource is a call to:
q.explanation: Responsibility and commitment with active community participation is a call to every citizen.

q.q: People are increasingly converting forest land to pasture land, expanding grazing at the expense of forest.
q.explanation: The textbook states that forest land is increasingly converted to pasture land.

q.q: Ethiopia is the second richest African country in water-resource potential, after:
q.explanation: Ethiopia follows the Democratic Republic of Congo in water-resource potential.

q.q: Drought in Ethiopia recurs every how many years?
q.explanation: The textbook states drought is recurring every 3 to 5 years.

q.q: Two Rift Valley lakes named in the textbook as disappearing or on the verge of disappearance are:
q.explanation: Lake Abijata and Lake Cheleklektu are disappearing or on the verge of disappearance.

q.q: The volume and purity of Ethiopia's rivers are decreasing.
q.explanation: The textbook states both volume and purity of rivers are decreasing.

q.q: Name three pollutants increasingly contaminating Ethiopia's water resources.
q.answer: sewage, organic wastes, fertilizers|sewage, organic waste and fertilizer
q.explanation: Sewage, organic wastes and fertilizers are the named pollutants.

q.q: Why is the growing human population a water problem in Ethiopia?
q.answer: crucial growing demand for potable water|more people need potable water
q.explanation: Rapid population growth creates a crucial and growing demand for potable water.

q.q: According to the national water strategy, the interface between water bodies and land, such as lake shores and river banks, should be:
q.explanation: The strategy promotes protection of the interface between water bodies and land.

q.q: The national strategy requires environmental-impact assessment before introducing exotic species into water ecosystems.
q.explanation: Proposed introductions of exotic species are subject to detailed studies and environmental-impact assessment.

q.q: Which two groups of water-resource users does the strategy specifically involve in local planning and follow-up?
q.answer: women and animal herders|women and herders
q.explanation: The strategy involves water-resource users, particularly women and animal herders.

q.q: Natural ecosystems such as wetlands and upstream forests are recognized by the strategy as:
options: fundamental for regulating water quality and quantity
q.explanation: The strategy recognizes wetlands and upstream forests as fundamental for regulating water quality and quantity.

q.q: The Federal government adopted a national strategy to conserve and manage water resources in Ethiopia.
q.explanation: The Federal government adopted such a national strategy in response to degradation.

q.q: The Green Legacy Initiative was launched in 2019 by:
q.explanation: The Initiative was launched in 2019 by Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

q.q: The Green Legacy movement is aimed at building an irrigation dam to enhance agricultural productivity.
q.explanation: The review exercise lists this statement as false; the movement is a tree planting campaign.

q.q: How many seedlings does the Green Legacy plan to plant across the country, and over which years?
q.answer: 20 billion in 2020-2023|20 billion over four years
q.explanation: The plan is 20 billion seedlings over four years (2020-2023).

q.q: Which of the following is encompassed by the Green Legacy movement?
options: Integrated water and soil resources management
q.explanation: The movement encompasses agroforestry, forest sector development, urban greening and renewal, and integrated water and soil resources management.

q.q: Name the post-planting care actions carried out to raise seedling survival rates.
q.explanation: Post-planting care includes watering, weeding and replacement planting.

q.q: Which guiding document is NOT named in the lesson?
options: Ten-Year National Forest Sector Development Program
Bamboo Development Strategy and Action Plan
q.explanation: The named documents are the CRGE Strategy, the Ten-Year National Forest Sector Development Program and the Bamboo Development Strategy and Action Plan.

q.q: The Green Legacy movement supports Ethiopia's commitments under the Paris Climate Change Agreement, the UN 2030 Agenda, and African Agenda 2063.
q.explanation: The movement contributes toward these international commitments.

q.q: List any three overall goals of the Green Legacy movement.
q.answer: curb climate change and deforestation; improve food security; ensure gender equality|battle desertification and soil erosion; prevent environment-related conflicts; climate resilient green economy; climate-smart agriculture
q.explanation: Goals include curbing climate change and deforestation, climate-smart agriculture, food security, preventing conflicts, battling desertification and erosion, a climate-resilient green economy, and gender equality.

q.q: According to the National Forest Inventory report of 2018, forest area coverage has been raised to about:
q.explanation: Forest coverage was raised to about 15.7 percent, as indicated by the National Forest Inventory report of 2018.

q.q: Explain why planting alone cannot guarantee a successful Green Legacy program.
q.answer: post-planting care is needed|survival depends on watering, weeding, replacement
q.explanation: Without post-planting care such as watering, weeding and replacement planting, seedling survival rates fall.

q.q: The Green Legacy movement's efforts on the ground are guided by strategic documents aligned with global goals.
q.explanation: The efforts are guided by documents such as the CRGE Strategy, aligned with global goals.

q.q: A map shows the earth's surface as if seen from directly above. This view is called:
q.explanation: Maps show the surface as viewed vertically from above, called a bird's-eye view.

q.q: All maps are smaller than the area they represent.
q.explanation: A basic feature of maps is that they are always smaller than the areas they represent.

q.q: Which statement about traditional map-making is correct?
options: Each measurement was made by hand through fieldwork
It began in the seventeenth century
It used computers at every stage
q.explanation: In traditional map-making each measurement was made by hand, through laborious fieldwork.

q.q: Modern scientific mapping has its roots in:
q.explanation: Modern scientific mapping has its roots in the seventeenth century.

q.q: Name the two main stages of the historical development of map-making.
q.answer: traditional and modern map-making|traditional and modern map making
q.explanation: The two stages are traditional map-making and modern map-making.

q.q: Which component of a map explains the meaning of the signs and symbols used?
q.explanation: The legend or key explains the meaning of the symbols used by the cartographer.

q.q: A reader wants to know the extent to which the mapped area has been reduced. Which component gives this?
q.explanation: The scale indicates the extent to which the represented area has been reduced.

q.q: By convention, cartographers place North at the top of maps.
q.explanation: By convention, map makers place North at the top of maps.

q.q: Why is the year of publication printed on a map important to the reader?
q.answer: it shows how old the map is and whether its contents are current or out of date|to judge whether the contents are current or outdated
q.explanation: The date identifies the year of publication, letting readers judge whether contents are current or out of date.

q.q: Arrange the steps a careful map reader should follow.
options: Check the legend for symbol meanings
Read the title to learn what and where
Convert the scale to measure ground distances
Check the date of publication for currency
q.explanation: First the title (what and where), then the legend, then scale-based measurement, while the date checks currency.

q.q: On a map drawn at scale 1:1,000,000, two places measure 3 cm apart. Their ground distance is:
What is a sketch map?
q.answer: an outline map drawn from observation rather than exact survey measurements showing only the main features|outline map drawn from observation
q.explanation: A sketch map is an outline map drawn from observation, showing only the main features.

q.q: Sketch maps are usually drawn:
options: free hand on a blackboard or drawing pad
q.explanation: Sketch maps are free-hand maps drawn on a blackboard or drawing pad.

q.q: Sketch mapping minimizes irrelevant detail and maximizes major geographic points.
q.explanation: That is why sketch maps are called the ultimate in geographic simplification.

q.q: When sketching a map of your community, a good reference point would be:
q.explanation: For a community map, a major street or river might be the reference point.

q.q: The larger the area you want to represent on a sketch map, the less detail you will need.
q.explanation: Detail must fall as the represented area grows.

q.q: A football pitch and a school yard have equal areas in reality. On a good sketch map they should:
options: be drawn in different proportions for effect
q.explanation: Things of equal size in reality should have the same size on the map.

q.q: You cannot remember the exact shape of a lake while sketching. You should:
options: draw it with circles, rectangles and triangles as a general shape
measure it precisely with a planimeter
q.explanation: If exact shapes are unknown, use circles, rectangles and triangles.

q.q: Arrange the first steps of drawing a sketch map in the correct order.
options: Decide what region the map will show
q.explanation: First the region, then orientation, then reference points, then general shapes.

q.q: You should spend more than an hour perfecting your sketch map.
q.explanation: Do not spend more than an hour, and do not try to make the sketch perfect or overly detailed.

q.q: Explain why sketch maps are described as the ultimate in geographic simplification.
q.answer: they minimize irrelevant detail and maximize major geographic points|they strip away extra detail to show only the main features
q.explanation: Sketch mapping minimizes irrelevant detail and maximizes the major geographic points.

q.q: A compound 200 m wide is sketched 20 cm wide. The implied scale statement is:
q.explanation: 20 cm to 200 m gives 1 cm to 10 m (RF 1:1,000).

q.q: The meaning of symbols on a map can be obtained from the:
q.explanation: The legend or key explains the meaning of the signs and symbols used in the map.

q.q: Conventional signs and symbols are used on maps through the agreement of all map-makers of the world.
q.explanation: By agreement, they represent the same detail on maps in all countries.

q.q: In the textbook's line graph of Ethiopia's population growth, the x-axis represents:
q.explanation: The x-axis represents years and the y-axis represents population size.

q.q: On conventional maps, cities and towns are usually indicated by:
q.explanation: Cities and towns are indicated by dots or patches of shading.

q.q: In a pie chart, one percent of the data equals how many degrees of the circle?
q.explanation: 1 percent of the whole circle is equivalent to 3.6 degrees.

q.q: In a bar graph drawn for comparison, all bars must start at zero and be drawn on the same scale.
q.explanation: Bars start at zero and comparison bar graphs must use the same scale.

q.q: Which diagram is most suitable for showing Ethiopia's export destinations as shares of a total?
q.explanation: Pie charts show the sizes of parts in relation to a single whole.

q.q: According to the monthly rainfall data of Kokosa town (2011), the wettest month is:
q.explanation: May records the maximum rainfall, 206.3 mm.

q.q: State the two primary uses of pie charts in geography.
q.answer: show sizes of parts in relation to a whole and sizes of parts in relation to each other|parts of a whole; parts relative to each other
q.explanation: Pie charts show parts in relation to the whole and to each other.

q.q: Ethiopia's population was 19.2 million in 1950 and 114.9 million in 2020. The increase is about:
Arrange the steps of drawing a pie chart in order.
options: Draw the segments with a protractor
Convert each percentage using 3.6 degrees per percent
Draw the circle of convenient size
q.explanation: Draw the circle first, then convert percentages to degrees, draw the segments, and label them.

q.q: Which of the following scales is for a small-scale map?
q.explanation: Small-scale maps have scales less than or equal to 1:250,000.

q.q: Large-scale maps are best described as maps that:
options: cover large areas with little detail
cover smaller areas than small-scale maps and show greater detail
are used to cover a large area in detail
q.explanation: Large-scale maps cover a smaller geographic area and show greater detail.

q.q: The three ways of expressing map scale are the scale statement, the representative fraction and the graphic scale.
q.explanation: Scales are expressed as statements, representative fractions and graphic scales.

q.q: Name the three classes of maps based on scale differences.
q.answer: large scale, medium scale and small scale|large, medium and small scale maps
q.explanation: Maps are classified into large-scale, medium-scale and small-scale maps.

q.q: A graphic scale is usually drawn:
options: in the lower margin of the map
next to the north arrow only
on the back of the map
q.explanation: The graphic scale is mostly drawn in the lower margin of the map.

q.q: Distances on the field are not usually measured in centimetres.
q.explanation: Field distances are measured in metres or kilometres; centimetres serve map measurements.

q.q: To measure the distance along a winding river on a map, a geographer uses a ruler together with:
options: thread, string or the edge of a pair of dividers
q.explanation: Curved-line distances need threads, strings or the edge of a pair of dividers.

q.q: An instrument used to get accurate areas of both regular and irregular shaped features from maps is the:
q.explanation: The planimeter gives accurate areas of regular and irregular shapes.

q.q: Convert the RF 1:250,000 into a statement scale.
q.explanation: 250,000 / 100,000 = 2.5, so the statement is 1 cm to 2.5 km.

q.q: An irregular lake is drawn at 1 cm to 2 km and its boundary covers 10 grid squares of 1 cm by 1 cm. Explain how to find the lake's ground area.
q.answer: each square is 4 sq km so the lake is about 40 sq km|10 squares x 4 sq km = 40 sq km
q.explanation: Each 1 cm square equals 2 km x 2 km = 4 sq km, and 10 squares give about 40 sq km.

q.q: The map distance between two towns is 4 cm on a map of scale 1:800,000. The ground distance is:
Imaginary lines that join all points with the same latitude are called:
q.explanation: Parallels run around the globe parallel to the equator and join points of equal latitude.

q.q: Name the imaginary lines that run from the North Pole to the South Pole and join points of the same longitude.
q.explanation: These lines are meridians.

q.q: The geographic grid is composed of parallels of latitude and meridians of longitude.
q.explanation: The geographic grid is a network of parallels and meridians.

q.q: In the national grid of Ethiopia, the grid origin lies:
options: at the point in south-west Kenya where the 34 degrees 30 minutes E meridian crosses the equator
q.explanation: Ethiopia's grid origin is the southwestern point where the 34 degrees 30 minutes E meridian crosses the equator.

q.q: Which statement about a grid reference is correct?
options: It always stands for a point, the intersection of two lines
q.explanation: A grid reference never indicates an area; it stands for a point where two lines cross.

q.q: The four cardinal points of the compass are:
q.explanation: The cardinal points are North, East, South and West.

q.q: If the angular bearing of point A from point B is 135 degrees, the cardinal direction is:
q.explanation: 135 degrees lies between 90 (E) and 180 (S), so it coincides with Southeast.

q.q: Direction on maps is always measured clockwise starting from north.
q.explanation: Degrees start at north from 0 and increase in the clockwise direction.

q.q: A point lies 5 tenths across from easting line 55 and 5 tenths above northing line 25. Give its four-digit grid reference.
q.explanation: Eastings 55, northings 25, giving 5525.

q.q: In a six-digit grid reference, the first three digits always refer to:
q.explanation: The three first digits refer to the eastings; the three last digits refer to the northings.

q.q: Explain the difference in accuracy between a four-figure and a six-figure grid reference.
q.answer: four-figure gives accuracy to the nearest kilometre while six-figure reaches the nearest 100 metres|four figure: nearest km; six figure: nearest 100 m
q.explanation: Four-figure references suit small-scale maps (nearest kilometre); six-figure references on larger-scale maps give accuracy to the nearest 100 metres.

q.q: The word history comes from the Greek word Istoria, which means:
q.explanation: Istoria means inquiry or an account of one's inquiries.

q.q: According to the textbook, history began about how many years ago?
q.explanation: History began about 5,500 years ago when people first began to write.

q.q: Prehistory is the time before people developed the art of writing.
q.explanation: Prehistory was the period before the art of writing was developed.

q.q: Every statement written in a history book is a historical fact.
q.explanation: Writers can mix opinions with facts; an opinion cannot be proved.

q.q: Name the people who study and write about the human past.
q.explanation: Historians are people who study and write about the human past.

q.q: Give the term for the study of the distant past, before writing was invented.
q.explanation: This is the definition of prehistory.

q.q: Which one best describes a historical fact?
options: A statement about the past that can be proved with supporting information
A story invented to entertain readers
q.explanation: A fact is a statement that can be proved with supporting information.

q.q: Which of these are primary needs that human beings produced by interacting with the natural environment?
q.explanation: People produced their primary needs, such as food, shelter and cloth, from nature.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why archaeologists and anthropologists are important for the study of prehistory.
q.answer: there are no written records|prehistory has no writing
q.explanation: Because prehistory left no written records, scholars must recover clues from material remains.

q.q: Arrange these steps in the order a historian follows to turn evidence into history.
options: Write an interpretation of what happened and why
Find and examine sources as evidence
Decide whether each source can be trusted
q.explanation: The historian first finds sources, then evaluates them, and finally writes an interpretation.

q.q: According to the lesson, history is a branch of which field?
q.explanation: History is a branch of social science that deals with what human beings did in the past.

q.q: History helps us know the past, understand the present and foresee future developments.
q.explanation: This is the importance of history stated in the textbook.

q.q: Who is often called the father of history?
q.explanation: The first use of the term is attributed to Herodotus (c. 484-425 BC).

q.q: Leopold Von Ranke (1795-1886) is considered the father of:
q.explanation: Ranke established history as an independent discipline and is called the father of modern historiography.

q.q: Give the term for sources that are contemporary with the events under study.
q.explanation: Primary sources are contemporary with the events they describe.

q.q: Give the name for the study of how knowledge of the past is attained and transmitted.
q.explanation: This is the definition of historiography.

q.q: Which of the following is a secondary source?
options: A chronicle written at the time
A coin minted in the period
A letter written by a witness
q.explanation: A textbook derives its information from primary sources.

q.q: The Ethiopian calendar is:
options: exactly the same as the Gregorian calendar
seven to eight years behind the Gregorian calendar
ten years ahead of the Gregorian calendar
q.explanation: Ethiopia uses its own calendar, which is seven to eight years behind the Gregorian calendar.

q.q: The Islamic calendar counts time from the Hijra, the flight of the prophet Mohammed from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD.
q.explanation: The Hijra of 622 AD begins the Islamic calendar, with BH before it and AH after it.

q.q: Explain why the textbook says that where there are no sources there is no history.
q.answer: history is based on evidence from sources|without sources there is no evidence
q.explanation: History rests on evidence arising from sources, so no sources means no evidence and no history.

q.q: Arrange these steps in the order a historian follows when writing history.
options: Write an interpretation of what happened and why
Select a topic or problem to study
q.explanation: The historian selects a topic, collects and evaluates sources, then writes an interpretation.

q.q: All human beings living today belong to which species?
q.explanation: All human beings now living belong to the species Homo sapiens.

q.q: All hominids are characterised by bipedalism, that is walking on two feet in an upright position.
q.explanation: Bipedalism is a distinguishing feature of all hominids.

q.q: What name did Donald Johanson give to the fossil skeleton he found in Ethiopia in 1974?
q.explanation: He named his find Lucy, also known as Dinkinesh.

q.q: Homo erectus was the first hominid to:
options: leave Africa and move into Europe and Asia
q.explanation: Homo erectus were the first to leave Africa, using fire to keep warm in colder areas.

q.q: Which two major opposing theories explain the origin of human beings?
q.explanation: The two major opposing theories are the creationist and the evolutionist theories.

q.q: Give the term for the slow and natural process by which living things change from earlier forms.
q.explanation: This slow and natural process is called evolution.

q.q: Who formulated the scientific theory of evolution?
q.explanation: The evolutionist theory was formulated by the English scientist Charles Darwin (1809-1882).

q.q: Explain why Ethiopia is important in the study of human evolution.
q.answer: fossils of hominids were found in ethiopia|remains of homo species were found in ethiopia|ethiopia and the horn have sites of all three homo species
q.explanation: Ethiopia has sites showing all three Homo sub-species in succession, along with the earliest hominid found at Aramis.

q.q: The earliest hominid found in Ethiopia was discovered at Aramis in the Middle Awash of the Afar region.
q.explanation: It was described by a team led by Tim White and dated to about 4.4 million years ago.

q.q: Name the genus to which Homo habilis, Homo erectus and Homo sapiens belong.
q.explanation: All three species belong to the genus Homo.

q.q: Arrange these hominids from the earliest to the latest.
q.explanation: The order is Australopithecus afarensis, Homo habilis, Homo erectus and Homo sapiens.

q.q: Which of these is one of the basic distinguishing features of the human species?
options: The ability to live in water
The ability to write from birth
q.explanation: One basic distinguishing feature of the human species is the ability to make tools.

q.q: The Paleolithic Age is also known as the:
q.explanation: Paleolithic is Greek for old stone, so it is the Old Stone Age.

q.q: The Neolithic Age started around 8,000 BC and lasted until about 4,000 BC.
q.explanation: These are the dates given for the Neolithic Age in the textbook.

q.q: During which period did human beings domesticate plants and animals?
q.explanation: Systematic agriculture and domestication belong to the Neolithic Age.

q.q: Give the term for the shift from hunting animals and gathering food to keeping animals and growing crops regularly.
q.explanation: This shift is called the Neolithic Revolution or Agricultural Revolution.

q.q: Which tools appeared during the Neolithic Age?
options: The hoe, the yoke and the wheel
q.explanation: New and better tools such as the hoe, the yoke and the wheel appeared in the Neolithic Age.

q.q: The Mesolithic Age lasted from 9000 BC to 8000 BC.
q.explanation: The Mesolithic Age lasted from 9000 BC to 8000 BC.

q.q: Name one plant domesticated in Ethiopia during the Neolithic age.
q.explanation: Teff, dagussa, nug and enset were among the domesticated plants.

q.q: Explain one major consequence of the Neolithic Revolution.
q.answer: sedentary way of life|people became food producers|complex social organisation|stone houses and granaries were built
q.explanation: The revolution produced settled life, food production and more complex society.

q.q: Which of these is a Neolithic archaeological site in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: Ethiopian Neolithic sites include Aksum, Lalibela, and places near Chercher in Hararghe and Metehara.

q.q: Arrange the three periods of the Stone Age from earliest to latest.
q.explanation: The order is Paleolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic.

q.q: A state is best defined as:
options: a group of families living together
a politically organised body of people with a defined territory, a legitimate government and sovereignty
q.explanation: This is the definition of a state given in the textbook.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the features a state must have?
q.explanation: The features listed are population, territory, government, sovereignty and recognition, not language.

q.q: For a state to exist it must have population, territory, government, sovereignty and recognition.
q.explanation: These five features are listed in the textbook.

q.q: Give the term for the early states that were ruled by priests.
q.explanation: Early states ruled by priests were known as theocratic states.

q.q: According to the trade theory, who gradually replaced priests with the emergence of markets?
q.explanation: Village chiefs who controlled trade gradually replaced priests as markets emerged.

q.q: In the agricultural theory of the state, rich people who gained higher status because of their surplus are called:
q.explanation: Elites are rich people who attained higher status in society due to their wealth.

q.q: A state is exactly the same thing as a kingdom or an empire.
q.explanation: The textbook states clearly that a state differs from a kingdom and an empire.

q.q: According to one theory, villages combined to establish states under powerful local chiefs by what means?
q.explanation: War or conflict could lead small villages to combine under powerful local chiefs by force.

q.q: Explain how agriculture is said to have led to the emergence of the state.
q.answer: surplus produced elites who gained control over others|society divided into higher and lower classes
q.explanation: Agricultural surplus created economic classes and wealthy elites, whose control over others led to the state.

q.q: The Neolithic way of life that preceded the state was based on:
q.explanation: The Neolithic age produced sedentary ways of life based on farming.

q.q: The civilization of ancient Egypt began at about:
q.explanation: The textbook states that the civilization of Ancient Egypt began at about 3000 BC.

q.q: Who, according to tradition, unified Upper and Lower Egypt?
q.explanation: According to tradition, Upper and Lower Egypt were unified by Menes around 3200 BC.

q.q: The viziers acted as mayors, tax collectors and judges.
q.explanation: The king ruled Egypt through officials named viziers, who acted as mayors, tax collectors and judges.

q.q: What is the name of the process of preserving a body, which helped Egyptians advance in medicine?
q.explanation: The process of preserving the body is called mummification.

q.q: The Egyptian art of writing developed around 3000 BC is called:
q.explanation: Hieroglyphics was a combination of pictograms, ideograms, phonograms and determinatives.

q.q: Give the term for the paper-like substance that the ancient Egyptians introduced.
q.explanation: The Egyptians introduced papyrus, a paper-like substance.

q.q: Meroe was important mainly because of its flourishing iron industry.
q.explanation: Meroe was a centre of metal products such as gold, copper, silver and iron, indicating a flourishing iron industry.

q.q: The kingdom of Kush lasted until about 350 AD, when it was destroyed by:
q.explanation: At about 350 AD, the Aksumite king Ezana invaded and destroyed Meroe.

q.q: Explain why the Nile was central to the Egyptian economy.
q.answer: silt replenished the soil|farming and trade depended on the Nile
q.explanation: Silt from the Nile replenished the fertility of the soil, allowing large crops, and trade also used the river.

q.q: Arrange these events in correct chronological order from earliest to latest.
options: Kush first exists along the Nile
q.explanation: The order is: Menes unifies Egypt (c. 3200 BC), Kush exists (c. 2000 BC), the Kushites conquer Egypt (8th century BC), Ezana destroys Meroe (c. 350 AD).

q.q: Name one crop produced by the Egyptian peasantry.
q.explanation: The Egyptian peasantry produced wheat and barley.

q.q: The earliest great river valley civilization was found between which two rivers?
q.explanation: The Sumerian civilization was found between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates.

q.q: The large Sumerian stepped temple towers built of sun-dried mud bricks were called:
q.explanation: Large temples of this kind were called ziggurats, or stepped towers.

q.q: Cuneiform was a simple alphabet system.
q.explanation: Cuneiform was not an alphabet system; it was a highly complex system of ideographs.

q.q: Who founded the first Persian Empire around 550 BC?
q.explanation: The first Persian Empire was founded by Cyrus the Great around 550 BC.

q.q: Name the Persian religion founded by a prophet called Zoroaster.
q.explanation: Their religion was known as Zoroastrianism, founded by a prophet called Zoroaster.

q.q: The first Indian civilization began in the Indus Valley at about:
q.explanation: The first Indian civilization began in the Indus Valley at about 2500 BC and reached its apex at about 1500 BC.

q.q: Buddhism emerged from Hinduism as a reform movement and spread outside India.
q.explanation: Buddhism emerged from Hinduism as a reform movement and spread to South East Asia, China and Japan.

q.q: The first dynasty in China (c. 1700-1122 BC) was the:
q.explanation: The first dynasty in China was the Shang dynasty (c. 1700-1122 BC).

q.q: Explain why the Chinese constructed the Great Wall of China.
q.answer: to keep out invaders from central Asia|defence against invaders
q.explanation: The Great Wall was built to keep out invaders from central Asia.

q.q: Name the philosopher (551-479 BC) whose teaching is known as Confucianism.
q.explanation: Confucius (551-479 BC) was the most influential philosopher in Chinese history; his teaching was Confucianism.

q.q: Arrange these Asian civilizations or states from earliest to latest foundation.
q.explanation: Order: Sumerian cuneiform c. 3200 BC, Indus Valley c. 2500 BC, Shang dynasty c. 1700 BC, Persian Empire c. 550 BC.

q.q: The Maya civilization was at its peak from about:
q.explanation: The Maya civilization was at its peak from about 250-900 AD.

q.q: The Maya developed an accurate yearly calendar.
q.explanation: The Maya made outstanding achievements in astronomy and mathematics and developed an accurate yearly calendar.

q.q: What was the capital of the Inca Empire?
q.explanation: Its capital was Cusco, in southern Peru.

q.q: The Inca Empire began to expand at about:
q.explanation: The Inca Empire began to expand at about 1438.

q.q: The Aztec capital, which stood on the site of present-day Mexico City, was:
q.explanation: The largest city was the capital Tenochtitlan, on the site of present-day Mexico City.

q.q: Name the form of writing used by the Aztecs.
q.explanation: They used a form of writing called pictographic writing.

q.q: The Inca built a network of roads and were skilled in engineering.
q.explanation: The Inca were skilled in engineering and crafts and built a network of roads.

q.q: The Aztec empire was destroyed by the Spaniards in:
q.explanation: The Aztec empire was destroyed by the Spaniards in 1521.

q.q: Explain what the Maya built for worship and where the temples were placed.
q.answer: tall limestone pyramids with small temples on top|limestone pyramids
q.explanation: The Maya built tall pyramids of limestone with small temples on top.

q.q: What craft material did Inca craftworkers use besides cotton and wool?
q.explanation: Inca craftworkers made fine artifacts from gold, silver and other materials.

q.q: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
options: The Spaniards destroy the Aztec empire
The Maya civilization is at its peak
The Inca Empire begins to expand
Spanish forces conquer the Inca Empire
q.explanation: Order: Maya peak 250-900 AD, Inca expansion c. 1438, Aztec fall 1521, Inca conquest after 1532.

q.q: The smaller political unit in which Greek culture developed was the:
q.explanation: Greek culture developed chiefly in small city-states called polis.

q.q: The two best-known Greek city-states were:
q.explanation: The best-known city-states were Athens and Sparta.

q.q: The Greek city-states were united into a single nation.
q.explanation: The city-states never became united into a nation, though they shared language, religion and culture.

q.q: Who was the Greek physician who began the tradition of modern medicine in Europe?
q.explanation: Hippocrates began the tradition of modern medicine in Europe.

q.q: The Roman Republic was established in:
q.explanation: The Roman Republic was established in 509 BC after the Roman nobles overthrew the king.

q.q: In the Roman Republic, who served for only one year?
q.explanation: Two elected consuls headed the government, and a consul served for only a year, while senators served for life.

q.q: Give the name of the temple of Athena in Athens, the finest example of Greek architecture.
q.explanation: The temple of Athena in Athens, the Parthenon, is the finest example of Greek architecture.

q.q: The Roman Republic lasted nearly 500 years, until 27 BC.
q.explanation: The Roman Republic lasted nearly 500 years, until 27 BC, when the Empire was established.

q.q: Explain the main difference between the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire.
q.answer: the Republic was democratic and the Empire was run by one man|rule by one man
q.explanation: The former was a democratic society and the latter was run only by one man.

q.q: Against which city did Rome fight the Punic wars (264-146 BC)?
q.explanation: The bloodiest wars of Rome were the repetitive Punic wars fought against Carthage.

q.q: Arrange these Roman and Greek events in correct chronological order.
q.explanation: Order: Rome founded c. 753 BC, Republic 509 BC, Empire 27 BC, Rome falls 476 AD.

q.q: Christianity began in Palestine in the:
q.explanation: Christianity began in Palestine in the first century AD.

q.q: In which town was Jesus born?
q.explanation: Jesus was born in Bethlehem, in the Judea part of Palestine.

q.q: The Roman government began persecuting Christians during the reign of Nero (AD 54-68).
q.explanation: The Roman government began persecuting Christians during the reign of Nero (AD 54-68).

q.q: The Edict of Milan, which ordered religious toleration, was issued in:
q.explanation: Constantine ordered religious toleration in the Edict of Milan in 313 AD.

q.q: Give the term for the belief in one God.
q.explanation: Monotheism is the belief in one God.
