q.q: Under which ruler did the Romans adopt Christianity as their official religion in 392 AD?
q.explanation: Under Theodosius the Great, who ruled from 378 to 395, the Romans adopted Christianity as their official religion in 392 AD.

q.q: In 1054 the Christian Church split into two parts. These were:
q.explanation: In 1054 the Church split into the Roman Catholic Church at Rome and the Eastern Orthodox Church at Constantinople.

q.q: The Edict of Milan made Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire.
q.explanation: The Edict of Milan granted religious toleration; Christianity became the official religion only in 392 AD under Theodosius.

q.q: Explain why the Roman government persecuted Christians.
q.answer: they were seen as a threat to the unity of the Empire|a threat to the unity of the Empire
q.explanation: The Roman governments considered the Christians a threat against the unity of the Empire.

q.q: What event in 1517 divided Western Christianity into the Roman Catholic Church and Protestantism?
q.explanation: In 1517 a Reformation movement began, dividing Western Christianity into the Roman Catholic Church and Protestantism.

q.q: Arrange these events in correct chronological order.
options: Christianity becomes the official religion in 392 AD
q.explanation: Order: persecution under Nero (AD 54-68), Edict of Milan (313 AD), official religion (392 AD), the split of 1054.

q.q: How many major language super-families do linguists identify in Ethiopia and the Horn?
q.explanation: The two super-families are Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan.

q.q: Which language family is spoken by the largest number of people in Ethiopia and the Horn?
q.explanation: Cushitic speakers form the vast majority in both area and numbers.

q.q: The Beja language represents which branch of Cushitic?
q.explanation: North Cushitic is represented only by the Beja people's language.

q.q: Agaw languages such as Qimant and Awign belong to:
q.explanation: Central Cushitic is represented by Bilen and the Agaw languages.

q.q: Gafat is an example of an Ethiopian language that has disappeared.
q.explanation: Gafat, a Southern Semitic language, is now extinct.

q.q: The Nilo-Saharan super-family in Ethiopia is divided into Chari-Nile and Koman.
q.explanation: These are the two families of the Nilo-Saharan super-family.

q.q: Name the two major language super-families of Ethiopia and the Horn.
q.explanation: They are Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan.

q.q: Give the term for the mixing of religious beliefs and practices, such as indigenous customs fused with Christianity or Islam.
q.explanation: This mixing is known as syncretism.

q.q: Christianity became the state religion of Aksum after Frumentius converted:
q.explanation: Frumentius converted King Ezana (r. 320-350 AD).

q.q: In which year AD did the first group of Muslim refugees arrive at Aksum?
q.explanation: The refugees arrived in 615 AD.

q.q: Arrange these events in the correct chronological order.
options: The first Muslim refugees arrive at Aksum
The Nine Saints arrive in Ethiopia
q.explanation: The order is: Frumentius converts Ezana about 330, the Nine Saints arrive at the end of the fifth century, refugees arrive in 615, Adulis is destroyed in 702.

q.q: Which state had trade relations with Egypt since the third millennium BC?
q.explanation: Egyptian records place Punt south of Egypt with trade since the third millennium BC.

q.q: Historians place the territory of Punt in the coastal parts of present-day:
q.explanation: Punt lay along the Red Sea and Indian Ocean coasts of these present-day countries.

q.q: Which of the following was an export of Punt to Egypt?
q.explanation: Ostrich feathers were exported by Punt; hatchets, daggers and necklaces were sent by Egypt.

q.q: Yeha is located about 30 kilometres north-east of Aksum.
q.explanation: The textbook places Yeha 30 km north-east of Aksum.

q.q: Between which two years BC did the wealth of Yeha reach its peak?
q.explanation: Yeha's wealth peaked between 750 and 500 BC.

q.q: Damat's rulers adopted which South Arabian political and religious title?
q.explanation: The rulers of Damat adopted the South Arabian title Mukarib.

q.q: Which Red Sea port did Damat use for its trade?
q.explanation: Damat used the Red Sea coast port of Adulis.

q.q: Why do historians no longer believe that Aksum was the first centralised polity in Ethiopia and the Horn?
options: States such as Punt, Yeha and Damat existed before Aksum
q.explanation: Several principalities emerged and declined before the rise of Aksum.

q.q: The other pre-Aksumite states named in the lesson emerged from about 1000 BC.
q.explanation: These states emerged from about 1000 BC.

q.q: Arrange these centres from earliest to latest.
q.explanation: The order is: Punt (third millennium BC), Yeha (about 1000 BC), Damat, then Aksum (first century AD).

q.q: Aksum emerged in the first century AD with its nucleus at:
q.explanation: The city of Aksum was the political and religious centre of the kingdom.

q.q: Which port was the main outlet for Aksumite external trade?
q.explanation: Aksum generated income from trade through the port of Adulis.

q.q: Aksumite kings minted coins of:
q.explanation: Coins of bronze, silver and gold were minted to facilitate trade.

q.q: Which sequence correctly explains the decline of Aksum?
options: Loss of the Red Sea trade after Adulis fell in 702 AD, then internal rebellion and Beja pressure
Defeat by the Zagwe in 1150 AD
Conquest by Portugal in the sixteenth century
The founding of Ifat in 896 AD
q.explanation: The decline began with the loss of the Red Sea trade and was worsened by rebellion and Beja attacks.

q.q: Between the fourth and sixth centuries Aksum expanded beyond the Red Sea into southern Arabia.
q.explanation: Aksumite kings expanded east beyond the Red Sea into southern Arabia.

q.q: Who was the last Aksumite king deposed by the Zagwe around 1150 AD?
q.explanation: Dil Naod was the last Aksumite king, deposed around 1150 AD.

q.q: Name the language that served as the lingua franca of the Red Sea and the Mediterranean before Geez spread in Aksum.
q.explanation: Greek was the lingua franca of the Red Sea and Mediterranean region at that time.

q.q: King Kaleb controlled South Arabia in:
q.explanation: Kaleb controlled South Arabia in 525 AD.

q.q: Aksum lost control of the trade on the other side of the Red Sea after the South Arabians expelled its governors between 580 and 590 AD.
q.explanation: The expulsion ended Aksumite control of South Arabia.

q.q: By the late ninth century the Aksumite state had taken refuge in an area inhabited mainly by:
q.explanation: After being pushed to Kubar, the state took refuge among the Agaw people.

q.q: The Zagwe dynasty was founded around 1150 AD by:
q.explanation: Mera Tekle Haymnot founded the dynasty around 1150 AD.

q.q: The capital of the Zagwe dynasty was at:
q.explanation: Mera Tekle Haymnot established a new capital at Adefa (Roha) in Lasta.

q.q: The Zagwe dynasty is best known in Ethiopian history for its:
q.explanation: Zagwe is remembered for the rock-hewn churches at Roha.

q.q: How many rock-hewn churches were built during the reign of Emperor Lalibela?
q.explanation: Eleven rock-hewn churches survive from the reign of Emperor Lalibela.

q.q: The rise of the Zagwe was a shift of power to the Cushitic-speaking Agaw rather than the creation of a new kingdom.
q.explanation: The founding of Zagwe was a political power shift, not a new kingdom.

q.q: Which Amhara chief defeated the last Zagwe king in 1270 AD?
q.explanation: Yekuno Amlak organised the movement and defeated the last Zagwe king.

q.q: Name the last Zagwe king defeated in 1270 AD.
q.explanation: Yetbarek was the last Zagwe king.

q.q: Which two regions provided the strongest opposition to Zagwe rule?
q.explanation: Strong opposition came from Tigray and Amhara.

q.q: What was the main economic base of the Zagwe dynasty?
options: Sea trade in the Red Sea only
Agriculture, with trade bringing additional income
q.explanation: The economy was based on agriculture, with trade adding income.

q.q: Which port was the main outlet during the Zagwe period?
q.explanation: The Zeila port was the main outlet during Zagwe times.

q.q: Yekuno Amlak claimed descent from Dil Naod and restored the so-called Solomonic dynasty.
q.explanation: His genealogy linked him to the last Aksumite king, Dil Naod.

q.q: Which Muslim sultanate was established first in the region?
q.explanation: The sultanate of Shewa was the first to be established.

q.q: The sultanate of Shewa was founded in:
q.explanation: The sultanate of Shewa was established in 896 AD.

q.q: Because its founders claimed descent from a clan of southern Arabia, the ruling dynasty of Shewa was known as the:
q.explanation: Its founders claimed descent from the Makhzunmite clan, so the dynasty was called Makhzunmite.

q.q: The sultanate of Shewa was located in the hot lowland region on the left of the Awash River.
q.explanation: The textbook places Shewa on the left of the Awash in the hot lowlands.

q.q: Which port became the most crucial gateway for Islam into the Horn of Africa?
q.explanation: Zeila became the most crucial gateway for Islam into the Horn.

q.q: Who founded the Walasma dynasty of Ifat in 1285 AD?
q.explanation: Umar Walasma founded Ifat in 1285 AD.

q.q: What was the main source of conflict between Ifat and the Christian highland state after 1270?
q.answer: control of the zeila trade|the zeila trade|trade routes
q.explanation: The need to control the Zeila trade became the main source of conflict.

q.q: An internal power struggle within the ruling family contributed to the final decline of Shewa.
q.explanation: The ruling family's internal struggle later led to the state's final decline.

q.q: The main reason northern Ethiopian trade declined was:
options: Arab control of the Red Sea and the destruction of Adulis
the fall of Shewa in 896 AD
q.explanation: Arab control of the Red Sea and the destruction of Adulis reduced northern trade.

q.q: Which state became the strongest Muslim sultanate and the main rival of the Christian highland kingdom?
q.explanation: Ifat became the strongest Muslim sultanate and the strongest rival of the Christian highland state.

q.q: The Dark Age in Western Europe is dated:
q.explanation: The Dark Age was a period of West European history from 500 AD to 1000 AD.

q.q: In feudalism, a fief was:
q.explanation: A fief, or feud, is a piece of land given by a higher lord to a lower lord.

q.q: The basic units of European feudalism were manors, or villages.
q.explanation: The basic units of European feudalism were manors, or villages, and the manorial lord held power over the peasants.

q.q: The Byzantine Empire was the:
q.explanation: The Byzantine Empire was the East Roman Empire which continued after the fall of the West Roman Empire.

q.q: In which year was the Battle of Manzikert fought?
q.explanation: Byzantium suffered a disastrous defeat at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071.

q.q: Give the name of the system in which a higher lord gave land to a lower lord who then owed service.
q.explanation: This is the vassalage system, the core of feudalism.

q.q: The Orthodox Church officially separated from the Roman Catholic Church in:
q.explanation: The Orthodox Church was officially separated from the Roman Catholic Church in 1054.

q.q: West European feudal society gave peasants, craftsmen and traders real political power.
q.explanation: The mass of feudal society had no political and economic power and was exploited.

q.q: Explain one merit and one demerit of the medieval period.
q.answer: merit: stability and church schools and castles|demerit: exploitation war and blood feuds
q.explanation: The period produced churches, castles and record keeping, but also war, murder, blood feuds and the exploitation of peasants.

q.q: The Crusades began in the 1090s mainly in order to:
options: liberate the Christian holy lands from the Seljuk Turks
q.explanation: The crusades were wars of Christian Europe against the Seljuk Turks to liberate Christian holy lands.

q.q: Which emperor brought the Byzantine Empire to the height of its territory and power?
q.explanation: The Byzantine Empire was at its height under Emperor Justinian (r. 527-565).

q.q: Islam began in the Arabian Peninsula with the teaching of the Prophet Mohammed in Mecca around:
q.explanation: Islam began around 610 AD with the Prophet's life and teaching in Mecca.

q.q: What is the name of the journey from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD?
q.explanation: The journey is called the Hejira, and it began the Islamic calendar.

q.q: The term Islam means submission to the will of Allah (God).
q.explanation: Islam means submission to the will of Allah, and worshippers are called Muslims.

q.q: In 1453 the Ottoman Turks captured:
q.explanation: The Ottomans conquered Constantinople in 1453 and renamed it Istanbul.

q.q: The highly trained soldiers of the Ottoman Empire were called:
q.explanation: The Ottomans formed a group of highly trained soldiers called janissaries.

q.q: Give the term for the authority and legitimacy to rule China, which a corrupt dynasty was believed to lose.
q.explanation: A corrupt and weak dynasty lost the mandate of Heaven and was replaced.

q.q: Arrange the four groups of Ottoman society from highest to lowest rank.
q.explanation: The order is Sultan, grand viziers, janissaries, occupational groups.

q.q: Turkish expansion in Europe was ended in 1571 by the:
q.explanation: European fleets defeated the Turkish navy at the Battle of Lepanto near Greece in 1571.

q.q: The Ottomans banned European merchants from going to the Far East.
q.explanation: The Ottomans controlled the trade route from Europe to Asia and banned European merchants from the Far East.

q.q: Explain how a dynasty lost the mandate of Heaven in the Chinese dynastic cycle.
q.answer: it became corrupt and weak and lost the support of the people|corruption and weak rule cost it legitimacy
q.explanation: When a dynasty ruled well it kept the mandate; when it became corrupt, weak and unsupported it lost it and was replaced.

q.q: After the death of the Prophet, under which two dynasties did Muslims come?
q.explanation: Muslims came under the Arab Caliphates of the Umayyad and then the Abbasid dynasties.

q.q: What distinguished capitalism from previous systems?
options: Spending wealth on pyramids and cathedrals
Using accumulated capital to enlarge productive capacity
q.explanation: Capitalism used accumulated capital to enlarge productive capacity rather than invest in unproductive enterprises.

q.q: Old Roman cities were restored and became centres of production and exchange.
q.explanation: Trade revived slowly and old Roman cities were restored as centres of production and exchange.

q.q: Which of the following was a problem for long-distance trade?
q.explanation: Heavy tolls, transport difficulties and insecurity from war and robbery were the chief trade problems.

q.q: Give the term for heavy taxes charged on the transit of commodities.
q.explanation: Heavy tolls were taxes charged on the transit of commodities.

q.q: City-states were the political, economic and social life centres of:
q.explanation: City-states were the political, economic and social life centres in Renaissance Italy.

q.q: Explain what merchants learned to do in the revived towns.
q.answer: buy raw materials have workers manufacture and sell finished products at the best prices|organise production and exchange
q.explanation: Merchants bought raw materials, had workers manufacture goods and sold the finished products at the best prices.

q.q: The Crusades contributed to the revival of trade in the Middle Ages.
q.explanation: The crusades contributed to the revival of trade in the Middle Ages.

q.q: Explain how the discoveries and colonial conquest promoted capitalism.
q.answer: profits from trade and colonies were reinvested|big profits promoted faster development of capitalism
q.explanation: After the discoveries big profits were made, and colonial conquest helped promote the faster development of capitalism.

q.q: Which statement best describes capital in early capitalism?
options: Accumulated wealth invested in production and trade
A tax paid to a lord
q.explanation: Capital is accumulated wealth that early capitalists invested to enlarge productive capacity.

q.q: In which country did city-states become centres of economic and political life?
q.explanation: City-states were the life centres in Renaissance Italy.

q.q: The age of European explorations and discoveries took place in the:
q.explanation: The age of European explorations and discoveries was in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

q.q: Which explorer discovered a new sea route to India in 1498?
q.explanation: The Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama reached India by a new sea route in 1498.

q.q: Which of the following explorers reached America in 1492?
q.explanation: Christopher Columbus was the first European explorer to reach America in 1492.

q.q: America was named after the Italian mapmaker Amerigo Vespucci.
q.explanation: The land came to be known as America from the name of the Italian mapmaker Amerigo Vespucci.

q.q: Explain the main reason why Europeans wanted to bypass the old trade route to the Far East.
q.answer: the Ottoman Turkish blockade of the trade route|Ottoman control and tolls on the route
q.explanation: The explorations were partly initiated by the need to bypass the Ottoman Turkish blockade of the old long-distance trade route.

q.q: Arrange these events in correct chronological order, earliest first.
q.explanation: The Ottoman conquest was 1453, Columbus 1492, Vasco da Gama 1498 and Magellan 1519-1522.

q.q: Who circumnavigated the world between 1519 and 1522?
q.explanation: The Portuguese Ferdinand Magellan circumnavigated the world between 1519 and 1522 in the service of Spain.

q.q: Name the two leading European nations in exploration and discoveries in the 15th and 16th centuries.
q.explanation: Spain and Portugal were the leaders, closely followed by Holland, Britain, France and Russia.

q.q: The discoveries reduced the development of capitalism in Europe.
q.explanation: The voyages, with colonial conquest, promoted the faster development of capitalism.

q.q: Which invention mentioned in the lesson helped sailors on long voyages?
q.explanation: New inventions such as the compass aided European long-distance exploration.

q.q: Explain one economic impact of the discoveries on Europe.
q.answer: huge profits from local trade networks|faster development of capitalism|growth of globalisation
q.explanation: Europeans gained huge profits from trade networks, which enhanced globalisation and, with colonial conquest, promoted capitalism.

q.q: The word Renaissance means:
q.explanation: The word renaissance indicates the rebirth of learning.

q.q: The Renaissance began in Italy and spread to the rest of Europe.
q.explanation: The Renaissance began in Italy and spread mainly to England, France, Germany, Spain and Holland.

q.q: Who painted the Last Supper and the Monalisa?
q.explanation: The Italian Leonardo da Vinci painted the Last Supper and the Monalisa.

q.q: Which Polish thinker declared that the earth revolved around the sun?
q.explanation: The Polish Nicholas Copernicus declared that the earth revolved around the sun.

q.q: Give the term for the national language used in Renaissance writing instead of Latin.
q.explanation: Renaissance writers used the vernacular, such as Italian and English, rather than Latin.

q.q: Which of these was written by the Englishman Thomas More?
q.explanation: Utopia was written by the Englishman Thomas More.

q.q: The Renaissance began in the 14th century and ended in the 17th century.
q.explanation: It began in the 14th century and ended in the 17th century.

q.q: Explain the new view of human beings that emerged in Renaissance Italy.
q.answer: emphasis on individual ability|people emphasised individual ability and human potential
q.explanation: A new view of human beings emerged as people emphasised individual ability.

q.q: Which Renaissance figure studied human anatomy?
q.explanation: The Belgian Vesalius studied human anatomy.

q.q: Arrange the three features of Renaissance Italy in the order given in the lesson.
options: An age of recovery from the disasters of the fourteenth century
A new view of human beings emphasising individual ability
q.explanation: First it was an urban society; second an age of recovery; third a new view of human beings.

q.q: Explain how the Renaissance influenced the modern world.
q.answer: new focus on humanism|recognition of human potential and scientific inquiry|turning away from church-dominated ideas
q.explanation: The Renaissance brought a new focus on humanism and recognition of human potential and scientific inquiry, which still influence societies today.

q.q: The Reformation began in Germany, led by:
q.explanation: It began in Germany led by Martin Luther in 1517.

q.q: The Calvinist followers in France were called Huguenots.
q.explanation: The Calvinist followers in French were called Huguenots.

q.q: In Britain, the Protestant national church established during the Reformation was known as:
q.explanation: The English Protestants established a national church called the Anglican Church.

q.q: In which year did Martin Luther begin the Reformation?
q.explanation: The Reformation began in Germany led by Martin Luther in 1517.

q.q: The Society of Jesus was founded in Spain in 1534 by:
q.explanation: The Society of Jesus was formed in Spain by Ignatius Loyola in 1534.

q.q: Give the name of the Catholic reform movement carried out in response to the Protestant challenge.
q.explanation: The Catholic Church carried out the Counter-Reformation to reform itself in response to Protestantism.

q.q: John Knox founded the Anglican Church in England.
q.explanation: John Knox founded Presbyterianism in Scotland; the Anglican Church came from Henry VIII and Elizabeth I in England.

q.q: Which 1648 peace ended the Thirty Years' War in Germany?
q.explanation: The Peace of Westphalia ended the war in Germany in 1648.

q.q: Explain the four kinds of causes of the Reformation.
q.answer: social political religious and economic causes
q.explanation: The causes of the Reformation were social, political, religious and economic.

q.q: The Thirty Years' War lasted from:
q.explanation: The Reformation played an essential role in the Thirty Years' War, which lasted from 1618 to 1648.

q.q: Arrange these events in the correct order, earliest first.
options: The Society of Jesus is founded
q.explanation: The order is 1517 Luther, 1534 Society of Jesus, 1560 Knox, 1648 Peace of Westphalia.

q.q: The Industrial Revolution means the invention and use of machines in place of:
q.explanation: The term means the invention and use of machines in place of hard labour.

q.q: The Industrial Revolution began in:
q.explanation: It began in Great Britain in the 1780s and spread over several decades.

q.q: Steam power replaced the early wind and water power.
q.explanation: The new steam power replaced the early wind and water power.

q.q: Who improved the steam engines between 1782 and 1784?
q.explanation: James Watt improved the steam engines and applied them to all kinds of machinery.

q.q: The first railway locomotive was built in:
q.explanation: The first railway locomotive was built in 1804.

q.q: Give one reason why Great Britain was the starting place of the Industrial Revolution.
q.answer: abundant natural resources|large labour force|readiness to invest in the new machines
q.explanation: Britain had abundant natural resources, a large labour force and the readiness to invest in the new industrial machines.

q.q: By the mid-nineteenth century, Great Britain had become the world's first and richest industrial nation.
q.explanation: By the mid-nineteenth century Britain was the world's first and richest industrial nation.

q.q: Which countries were the first to be industrialised in continental Europe?
q.explanation: The first to be industrialised in continental Europe were Belgium, France and Germany.

q.q: Arrange these steam milestones in correct order, earliest first.
options: James Watt improves the steam engine
Savry builds an early steam device
The Industrial Revolution reaches the United States
q.explanation: The order is Savry 1698, Watt 1782-1784, railway locomotive 1804, United States 1800.

q.q: Explain how steam power changed transport in the Industrial Revolution.
q.answer: applied to steamboats on rivers then steamships at sea and finally railways|steam powered boats ships and railway locomotives
q.explanation: Steam power was applied to transport: the first steamboat on rivers, then steamships at sea, and finally railways on land.

q.q: Which statement about the cotton industry is correct?
options: It was equal in size to all other European industries combined by 1850
It existed only in the United States
q.explanation: Britain's cotton industry alone in 1850 was equal in size to the industries of all other European countries combined.

q.q: Linguists classify the peoples of Africa into how many super-families of languages?
q.explanation: The four super-families are Congo-Kordofanian, Afro-Asiatic, Nilo-Saharan and Khoisan.

q.q: Which sub-group of Afro-Asiatic is spoken only in Ethiopia?
q.explanation: The Omotic sub-family is spoken only in Ethiopia.

q.q: Afro-Asiatic is divided into six sub-groups including Berber, Cushitic and Omotic.
q.explanation: Its six sub-groups are Berber, Chadic, Coptic, Cushitic, Omotic and Semitic.

q.q: Arabic is a native African language that developed in the Sahara.
q.explanation: Arabic was brought to Africa by the Muslim Arabs between the seventh and eleventh centuries.

q.q: Name the hills south of the Republic of Sudan where Kordofanian languages are spoken.
q.explanation: Kordofanian languages are spoken in a small area in the Nuba hills.

q.q: Give the term for a large group of related African languages such as Nilo-Saharan.
q.explanation: Linguists group Africa's languages into four super-families.

q.q: Which language belongs to the Bantu family and mixes African and Arab cultures?
q.explanation: Kiswahili is a mixture of African and Arab cultures and belongs to the Bantu group.

q.q: Kiswahili, spoken widely in East Africa, belongs to which super-family through its Bantu roots?
q.explanation: Bantu is part of Niger-Congo, which belongs to the Congo-Kordofanian super-family.

q.q: Arrange these families from the one with the most speakers to the one with the fewest, as the textbook suggests.
q.explanation: The order is Congo-Kordofanian, Afro-Asiatic, Nilo-Saharan and Khoisan.

q.q: Explain one way in which living along a border, such as at Moyale, encourages multilingualism.
q.answer: people interact with neighbours|trade and contact with other cultures
q.explanation: Living along a border allows people to interact with peoples of diverse cultures and languages.

q.q: Name one non-native language that Muslim Arabs brought to northern Africa.
q.explanation: Arabic was brought to Africa by the Muslim Arabs.

q.q: Who founded the dynasty that ruled Egypt from 1250 to 1517?
q.explanation: The Mamluks founded the dynasty that ruled Egypt from 1250 to 1517.

q.q: The Mamluks were of Turkish origin.
q.explanation: The textbook states that the Mamluks were of Turkish origin.

q.q: Egypt declared its independence from the rule of Baghdad in which year?
q.explanation: The Fatimids declared Egyptian independence from Baghdad in 969 AD.

q.q: Relations between Mamluk Egypt and Christian Ethiopia were always peaceful.
q.explanation: During Mamluk rule, Ethio-Egyptian relations were full of conflicts.

q.q: Name the capital of the Funj sultanate.
q.explanation: The Funj established their sultanate in 1504 with its capital at Sennar.

q.q: Give the name of the Ethiopian ruler (r. 1434-1468) who tried to build smooth relations with Mamluk Egypt.
q.explanation: Zera Yacob (r. 1434-1468) tried to create smooth relations, but their relation was short-lived.

q.q: Which advantage helped the Ottoman Turks defeat the Mamluks?
q.explanation: Firearms helped the Ottoman Turks to defeat the Mamluk force in Palestine.

q.q: The army of which Ethiopian king destroyed the Funj in about 1620?
q.explanation: The army of King Susenyos destroyed the Funj in about 1620.

q.q: Explain the main reason given in the textbook for conflict between the Funj and the Christian kingdom of Ethiopia.
q.explanation: The Funj fought Ethiopia due to rivalry over trade routes.

q.q: Which power conquered the Funj sultanate in the 1820s?
q.explanation: Muhammed Ali of Egypt conquered the Funj sultanate in the 1820s.

q.q: Who founded the Ancient Ghana Empire?
q.explanation: Ancient Ghana was founded by the Soninke people in the fourth century AD.

q.q: Which empire captured Kumbi Saleh in 1076 and ended Ancient Ghana?
q.explanation: Ancient Ghana came to an end in 1076 when the Almoravids captured Kumbi Saleh.

q.q: Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire of the Mandinka people.
q.explanation: Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire of the Mandinka people.

q.q: Mansa Musa ruled Mali during which period?
q.explanation: Mansa Musa ruled as the greatest king of Mali from 1312 to 1337.

q.q: Give the name of the capital of Mali that became a leading centre of Islamic learning.
q.explanation: Timbuktu, the capital of Mali, became one of the most important Islamic learning and culture centres.

q.q: Name the capital of the Songhai empire.
q.explanation: The Songhai established their empire with its capital at Gao.

q.q: The battle of Tondibi in 1591 led to the defeat of Songhai by which force?
q.explanation: The Songhai Empire ended in 1591 when a Moroccan army defeated Songhai at Tondibi.

q.q: Which was the most famous walled city of the Hausa states?
q.explanation: The most famous of the Hausa city-states was the walled city of Kano.

q.q: Explain why control of the trans-Saharan trade made the West African empires powerful.
q.answer: they taxed the trade|trade brought wealth
q.explanation: By controlling the trade route the empires gained wealth to build armies and administer large territories.

q.q: Kanem-Bornu probably declined after trade centres shifted to the Atlantic coast.
q.explanation: Kanem-Bornu began to decline because trade centres shifted from inland routes to the Atlantic coast.

q.q: Arrange the three empires in the order in which they rose.
q.explanation: The order is Ghana, then Mali, then Songhai.

q.q: What is the meaning of the word Swahili in Arabic?
q.explanation: The mixed Bantu-Arab stocks called their language Swahili, meaning coasters in Arabic.

q.q: The kingdom of Kongo was founded by which people?
q.explanation: Bantu people founded the kingdom of Kongo in the late fourteenth century.

q.q: Bantu-speaking peoples moved into eastern Africa as small communities, not as invading hordes.
q.explanation: They moved slowly, not as invading hordes but as small communities.

q.q: Name the Swahili city that became the main centre of the East African gold and ivory trade.
q.explanation: Kilwa became the main centre of the East African gold and ivory trade.

q.q: In which years did explorers reach the Kongo?
q.explanation: The explorers reached the Kongo in 1482 and 1491.

q.q: Give the term for the blending of Arabic, Persian and Bantu traditions that produced Swahili civilization.
q.explanation: The Swahili civilization is an example of cultural diffusion.

q.q: Where did the Portuguese establish a trading fort in 1505?
q.explanation: The Portuguese established a trading fort at Sofala in 1505.

q.q: Swahili city-states traded with Arabia, Persia, India and China long before the Portuguese arrived.
q.explanation: Their commercial relations with Arabia, the Persians, India and China existed long before the Portuguese arrival.

q.q: Explain the main economic activity that made Kilwa wealthy.
q.answer: gold and ivory trade|trade in gold and ivory
q.explanation: Kilwa became the main centre of the East African gold and ivory trade.

q.q: Which language is now a common language in East African countries?
q.explanation: Swahili is now a common language in East African countries.

q.q: Who founded Great Zimbabwe?
q.explanation: The founders of Great Zimbabwe were the Bantu-speaking people of Shona.

q.q: The name Zimbabwe comes from a Shona word meaning what?
q.explanation: Zimbabwe is a Shona word meaning stone houses.

q.q: Great Zimbabwe was part of a trading empire that controlled much of the East African coast.
q.explanation: It was part of a wealthy African trading empire that controlled much of the East African coast.

q.q: After 1450 AD, which empire did the Rozwi clan kings establish?
q.explanation: After 1450 AD the Rozwi clan kings of the Shona established Mwene Mutapa.

q.q: Which European power conquered Mwene Mutapa in the late sixteenth century?
q.explanation: The Portuguese conquered Mwene Mutapa in the late sixteenth century.

q.q: Since 1000 AD the Khoikhoi mainly practised what?
q.explanation: Since 1000 AD the Khoikhoi changed to sheep and cattle breeding.

q.q: The San are farmers who cultivate crops in the Kalahari Desert.
q.explanation: The San lived by hunting and gathering, not farming.

q.q: Give the name Europeans used for the San people.
q.explanation: Europeans called the San Bushmen.

q.q: What happened to both the Khoikhoi and the San after Dutch settlers arrived?
options: They were driven into the Kalahari Desert
q.explanation: Both peoples were driven out of their land to the Kalahari Desert.

q.q: Explain why Great Zimbabwe is called a trading empire.
q.answer: it controlled gold and coastal trade|control of gold and trade
q.explanation: Its wealth came from cattle, crops and gold, and it traded along the East African coast.

q.q: After the introduction of which animal did trade across the Sahara become better organised?
q.explanation: Trade became better organised after the introduction of the camel.

q.q: The trans-Saharan caravan trade began regularly in the fourth century.
q.explanation: The caravan trade began regularly beginning in the fourth century.

q.q: Which two goods were the most important in the trans-Saharan trade?
q.explanation: The important traded items were gold from West Africa and salt mined in north-west Africa.

q.q: After which group emerged in the seventh century did enslaved people become important trade goods?
q.explanation: Enslaved people became important trade goods after the emergence of the Arabs in the seventh century.

q.q: Which region was connected to West Africa by a sub-branch of the trans-Saharan trade routes?
q.explanation: A sub-branch linked West Africa and Egypt.

q.q: Give the term for relations that occur between two or more continents.
q.explanation: Intercontinental relations occur between two or more continents.

q.q: Give the term for relations that occur within a continent.
q.explanation: Intracontinental relations occur within a continent.

q.q: Why did Ghana, Mali and Songhai become powerful?
options: They controlled the trans-Saharan trade route
They were protected by the sea
q.explanation: They became powerful because they could control the trans-Saharan trade route.

q.q: The trans-Saharan trade helped spread Islam in West and West-Central Africa.
q.explanation: The trade facilitated the spread of Islam and Islamization in West and West-Central Africa.

q.q: Which trade opened as a result of Afro-European contact during the era of exploration?
q.explanation: The outcome of Afro-European contact during the exploration era was the opening of the trans-Atlantic slave trade.

q.q: Name one group of outside peoples who had early contact with the East African coast.
q.explanation: Early contacts were mainly with Arabs, Greeks, Persians, Romans, Chinese, Indians, Spain and Portuguese.

q.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four language super-families of Africa?
q.explanation: The four super-families are Congo-Kordofanian, Afro-Asiatic, Nilo-Saharan and Khoisan.

q.q: Egypt became great under the Turkish Mamluk rule, who founded their dynasty from 1250 to 1517.
q.explanation: The Mamluks founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt from 1250 to 1517.

q.q: All languages spoken in Africa are native to the continent.
q.explanation: Arabic, English, French, Spanish and Portuguese are a few non-native languages.

q.q: Britain and France were the first countries determined to dominate Africa.
q.explanation: Europeans, especially Portugal and Spain, were the first determined to dominate Africa.

q.q: Which of the following was the main factor that contributed to the greatness of Ghana?
q.explanation: Ghana relied on the trans-Saharan trade and its rulers built a vast empire.

q.q: Who ruled Egypt between 969 and 1171?
q.explanation: The Fatimids declared Egyptian independence from Baghdad in 969 AD.

q.q: Which European country reached the Congo first?
q.explanation: The Portuguese reached the Kongo, and they colonised the kingdom.

q.q: Since 1000 AD the Khoikhoi mainly practised what?
q.explanation: Since 1000 AD the Khoikhoi changed to sheep and cattle breeding.

q.q: Give the empire named after the Shona word for stone houses.
q.explanation: Zimbabwe is a Shona word meaning stone houses, and Great Zimbabwe was its greatest city.

q.q: Arrange these events in time order, earliest first.
q.explanation: Order: Kumbi Saleh 1076, Mamluk dynasty 1250, Funj 1504, Tondibi 1591.

q.q: Name the capital of the Funj sultanate.
q.explanation: The Funj established their sultanate in 1504 with its capital at Sennar.

q.q: Portugal established early contacts with which part of Africa?
q.explanation: Portugal was the European country that established early contacts with the coastal regions of West Africa.

q.q: Portugal's distant objective was to reach India.
q.explanation: The textbook states that reaching India was their distant objective.

q.q: Name the Portuguese prince who sponsored the exploration of Africa.
q.explanation: Henry the Navigator sponsored Portuguese exploration of Africa.

q.q: In 1482 the Portuguese built their first permanent trading post, known as:
q.explanation: The Castle of Elmina was built in 1482 on the western coast of present-day Ghana.

q.q: Give the year in which the Portuguese seized Ceuta.
q.explanation: Ceuta was seized in 1415, the first step in Portuguese expansion along the Atlantic coast.

q.q: The Portuguese left the Gold Coast permanently after:
options: the loss of Elmina to the Dutch in 1642
q.explanation: With the loss of Elmina in 1642 the Portuguese left the Gold Coast permanently.

q.q: American crops such as maize and cassava were spread through contact with the Gold Coast.
q.explanation: Intensive contact with the Gold Coast spread American crops, notably maize and cassava.

q.q: From which West African region did perhaps a third of enslaved Africans exported in the sixteenth century come?
q.explanation: About a third of enslaved Africans exported in the sixteenth century came from Senegambia.

q.q: Arrange these Portuguese milestones from earliest to latest.
q.explanation: The order is Ceuta in 1415, Cape Blanc in 1441, Sierra Leone in 1460 and the Castle of Elmina in 1482.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the Portuguese wanted to bypass Muslim North Africa.
q.answer: to reach West African gold directly|to gain direct access to gold
q.explanation: Their immediate goal was to bypass Muslim North Africa and gain direct access to the gold-producing region.

q.q: The Trans-Atlantic slave trade is also called:
q.explanation: It is called the triangular trade because it connected three continents.

q.q: Slavery first began in the world with the Trans-Atlantic slave trade.
q.explanation: Slavery has a long history in Africa, Europe and Asia before the Atlantic trade.

q.q: According to historical records, how many native Africans were enslaved and deported?
q.explanation: Historical records indicate that more than twelve million native Africans were enslaved and deported.

q.q: The first phase of the Atlantic slave trade, from the fifteenth century to the 1580s, was called:
q.explanation: The first phase was the piratic slave trade, run by individual traders and sea robbers.

q.q: Before the Atlantic trade, the primary market for enslaved Africans was:
q.explanation: The primary market was Southwest Asia, where most enslaved people worked as domestic servants.

q.q: Give the year of the discovery of America that laid the background for the Atlantic slave trade.
q.explanation: The discovery of America in 1492 laid the background for the trade.

q.q: Which of these was NOT one of the three circumstances that began the trade in West Africa?
options: Fragmentation of Ghana, Mali and Songhai
The region's growing importance as a source of slaves
Coastal states exchanging slaves for arms
q.explanation: The three circumstances were the fragmentation of states, the region's importance as a source of slaves and coastal conflict and cooperation.

q.q: The wealth created by the triangular trade helped Western Europe to industrialise in the nineteenth century.
q.explanation: The accumulated wealth led to the industrialisation of Western Europe in the nineteenth century.

q.q: Name the two continents, besides Africa, that the triangular trade connected.
q.explanation: The triangular trade connected Africa, America and Europe.

q.q: In which West African state were large numbers of slaves used in agriculture and seen as symbols of wealth?
q.explanation: In the West African state of Benin large numbers of slaves worked in agriculture and symbolised wealth.

q.q: Legitimate trade refers to:
options: trade in commodities between Africans and European merchants
q.explanation: Legitimate trade was the trade in commodities between Africans and European merchants.

q.q: Legitimate trade grew after Europeans began to outlaw the slave trade.
q.explanation: As Europeans gradually outlawed the slave trade, they found West Africa a fertile field for legitimate commerce.

q.q: Name one West African commodity that replaced the export of captives.
q.explanation: Palm produce, rubber, cotton, skins and cocoa were among the new commodities.

q.q: Gum arabic was exported mainly from:
q.explanation: Gum arabic was exported from Senegal.

q.q: The high European demand for African raw materials was caused mainly by:
q.explanation: The products were in high demand in Europe because of the Industrial Revolution.

q.q: Which product was exported from most coastal forest zones of West Africa?
q.explanation: Palm oil came from most coastal forest zones.

q.q: Legitimate trade gave African states real opportunities to build economic strength and independence.
q.explanation: The textbook states that the export trade in raw materials did not provide African states with real opportunities to develop economic strength and independence.

q.q: Which was an effect of legitimate trade?
options: Intensive exploitation of African natural resources
The end of Christianity in Africa
q.explanation: It led to intensive exploitation of African natural resources such as minerals and crops.

q.q: Give the term for crops grown mainly for sale and export rather than for the farmer's own use.
q.explanation: Legitimate trade exchanged African raw materials, especially cash crops, for European goods.

q.q: Name the West African region that exported groundnuts.
q.explanation: Groundnuts were exported from Guinea.

q.q: In 1652 the Dutch trading company established a settlement to regulate trade with the:
q.explanation: The Dutch settlement was set up to regulate trade with the Khoisan.

q.q: The word Boers means farmers.
q.explanation: Boers were released to set up their own business as Boers, which means farmers.

q.q: Which company commander released soldiers to become Boers in 1657?
q.explanation: Van Riebeck released soldiers from their contracts in 1657.

q.q: The first Khoi-Dutch war took place in:
q.explanation: The first Khoi-Dutch war was in 1659.

q.q: In the second Khoi-Dutch war of 1673 to 1677 the Khoisan defeated the Dutch.
q.explanation: In the second war the natives could not win over the Dutch.

q.q: Britain seized the Cape Colony in 1795 in order to:
options: prevent it from falling to the French
q.explanation: The British occupied the Cape to prevent it from falling into the hands of the French.

q.q: Give the name of the movement in which the Boers left the Cape northwards from 1835.
q.explanation: This movement northwards is known as the Great Trek.

q.q: Which was a reason for the Great Trek?
options: the discovery of gold at Elmina
the law giving freedom to Africans and coloured people
the settlement of British immigrants at Elmina
q.explanation: The Boers reacted against the freedom law and the new ideas of equality.

q.q: Name the fertile grazing land where violence between the Trek Boers and the Xhosa began in the 1770s.
q.explanation: Violence began as settlers moved into the fertile grazing land of Zuurveld.

q.q: Arrange these events in the correct order.
q.explanation: The Dutch settled in 1652, the first Khoi-Dutch war was in 1659, Britain seized the Cape in 1795 and the Great Trek began in 1835.

q.q: European explorers travelled to the heart of Africa mainly between:
q.explanation: Between the 1780s and 1870s many European explorers travelled to the heart of Africa.

q.q: Portuguese Catholic missionaries closely followed the early Portuguese coastal penetration of Africa.
q.explanation: Roman Catholic missionaries from Portugal closely followed the early Portuguese penetration of tropical Africa.

q.q: In which kingdom did a Christian convert become king in 1506?
q.explanation: Greater success was achieved in Kongo, where a Christian convert became king in 1506.

q.q: Which was the main motive of those who financed European explorers?
options: the chance of greater future trading profit
mapping rivers for their own sake
q.explanation: The people who financed the journeys were interested in the chance of more significant trading profit in the future.

q.q: In which African state was the attempt to convert the Oba abandoned in the early sixteenth century?
q.explanation: The attempt to convert the Oba of Benin was abandoned in the early sixteenth century.

q.q: The Jesuit missionaries in Ethiopia were expelled in the mid-seventeenth century because:
options: they were defeated by the Ottomans
q.explanation: They were expelled for political interference.

q.q: European Christianity had a huge impact on the peoples of Sub-Saharan Africa by the eighteenth century.
q.explanation: Looking back from the eighteenth century, European Christianity had virtually no impact on the peoples of Sub-Saharan Africa.

q.q: Which missionary society was prominent in Sierra Leone?
q.explanation: The British-based Anglican Church Missionary Society was prominent in Sierra Leone.

q.q: Name one thing African rulers wanted from Europeans in return for contact.
q.explanation: Rulers wanted new trading openings, technical assistance and firearms.

q.q: Which missionary society initially worked mainly in South Africa?
q.explanation: The London Missionary Society initially worked mainly in South Africa.

q.q: The 'Solomonic' dynasty came to power in:
q.explanation: Yekuno-Amlak restored the dynasty in 1270.

q.q: Yekuno-Amlak claimed to be a descendant of the Aksumite kings.
q.explanation: He claimed to be the descendant of the Aksumite kings.

q.q: In which 14th-century book was the legend of Solomon and Sheba elaborated?
q.explanation: The Kibre Negest ('Glory of Kings') elaborated the claim in the 14th century.

q.q: The first 'Solomonic' king to pursue a wider and rapid territorial expansion policy was:
q.explanation: Amde-Tsion (r. 1314-1344) was the first 'Solomonic' king to embark on a wider and rapid expansion.

q.q: The royal prison at Amba-Gishen was established in:
q.explanation: It was established in 1300 during the reign of Widim-Ra'ad.

q.q: Give the name of the official who held the right to collect tribute under the gult system.
q.explanation: An official given this right by the state was known as bale-gult or gult owner.

q.q: Rist right was not hereditary and lasted only while the official remained loyal.
q.explanation: That describes gult right; rist right was a hereditary communal claim to land.

q.q: Medieval kings ruled through mobile courts mainly because:
options: the large court needed daily food and firewood
q.explanation: Mobile camps were necessitated by the need to obtain daily food supplies and firewood for the large court.

q.q: Arrange these events in the order in which they happened.
q.explanation: The order is: Yekuno-Amlak in 1270, the prison in 1300, Amde-Tsion in 1314-1344, and the destruction of Amba-Gishen in 1540.

q.q: Which trade route strengthened the economic power of Yekuno-Amlak?
q.explanation: Control over the Zeila trade route helped Yekuno-Amlak strengthen his economic power.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the name 'Solomonic' is written in quotation marks.
q.answer: the descent claim is legendary|it cannot be historically proven|it is a legend
q.explanation: The claim of descent from King Solomon is legendary and cannot be historically proven.

q.q: Which route served as the most important gateway of Islam to the interior of Ethiopia?
q.explanation: The Zeila trade route served as the most important gateway of Islam to the interior.

q.q: Ifat was founded by Umar Walasma, the founder of the Walasma dynasty.
q.explanation: Umar Walasma founded Ifat and hence the Walasma dynasty.

q.q: In which year did Ifat destroy the older Makhzumite dynasty?
q.explanation: In 1285 AD Ifat destroyed the Makhzumite dynasty and became the strongest sultanate.

q.q: Ifat was defeated by the Christian forces of Amde Seyon in:
q.explanation: Frequent skirmishes resulted in the defeat of Ifat in 1332 AD.

q.q: The Sultanate of Adal was founded around Harar in:
q.explanation: A branch of the Walasma family established Adal around Harar in 1367.

q.q: Give the name of the trade route whose control was the primary source of conflict between Ifat and the Christian kingdom.
q.explanation: Control of the Zeila trade was the primary source of conflict between the two states.

q.q: Trade was only a source of cooperation and never a source of conflict between the states.
q.explanation: Trade was a source of livelihood and state formation, but it remained a major source of conflict.

q.q: Which smaller sultanate was located between the middle Awash River and the upper Wabe-Shebele?
q.explanation: Dawaro was located between the middle Awash River and the upper Wabe-Shebele.

q.q: Arrange these events of Ifat and Adal from earliest to latest.
q.explanation: The order is: Ifat emerges in the mid-13th century, Ifat is defeated in 1332, Adal is founded in 1367, and Awsa becomes its capital in 1576/7.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why a branch of the Walasma family left Ifat and founded Adal.
q.answer: Ifat was too exposed to the Christian kingdom|to find a safer base|Ifat became an easy target
q.explanation: They realized Ifat was becoming an easy target for the Christian kingdom because of its location.

q.q: Which statement about Sharka is correct?
options: It was the strongest sultanate of the region
It existed as a tributary to the Christian kingdom from the 14th century
It replaced Ifat as the gateway of Islam
q.explanation: From the 14th century onwards Sharka existed as a tributary to the Christian kingdom until the first quarter of the 16th century.

q.q: The primary source of conflict among the peoples and states of Ethiopia and the Horn was:
options: the desire to monopolize long-distance trade
q.explanation: The primary source of conflict was the desire to monopolize long-distance trade.

q.q: The height of the war between the Christian kingdom and Adal came between 1529 and 1543.
q.explanation: The textbook states the height of the war came between 1529 and 1543.

q.q: Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi won a victory at Shimbra Kure in:
q.explanation: In March 1529 the Muslim force achieved victory at Shimbra Kure near Mojjo.

q.q: At which battle in 1543 was Imam Ahmad killed?
q.explanation: He was attacked and killed at the battle of Woyna-Dega on 25 February 1543.

q.q: Which European country sent soldiers who fought alongside the Christian kingdom?
q.explanation: Portuguese soldiers arrived at the Christian court in 1541.

q.q: Give the name of the wife of Imam Ahmad who accompanied him on his expeditions.
q.answer: Bati Del Wanbara|Bati dil-Wonberra|Bati Dil Wanbara
q.explanation: Bati Del Wanbara, daughter of the commander Mahfuz, accompanied her husband throughout his expeditions.

q.q: The Christian army won the battle of Ofla in August 1542.
q.explanation: In August 1542 the Christian army was defeated at Ofla, and about two hundred Portuguese were killed.

q.q: By 1535 Imam Ahmad's empire stretched from:
q.explanation: By 1535 his empire stretched from Zeila to Massawa on the coast.

q.q: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
options: Ofla defeat of the Christian army
q.explanation: The order is: expeditions begin in 1527, Shimbra Kure in 1529, Ofla in 1542, and Woyna-Dega in 1543.

q.q: Explain in one sentence how the wars affected the Christian kingdom and Adal.
q.answer: both were exhausted and weakened|loss of human and material wealth
q.explanation: Both states were exhausted and weakened at the end of the war due to the loss of enormous human and material wealth.

q.q: Which statement best explains why the Oromo population movement later succeeded more easily?
options: The wars had exhausted and weakened both the Christian kingdom and Adal
There were no other peoples in the region
q.explanation: The exhaustion of both states paved the way for the easy penetration and success of the Oromo population movement.

q.q: Which state was probably the earliest of the central and southern states?
q.explanation: Damot was probably the earliest of these states.

q.q: Damot was annexed into the Christian state by King Amde Seyon in 1316.
q.explanation: Amde Seyon annexed Damot into the Christian state in 1316.

q.q: Who converted the Damot ruler Motalami to Christianity?
q.explanation: Motalami was converted to Christianity by Abune Tekle Haymanot in the late thirteenth century.

q.q: The Agaw kingdom of Gojjam was incorporated into the Christian state by:
q.explanation: Amde Tsiyon (r. 1314-1344) incorporated Gojjam in the early fourteenth century.

q.q: Which kingdom remained independent of the Christian highland state?
q.explanation: Kafa was an independent kingdom from the Christian highland state.

q.q: Give the name of the ruling dynasty of Wolaita.
q.explanation: The ruling dynasty of Wolaita was known as Wolaita-Malla.

q.q: All societies of the southern and central region had highly organized states.
q.explanation: Other societies lived there without highly organized states, led by chiefs and local elderly councils.

q.q: The main trade items of the southern and central states included:
q.explanation: The main trade items were enslaved people, civets, ivory and other natural products.

q.q: Which preacher from a Lake Tana island monastery evangelized the Agaw villages?
q.explanation: Abba Za Yohannes marched southwards to the Agaw villages and attempted to evangelize the people.

q.q: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
options: Wolaita pays tribute to King Yeshaq
q.explanation: The order is: Motalami is converted in the late thirteenth century, Gojjam is incorporated in the early fourteenth century, Damot is annexed in 1316, and Yeshaq reigns from 1413 to 1430.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the less centralized frontier societies were important.
q.answer: they were agents of frontier trade and cultural relations|primary agents of frontier trade
q.explanation: They were the primary agents of frontier trade and cultural relations between the Ethiopian interior and its neighbours.

q.q: The largest population movement and expansion of the sixteenth century was that of the:
q.explanation: The largest population movement and expansion of the period was that of the Oromo.

q.q: The Oromo are an indigenous Cushitic people of Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa.
q.explanation: The Oromo are described as an indigenous Cushitic people of Ethiopia and the Horn.

q.q: What was the political and religious centre of the Oromo settlement area?
q.explanation: The political and religious centre of the Oromo settlement area was Madda Walabu.

q.q: Which two confederacies made up the Oromo people before they began to move?
q.explanation: The Barentu and the Borana confederacies were the two main groups that made up the Oromo people.

q.q: During the expansion, the Barentu headed mainly:
q.explanation: The Barentu headed north-east while the Borana took a north-westerly direction.

q.q: Give the name of the adoption system by which non-Oromos were incorporated into a clan through an oath of allegiance.
q.explanation: Moggasa was the practice of incorporating individuals or groups into a clan through an oath of allegiance.

q.q: The Somali population movement lasted long after the defeat of Imam Ahmad in 1543.
q.explanation: The Somali returned to their home base after the defeat of Imam Ahmed in 1543.

q.q: Which of the following helped the Oromo expansion succeed?
options: The Gadaa system and the exhaustion of the two warring states
The use of firearms supplied by Turkey
The help of the Ottoman navy
q.explanation: The Gadaa system provided training and organisation, and the movement took place when both states were exhausted.

q.q: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
options: Mudena expands to the west and north
q.explanation: The order is: Melba in 1522-1530, Kilole in 1538-1546, Mul'ata in 1586-1594, and Mudena in 1610-1618.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the Oromo expansion weakened the Christian kingdom.
q.answer: it lost territory and wealth|its centre shifted north|territorial and financial strength weakened
q.explanation: The kingdom's territorial and financial strength was highly weakened, and it shifted its centre from Shewa to the Lake Tana area and Gondar.

q.q: The Gadaa system was based on:
q.explanation: The Gadaa system was based on age grades.

q.q: In the Gadaa system, power was transferred peacefully every eight years.
q.explanation: There was a peaceful transfer of political power from one Gadaa class to the other every eight years.

q.q: What does the title Abba Gadaa literally mean?
q.explanation: Abba-Gadaa literally means 'father of the period'.

q.q: Supreme authority in the Gadaa system rested with the:
q.explanation: The supreme authority rested on the assembly (chaffe).

q.q: How many years made one Gadaa period?
q.explanation: Eight years represented one Gadaa period.

q.q: Give the name of the institution through which Oromo women maintained their rights.
q.explanation: Women maintained their rights by the Sinqe institution, which helped them form sisterhood and solidarity.

q.q: The Abba Gadaa exercised absolute power over the Oromo nation.
q.explanation: He served as spokesman of the reigning set but did not have absolute power.

q.q: Five Gadaa periods, or forty years, represented one:
q.explanation: Five Gadaa periods or 40 years represented one generation.

q.q: Which assembly mainly served as the law-making body of the Gadaa system?
q.explanation: The Gumi-Gayo was the assembly of representatives of the entire society and mainly served as the law-making body.

q.q: Arrange these Gadaa age grades from the youngest to the oldest.
q.explanation: The order is: Dabale, then Qondala, then Raba-Dori, then Gadaa.

q.q: Explain in one sentence how the Gadaa system checked the power of leaders.
q.answer: regular succession every eight years|assembly held supreme authority|check and balance
q.explanation: Power rotated every eight years under the authority of the assembly, providing check and balance.

q.q: The Sidama indigenous system of governance was led by the:
q.explanation: The Sidama had an indigenous system of governance led by the Mote (king).

q.q: The Gedeo traditional governance system is known as ballee.
q.explanation: The Gedeo traditional governance system is known as ballee.

q.q: What is the name of the Gedeo general council that elected the ballee officials?
q.explanation: The leaders of the ballee were elected by the general council called Yaa.

q.q: Political organisation among the Konso was:
q.explanation: The Konso had a decentralized political structure in which various people and groups shared authority.

q.q: The Konso village council of elders was called:
q.explanation: Each Konso village was ruled by a council of elders called hayyota.

q.q: Give the name of the Konso priest in charge of the clan's welfare and disputes.
q.explanation: The poqalla, a priest, was in charge of the clan's welfare and served as a peacemaker.

q.q: The Burji basha system was a hereditary rather than an elective system.
q.explanation: Traditional Burji administration had an elective system known as basha (shumet).

q.q: The five named generations of the Sidama luwa included:
q.explanation: The five luwa generations were Fulasa, Wawasa, Darara, Hirbora and Mogisa.

q.q: What was the moral standard, proclaimed by the Sidama elders, that required honesty and the avoidance of crime?
q.explanation: According to the halal, an elder was expected to live according to the halale, the moral standard.

q.q: Arrange these Sidama structures from the smallest to the largest unit.
q.explanation: The order is: the family unit, then the village, then the gare, and finally the woma-songo assembly of subtribal kings.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the Konso are described as having an egalitarian system.
q.answer: authority was shared|no central sovereign power|council of elders ruled
q.explanation: Authority was shared among village councils, the poqalla and the tselta, with no central sovereign power.

q.q: The king of the Kingdom of Kafa bore the title:
q.explanation: The ruler of Kafa was called Tato; his crown was a helmet of gold and silver.

q.q: The advisory council of nobles that chose the Kafa king's successor was called the:
q.explanation: The Mikkerecho assisted the king and chose his successor.

q.q: Wolaita and Gamo were led by a hereditary king called Kawo.
q.explanation: Wolaita and Gamo used the title Kawo; Dawuro and Konta used Kati.

q.q: Which title did the Dawuro and Konta peoples use for their rulers?
q.explanation: The Dawro and Konta people called their ruler Kati.

q.q: Give the name of the fortification walls built by the Omotic states.
q.explanation: Kella were defensive fortifications, such as the Amado Kella of Wolaita.

q.q: Give the term for the body of local cultural norms used as an unwritten law by the Highland East Cushitic peoples.
q.explanation: Sera is a set of local cultural norms regulating communal social structure.

q.q: The Gadaa system transferred power once every:
q.explanation: Gadaa transferred power every eight years, as did the Sidama luwa ceremonies.

q.q: The Somali council of elders that decided criminal and civil cases was the:
q.explanation: The Guurti was the highest political council of the Somali.

q.q: Explain one reason why the Oromo gradually abandoned the Gadaa system in the Gibe region.
q.answer: war strengthened abba dula|change from pastoral to agrarian|class differentiation
q.explanation: War, a shift to farming and growing class differences gave power to war leaders over the Gadaa councils.

q.q: Which Gibe state was the earliest, with its centre at Saqqa?
q.explanation: Limmu-Ennarya was the earliest Gibe state, with its centre at Saqqa.

q.q: Arrange the political hierarchy of Kafa from the top downwards.
q.explanation: The order is king (Tato), Mikkerecho council, district chiefs, then the sub-district chief woraafe rasho.

q.q: Gondar was founded as a permanent capital around 1636 by:
q.explanation: Fasiladas founded Gondar around 1636.

q.q: Before Gondar, the kings of the Christian Kingdom ruled from mobile capitals.
q.explanation: Kings rested at places such as Denqez, Gorgora, Azezo, Dembiya and Qoga.

q.q: Gondar's prosperity during its first three kings was based above all on:
options: the long-distance trade route and its urban market
q.explanation: Gondar sat on the route to Massawa and Mettema and had a busy daily market.

q.q: Name the Ethiopian Muslim traders who were the main merchants of Gondar.
q.explanation: Traders in Gondar were mostly Ethiopian Muslims known as the Jeberti.

q.q: The craft community of Gondar engaged in masonry, pottery and ironwork was the:
q.explanation: The Bete Israel were engaged in masonry, pottery, basketry and ironworks.

q.q: At its height Gondar had about how many inhabitants?
q.explanation: Gondar had about 70,000 inhabitants.

q.q: Explain why Gondar declined after the reign of Iyasu I.
q.answer: military weakness|court intrigues|warlords|unable to control regional lords
q.explanation: Court intrigue, poisoning, assassination and military weakness let warlords take over.

q.q: In which year was Iyasu I assassinated?
q.explanation: After Iyasu I was assassinated in 1706 the court had to be guarded by warlords.

q.q: Mentewab gave her brother Welde Leul the title of:
q.explanation: She bestowed on Welde Leul the prestigious title of Ras Bitweded.

q.q: In 1769 Mentewab lost power to the Tigrean warlord:
q.explanation: Ras Mikael Sehul came to Gondar, killed Iyoas and took the title Ras Bitweded.

q.q: The Ethiopian king who declared Catholicism the official religion of the country was:
q.explanation: The unit review names Susenyos as the king who declared Catholicism official.

q.q: Zemene-Mesafint is best translated as:
q.explanation: Zemene-Mesafint means the period of regional warlords.

q.q: The Zemene-Mesafint is dated from 1769 to 1855.
q.explanation: It runs from the assassination of Iyoas in 1769 to the crowning of Tewodros II in 1855.

q.q: Who represented the Quara faction in the Gondar power struggle of 1767-1769?
q.explanation: Quara was represented by Itege Mentewab, who controlled power for her grandson Iyoas.

q.q: The Wollo faction was represented by Wubit, who was:
options: the wife of Iyassu II and mother of Iyoas
q.explanation: Wubit was the wife of Iyassu II and the mother of the young king Iyoas.

q.q: At which battle in 1771 was Ras Mikael Sehul defeated and forced back to Tigrai?
q.explanation: A coalition of Gojjam, Amhara, Lasta and Wollo lords defeated him at Sarba-Kussa.

q.q: Which of the following was NOT an objective of the Zemene-Mesafint warlords?
options: Holding the title of Ras Bitweded
Collecting tribute in the name of weak kings
q.explanation: The warlords wanted to control the weak monarchy, not to restore a strong central one.

q.q: Explain how the doctrinal controversy in the Orthodox Tewahedo Church made the power struggle worse.
q.answer: gave it an ideological dimension|the Church could not enforce unity|divisions took a regional character
q.explanation: Church divisions had a regional character and gave the conflict an ideological edge, weakening both state and Church.

q.q: What name was given to the bandits who forced peasants to supply them food?
q.explanation: The many shiftas, or bandits, forced the peasants to feed them.

q.q: Explain two ways in which the endless wars harmed the peasantry.
q.answer: forced to feed armies|farmlands became battlefields|villages burnt|discouraged surplus production
q.explanation: Peasants fed the armies, lost their land as battlefields, had villages burnt and were discouraged from producing a surplus.

q.q: An important trade item that increased in supply because of the feudal wars was:
q.explanation: War captives increased the supply of enslaved people, who were in high demand in Arabia.

q.q: The Zemene-Mesafint ended in 1855 when Kasa Hailu was crowned as:
q.explanation: Kasa Hailu of Qwara was crowned as Tewodros II in 1855.

q.q: The Yejju dynasty was also known as the:
q.explanation: Ali founded the Yejju dynasty, also called the Warra Sheh.

q.q: Who founded the Yejju dynasty in 1786?
q.explanation: Ali Gwangul (Ali I) of the Yejju Oromo family founded it in 1786.

q.q: The centre of the Yejju dynasty was:
q.explanation: The Yejju dynasty was the leading power with its centre at Debre-Tabor.

q.q: Which ruler is described as the strongest of the Yejju dynasty?
q.explanation: The dynasty strengthened its power during its strongest ruler, Ras Gugsa (1803-1825).

q.q: The Yejju dynasty placed its own kings directly on the Gondarine throne.
q.explanation: It ruled in the name of the puppet kings of Gondar.

q.q: The battle of May-Aslamay in 1831 was fought near:
q.explanation: May-Aslamay was near Debre Abay in western Tigrai.

q.q: At the battle of May-Aslamay, both Ras Marye and Dejjazmach Sabagadis were killed. Who won the battle?
q.explanation: The final victory went to the Yejju dynasty.

q.q: Who succeeded Ras Marye and ruled the Yejju dynasty from 1831 to 1853?
q.explanation: Ras Ali Alula, or Ali II, ruled from 1831 to 1853.

q.q: The ruler who put an end to the Zemene-Mesafint era was:
q.explanation: Kasa Hailu of Qwara fought from the 1840s until 1855 and ended the era.

q.q: Name one Tigrian ruler who resisted Ras Gugsa in the north.
q.explanation: Ras Walda Sellase of Indarta and Dejjazmach Sabagadis both resisted Gugsa.

q.q: Explain how Ras Gugsa managed to control so many regional lords.
q.explanation: He combined military force with marriage relations and diplomacy to neutralize and control rivals.

q.q: The Shewan kingdom emerged in the area of:
q.explanation: The Shewan kingdom emerged in the area of Manz.

q.q: Who was the founder of the Shewan kingdom?
q.explanation: The founder was a local chief known as Negasi.

q.q: The centre of the Shewan kingdom under its consolidated rulers was:
q.explanation: Successive rulers consolidated the Shewan kingdom with their centre at Ankober.

q.q: The Christian Kingdom moved its centre from Shewa to the Lake Tana area because of Adal pressure and Oromo expansion.
q.explanation: The shift was caused by the pressure from Adal and the Oromo expansion of the 16th century.

q.q: Which Gondarine ruler sent military expeditions to control Shewa?
q.explanation: Iyassu I (r. 1682-1706) sent military expeditions to Shewa.

q.q: The Shewan kingdom reached its heyday under:
q.explanation: The kingdom reached its heyday under Nigus Sahle Sellase (r. 1813-1847).

q.q: Explain the main advantage Shewa gained from being isolated from the wars of the Zemene-Mesafint.
q.answer: peace and stability|maintained law and order|it could consolidate the kingdom
q.explanation: Isolation let the rulers keep peace, maintain law and order and consolidate the kingdom.

q.q: Which two European countries did Sahle Sellase establish independent foreign relations with?
q.explanation: He established independent foreign relations with Britain and France.

q.q: Stability under Sahle Sellase helped Shewa because it:
options: enabled foreign travellers to visit and relations to open
q.explanation: Stability enabled foreign travellers to visit, which helped open relations with Britain and France.

q.q: Explain why the central highlands of Shewa lost their role as the political centre of the Christian Kingdom.
q.answer: capital shifted to Lake Tana|pressure from Adal|the Oromo expansion
q.explanation: Adal pressure and the Oromo expansion drove the capital to the Lake Tana area, leaving Shewa detached.

q.q: Nigus Sahle Sellase ruled from:
q.explanation: Sahle Sellase ruled from 1813 to 1847.

q.q: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin in the late 1700s?
q.explanation: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain in the late 1700s.

q.q: Industrial capitalism is best described as:
options: a mode of production based on large, centrally controlled accumulations of capital used to finance production
q.explanation: Industrial capitalism consists of large, centrally controlled accumulations of capital used to finance production of commodities.

q.q: Which two resources did Britain have in plenty to power and build its factories?
q.explanation: Britain had plenty of coal and iron, which powered and built machines for the factories.

q.q: Which class owned the factories, machines, raw materials and finished goods?
q.explanation: The bourgeoisie owned the factory, machine, raw materials and finished goods, while the proletariat sold their labour for wages.

q.q: By the mid-19th century Britain had fully embraced which economic policy?
q.explanation: By the mid-19th century Britain had fully embraced the laissez-faire economy.

q.q: The Industrial Revolution increased wealth and the standard of living but also brought pollution, poor sanitation and child labour.
q.explanation: The textbook lists both the positive effects such as higher living standards and the negative effects such as pollution and child labour.

q.q: Give one new technology that helped business during the Industrial Revolution.
q.explanation: The telephone, the typewriter and electricity were new technologies that helped business.

q.q: Name the two new social classes that emerged during the Industrial Revolution.
q.explanation: The bourgeoisie owned the means of production; the proletariat sold their labour for wages.

q.q: In North America the first transcontinental railroad opened in 1869.
q.explanation: The first transcontinental railroad opened in North America in 1869.

q.q: Explain why the mechanization of labour caused social unrest in the 19th century.
q.answer: it displaced thousands of labourers|workers lost jobs and protested|it went with strikes and labour protests
q.explanation: The mechanization of labour displaced thousands of labourers and went hand in hand with strikes and other labour protests.

q.q: Arrange these Industrial Revolution developments in the order given by the textbook.
options: Making cloth moves to large factories
Capitalism emerges in the 16th to 17th centuries
q.explanation: Capitalism emerged first in the 16th to 17th centuries, then cloth moved to factories, then Britain became the world's workshop, and railways followed in the early 19th century.

q.q: The French Revolution began in which year and lasted how long?
q.explanation: The Revolution began in 1787 and ended in 1799, lasting ten years.

q.q: The two privileged classes in France before the revolution were:
q.explanation: The First Estate was the clergy and the Second Estate was the nobility; both held privileges and paid no taxes.

q.q: The action which marked the outbreak of the French Revolution in 1789 was carried out by the:
q.explanation: The immediate action came from the poor of Paris, who found it difficult to overcome the high price of bread.

q.q: What was the fundamental cause of the French Revolution of 1789?
options: Food shortage caused by poor harvest
Injustices under the old feudal order
q.explanation: The fundamental cause was the injustice of the old feudal order; the other factors were contributing or immediate causes.

q.q: The Estates General was transformed into the National Assembly on:
q.explanation: On June 17, 1789 the Estates General was transformed into the National Assembly.

q.q: Louis XVI was executed on January 21, 1793.
q.explanation: Louis XVI was found guilty and executed on January 21, 1793.

q.q: Name the prison that revolutionaries stormed on July 14, 1789.
q.explanation: The revolutionaries stormed the royal castle and prison of the Bastille.

q.q: Give the name of the Jacobin leader who headed the Reign of Terror.
q.explanation: The Reign of Terror reached its highest stage when Robespierre took over the Jacobin leadership.

q.q: Which group represented the big and middle bourgeoisie during the Revolution?
q.explanation: The Girondists represented the big and middle bourgeoisie and formed the extreme right political wing.

q.q: The Girondists were the left wing of the Revolution.
q.explanation: The Girondists represented the extreme right political wing; the Jacobins led the left wing.

q.q: Explain one way the French Revolution affected the world beyond France.
q.answer: rise of modern nationalism|spread of liberalism|lessened importance of religion|ignited the age of revolutions
q.explanation: Its repercussions included lessening the importance of religion, the rise of modern nationalism, the spread of liberalism and igniting the Age of Revolutions.

q.q: The Napoleonic Era covers the years:
q.explanation: The period of Napoleon's rule in France and Europe is known as the Napoleonic Era, 1799 to 1815.

q.q: The battle that marked Napoleon's final defeat was:
q.explanation: Napoleon was finally defeated at the Battle of Waterloo on June 18, 1815.

q.q: Napoleon Bonaparte met the strongest and most challenging resistance of all in:
q.explanation: In Russia Napoleon met the strongest and most successful resistance, and the 1812 campaign became the beginning of the end.

q.q: In which year was the Napoleonic Code completed, guaranteeing civil equality regardless of birth, wealth and rank?
q.explanation: The Napoleonic Code of Laws was introduced in 1804.

q.q: Napoleon made himself Emperor of France on:
q.explanation: Napoleon made himself Emperor of France on 2 December 1804.

q.q: Napoleon's rule allowed full political democracy to the French people.
q.explanation: His rule kept the fruits of the Revolution such as civil equality, but it did not allow political democracy to the people.

q.q: Name the island where Napoleon was first exiled in 1814.
q.explanation: After his abdication in 1814 Napoleon was exiled to the island of Elba.

q.q: Give the term for the blockade Napoleon imposed on British trade with mainland Europe from 1806 to 1810.
q.explanation: Napoleon imposed a blockade on British trade known as the Continental System.

q.q: Napoleon built a Grand Army of about how many troops by 1812?
q.explanation: Napoleon built a Grand Army that had 600,000 troops by 1812.

q.q: Explain why the campaign to conquer Russia became the beginning of the end of the Napoleonic Empire.
q.answer: hunger cold and disease destroyed the Grand Army|the Russian winter and scorched earth destroyed his army
q.explanation: The Russian strategy of withdrawal and scorched earth, together with the winter, and hunger, cold and disease, destroyed the Grand Army.

q.q: Napoleon died in exile on the island of St. Helena in 1821.
q.explanation: He was exiled to St. Helena in the southern Atlantic Ocean, where he stayed until his death in 1821.

q.q: The American War of Independence was fought between:
q.explanation: The war was fought between 1775 and 1783.

q.q: Which country ruled the thirteen North American colonies before the war?
q.explanation: The thirteen colonies were colonies of Great Britain.

q.q: Which of the following was NOT an effect of the American War of Independence?
options: It liberated the American people from British rule
It influenced the French and Latin Americans
q.explanation: The war did not abolish slavery; it was an essential step towards creating the USA but left slavery in place.

q.q: Who drafted the Declaration of Independence in 1776?
q.explanation: Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence.

q.q: The Constitution of the United States was signed on:
q.explanation: The majority of delegates signed the constitution on September 17, 1787.

q.q: The American War of Independence abolished slavery and made the Red Indians citizens.
